# theAuth documentation

# theAuth

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/

**Auth for AI agents and for the humans behind them.** theAuth gives every agent its own identity, checks permissions at call time and writes an audit row for every decision. It also ships human auth: email and password, magic link, passkeys, TOTP and more, plus 48 OAuth providers. Use either half alone, or both. Runs on Node, edge, Workers, Deno and Bun.

<Note>Building in Go? See the [theAuth Go library docs](/go/getting-started/overview).</Note>

## Pick your track

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="Add agent auth" icon="robot" href="/quickstart#track-a-add-agent-auth">
    Give agents an identity, scoped permissions, delegation and an audit trail. About five minutes.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Add human auth" icon="user" href="/quickstart#track-b-add-human-auth">
    Sign-up, sign-in, verification and reset with email and password, then add passkeys, OAuth and more. About five minutes.
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

### Agent auth in one screen

```ts
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite', url: ':memory:' },
  agents: { enabled: true },
});

// The owner must exist (human auth creates these for you).
const owner = await theauth.user.create({ email: 'owner@example.com', name: 'Owner' });

const agent = await theauth.agent.create({
  ownerId: owner.id,
  name: 'code-reviewer',
  type: 'autonomous',
  permissions: [{ resource: 'mcp:github:*', actions: ['read'] }],
});

const { allowed, auditId } = await theauth.authorize(agent.id, {
  action: 'read',
  resource: 'mcp:github:repos',
});
```

### Human auth in one screen

```ts
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { emailPassword } from '@glinr/theauth-email';

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite', url: ':memory:' },
  plugins: [
    emailPassword({
      appUrl: 'http://localhost:3000',
      sendVerificationEmail: async (email, _token, url) => console.log(email, url),
      sendResetEmail: async (email, _token, url) => console.log(email, url),
    }),
  ],
});

// Routes served by the email plugin (only while it is installed):
// POST /auth/sign-up, /auth/sign-in, /auth/verify-email, /auth/request-reset ...
const res = await theauth.plugins.handleRequest(request);
```

## What's in the box

<Columns cols={3}>
<div>
**Agent identity** as a first-class entity, not an extension of a user.
</div>
<div>
**Resource wildcards** with rate limits, time windows, and IP allowlists.
</div>
<div>
**Delegation chains** with depth, expiry, and revocation that takes effect on the next call.
</div>
<div>
**Audit log** of every decision, with JSON and CSV export.
</div>
<div>
**MCP OAuth 2.1** authorization server, PKCE, DCR and revocation-bound tokens.
</div>
<div>
**Trust scoring** per agent from audit history, plus budget policies.
</div>
<div>
**Ten adapters** for Node, edge, Workers, Deno, Bun.
</div>
<div>
**Databases**: SQLite and Postgres, plus Cloudflare D1. MySQL is not supported. See [what is tested](/choose-storage#what-is-tested-per-database).
</div>
<div>
**Web Crypto only** in core, no Node-specific APIs.
</div>
<div>
**Devices** with their own credentials, enrollment, live revocation and signed offline policy bundles.
</div>
<div>
**Robotics** with ROS 2 permissions exported to SROS2 and DDS Security files, plus a gate node for hazardous commands.
</div>
</Columns>

Devices and robots use the same model as agents. A sensor, gateway or machine is a principal with its own credentials, permissions and audit rows, so one policy and one audit trail cover people, agents and hardware. Start with [IoT devices](/iot-devices) or [robotics and ROS 2](/robotics-ros2).

## How it fits with your stack

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  User([Human user]) -->|signs in| HumanAuth[theAuth human auth, or Clerk / Auth.js / better-auth]
  HumanAuth -->|user ID| TheAuth[TheAuth]
  TheAuth -->|agent.create| Agents[(Agents)]
  TheAuth -->|authorize| Decision{allowed?}
  Decision -->|yes| Tools[MCP servers, APIs, databases]
  Decision -.->|logged either way| Audit[(Audit trail)]
```

<Info>
theAuth includes human auth, but you do not have to use it. If you already run Clerk, Auth.js, better-auth or your own login, keep it and pass the user ID as the agent's owner. theAuth's own methods (see [Authentication](/auth)) cover sign-in forms, password reset and social OAuth when you want one library for both.
</Info>

# Core concepts

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/concepts

A theAuth app has one loop: a user signs in, creates agents, agents call `authorize()` before acting, and every decision lands in the audit trail. Everything else is detail on top of that loop.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  U([User]) -->|creates| A[(Agent)]
  A -->|token| C[Agent call]
  C -->|authorize| K[TheAuth]
  K -->|yes / no| Out{Decision}
  K -.->|logs| Log[(Audit)]
  K -.->|adjusts| T[Trust score]
```

## User vs agent

A **user** is a human. They have email, password, sessions, OAuth accounts. theAuth can run human auth for you (see [Authentication](/auth)) or plug into Clerk, Auth.js, better-auth.

An **agent** is a program acting on a user's behalf. One human can own many agents. Agents do not sign in. They authenticate with a bearer token (`ta_...`) that is issued once and hashed at rest. No password, no session, no OAuth.

<Info>
If you reach for password reset, email verification, or social sign-in on an agent, you want a user, not an agent. Agents are non-interactive by design.
</Info>

## Permission model

Permissions are strings that describe what the agent may do, scoped to resources it may touch.

```ts
permissions: [
  {
    resource: 'mcp:github:*',        // wildcard on tool namespaces
    actions: ['read'],
    constraints: {
      maxCallsPerHour: 100,          // rate limit
      requireApproval: true,         // authorize() denies until approval is wired up
      ipAllowlist: ['10.0.0.0/8'],   // where the agent may run from
      timeWindow: { start: '09:00', end: '18:00' },  // server local time
    },
  },
]
```

Three shapes carry most of the real work: the **resource string** (free-form, convention-driven, usually `kind:namespace:id`), the **action list** (`read`, `write`, `execute`, domain-specific verbs), and **constraints** (rate, approval, IP, time, argument patterns). `authorize()` evaluates all three. `allowedArgPatterns` are regular expressions, and every string argument must match every pattern.

<Tip>
Resource strings are conventions, not enforced syntax. Pick `mcp:github:*`, `db:users:write`, `s3:bucket:objects`, whatever reads in logs. Consistency matters more than syntax.
</Tip>

## Delegation

An agent can hand a subset of its permissions to a sub-agent. Every hop carries a depth counter, an expiry, and can be revoked independently. Revoking a delegation cascades: every delegation made onward from that link is revoked too, so those agents lose the delegated permissions the next time they call `authorize()`.

```ts
await theauth.delegate({
  fromAgent: parent.id,
  toAgent: child.id,
  permissions: [{ resource: 'mcp:github:issues', actions: ['read'] }],
  expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 3_600_000),
  maxDepth: 2,
});
```

An agent cannot delegate permissions it does not hold. Attempts to escalate are rejected at delegation time, not at the next `authorize()` call. `maxDepth` limits chain length: the new link's depth must be less than or equal to it (default 3).

## Audit trail

When `agents.auditAll` is on (the default), every `authorize()` and `authorizeByToken()` call against a known agent writes one row:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `agentId` | Which agent asked |
| `userId` | The human the agent belongs to |
| `action`, `resource` | What they tried to do |
| `parameters` | The `arguments` passed to `authorize()` |
| `result` | `allowed` or `denied` |
| `reason` | Why, if denied (free text, or `agent_revoked` / `agent_expired` for a revoked or expired agent) |
| `durationMs` | Evaluation latency in ms |

The IP address and user agent are stored too, when the request carried them. Nothing in the API edits entries; `theauth.audit.cleanup({ retentionDays })` deletes entries older than the retention window. Export as JSON or CSV for compliance.

## Agent types

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="autonomous" icon="robot">
    Acts on its own. No human approval unless a permission constraint says so. Background jobs, cron, assistants that run unattended.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="delegated" icon="link">
    Gets permissions from a parent agent via delegation. Use for ephemeral sub-agents created to finish one task, then discarded.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="service" icon="server">
    Long-lived infrastructure identity. MCP servers, internal microservices, anything service-account-shaped.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Trust scoring

Every agent can have a score from 0 to 100, computed from its audit log when you call `theauth.trust.computeScore(agentId)` (it is not recomputed on each `authorize()` call). The score starts at 50 and moves with successful calls (up), denials (down), flagged denials (down more), and agent age (up).

The score maps to a level: `untrusted` (below 40), `limited` (40-59), `standard` (60-79), `trusted` (80-94), `elevated` (95+).

See [Trust scoring](/trust) for the full formula and [Policy templates](/policies/templates) for policies you can pair with the level.

## MCP OAuth

theAuth ships an OAuth 2.1 authorization server for Model Context Protocol tool servers. Your MCP servers register as OAuth clients, and they get scoped JWT access tokens. The OAuth server comes from `createMcpModule` in `@glinr/theauth/mcp`; token validation is separate from agent `authorize()` and does not write audit entries.

Three relevant standards: **PKCE S256** (RFC 7636), **Protected Resource Metadata** (RFC 9728), **Dynamic Client Registration** (RFC 7591). Full details in [MCP OAuth 2.1](/mcp).

# Quickstart

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/quickstart

<Note>Building in Go? See the [theAuth Go library docs](/go/getting-started/overview).</Note>

theAuth does two jobs, and you can use either one alone or both together. Pick the track that matches what you are building. Each takes under five minutes and the code runs as pasted (SQLite, no other services).

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="Add agent auth" icon="robot" href="#track-a-add-agent-auth">
    Identity, scoped permissions, delegation and an audit row for every AI agent.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Add human auth" icon="user" href="#track-b-add-human-auth">
    Sign-up, sign-in, email verification and password reset for your users.
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

Want a full app instead? `pnpm create @glinr/theauth-app` scaffolds a Next.js SaaS, a Hono MCP server or a Cloudflare Worker with theAuth wired up (also `npm create`, `yarn create`, `bun create`). The CLI asks for a directory, a template, a package manager and a database driver. It writes a `.env` with generated secrets and adds a `doctor` script. The generated code creates the owner with `theauth.user.create` and stores data in a SQLite file. The Hono MCP template still keeps MCP clients, codes and tokens in memory, because database backed MCP stores are not available yet.

## Fastest start: theauth init

In an existing project, `theauth init` writes a working server, creates the owner user and a demo agent, and prints the next steps. It reads `package.json` to pick the framework (Hono, Express, Fastify, Next.js, SvelteKit or Nuxt) and the package manager, and it stores data in a SQLite file so it survives restarts.

```bash title="terminal"
npx theauth init --yes
```

```text title="output"
TheAuth init
Framework: hono, database: sqlite

created     src/theauth.ts
created     src/seed.ts
created     src/server.ts
created     .env.example
created     .gitignore
created     .env (generated secrets, gitignored)

Note: Detected hono from package.json.

Next steps

  1. Install dependencies:
       npm install @glinr/theauth @glinr/theauth-hono better-sqlite3 hono @hono/node-server zod
       npm install -D tsx
  2. Start the server (it creates the owner user and a demo agent on boot):
       npx tsx --env-file=.env src/server.ts
  3. List agents through the mounted routes:
       curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $(grep '^ADMIN_API_KEY=' .env | cut -d= -f2)" http://localhost:3000/api/theauth/agents
  4. Check the setup, including the running server:
       theauth doctor --live http://localhost:3000/api/theauth

Docs: https://theauth.dev/docs
```

After you install and start the server:

```text title="server log"
Owner user: owner@example.com (50005a21-0612-4ca0-a085-0c6f0ea04706)
Demo agent created: 72bab466-1fc7-41ad-93f9-502e02b56c23
Agent token (shown once, store it safely): ta_x8tSbjRs7NnH21WA1_-yGKZRqmucw7a_u4Yo0wkhKjU
Listening on http://localhost:3000
```

The curl from step 3 returns the demo agent:

```json title="response"
{"data":[{"id":"72bab466-1fc7-41ad-93f9-502e02b56c23","ownerId":"50005a21-0612-4ca0-a085-0c6f0ea04706","name":"demo-agent","type":"autonomous","token":"","permissions":[{"resource":"documents","actions":["read","write"]}],"status":"active", ...}]}
```

The same call without the `Authorization` header answers 401. The seed creates the owner with `theauth.user.create` before the agent, so the foreign key on `owner_id` holds. Running `init` again skips every file that exists, so it never overwrites your edits (pass `--force` to replace the generated files; `.env` is only ever created). See [CLI tools](/cli-tools#init) for every flag. The two tracks below show the same calls by hand.

## Track A: Add agent auth

<Steps>

<Step>

### Install

```bash title="terminal"
pnpm add @glinr/theauth better-sqlite3
```

`npm install` and `yarn add` work the same way. The Node SQLite driver is `better-sqlite3`; on Bun, Deno and Workers use the matching [database provider](/database).

The unscoped `theauth` package is an alias for `@glinr/theauth-cli`, so `npx theauth init` sets up agent identity and MCP OAuth 2.1 without a separate CLI install. To keep the command on your PATH, install it globally with `npm install -g theauth`.

</Step>

<Step>

### Create an instance and an owner

Every agent has an owner: a user ID that exists as a row in `theauth_users` (the `owner_id` column is a foreign key, so creating an agent for an unknown ID fails). Human auth in the next track creates these rows for you; if you already have users in another system, call `theauth.user.create()` for each one you want to own agents. It validates and lowercases the email, and returns the existing row if the email is already registered.

```ts title="agent.ts"
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite-native', url: './theauth.db' }, // a file on disk, kept across runs
  agents: { enabled: true, maxPerUser: 10, auditAll: true, tokenExpiry: '24h' },
});

// Owner row. Skip this if the user came from the human auth track.
const owner = await theauth.user.create({
  id: 'user-123', // optional, generated when omitted
  email: 'owner@example.com',
  name: 'Owner',
});
```

</Step>

<Step>

### Create an agent

```ts title="agent.ts"
const agent = await theauth.agent.create({
  ownerId: 'user-123',
  name: 'github-reader',
  type: 'autonomous',
  permissions: [
    { resource: 'mcp:github:*', actions: ['read'] },
    {
      resource: 'mcp:deploy:production',
      actions: ['execute'],
      constraints: {
        requireApproval: true,   // authorize() denies until approval is wired up
        maxCallsPerHour: 5,
      },
    },
  ],
});

// agent.token is the bearer token. Agent tokens start with "ta_".
console.log(agent.token);
```

<Warning>
The token is shown once, at creation. Store it in your secrets manager or hand it straight to the agent. It cannot be recovered, only rotated.
</Warning>

New agent tokens start with `ta_`. Tokens issued by earlier versions start with `kv_` (the old Kavach name) and keep working until you rotate them (see [RENAME-MAP.md](https://github.com/glincker/theauth/blob/main/RENAME-MAP.md)).

There are three agent types:

| Type | When to use |
|---|---|
| `autonomous` | Runs without human involvement. Default for most agents. |
| `delegated` | Receives permissions from another agent via a delegation chain. |
| `service` | Long-lived service account identity. |

</Step>

<Step>

### Authorize an action and read the audit trail

`authorize` returns `{ allowed, reason?, auditId }`. `reason` explains a denial. Budget policies are not checked here; call `theauth.policies.checkBudget()` yourself if you use them.

```ts title="agent.ts"
const result = await theauth.authorize(agent.id, {
  action: 'read',
  resource: 'mcp:github:repos',
});
if (!result.allowed) throw new Error(`Denied: ${result.reason}`);

// With only the raw bearer token (from an incoming HTTP request):
const byToken = await theauth.authorizeByToken(agent.token, {
  action: 'read',
  resource: 'mcp:github:repos',
});

// Every decision is logged while auditAll is on (the default).
const logs = await theauth.audit.query({ agentId: agent.id });
const denied = await theauth.audit.query({ agentId: agent.id, result: 'denied' });
const csv = await theauth.audit.export({ format: 'csv' });
```

Run it with `npx tsx agent.ts`.

</Step>

</Steps>

## Track B: Add human auth

theAuth ships 14 human auth methods and 48 OAuth providers as plugins and modules; this track uses email and password, the most common starting point. See [Authentication](/auth) for the rest.

<Steps>

<Step>

### Install

```bash title="terminal"
pnpm add @glinr/theauth @glinr/theauth-email better-sqlite3
```

</Step>

<Step>

### Add the plugin

`emailPassword()` registers `POST /auth/sign-up`, `/auth/sign-in`, `/auth/verify-email`, `/auth/request-reset`, `/auth/reset-password` and `/auth/change-password`. You supply the email transport; the callbacks below just log. Passwords are hashed before storage. These routes exist only while `@glinr/theauth-email` is installed: the core on its own serves `/auth/username/sign-up` and `/auth/username/sign-in` instead.

```ts title="human.ts"
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { emailPassword } from '@glinr/theauth-email';

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite', url: ':memory:' },
  plugins: [
    emailPassword({
      appUrl: 'http://localhost:3000',
      requireVerification: false, // development only, default is true
      sendVerificationEmail: async (email, _token, url) => console.log('verify', email, url),
      sendResetEmail: async (email, _token, url) => console.log('reset', email, url),
    }),
  ],
});
```

</Step>

<Step>

### Sign up and sign in

The plugin endpoints take standard `Request` objects, so you can call them directly or mount them with a [framework adapter](/adapters).

```ts title="human.ts"
const post = (path: string, body: unknown) =>
  theauth.plugins.handleRequest(
    new Request(`http://localhost${path}`, {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
    }),
  );

const signUp = await post('/auth/sign-up', { email: 'ada@example.com', password: 'correct horse battery', name: 'Ada' });
console.log(signUp?.status); // 201

const signIn = await post('/auth/sign-in', { email: 'ada@example.com', password: 'correct horse battery' });
console.log(await signIn?.json()); // { user, session: { token, expiresAt } }
```

Run it with `npx tsx human.ts`. With `requireVerification` left at its default of `true`, sign-in fails with `EMAIL_NOT_VERIFIED` until the user posts the token from the verification email to `/auth/verify-email`.

</Step>

<Step>

### Give the user an agent

The sign-up response contains `user.id`. Pass it as `ownerId` in Track A and the foreign key is satisfied with no manual seeding.

```ts title="human.ts"
const { user } = await signUp!.json();
const agent = await theauth.agent.create({
  ownerId: user.id,
  name: 'assistant',
  type: 'autonomous',
  permissions: [{ resource: 'mcp:github:*', actions: ['read'] }],
});
```

</Step>

</Steps>

Prefer to keep Clerk, Auth.js, better-auth or your own login? Skip Track B and pass your user ID as `ownerId`, or wrap your resolver with `customAuth` ([details](/auth/email-password)).

## Delegation

An orchestrator agent can delegate a subset of its permissions to a sub-agent. The delegation has its own expiry and a `maxDepth` (default 3) to prevent unbounded chains: the new link's depth must be less than or equal to `maxDepth`.

```ts
const sub = await theauth.agent.create({
  ownerId: 'user-123',
  name: 'sub-reader',
  type: 'delegated',
  permissions: [],  // starts empty; receives permissions via delegation
});

await theauth.delegate({
  fromAgent: agent.id,
  toAgent: sub.id,
  permissions: [{ resource: 'mcp:github:issues', actions: ['read'] }],
  expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 3_600_000),  // 1 hour
  maxDepth: 2,
});

// Permissions this agent currently holds through active delegations
const perms = await theauth.delegation.getEffectivePermissions(sub.id);
```

<Info>
An agent cannot delegate permissions it does not hold itself. Attempts to escalate are rejected at the point of delegation, not at authorization time.
</Info>

## Full working example

<Expandable title="Self-contained script: create, authorize, rotate, delegate, export">

Covers agent creation, authorization by ID and token, token rotation, delegation, and audit export.

```ts
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite', url: ':memory:' },
  agents: { enabled: true, maxPerUser: 10, auditAll: true, tokenExpiry: '24h' },
});

// The owner must exist in theauth_users (see Track A, step 2)
await theauth.user.create({ id: 'user-123', email: 'owner@example.com', name: 'Owner' });

// Create an agent with wildcard read on github resources
const agent = await theauth.agent.create({
  ownerId: 'user-123',
  name: 'github-reader',
  type: 'autonomous',
  permissions: [
    { resource: 'mcp:github:*', actions: ['read'] },
    { resource: 'mcp:github:issues', actions: ['read', 'comment'] },
  ],
});

// Allowed: mcp:github:repos matches mcp:github:*
const r1 = await theauth.authorize(agent.id, {
  action: 'read',
  resource: 'mcp:github:repos',
});
console.log(r1.allowed);  // true

// Denied: no write permission
const r2 = await theauth.authorize(agent.id, {
  action: 'write',
  resource: 'mcp:github:repos',
});
console.log(r2.allowed);  // false

// Authorize using the raw bearer token
const r3 = await theauth.authorizeByToken(agent.token, {
  action: 'read',
  resource: 'mcp:github:issues',
});
console.log(r3.allowed);  // true

// Rotate: old token is immediately invalid
const rotated = await theauth.agent.rotate(agent.id);
console.log(rotated.token);  // new ta_... token

// Delegate a subset to a sub-agent
const sub = await theauth.agent.create({
  ownerId: 'user-123',
  name: 'sub-reader',
  type: 'delegated',
  permissions: [],
});

await theauth.delegate({
  fromAgent: agent.id,
  toAgent: sub.id,
  permissions: [{ resource: 'mcp:github:issues', actions: ['read'] }],
  expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 3_600_000),
  maxDepth: 2,
});

const perms = await theauth.delegation.getEffectivePermissions(sub.id);
console.log(perms);
// [{ resource: 'mcp:github:issues', actions: ['read'] }]  (delegated permissions only)

// Export the audit trail (up to the 10,000 most recent entries)
const csv = await theauth.audit.export({ format: 'csv' });
```

</Expandable>

## Cloudflare Workers

theAuth runs on Workers with no changes. Pass a D1 binding as the database and use the Hono adapter.

```typescript
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { Hono } from 'hono';

type Env = { THEAUTH_DB: D1Database };

const app = new Hono<{ Bindings: Env }>();

app.get('/health', async (c) => {
  const theauth = await createTheAuth({
    database: { provider: 'd1', binding: c.env.THEAUTH_DB },
    agents: { enabled: true },
  });

  const agent = await theauth.agent.create({
    ownerId: 'user-1',
    name: 'my-agent',
    type: 'autonomous',
    permissions: [{ resource: 'mcp:github:*', actions: ['read'] }],
  });

  return c.json({ agent });
});

export default app;
```

Bind a D1 database in your `wrangler.toml`:

```toml
[[d1_databases]]
binding = "THEAUTH_DB"
database_name = "theauth"
database_id = "<your-database-id>"
```

Run `npx wrangler d1 execute theauth --file=./theauth-schema.sql` to apply the schema yourself (and set `skipMigrations: true` inside `database`), or leave it at its default of `false` and theAuth creates the tables with `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` on startup.

<Info>
`createTheAuth` is always async, not only with D1. Workers and Deno both support top-level await, so you can also initialize outside the handler if you use a module worker.
</Info>

## Troubleshooting

### "Email address has not been verified" after sign-up

With the `@glinr/theauth-email` plugin, sign-in requires email verification by default and fails with `EMAIL_NOT_VERIFIED` (HTTP 401). Either:
1. Post the token from the verification email (the one passed to your `sendVerificationEmail` callback) to `/auth/verify-email`
2. Set `requireVerification: false` in the `emailPassword()` config (development only)

### "FOREIGN KEY constraint failed" when creating agents

The `ownerId` must match a row in `theauth_users`. Sign the user up with the email plugin (Track B), or create one with `theauth.user.create()` as shown in step 2 of Track A.

### Session not persisting after page reload

The React hooks store sessions in `localStorage`. Make sure your app is wrapped in `<TheAuthProvider>`. If using SSR (Next.js), wrap the provider in a `"use client"` component.

# Dev mode: local agent auth server in one command

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/dev-mode

Start a local server with a demo user, a delegation and a policy check. No config, database or account is needed.

```bash
npx theauth dev
```

The server listens on `127.0.0.1` with an in-memory SQLite database. It seeds:

1. A demo user, `demo@theauth.dev`.
2. A `planner-agent` owned by that user, with read access to repos and write access to issues.
3. A `worker-agent` that starts with no permissions of its own.
4. A delegation from the planner to the worker that grants only `read` on `mcp:github:repos`.

It then runs three guarded tool calls and prints each result:

| Call | Result | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| worker reads a repo | allowed | The delegation covers it |
| worker deletes a repo | denied | The delegation does not cover it |
| planner writes an issue | allowed | The planner holds that grant itself |

Every call lands in the audit log. The command verifies the audit hash chain and reports the count.

## Command-line options

| Option | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--port <n>` | `3100` | Also settable with the `THEAUTH_DEV_PORT` environment variable |
| `--smoke` | off | Run the walkthrough, check the server answers, then exit with code 0 or 1 |

## Dashboard

When the dashboard build is present, the walkthrough prints a dashboard URL for browsing agents, delegations and audit entries. Without the build, only the API URL is printed and everything else still works. Try `curl http://localhost:3100/api/agents`.

## Limits

- Dev mode turns off authentication on the management routes and binds to localhost only. Do not expose it.
- Data is in memory and is gone when the process exits. Press Ctrl+C to stop.
- For a real setup, run `npx theauth init`.

## Something missing?

If your provider speaks OIDC, `genericOIDC` covers it with a discovery URL and a client ID. For a framework without an adapter, the core is plain Web `Request` and `Response`, so it mounts anywhere. See [more providers](/auth/more-providers) and the [adapter overview](/adapters).

# What's new

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/whats-new

This page covers three rounds of work on `@glinr/theauth`. The first two aim to make an agent's actions checkable before and after they run. The third makes revocation reach the tokens an agent already holds. The changes sit in pending changesets in the repository and are merged to main. This page does not name a release number. Check the [GitHub releases](https://github.com/glincker/theauth/releases) for what has been published, and the changelog for breaking changes.

The pending set now includes `major` changesets (hooks, the HTTP handler, audit v2, the MCP stores, SAML, cookies and more). Read [Upgrading to 2.0](/upgrading-to-2) before you upgrade, and the "Behavior changes" list below.

## Accountability at runtime (first round)

- **Three way decisions.** `policy.evaluate` returns `allow`, `deny` or `escalate`. Risk tiers map an amount, currency or data class to no approval, human approval or step up. See [Agent accountability](/accountability) and [Policy engine](/policy-engine).
- **Delegation keeps its limits.** A delegated permission carries its constraints, narrowed against the parent, and a child that does not overlap the parent now gets a deny instead of the parent's wider value. See [Delegation](/delegation).
- **Revoking an agent cuts its delegations.** `agent.revoke()` also revokes the chains where the agent is source or target, and everything downstream. See [Cascading revocation](/delegation#cascading-revocation).
- **Richer audit rows.** Rows record the accountable human, the acting agent, the policy version, the approver and the delegation chain. Delegation and approval events join the hash chain. See [Tamper evident audit trail](/audit-trail).
- **Fail closed fixes.** `maxCallsPerHour: 0` denies, malformed time windows and IP lists deny, a revoked or suspended agent is denied by `evaluate`, and an unknown agent id is denied.

## Tools, approvals and proofs (second round)

- **Single use approvals.** `authorize()` and `policy.evaluate()` accept an `approvalId`. An approval is checked against the agent, action and resource, then spent once. See [Approval flows](/approval).
- **Tool guard.** `guardTool` and `guardTools` put the policy engine in front of any tool with an `execute` function. Walkthroughs for the [Vercel AI SDK](/vercel-ai-sdk) and the [OpenAI Agents SDK](/openai-agents-sdk), with the shared pieces in [Guard agent tools](/agent-tools). LangChain appears as a hand wrapped example, not a supported integration.
- **Taint guard.** Tool arguments can carry labels for where they came from, and policy decides which labels may reach which tools. The labels are written to the audit row. See [Taint aware tool guard](/taint-guard).
- **Policy shrink.** `analyzeUsage`, `suggestShrink` and `verifyShrink` compare what an agent may do with what it did, and report which recorded decisions would change. They never edit permissions. See [Policy shrink](/policy-shrink).
- **Audit checkpoints and receipts.** Signed checkpoints over the audit log, with inclusion and consistency proofs and receipts that verify offline with a public key. See [Audit checkpoints and receipts](/audit-checkpoints).
- **MCP live delegation check.** With `delegationStore` set, a token's `act` chain is re-checked against live links, and `resolveActorAgentId` maps actors to agent ids. The third round replaces this with a signed binding that needs no config. See [MCP OAuth 2.1](/mcp#security-hardening).
- **Session and audit fixes.** Session refresh and `maxConcurrent` no longer race, a failing audit write no longer makes `authorize()` throw, and `canonicalJson` rejects cycles.

## Revocation, remote guards and storage (third round)

- **Revocation reaches MCP tokens.** Exchanged tokens carry a signed `theauth_dlg` binding to their delegation links and agents. With `auth`, revoking a link, an agent, a user's sessions or a token fails the next request on every instance that shares the database. Modes are `live`, `cached` and `offline`. See [MCP token revocation](/mcp-revocation).
- **Introspection.** `POST /mcp/introspect` (RFC 7662) gives resource servers the live answer. Only the token's client and listed resource servers learn the inactive reason.
- **Client ID metadata documents.** A client can use an `https` URL as its `client_id`, behind a required consent page, host rules, size and time limits and an admin block list. See [Client ID metadata documents](/mcp-client-id-metadata).
- **Database backed MCP server.** Clients, codes, tokens and refresh families live in the theAuth database, and an OAuth client can be bound to an agent.
- **One HTTP handler.** `createTheAuthHandler` serves every route for every framework adapter, with identical status codes. See the [route reference](/adapters/routes).
- **Explain and policy tests.** `explain()` returns the matched grant, the delegation chain and near misses. `@glinr/theauth/testing` and `theauth policy test` run policy suites. See [Explain a decision](/explain) and [Policy testing](/policy-testing).
- **Remote guards.** `httpGuard` and `guardHook` put a signed, fail closed external check in `beforeAuthorize`. See [Remote guards](/guards).
- **Observability.** One typed event per decision, an OpenTelemetry mapping and a logger interface. See [Observability](/observability).
- **Audit API v2.** Explicit order, cursor paging, an `event` column and `decision_code` filters.
- **Schema ledger.** Every schema change is recorded in `theauth_schema_migrations`, with `theauth db status | up | sql`.
- **Typed decision codes and typed permissions.** `authorize()` returns a `code`, and `definePermissions` turns resource and action typos into compile errors.
- **Security fixes.** Strict SAML signature verification, a signed session cache in `@glinr/theauth-nextjs-auth`, `Secure` cookies by default and PBKDF2 at 600000 iterations, and revoked or expired delegators no longer lend permissions.
- **Storage.** Postgres works across the instance with epoch second timestamps, and `provider: "sqlite"` refuses a file URL (use `sqlite-native`).
- **Tooling.** `theauth init` and `theauth doctor` are rebuilt, and `theauth.user.create` replaces hand written inserts.

## Behavior changes to check

- ABAC `requireApproval` now escalates instead of returning a plain deny. `allowed` is still false.
- `policy.evaluate` writes an audit row on every call, and the row joins the hash chain.
- A permission with `requireApproval: true` is denied until the call carries a valid `approvalId`.
- Delegated constraints that do not overlap the parent now deny every call.
- `checkLiveDelegation` takes an options object as its fourth argument in place of the `now` date.
- Rows written before the new audit columns verify as erased history, not as tampered.
- With `auth`, MCP validation reads the database on every request by default (`live` mode). Set `revocation.mode: "cached"` above roughly a thousand validations per second per instance.
- Agent tokens start with `ta_`. Existing `kv_` tokens keep working.

The rest, with the action to take for each, is in [Upgrading to 2.0](/upgrading-to-2).

- [Stop prompt injection from making an agent send email](/tutorials/prompt-injection-tool-guard)
- [Find and remove unused agent permissions](/tutorials/remove-unused-agent-permissions)
- [Give a counterparty a receipt they can verify offline](/tutorials/verifiable-agent-receipts)

## Limits that still apply

- `input_provenance` holds the labels you supply. The SDK does not infer where an input came from.
- The approver is stored on the approval's audit row and on the decision that spends it, not on every decision row.
- `CheckpointStore` ships with an in memory implementation. There is no database backed store.
- The MCP adapters do not serve the `/mcp/revoke` or `/mcp/jwks` routes that the metadata advertises.

---

# Add to an existing app

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/add-to-existing-app

You already have users. You just added agents. This is the ten-minute recipe.

<Info>
theAuth does not replace your human auth. It runs alongside it. This guide assumes you already have a way to get a stable `userId` for every request.
</Info>

## What you need before you start

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="A user ID on every request" icon="user-check">
    Your existing auth must expose a stable string ID, anything from Clerk's `userId`, Auth.js's `session.user.id`, or a row id from your own users table. theAuth needs a matching row in its `theauth_users` table (see step 4).
  </Card>
  <Card title="A database" icon="database">
    Postgres, MySQL, SQLite, or Cloudflare D1. theAuth creates its own tables, prefixed `theauth_`, alongside yours.
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

<Tip>
Want the files below generated for you? Run `npx theauth init --framework nextjs` (or `hono`, `express`, `fastify`, `sveltekit`, `nuxt`) in your project. It writes `src/theauth.ts`, a seed script that creates the owner user and a demo agent, the route file, and a `.env` with generated secrets, then prints the install command for your package manager and a `curl` against the mounted routes. For Next.js it detects an existing `src/` folder and writes `src/app/api/theauth/[...theauth]/route.ts` (or `app/...` without one):

```text title="npx theauth init --yes (Next.js, pnpm)"
created     src/theauth.ts
created     src/seed.ts
created     src/app/api/theauth/[...theauth]/route.ts
created     .env.example
created     .gitignore
created     .env (generated secrets, gitignored)

Next steps

  1. Install dependencies:
       pnpm add @glinr/theauth @glinr/theauth-nextjs better-sqlite3 zod
       pnpm add -D tsx
  2. Create the owner user and a demo agent:
       pnpm exec tsx --env-file=.env src/seed.ts
  3. Start your app:
       pnpm dev
  4. List agents through the mounted routes:
       curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $(grep '^ADMIN_API_KEY=' .env | cut -d= -f2)" http://localhost:3000/api/theauth/agents
  5. Check the setup, including the running server:
       theauth doctor --live http://localhost:3000/api/theauth
```

The generated `authenticate` checks a bearer `ADMIN_API_KEY`. In an app that already has human auth, replace it with your own check as shown in step 3. Re-running `init` never overwrites a file that exists.
</Tip>

## Steps

<Steps>

<Step title="Install">

```bash
pnpm add @glinr/theauth @glinr/theauth-nextjs
```

Substitute the adapter for your framework: `@glinr/theauth-hono`, `@glinr/theauth-express`, `@glinr/theauth-fastify`, and so on. See [Framework adapters](/adapters).

</Step>

<Step title="Create the theAuth instance">

```ts title="lib/theauth.ts"
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';

let instance: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof createTheAuth>> | null = null;

export async function getTheAuth() {
  if (!instance) {
    instance = await createTheAuth({
      database: {
        provider: 'postgres',
        url: process.env.DATABASE_URL!,
      },
      agents: { enabled: true },
      secret: process.env.THEAUTH_SECRET!,
    });
  }
  return instance;
}
```

The singleton makes sure the instance (and its database connection) is created once per process. Passing `agents` is what makes theAuth create the agent, permission, delegation, and audit tables; without it those tables do not exist and `agent.create` fails.

</Step>

<Step title="Wire the route handler">

```ts title="app/api/theauth/[...theauth]/route.ts"
import { theAuthNextjs } from '@glinr/theauth-nextjs';
import { getTheAuth } from '@/lib/theauth';

const theauth = await getTheAuth();

// Return { id } for callers allowed to use the management routes, or null for a 401.
// Replace this with a check against your existing auth (Clerk, Auth.js, ...).
const authenticate = async (request: Request) => {
  const user = await theauth.auth.resolveUser(request);
  return user ? { id: user.id } : null;
};

export const { GET, POST, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS } = theAuthNextjs(theauth, { authenticate });
```

`theAuthNextjs` takes the resolved instance (not a function) and returns one handler per HTTP method. Export all five: the REST API uses `PATCH` and `DELETE` as well. Its default `basePath` is `/api/theauth`; pass `{ basePath }` if you mount it elsewhere. The agent, delegation, audit and dashboard routes require an authenticated caller: pass `authenticate` (as above), or configure `auth.session` to accept any signed-in user. With neither, `theAuthNextjs` throws at startup. See [Framework adapters](/adapters#authenticate-the-management-routes). The `authenticate` function above is a placeholder; with Clerk or Auth.js, call their server helpers and return `{ id: userId }`.

Pick a path that does not collide with your existing auth. `/api/theauth/*` lives next to `/api/auth/*` (Clerk / Auth.js) without stepping on it.

</Step>

<Step title="Create an agent when a user signs up or activates AI features">

Hook into your existing post-sign-in flow. For Clerk, that is a webhook or a server action. For Auth.js, the `signIn` event. For better-auth, the `onSignIn` hook.

<Warning>
`theauth_agents.owner_id` is a foreign key to `theauth_users.id`, and `agent.create` does not create the user for you. Call `theauth.user.create` with your provider's user ID before the first agent. Otherwise the insert fails with a foreign key error. `create` is idempotent on email, so calling it on every sign-in is safe. If the email already belongs to a different id, it throws `USER_EMAIL_CONFLICT` instead of returning the wrong row.
</Warning>

```ts title="wherever you create user-scoped resources"
import { getTheAuth } from '@/lib/theauth';

export async function createDefaultAgent(userId: string, email: string) {
  const theauth = await getTheAuth();

  // Ensures the owner row exists. Returns the existing row on later calls.
  await theauth.user.create({ id: userId, email });

  const agent = await theauth.agent.create({
    ownerId: userId,                     // stable ID from your auth provider
    name: 'default',
    type: 'autonomous',
    permissions: [
      { resource: 'app:read:*', actions: ['read'] },
    ],
  });

  // Persist agent.token somewhere the user can access, encrypted at rest.
  // It is returned once and cannot be recovered.
  return { agentId: agent.id, token: agent.token };
}
```

<Warning>
The token is shown once. Store it in your secrets store or hand it directly to the agent process. If you lose it, rotate with `theauth.agent.rotate(agentId)` to issue a new one. Agents also expire after `agents.tokenExpiry` (default `24h`) unless you pass `expiresAt` to `agent.create`.
</Warning>

</Step>

<Step title="Authorize in your handlers">

Anywhere your agent code runs, check authorization before the call.

```ts title="app/api/agent-action/route.ts"
import { getTheAuth } from '@/lib/theauth';

export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const token = req.headers.get('Authorization')?.replace('Bearer ', '');
  if (!token) return new Response('Missing token', { status: 401 });

  const theauth = await getTheAuth();

  const { allowed, reason, auditId } = await theauth.authorizeByToken(token, {
    action: 'read',
    resource: 'mcp:github:repos',
  });

  if (!allowed) {
    return Response.json({ error: reason, auditId }, { status: 403 });
  }

  // allowed. Do the work.
  const repos = await fetchGithubRepos();
  return Response.json({ repos, auditId });
}
```

</Step>

</Steps>

## Fitting in with Clerk, Auth.js, and better-auth

<Tabs>
<Tab title="Clerk">

```ts
import { auth } from '@clerk/nextjs/server';
import { getTheAuth } from '@/lib/theauth';

export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const { userId } = await auth();
  if (!userId) return new Response('Unauthorized', { status: 401 });

  const theauth = await getTheAuth();
  const agent = await theauth.agent.create({
    ownerId: userId,
    name: 'default',
    type: 'autonomous',
    permissions: [{ resource: 'app:read:*', actions: ['read'] }],
  });

  return Response.json({ agentId: agent.id, token: agent.token });
}
```

</Tab>
<Tab title="Auth.js">

```ts
import { auth } from '@/auth';
import { getTheAuth } from '@/lib/theauth';

export async function POST() {
  const session = await auth();
  if (!session?.user?.id) return new Response('Unauthorized', { status: 401 });

  const theauth = await getTheAuth();
  const agent = await theauth.agent.create({
    ownerId: session.user.id,
    name: 'default',
    type: 'autonomous',
    permissions: [{ resource: 'app:read:*', actions: ['read'] }],
  });

  return Response.json({ agentId: agent.id, token: agent.token });
}
```

</Tab>
<Tab title="better-auth">

```ts
import { auth } from '@/lib/auth';
import { getTheAuth } from '@/lib/theauth';
import { headers } from 'next/headers';

export async function POST() {
  const session = await auth.api.getSession({ headers: await headers() });
  if (!session?.user?.id) return new Response('Unauthorized', { status: 401 });

  const theauth = await getTheAuth();
  const agent = await theauth.agent.create({
    ownerId: session.user.id,
    name: 'default',
    type: 'autonomous',
    permissions: [{ resource: 'app:read:*', actions: ['read'] }],
  });

  return Response.json({ agentId: agent.id, token: agent.token });
}
```

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Common first-day questions

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="Do I need to run theAuth migrations manually?" icon="database">
No by default. theAuth runs its own migrations on first boot. Set `skipMigrations: true` inside the `database` config if you want to run them yourself with `npx theauth migrate` (from `@glinr/theauth-cli`).
</Accordion>
<Accordion title="Can I share the session cookie with my existing auth?" icon="cookie-bite">
Not directly. theAuth issues its own cookie for sessions created via its plugins. If you never use theAuth's human-auth plugins (because you have Clerk / Auth.js / better-auth), you never see that cookie and there is nothing to share.
</Accordion>
<Accordion title="What if my user IDs change shape later?" icon="arrows-rotate">
theAuth stores `ownerId` as a string and never interprets it, but `theauth_agents.owner_id` references `theauth_users.id`. Migrating from numeric IDs to UUIDs later means updating `theauth_users.id` and every referencing `owner_id` together, in one transaction.
</Accordion>
<Accordion title="Does theAuth emit events I can subscribe to?" icon="rss">
Yes, via [event streaming](/event-streaming) and [webhooks](/webhooks). Wire them to your analytics or to Stripe / PostHog / Slack.
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Configuration

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/configuration

`createTheAuth()` accepts a `TheAuthConfig` object. The only required field is `database`. Everything else is optional and enables features incrementally.

```typescript
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite-native', url: 'theauth.db' },
});
```

## Common development setup

A minimal config for local development with username and password sign-in, theAuth-managed sessions, and no email sending:

```typescript
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite-native', url: './theauth.db' },
  agents: { enabled: true },
  auth: {
    session: { secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET! }, // at least 32 characters
  },
  username: {}, // enables theauth.username (signUp, signIn, ...)
});
```

## Top-level options

<ParamField path="database" type="DatabaseConfig" required>Database connection config. Required.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="agents" type="AgentConfig">Agent identity settings.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="auth" type={`{ adapter?: AuthAdapter; session?: SessionConfig }`}>Human auth adapter and session config.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="approval" type="ApprovalConfig">CIBA async approval flow config. See [Approval flows](/approval).</ParamField>
<ParamField path="hooks" type="TheAuthHooks">Lifecycle hooks for sandboxing and custom validation. See [Hooks](/hooks).</ParamField>
<ParamField path="hookSafety" type="HookSafetyConfig">Timeout and failure policy for `beforeAuthorize` and `beforeAgentCreate`. Defaults: 2000 ms, deny on timeout or error for `beforeAuthorize`, throw for `beforeAgentCreate`. Environment variables `THEAUTH_HOOK_TIMEOUT_MS`, `THEAUTH_HOOK_ON_TIMEOUT` and `THEAUTH_HOOK_ON_ERROR` set the defaults. See [Hook safety](/hooks#hook-safety-timeout-and-fail-closed).</ParamField>
<ParamField path="policy" type="PolicyEngineConfig">Unified policy engine cache, combine strategy, and audit sampling. See [Policy engine](/policy-engine).</ParamField>
<ParamField path="did" type="{ web?: DidWebConfig }">did:web domain and path. See [DIDs](/did).</ParamField>
<ParamField path="plugins" type="TheAuthPlugin[]">Plugin factories such as `gdpr()`, `rateLimit()`, `twoFactor()`. See [Plugins](#plugins).</ParamField>
<ParamField path="baseUrl" type="string">Base URL for the auth server (e.g. https://auth.example.com). Read by plugins that build callback URLs or decide on secure cookies (OAuth, passkey, OAuth proxy).</ParamField>
<ParamField path="secondaryStorage" type={`"memory" | "database" | SecondaryStorage | { default?, rateLimit?, deviceCodes?, ... }`} default={`"memory"`}>Where short-lived state lives: rate limit counters, device login codes and similar. Memory is lost on restart and not shared between instances, so use `"database"` or Redis when you run more than one server. See [Secondary storage](/secondary-storage).</ParamField>
<ParamField path="trustedProxy" type="{ trustedProxyCount?: number; trustedHeader?: string }">How plugin endpoint rate limits find the real client IP. Forwarded headers are ignored unless you set the number of proxies you run or a header your edge overwrites (for example `cf-connecting-ip`). Without either, all clients share one rate limit bucket. See [Rate limiting](/rate-limiting).</ParamField>
<ParamField path="sessionFreshness" type="SessionFreshnessConfig">See [Session freshness config](#session-freshness-config).</ParamField>
<ParamField path="webhooks" type="WebhookConfig[]">Webhook endpoints to notify on auth events. See [Webhooks](/webhooks).</ParamField>
<ParamField path="passwordReset" type="PasswordResetConfig">Password reset flow. See [Password reset config](#password-reset-config).</ParamField>

Other optional top-level modules, each of which creates the matching `theauth.<name>` instance property when provided: `magicLink`, `emailOtp`, `emailVerification`, `totp`, `passkey`, `org`, `sso`, `admin`, `apiKeys`, `username`, `phone`, `captcha`, and `redirects`. Several of these require `auth.session` as noted in their own pages.

Options that `TheAuthConfig` declares but `createTheAuth()` does not act on:

- `mcp`: `createTheAuth()` does not read it. The OAuth 2.1 authorization server is built with `createMcpModule` from `@glinr/theauth/mcp`, which takes a `McpConfig` (see [MCP config](#mcp-config)). `theauth.mcp` on the instance is only the MCP tool server registry.
- `secret`: not read by `createTheAuth()`. Set the session secret in `auth.session.secret` and the MCP signing secret in `McpConfig.signingSecret`.
- `emitAgenticJwtClaims`: not read by `createTheAuth()`. See [Standards](/standards) for the places it does work.

There is no `trust` or `telemetry` option. The trust module is always created with its defaults.

## Database config

<ParamField path="provider" type={`"sqlite" | "sqlite-native" | "postgres" | "mysql" | "d1"`} required>Database driver to use.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="url" type="string">File path for SQLite, connection string for Postgres/MySQL. Required for every provider except D1.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="binding" type="D1Database">D1Database binding from the Worker environment. Required when provider is "d1".</ParamField>
<ParamField path="skipMigrations" type="boolean">Skip automatic CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS on init. Use when you manage migrations externally (Flyway, drizzle-kit push, etc.). Defaults to false.</ParamField>

```typescript
// Cloudflare D1 (edge)
const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: {
    provider: 'd1',
    binding: env.THEAUTH_DB,  // D1Database from Worker env
  },
});

// SQLite (Node.js)
const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite-native', url: './theauth.db' },
});

// PostgreSQL
const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'postgres', url: process.env.DATABASE_URL },
});

// MySQL
database: { provider: 'mysql', url: process.env.DATABASE_URL }

// In-memory SQLite (tests)
database: { provider: 'sqlite', url: ':memory:' }
```

## Agent config

Controls the agent identity lifecycle.

<ParamField path="enabled" type="boolean" required>Required by the type, but not read: agent management is always available. Set it to `true`.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="maxPerUser" type="number" default="10">Maximum number of active agents per owner. `agent.create()` throws when the owner is at the limit.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="defaultPermissions" type="string[]">Accepted but not applied: new agents get only the permissions you pass to `agent.create()`.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="auditAll" type="boolean" default="true">Write every `authorize()` outcome (allowed and denied) to the audit log. This includes attempts by revoked or expired agents (reason `agent_revoked` or `agent_expired`). Unknown agent ids and unknown tokens write no row. When `false`, no rows are written by the permission engine at all.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="tokenExpiry" type="string" default={`"24h"`}>Default agent lifetime when `agent.create()` is called without `expiresAt`. Format is a number followed by `s`, `m`, `h`, or `d` (for example `"30m"`, `"24h"`, `"7d"`); anything else makes `create()` throw. Every agent therefore has an expiry unless you pass `expiresAt`.</ParamField>

```typescript
agents: {
  enabled: true,
  maxPerUser: 10,
  defaultPermissions: [],
  auditAll: true,
  tokenExpiry: '30d',
},
```

## MCP config

Options for the OAuth 2.1 authorization server for MCP-compliant tool access. These are the fields of `McpConfig`, passed to `createMcpModule` from `@glinr/theauth/mcp` (see [MCP](/mcp)). Passing them as the `mcp` option of `createTheAuth()` has no effect today.

<ParamField path="enabled" type="boolean" required>Enable the MCP authorization server.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="issuer" type="string">Token issuer URL. Appears as the iss claim in JWTs.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="baseUrl" type="string">Base path for MCP endpoints.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="signingSecret" type="string" required>Secret used to sign JWTs. At least 32 characters; `createMcpModule` throws without it. It does not fall back to any other secret.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="accessTokenTtl" type="number">Access token lifetime in seconds. Defaults to 3600 (1 hour).</ParamField>
<ParamField path="refreshTokenTtl" type="number">Refresh token lifetime in seconds. Defaults to 604800 (7 days).</ParamField>
<ParamField path="codeTtl" type="number">Authorization code lifetime in seconds. Defaults to 600 (10 minutes).</ParamField>
<ParamField path="enforceAuth" type="boolean">Reject all MCP requests without a valid Bearer token.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="scopes" type="string[]">Custom OAuth scopes supported by this server.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="allowedResources" type="string[]">Allowed resource URIs for RFC 8707 resource indicators.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="loginPage" type="string">URL of your login page. Users are redirected here when unauthenticated.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="consentPage" type="string">URL of your consent page. Users are redirected here to approve scopes.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="preRegisteredClients" type={`Array<{ clientId, clientSecret?, redirectUris, clientName?, scope? }>`}>OAuth clients registered at startup (first-party apps, CLIs, test fixtures).</ParamField>
<ParamField path="getAdditionalClaims" type={`(userId: string, scopes: string[]) => Promise<Record<string, unknown>>`}>Async function to add custom claims to issued tokens.</ParamField>

<ParamField path="emitAgenticJwtClaims" type="boolean">Emit `agent_id`, `agent_type`, and `trust_tier` on access tokens, using `getAgenticContext`. See [Standards](/standards).</ParamField>
<ParamField path="getAgenticContext" type="(userId: string) => Promise<{ agentId?, agentType?, trustTier? }>">Supplies the values for those claims.</ParamField>

```typescript
const mcpConfig = {
  enabled: true,
  issuer: 'https://auth.example.com',
  baseUrl: 'https://auth.example.com',
  signingSecret: process.env.THEAUTH_SIGNING_SECRET!,
  accessTokenTtl: 3600,
  refreshTokenTtl: 604800,
  enforceAuth: true,
  loginPage: 'https://example.com/login',
  consentPage: 'https://example.com/consent',
};
```

## Auth config

Connects theAuth to your existing auth provider so it can resolve the human user behind incoming requests.

```typescript
auth: {
  adapter: betterAuthAdapter(auth),   // resolves user from request
  session: {                          // optional: TheAuth-managed sessions
    secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET,
    maxAge: 60 * 60 * 24 * 30,       // 30 days in seconds
  },
},
```

When `auth` is omitted, `theauth.auth.resolveUser()` always returns `null` (manual user management mode).

Built-in adapters exported from `@glinr/theauth/auth` include `betterAuthAdapter`, `authJsAdapter`, `clerkAdapter`, `bearerAuth`, `cookieAuth`, `headerAuth`, `apiKeyAdapter`, and `customAuth`.

## Secret rotation

Secrets that sign or encrypt data accept a list so you can rotate without invalidating what is already issued: `secret: [current, ...previous]`. The first entry signs and encrypts, every entry verifies and decrypts. Add the new secret at the front and deploy, then remove the old one after the longest lifetime of anything it signed. Entries can also be `{ id, secret }`, and the id is emitted with the signature (`X-TheAuth-Key-Id` for webhooks, a cookie field for sessions) so verifiers try that key first. Entries must be at least 32 bytes, and empty or duplicate entries throw at startup. The list form is supported by webhook endpoint `secret` (see [Webhooks](/webhooks)), `createStatelessSessions` and `createSessionCookieCache` (see [Session hardening](/session-hardening)). `auth.session.secret` and `McpConfig.signingSecret` remain single strings.

## Session config

<ParamField path="secret" type="string" required>Signing secret for session JWTs. Min 32 characters.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="maxAge" type="number" default="604800 (7 days)">Session lifetime in seconds.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="cookieName" type="string" default="'theauth_session'">Declared on the type but not read: plugins that set the session cookie (OAuth, passkey) and the default token lookup always use `theauth_session`. To rename the cookie, use `sessionName` on `createCookieSessionManager` (see [Cookie options](/cookies)).</ParamField>

<ParamField path="maxConcurrent" type="number" default="no limit">Maximum non-expired sessions per user. Enforced inside `sessionManager.create`. Impersonation sessions are not counted.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="onLimit" type={`'evict-oldest' | 'reject'`} default="'evict-oldest'">What to do when `maxConcurrent` is reached. `reject` makes `create` throw `MultiSessionLimitError`.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="onRevoke" type="(revoked: Session[]) => Promise<void> | void">Called after sessions are revoked by `revoke`, `revokeAll` or limit eviction. Errors are swallowed. Used to fan out [OIDC back-channel logout](/auth/oidc-logout).</ParamField>

## Sign-in gate config

A top-level `signInGate` option. It controls forced password changes, required second factors and trusted devices on every session-issuing path. Without it only the forced password change is enforced. See [Sign-in gate](/sign-in-gate) for the response shapes and routes.

<ParamField path="require2faFor" type={`Array<'password' | 'social' | 'magic_link' | 'passkey'>`} default="['password', 'social', 'magic_link']">Methods that must pass a second factor when the user has one enabled. The default applies once the `signInGate` block is present. With no block, no method requires one.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="secret" type="string">HMAC secret for challenges and device cookies. Falls back to `auth.session.secret`.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="challengeTtlSeconds" type="number" default="300">Challenge lifetime.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="maxChallengeAttempts" type="number" default="5">Wrong codes allowed per challenge.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="trustedDevice" type="object">`{ enabled, trustDurationSeconds, maxDevices, cookieName }`. Off unless `enabled` is true. Defaults are 30 days, 10 devices and `theauth_trusted_device`.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="factors" type="TwoFactorFactor[]">Extra second factors besides TOTP.</ParamField>

## Password reset config

A top-level `passwordReset` option (not nested under `auth`). It requires `auth.session`, and its flow relies on the `username` module, so configure `username` too. If `auth.session` is missing, `theauth.passwordReset` is `null`. The caller provides an email-sending callback.

<ParamField path="sendResetEmail" type={`(email: string, token: string, url: string) => Promise<void>`} required>Callback to deliver the reset email. Receives email, raw token, and constructed URL.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="resetUrl" type="string" required>Base URL for the reset page. Token is appended as ?token=...</ParamField>
<ParamField path="tokenTtlSeconds" type="number" default="3600 (1h)">Reset token lifetime in seconds.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="revokeSessionsOnReset" type="boolean" default="true">Revoke all sessions when the password is successfully reset.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="minPasswordLength" type="number" default="8">Minimum new password length.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="maxPasswordLength" type="number" default="128">Maximum new password length.</ParamField>

<Warning>
  Always use an HTTPS URL for `resetUrl` in production. Reset tokens in plain HTTP links can be intercepted in transit or leaked via `Referer` headers.
</Warning>

```typescript
auth: {
  adapter: betterAuthAdapter(auth),
  session: {
    secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET!,
    maxAge: 60 * 60 * 24 * 7, // 7 days
  },
},
username: {},
passwordReset: {
  resetUrl: 'https://example.com/reset-password',
  tokenTtlSeconds: 3600,
  revokeSessionsOnReset: true,
  minPasswordLength: 10,
  sendResetEmail: async (email, token, url) => {
    await mailer.send({
      to: email,
      subject: 'Reset your password',
      html: `<a href="${url}">Reset password</a>`,
    });
  },
},
```

## Session freshness config

Controls when sessions are considered "fresh" for sensitive operations. Pass it as the top-level `sessionFreshness` option; it backs `theauth.sessionFreshness`.

<ParamField path="freshAge" type="number" default="300 (5 minutes)">Maximum session age in seconds to be considered fresh.</ParamField>

## Plugins

Plugins are factories passed in the `plugins` array. They register HTTP endpoints and lifecycle hooks. All of these are exported from `@glinr/theauth/auth`:

| Plugin | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `passkey(config)` | WebAuthn/FIDO2 endpoints (requires a `PasskeyConfig`) |
| `magicLink(config)` | Passwordless email links |
| `emailOtp(config)` | One-time password codes via email |
| `twoFactor(config?)` | TOTP two-factor endpoints |
| `organization(config?)` | Organization endpoints with RBAC |
| `apiKeys(config?)` | Static API key endpoints |
| `admin(config?)` | User management, banning, impersonation |
| `stripe(config)` | Stripe billing integration |
| `polar(config)` | Polar payment integration |
| `gdpr()` | Data export, delete, and anonymize endpoints |
| `rateLimit(config?)` | Per-IP limits on `/auth/*` endpoints |
| `oauth(config)` | Social OAuth sign-in endpoints |

`emailPassword()` is not part of `@glinr/theauth`. It ships in the separate `@glinr/theauth-email` package (see [Email and password](/auth/email-password)). Inside core, username and password sign-in is the top-level `username` option (with `passwordReset` and `emailVerification` alongside it). `deviceAuth()` (see [Device authorization](/auth/device)) and `agentRegistration()` (see [Agent registration tokens](/agent-registration-tokens)) are exported from `@glinr/theauth/auth` too. Multi-session support lives in the session module, see [Multi-session](/multi-session).

## Environment variables pattern

Never hardcode secrets in config. Pass them through environment variables:

```typescript
const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: {
    provider: 'postgres',
    url: process.env.DATABASE_URL!,
  },
  auth: {
    session: { secret: process.env.THEAUTH_SESSION_SECRET! },
  },
});
```

## Dev vs production example

```typescript
// config/theauth.ts
const isDev = process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production';

export const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: isDev
    ? { provider: 'sqlite-native', url: './theauth-dev.db' }
    : { provider: 'postgres', url: process.env.DATABASE_URL! },

  baseUrl: process.env.THEAUTH_BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000',

  auth: {
    session: { secret: process.env.THEAUTH_SESSION_SECRET! },
  },

  agents: {
    enabled: true,
    maxPerUser: isDev ? 100 : 25,
    auditAll: true,
    tokenExpiry: '30d',
  },
});
```

<Warning>
  `auth.session.secret` and the MCP `signingSecret` must be at least 32 characters. In production, generate them with `openssl rand -base64 32`.
</Warning>
