# Database setup

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/database

theAuth uses [Drizzle ORM](https://orm.drizzle.team) under the hood. You pick a provider and pass the connection URL; theAuth handles the rest.

## Choosing a provider

| Provider | Best for |
|----------|----------|
| `sqlite` | Local dev and small single-process deploys. Runs on `sql.js` (SQLite compiled to WebAssembly), no native build step |
| `sqlite-native` | Node.js servers that want the fastest SQLite. Uses `better-sqlite3`, which needs a native build |
| `postgres` | Production, high-concurrency, multi-tenant. Also Supabase and, with a bring your own handle, Neon |
| `libsql` | Turso and other libSQL servers, or a `file:` URL. See [Turso, Neon and Supabase](/hosted-databases) |
| `mysql` | Not supported in this release. Throws unless `experimental: true` is set |
| `d1` | Cloudflare Workers, using a D1 binding |

## Setup

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="SQLite">
    The `sqlite` provider uses `sql.js` (SQLite compiled to WebAssembly), which ships with `@glinr/theauth`. It needs no native build and runs on Node.js, Bun, Deno, and edge runtimes. It is in-memory only: it never writes a database file, so use it for tests, CI and throwaway demos. For a database file that survives a restart, use the **SQLite (native)** tab (`sqlite-native`) or Postgres.

    For in-memory SQLite (tests and CI), use `:memory:` as the URL:

    ```typescript
    const theauth = await createTheAuth({
      database: {
        provider: 'sqlite',
        url: ':memory:',
      },
    });
    ```

    `sql.js` keeps the database in memory and nothing is saved when the process exits. Passing a file path (for example `url: './theauth.db'`) throws `THEAUTH_SQLITE_NOT_PERSISTENT` at startup, because the file would never be written and your data would disappear on restart. theAuth turns on foreign keys (`PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`).
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="SQLite (native)">
    The `sqlite-native` provider uses `better-sqlite3`. Install it yourself, it is an optional peer dependency and needs C++ build tools:

    ```bash
    npm install better-sqlite3
    ```

    ```typescript
    import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';

    const theauth = await createTheAuth({
      database: {
        provider: 'sqlite-native',
        url: './theauth.db',
      },
    });
    ```

    theAuth enables WAL mode and foreign keys automatically for this provider:
    ```sql
    PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;
    PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Postgres">
    Install the `pg` peer dependency:

    ```bash
    npm install pg
    npm install --save-dev @types/pg
    ```

    ```typescript
    import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';

    const theauth = await createTheAuth({
      database: {
        provider: 'postgres',
        url: process.env.DATABASE_URL!,
        // postgresql://user:password@host:5432/dbname
      },
    });
    ```

    theAuth uses `drizzle-orm/node-postgres` with a connection pool via `pg.Pool`. The `pg` package is loaded with a dynamic import, so it stays an optional peer dep.

    Timestamps are stored as integer epoch seconds, the same as SQLite. When you query the tables yourself, wrap timestamp columns in `to_timestamp(...)`, for example `SELECT id, to_timestamp(created_at) AS created FROM theauth_users;`. Other Postgres drivers (postgres.js, Neon serverless, PGlite) are not supported yet.
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="MySQL">
    MySQL is not supported in this release. `provider: 'mysql'` throws `THEAUTH_MYSQL_UNSUPPORTED` unless you pass `experimental: true`, and even then the baseline schema does not apply on a real server. Do not use it in production.
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Cloudflare D1">
    Pass the D1 binding from your Worker environment. The `drizzle-orm/d1` driver is loaded with a dynamic import.

    ```typescript
    import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';

    export default {
      async fetch(request: Request, env: { DB: D1Database }) {
        const theauth = await createTheAuth({
          database: {
            provider: 'd1',
            binding: env.DB,
          },
        });
        // ...
      },
    };
    ```

    The D1 provider takes a `binding` instead of a `url`. Set `skipMigrations: true` if you create the tables yourself.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Auto-migration

By default, theAuth migrates the database at startup: it creates the tables your config needs (`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`) and applies any pending versioned migration, recording each one in the `theauth_schema_migrations` ledger (see [Schema migrations](#schema-migrations)). This is safe to run on every start, and there is no manual migration step for a new project or an upgrade.

Tables are created per feature, so a small config gives you a small schema. Users and the secondary storage table are always created. Everything else depends on the config:

| Config | Tables created |
|--------|----------------|
| `agents` (or `did`) | agents, permissions, delegation chains, agent cards, approval requests, trust scores, registration tokens, DIDs, ephemeral sessions, tenants, audit logs, cost and stream events, rate limits, budget policies, ReBAC |
| `auth.session` | sessions, trusted devices, login history, JWT refresh tokens and token families |
| `mcp` | MCP servers |
| `oauth()` plugin | OAuth accounts and states, plus OAuth client, token and code tables |
| `magicLink`, `emailOtp`, `totp`, `passkey`, `username`, `phone`, `org`, `sso`, `apiKeys` | The matching table(s), whether you use the config key or the plugin form (for example `plugins: [magicLink(...)]`) |
| `passwordReset`, `magicLink`, `emailOtp` | One-time tokens |

If you add a feature later, restart once and the new tables appear. Add `agents: { enabled: true }` if you use agents, since agent tables are not created without it. The `@glinr/theauth-email` plugin creates its own `theauth_email_accounts` table.

To disable this (e.g. when you manage migrations externally with Flyway, Liquibase, or `drizzle-kit push`), set `skipMigrations: true`:

```typescript
database: {
  provider: 'postgres',
  url: process.env.DATABASE_URL!,
  skipMigrations: true,
},
```

<Warning>
  When `skipMigrations: true`, you apply the schema yourself, and theAuth checks the ledger at startup. If migrations are pending it throws `SchemaOutdatedError` listing their ids, instead of failing on the first write. See [Using skipMigrations](#using-skipmigrations).
</Warning>

## Schema migrations

theAuth keeps a ledger table, `theauth_schema_migrations`, with one row per applied migration: `id`, `name`, `checksum` and `applied_at`. Migrations are numbered and append only:

| Id | Name | What it does |
|----|------|--------------|
| `0000` | `baseline` | Every table theAuth had when the ledger was introduced (the 1.x schema). |
| `0001` | `relation-and-cache-hit` | `theauth_permissions.relation` and `theauth_audit_logs.cache_hit`. |
| `0002` | `audit-decision-code` | `theauth_audit_logs.decision_code` and the index `theauth_audit_logs_code`. |
| `0003` | `audit-recorded-at-ms` | `theauth_audit_logs.recorded_at_ms`, a backfill from `timestamp`, and the index `theauth_audit_logs_order`. |
| `0005` | `audit-event` | `theauth_audit_logs.event`, a backfill for rows it can classify, and the index `theauth_audit_logs_event` on `(agent_id, event, recorded_at_ms)`. |

On startup theAuth runs every migration that is not in the ledger yet, in order, and records it. Rules that make this safe on an existing database:

- **A database from before the ledger is adopted, not rebuilt.** If the tables exist but the ledger does not, theAuth probes the columns, treats `0000` (and `0001`, when its columns are present) as already applied, records them, and runs the rest. Your rows are untouched.
- **Reruns are no-ops.** Applied migrations are skipped. Statements tolerate "already exists", so a half finished upgrade can be resumed.
- **Applied migrations cannot change.** The ledger stores a checksum of each migration's SQL. If it no longer matches the code, startup fails with `SchemaChecksumError` rather than guessing.
- **Features still decide which tables exist.** A migration that touches the audit table only applies when your config creates it. Enable the feature later and the next start creates the table and applies the migrations that were waiting.
- **The audit hash does not change.** `decision_code`, `recorded_at_ms` and `event` are not part of the hashed payload, so existing chains keep verifying.

Read the ledger from code:

```typescript
const status = await theauth.schema.status();
// { applied: [{ id: '0000', name: 'baseline', appliedAt: Date }, ...],
//   pending: [], baselineStamped: false, mismatched: [], unknown: [] }
```

Or from the shell, with the CLI:

```bash
theauth db status                      # applied and pending, exit 1 when behind
theauth db up                          # apply pending migrations
theauth db up --dry-run                # print the statements, change nothing
theauth db sql --dialect postgres      # print the SQL for a dialect
theauth db sql --dialect postgres --from 0002
```

`--db <url>` (or `DATABASE_URL`) picks the database; `--config <file>` loads your config module so only the tables your features need are considered. Add `--json` for machine readable output.

### Using skipMigrations

With `skipMigrations: true` theAuth never changes the schema, but it still reads the ledger and throws `SchemaOutdatedError` when migrations are pending. To keep the schema in step with the SDK:

1. Generate the SQL for your dialect: `theauth db sql --dialect postgres > theauth-schema.sql`. On a database that already has the 1.x tables, start at the first pending id instead, for example `--from 0002`. That output first creates the ledger and stamps the earlier migrations as applied.
2. Review it and run it with your own tooling (Flyway, Liquibase, `psql`). Each migration ends with an `INSERT` into the ledger, so theAuth sees it as applied.
3. Deploy the new SDK version. If anything is still pending the process fails at startup and names the ids.

The same SQL ships in the repository as generated files, `packages/core/src/db/migrations/sql/<dialect>/<id>.sql`. A test fails when they drift from the TypeScript migrations.

<Warning>
  Upgrading to 2.0 with `skipMigrations: true`: apply `0002` and `0003` (or run `theauth db sql --dialect <yours> --from 0002`) before deploying. The audit queries select `decision_code` and `recorded_at_ms`, and startup now fails with `SchemaOutdatedError` until the ledger shows them applied.
</Warning>

## Schema overview

The full set of tables theAuth can create is below. Which ones exist in your database depends on your config, see above.

| Table | Purpose |
|-------|---------|
| `theauth_secondary_storage` | Key/value rows used when `secondaryStorage: 'database'` (counters, device codes) |
| `theauth_users` | Human user identities (also holds ban, Stripe and Polar billing fields) |
| `theauth_tenants` | Multi-tenant isolation |
| `theauth_agents` | AI agent identities (the core entity) |
| `theauth_permissions` | Per-agent resource+action permissions with constraints |
| `theauth_delegation_chains` | Agent-to-agent delegation records |
| `theauth_audit_logs` | Log of every agent action. The nullable `decision_code` column holds the machine-readable outcome and the nullable `event` column holds what happened (both added in 2.0, neither part of the audit hash) |
| `theauth_rate_limits` | Per-agent call-rate counters |
| `theauth_mcp_servers` | Registered MCP servers |
| `theauth_sessions` | theAuth-managed human user sessions |
| `theauth_oauth_clients`, `theauth_oauth_access_tokens`, `theauth_oauth_authorization_codes` | OAuth 2.1 client registrations, issued tokens, and short-lived PKCE codes |
| `theauth_agent_cards` | A2A capability discovery cards |
| `theauth_agent_registration_tokens` | One-time tokens for [agent registration](/agent-registration-tokens) |
| `theauth_oauth_accounts`, `theauth_oauth_states` | Linked social accounts and in-flight OAuth state (`oauth()` plugin) |
| `theauth_approval_requests` | CIBA async approval flow records |
| `theauth_approval_votes` | One row per approver on a quorum approval request |
| `theauth_trust_scores` | Graduated autonomy trust scores per agent |
| `theauth_budget_policies` | Token and call budget caps per agent/user/tenant |
| `theauth_magic_links`, `theauth_email_otps`, `theauth_phone_verifications`, `theauth_totp` | Magic link, email OTP, phone OTP, and TOTP records |
| `theauth_username_accounts`, `theauth_passkey_credentials`, `theauth_passkey_challenges` | Username/password and passkey records |
| `theauth_organizations`, `theauth_org_members`, `theauth_org_invitations`, `theauth_org_roles`, `theauth_sso_connections`, `theauth_api_keys` | Organizations, SSO connections, and API keys |
| `theauth_trusted_devices`, `theauth_one_time_tokens`, `theauth_login_history`, `theauth_jwt_refresh_tokens`, `theauth_refresh_tokens`, `theauth_refresh_token_families` | Trusted devices, one-time tokens, login history, and refresh tokens |
| `theauth_ephemeral_sessions`, `theauth_agent_dids`, `theauth_cost_events`, `theauth_stream_events` | Ephemeral sessions, agent DIDs, cost attribution, and event streaming |
| `theauth_oidc_clients`, `theauth_oidc_auth_codes`, `theauth_oidc_refresh_tokens` | OIDC provider records |
| `theauth_rebac_resources`, `theauth_rebac_relationships` | ReBAC graph |
| `theauth_federation_instances`, `theauth_federation_tokens` | Federation records |

### Upgrading the audit table

Migrations `0002` and `0003` add `decision_code TEXT` (with the index `theauth_audit_logs_code`) and `recorded_at_ms` (`INTEGER` on SQLite, `BIGINT` on Postgres, with the index `theauth_audit_logs_order`). Old rows keep a NULL code, and `recorded_at_ms` is backfilled from the second-resolution `timestamp`. Audit reads order by `recorded_at_ms`, so rows written in the same second keep their write order. Migration `0005` adds a nullable `event TEXT` column (with the index `theauth_audit_logs_event`). It backfills `event` from `action` for rows whose action is itself an event name (`delegation.create`, `delegation.revoke`, `agent.cascade.revoked`, `approval.*`, `vault.read`, `audit.*`), marks policy engine rows `policy.evaluate`, marks the remaining rows that have a decision code `authorize`, and leaves every other row NULL. None of these columns is covered by the audit hash, so existing hash chains keep verifying. If you use `skipMigrations`, see [Using skipMigrations](#using-skipmigrations).

<Warning>
  Do not run TheAuth and `theauth-go` in the same database or schema. Both create `theauth_audit_secrets` with different column types. TheAuth detects the foreign layout before it migrates (and on every start with `skipMigrations`) and throws `AUDIT_SECRETS_LAYOUT_MISMATCH` without changing the table. Use a separate database or schema for each library. See [Audit receipts and chain vectors](/audit-receipts).
</Warning>

All table and column names use `snake_case`. IDs are `text`. Timestamps are integer epoch seconds on both SQLite and Postgres.

## Peer dependencies

| Provider | Required package |
|----------|-----------------|
| `sqlite` | `sql.js` (installed with core) |
| `sqlite-native` | `better-sqlite3` |
| `postgres` | `pg` |
| `libsql` | `@libsql/client` |
| `mysql` (not supported in this release) | `mysql2` |
| `d1` | `drizzle-orm/d1` (a Cloudflare Workers binding, no extra install) |

theAuth uses dynamic imports for the SQLite and Postgres drivers so they remain optional. You will get a clear error message at startup if the required package is missing, for example:

```
TheAuth: provider "postgres" requires the "pg" package.
Install it with: npm install pg
```

## Testing with in-memory SQLite

Use `:memory:` for fast, isolated tests that need no setup or teardown:

```typescript
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { describe, beforeEach, it } from 'vitest';

let theauth: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof createTheAuth>>;

beforeEach(async () => {
  theauth = await createTheAuth({
    database: { provider: 'sqlite', url: ':memory:' },
    agents: { enabled: true },
  });
});

it('creates an agent', async () => {
  const agent = await theauth.agent.create({
    ownerId: 'user_1',
    name: 'Test Agent',
    type: 'autonomous',
    permissions: [],
  });

  expect(agent.id).toBeDefined();
});
```

Each `createTheAuth()` call with `:memory:` gets a completely isolated database, so tests never share state.

# Bring your own Drizzle instance

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/bring-your-own-drizzle

Most apps that already use Drizzle have a connection pool, credentials and a driver choice that theAuth should not duplicate. Pass that instance in and theAuth queries it directly.

```ts
import { createTheAuth } from "@glinr/theauth";
import { drizzle } from "drizzle-orm/node-postgres";
import { Pool } from "pg";

const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

const auth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { drizzle: drizzle(pool), dialect: "postgres" },
});
```

`dialect` is `"sqlite"`, `"postgres"` or `"mysql"`. It picks the migration SQL, the same way `provider` does for the URL form. Everything else about the database section is unchanged: tables are created on boot, and `skipMigrations: true` makes boot fail with `SchemaOutdatedError` when the schema is behind (see [Database setup](/database#using-skipmigrations)).

## What you own

theAuth does not open this connection, so it never closes it. Shut the pool down yourself when the process exits.

Connection settings that `provider` applies for you become your job:

| Dialect | Set this on your own handle |
|---|---|
| `sqlite` | `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`. For a file, `PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL` is a good idea if more than one process opens it. |
| `mysql` | Create the pool with `timezone: "Z"`. The migration ledger stores UTC. Use a `utf8mb4` database with a binary collation (`utf8mb4_bin`) so ids compare case sensitively. |
| `postgres` | Nothing extra. Use a pooled connection string on serverless hosts. |

## Requirements for the handle

- It must expose the driver client at `db.$client`, because migrations and the schema check send raw SQL through it. The node-postgres, mysql2 and better-sqlite3 drivers do, and those are the ones this release tests. A driver that hides its client can still work if you run the migrations yourself (`theauth db sql`) and every query path goes through Drizzle, but boot calls the schema check even with `skipMigrations`, so that is untested territory.
- Do not pass a `schema` that renames or replaces theAuth's tables. theAuth uses its own table objects and never reads `db.query`, so a plain `drizzle(pool)` is enough.
- Reads must see your own writes. Single use tokens, refresh rotation and the audit chain read right after a write. If you route reads to a replica, pin auth traffic to the primary.

`createTheAuth` returns your handle as `auth.db`, and plugins receive it as `ctx.db`, so it is the same object you passed in.

## Hot path indexes

Migration `0014` adds seven indexes that agent token lookup, the delegation walks, the hourly rate limit read and the pending approval list depend on. Without them each of those scans its whole table. If you own the schema and skip theAuth migrations, create them yourself. Keep the names, so a later run of the migration finds them and leaves them alone.

| Index | Table | Columns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `theauth_agents_token_hash` | `theauth_agents` | `token_hash` |
| `theauth_agents_owner_status` | `theauth_agents` | `owner_id, status` |
| `theauth_delegation_chains_to` | `theauth_delegation_chains` | `to_agent_id, status` |
| `theauth_delegation_chains_from` | `theauth_delegation_chains` | `from_agent_id, status` |
| `theauth_rate_limits_lookup` | `theauth_rate_limits` | `agent_id, resource, window_start` |
| `theauth_approval_requests_status` | `theauth_approval_requests` | `status, created_at` |
| `theauth_permissions_agent` | `theauth_permissions` | `agent_id` (SQLite and Postgres only) |

The SQL for each dialect:

```sql
-- SQLite and Postgres
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS theauth_agents_token_hash ON theauth_agents (token_hash);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS theauth_agents_owner_status ON theauth_agents (owner_id, status);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS theauth_delegation_chains_to ON theauth_delegation_chains (to_agent_id, status);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS theauth_delegation_chains_from ON theauth_delegation_chains (from_agent_id, status);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS theauth_rate_limits_lookup ON theauth_rate_limits (agent_id, resource, window_start);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS theauth_approval_requests_status ON theauth_approval_requests (status, created_at);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS theauth_permissions_agent ON theauth_permissions (agent_id);

-- MySQL (TEXT columns need a prefix length; InnoDB already indexes the foreign key columns)
CREATE INDEX theauth_agents_token_hash ON theauth_agents (token_hash(191));
CREATE INDEX theauth_agents_owner_status ON theauth_agents (owner_id, status);
CREATE INDEX theauth_delegation_chains_to ON theauth_delegation_chains (to_agent_id(191), status(16));
CREATE INDEX theauth_delegation_chains_from ON theauth_delegation_chains (from_agent_id(191), status(16));
CREATE INDEX theauth_rate_limits_lookup ON theauth_rate_limits (agent_id, resource(191), window_start);
CREATE INDEX theauth_approval_requests_status ON theauth_approval_requests (status, created_at);
```

If you copy the table objects from `@glinr/theauth` into your own Drizzle schema, they already declare these indexes (SQLite dialect), so `drizzle-kit generate` emits them.

## Typed unique conflicts

Several flows use a unique index as the tiebreaker: creating a user, appending to the audit chain, a second vote from the same approver, banning twice, MCP client and revocation inserts, erasure tombstones. They now map a driver error through `toStoreConflict`, which returns a `StoreConflictError` (exported from `@glinr/theauth`, with `code: "STORE_CONFLICT"`, `model` and the driver error as `cause`).

Detection reads structured codes first: Postgres `23505`, MySQL `ER_DUP_ENTRY` or errno `1062`, SQLite `SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE` and `SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_PRIMARYKEY`, SQL Server `2627` and `2601`, Prisma `P2002`, MongoDB `11000`. The old text match stays as a fallback for drivers that wrap the code away, so behavior on the existing providers is unchanged.

## Run the contract suite against your backend

`@glinr/theauth-test-utils/store-contract` holds the checks that make a backend safe for auth: 24 parallel callers fighting over one single use row with exactly one winner (magic link, email OTP, approval decision and consumption, refresh rotation), the attempt limit on OTP guesses, unique conflicts, and an audit chain that stays gapless and verifies when two processes append for one agent.

```ts
import { createTheAuth } from "@glinr/theauth";
import { runStoreContract } from "@glinr/theauth-test-utils/store-contract";

const url = process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL;

runStoreContract(
  "my postgres",
  async () => {
    const mail = { magicTokens: [] as string[], otpCodes: [] as string[] };
    const auth = await createTheAuth({
      database: { drizzle: makeMyDrizzle(url), dialect: "postgres" },
      agents: { enabled: true, maxPerUser: 500 },
      audit: { tamperEvident: true, hmacKey: "test-key" },
      magicLink: {
        appUrl: "https://app.test",
        sendMagicLink: async (_email, token) => void mail.magicTokens.push(token),
      },
      emailOtp: { sendOtp: async (_email, code) => void mail.otpCodes.push(code) },
    });
    return { auth, mail, close: async () => {} };
  },
  { skip: !url },
);
```

Add `peer` (a second instance with its own handle on the same database) to include the two process audit check, `duplicateInsert` to check conflict typing with your driver, and `tokenFamilies` for the refresh rotation race. The repository runs this suite on sql.js, better-sqlite3 through both config forms, Postgres and MySQL; set `THEAUTH_TEST_PG_URL` and `THEAUTH_TEST_MYSQL_URL` to include the last two.

<Note>
  The suite needs `vitest` as a dev dependency. It runs against the instance's public surface, so it describes how today's Drizzle code behaves, not a future storage interface.
</Note>

# Turso, Neon and Supabase

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/hosted-databases

These three hosted databases are not special cases in the schema. Turso speaks SQLite, Neon and Supabase speak Postgres, and theAuth already runs on both dialects. What changes is how you connect.

| Host | How to connect | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| Turso or any libSQL | `provider: "libsql"` | `@libsql/client` |
| Supabase | `provider: "postgres"` with a Supabase URL | `pg` |
| Neon | `database: { drizzle, dialect: "postgres" }` with Neon's WebSocket `Pool` | `@neondatabase/serverless`, `ws` on older Node |

## Turso and libSQL

```bash
pnpm add @glinr/theauth @libsql/client
```

```ts
import { createTheAuth } from "@glinr/theauth";

const auth = await createTheAuth({
  database: {
    provider: "libsql",
    url: process.env.TURSO_DATABASE_URL!, // libsql://my-db-my-org.turso.io
    authToken: process.env.TURSO_AUTH_TOKEN!,
  },
});
```

`url` also takes `https://`, `wss://` and `file:./local.db`, so the same code runs against a local file in development. `authToken` is not needed for a `file:` URL. Tables are created on boot, and `skipMigrations: true` makes boot fail with `SchemaOutdatedError` if the schema is behind, like the other providers.

libSQL is SQLite on the wire, so the schema is the SQLite one: ids are text and timestamps are integer epoch seconds. Foreign keys are on by default in the client. The `libsql` provider does not set `journal_mode` or `busy_timeout`, because those belong to the server. If you open a `file:` database from more than one process, set them yourself with a bring your own handle ([Bring your own Drizzle instance](/bring-your-own-drizzle)).

Want your own client, for example an embedded replica with `syncUrl`? Pass it in:

```ts
import { createClient } from "@libsql/client";
import { drizzle } from "drizzle-orm/libsql";

const client = createClient({ url: "file:replica.db", syncUrl: process.env.TURSO_DATABASE_URL!, authToken: process.env.TURSO_AUTH_TOKEN! });
const auth = await createTheAuth({ database: { drizzle: drizzle(client), dialect: "sqlite" } });
```

The embedded replica form was not run. Writes on a replica go to the primary, and theAuth reads straight after writing (single use tokens, refresh rotation), so check that your replica sync mode gives read your writes before you rely on it.

## Supabase

Supabase is Postgres. Use the `postgres` provider with a connection string from the dashboard's Connect dialog. Which string you use matters:

| Mode | Port | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| Direct | 5432 | A long running server with IPv6 or the IPv4 add-on. Run migrations here. |
| Session pooler | 5432 | A long running server on an IPv4 only network. |
| Transaction pooler | 6543 | Serverless and edge functions. |

```ts
const auth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: "postgres", url: process.env.SUPABASE_DB_URL! },
});
```

Supabase asks for SSL, because many drivers default to `prefer`, which can fall back to plain text. With the `pg` driver the exact spelling matters. In `pg` 8.20, the version this repository tests with, `sslmode=require` is an alias for `verify-full`, so `pg` checks the server certificate against your system certificate store, and a Supabase certificate chain can fail that check. Pick one:

- Verify properly: download the root certificate from Database settings in the Supabase dashboard and use `?sslmode=verify-full&sslrootcert=/path/to/supabase-root.crt`.
- Encrypt without verifying, which is what Supabase's own `require` does: `?uselibpqcompat=true&sslmode=require`.

I did not run either against a real Supabase project. The alias behavior comes from running `pg-connection-string` 2.14.1 on those three URLs. The transaction pooler does not support prepared statements. theAuth never creates a named prepared statement, so nothing needs turning off. The suite below ran against a transaction mode pooler with prepared statements disabled and passed.

Two things to know:

- On serverless, keep the pool small. `provider: "postgres"` opens a `pg` pool with its default size, so a function that scales to many instances multiplies it. The transaction pooler absorbs that. If you need a size of one, use bring your own Drizzle with `new Pool({ connectionString, max: 1 })`.
- Do not point theAuth at the `auth` schema or reuse Supabase Auth tables. theAuth creates its own `theauth_*` tables in `public`. Row Level Security is off on them, so do not expose them through the Data API: turn on RLS with no policies, or revoke access for the `anon` and `authenticated` roles. Your server connects as a role that bypasses RLS.

## Neon

Neon serves Postgres over TCP and over WebSocket. The WebSocket `Pool` from `@neondatabase/serverless` is a drop in for `pg`, and supports the interactive transactions theAuth uses. The HTTP driver (`neon-http`) does not support them, so do not use it.

```bash
pnpm add @glinr/theauth @neondatabase/serverless drizzle-orm
```

```ts
import { createTheAuth } from "@glinr/theauth";
import { Pool } from "@neondatabase/serverless";
import { drizzle } from "drizzle-orm/neon-serverless";

const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

const auth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { drizzle: drizzle({ client: pool }), dialect: "postgres" },
});
```

On Node 21 and older there is no global `WebSocket`. Install `ws` and set `neonConfig.webSocketConstructor = ws` before you create the pool. Node 22 has one built in.

On an edge runtime a WebSocket cannot outlive the request. Create the pool and the instance inside the request handler and call `pool.end()` before you return, as Neon's driver docs describe. On a Node server, create them once.

If you are on a Node server and do not need Neon's WebSocket driver, `provider: "postgres"` with the normal Neon connection string works as well. Use the pooled (`-pooler`) host on serverless.

## What was run

- **libSQL.** The store contract suite (`runStoreContract`, 14 checks) against a real libSQL file database, with the `libsql` provider and with a bring your own `drizzle-orm/libsql` handle. It covers 24 parallel callers on one single use row, unique conflicts, an audit chain written by two handles and the hourly budget. Plus a restart that keeps data, and `skipMigrations` on an existing and an empty database. Not run: a remote Turso database, `libsql://` and `wss://` URLs, embedded replicas.
- **Supabase.** The same suite against local Postgres 14 behind PgBouncer 1.26 in transaction pooling mode with `max_prepared_statements = 0`, three runs, ten parallel callers. Not run: a real Supabase project, Supavisor, `sslmode=require` against Supabase's certificates.
- **Neon.** A scratch project with the packed `@glinr/theauth`, `@neondatabase/serverless` 1.2.0 and `ws`, using the WebSocket `Pool` through a small local bridge from WebSocket frames to a local Postgres 14 (Neon's wire protocol is plain Postgres messages inside the frames). Migrations ran, a user, an agent and allow and deny decisions worked, and 24 parallel calls against a budget of 10 admitted no more than 10. Not run: a real Neon endpoint, so the `-pooler` host, cold starts and Neon's own proxy are untested. The Neon driver is not a dependency of this repository, so this is a manual check and not part of the test suite.

The pooler suite is in `packages/core/tests/store-contract/pg-pooler.test.ts` and runs when `THEAUTH_TEST_PG_POOLER_URL` points at an empty database behind a transaction mode pooler.

One behavior to expect behind any pooler: the hourly call budget reserves before it checks, so when a burst is larger than the budget it can refuse calls that would have fit. It never admits more than the budget. Under a pooler that interleaves the reservations, a burst of 24 calls against a budget of 10 admitted between one and three.

# Which storage should I pick

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/choose-storage

theAuth has two separate storage decisions, and people often mix them up.

1. **The database** holds users, sessions, agents, delegations and the audit log. It has to be durable. You choose it with `database.provider`.
2. **Secondary storage** holds small, short-lived, high-churn values: rate-limit counters, device login codes. It only needs fast reads, writes and an atomic counter. You choose it with `secondaryStorage`.

The default for the second one is process memory, which is correct on a laptop and quietly wrong almost everywhere else. Most of the "it works locally" problems in [Troubleshooting](/troubleshooting) come from that default.

## Start from where you deploy

| You run | Database | Secondary storage |
|---|---|---|
| A laptop or CI job | `sqlite` with `:memory:` | memory (default) |
| One long-lived Node server, one process | `postgres`, or `sqlite-native` for a small app | memory is fine; `"database"` if you want counters to survive a restart |
| Several instances behind a load balancer | `postgres` | `"database"` (no new infrastructure) or Redis (more throughput) |
| Vercel or another serverless host | `postgres` through a pooled connection string (Supabase and Neon: see [Turso, Neon and Supabase](/hosted-databases)), or `libsql` for Turso | `"database"` or Redis over HTTP such as Upstash. Never memory. |
| Cloudflare Workers | `d1` | `"database"` on D1 for anything that must be exact, KV only for soft limits |

## The database, in one paragraph each

**`sqlite` (sql.js).** SQLite compiled to WebAssembly. No native build, runs on Node, Bun, Deno and edge runtimes. The whole database lives in memory and is never written to disk, so it only accepts `url: ":memory:"`. A file URL throws `THEAUTH_SQLITE_NOT_PERSISTENT` at startup instead of silently losing your data on restart. Good for tests, CI and throwaway demos. For a database file use `sqlite-native`.

**`sqlite-native` (better-sqlite3).** Real SQLite on disk, fast, one process at a time in practice. Needs a native build (install `better-sqlite3` yourself). A good fit for a single VPS where you want zero database operations. Back up the file.

**`postgres`.** The default recommendation for anything with more than one instance or any real traffic. Needs the `pg` package. Use a pooler on serverless.

**`mysql`.** Not supported in this release. `provider: "mysql"` throws `THEAUTH_MYSQL_UNSUPPORTED` unless you pass `experimental: true`. See [What is tested per database](#what-is-tested-per-database).

**`libsql`.** SQLite served by libSQL: Turso, or a local `file:` URL. Needs `@libsql/client`. See [Turso, Neon and Supabase](/hosted-databases).

**`d1`.** Cloudflare D1 through a Worker binding. Use it when the app lives on Workers. Pass the binding instead of a URL.

Setup snippets for each are on [Database setup](/database).

## What is tested per database

All providers share one versioned schema (`theauth_schema_migrations`, see [Database setup](/database#schema-migrations)). What the repository tests on each:

| Provider | Tested in CI | Tested by hand |
|----------|--------------|----------------|
| `sqlite`, `sqlite-native` | Every test file, on every change (fresh create, upgrade from the 1.2.0 schema, stamped baseline, rerun, checksum mismatch, `skipMigrations`) | n/a |
| `postgres` | Not yet | The dialect suite runs the full instance (users, sessions, agents, delegation, audit chain, MCP OAuth stores, GDPR erasure) against Postgres 14 when `THEAUTH_TEST_PG_URL` is set |
| `libsql` | Not yet | The store contract suite (14 checks) against a real libSQL file, through the provider and through a bring your own handle. A remote Turso database is untested |
| `mysql` | No | Not supported in this release |
| `d1` | Not yet | Not yet. The generated SQLite SQL (`theauth db sql --dialect sqlite`) is applied with `skipMigrations: true` |

> Postgres works through the `pg` driver. We run the full test suite against Postgres 14 by hand before each release; it is not in CI yet. Timestamps are stored as integer epoch seconds, the same as SQLite, so use `to_timestamp(created_at)` when you query the tables yourself. The store contract also ran behind a transaction mode pooler (PgBouncer) and, through a bring your own handle, on Neon's WebSocket driver against a local Postgres (see [Turso, Neon and Supabase](/hosted-databases)). Other Postgres drivers (postgres.js, PGlite) are not supported yet.
>
> MySQL is not supported in this release. `provider: "mysql"` throws unless you pass `experimental: true`, and even then the baseline schema does not apply on a real server. We will turn it on once the same suite passes on MySQL 8.4.

## Secondary storage, in one paragraph each

| Backend | Counts exactly | Shared between instances | Pick it when |
|---|---|---|---|
| memory | yes | no | One process, or you accept that every instance counts separately. |
| `"database"` | yes | yes | You already run a database and do not want another service. This is the safe default for multi-instance. |
| `redisStorage(client)` | yes | yes | High request volume, or you want counters off your main database. Works with ioredis, node-redis and `@upstash/redis`. |
| `cloudflareKvStorage(kv)` | no | eventually | Soft limits on Workers only. KV has no atomic increment and writes take time to appear elsewhere. |
| `defineSecondaryStorage({...})` | only if you provide `incr` | depends | You have a store the others do not cover. |

The `"database"` backend creates one table, `theauth_secondary_storage`, and increments counters with a single guarded `UPDATE`, so it is exact on every supported database. Expired rows are removed lazily; run `databaseStorage(db).purgeExpired()` from a cron if you have a large keyspace.

You can choose per feature. A common production setup on Workers is exact storage for device codes and soft storage for rate limits:

```ts
const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'd1', binding: env.DB },
  secondaryStorage: {
    default: 'database',
    rateLimit: cloudflareKvStorage(env.RATE_KV), // soft limits are fine
    deviceCodes: 'database',                     // must be reliable
  },
});
```

More detail, including the interface for a custom store, is on [Secondary storage](/secondary-storage).

## A few rules of thumb

- If you are unsure, use Postgres plus `secondaryStorage: 'database'`. It has one moving part and works on every deployment shape except Workers.
- Do not use memory for anything you would be upset to lose or to count twice: device codes and rate limits on a deployment with more than one instance.
- Do not put the main database on KV. KV is only an option for secondary storage.
- Moving from `sqlite` to Postgres later is a data copy. The table names are the same (`theauth_*`), so plan a one-off export and import, and run `createTheAuth` against the new database first so the tables exist.
- The Prisma adapter reads and writes theAuth tables from code that already uses Prisma. It does not replace the choice above. See [Prisma](/prisma).

Using the Go library instead? Its backends are different, see [Storage backends](/go/getting-started/storage-backends) and [Shared state for several replicas](/go/guides/pluggable-stores).

# Benchmarks

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/benchmarks

The harness lives in `benchmarks/` in the repository. It is not published to npm and has no dependencies of its own: it loads the built SDK and uses `performance.now()` for timing.

No results are published on this page yet. Numbers will be pasted in from a CI run (see below), with the hardware they came from. Until then, treat any performance claim about TheAuth as unmeasured.

## What it measures

| Scenario | What runs |
| --- | --- |
| createAgent | `agent.create`, for one owner with a growing agent count and for a fresh owner each call |
| Token issue and verify | `agent.rotate`, `agent.validateToken` (database lookup), JWT session `createSession` and `verifySession` (stateless) |
| authorize | allow and deny, direct permission and delegation depth 1, 2 and 3, with and without an audit row per call |
| simulate | the simulator, allow and deny, at the same depths |
| Sessions | session create and validate |
| Audit append | tamper evident off and on, with 1 to 64 concurrent writers on the same agent and on separate agents, plus multiple instances on one database (Postgres and MySQL) |
| Rate limit | the in-process limiter, the memory store, and the database counter behind `maxCallsPerHour` |
| Password hash | PBKDF2 hash and verify at the default cost |

Backends: SQLite through sql.js (in memory and file), SQLite through better-sqlite3 (in memory and file), and Postgres and MySQL when a connection URL is provided (`POSTGRES_URL`, `MYSQL_URL`, or `DATABASE_URL`). Backends without a URL are skipped.

For each row the report gives p50, p95 and p99 latency, operations per second, RSS change, and the Node version, CPU model and backend it ran on.

## Run it

The full run is heavy. Do not run it on a laptop. It is meant for the manual `Benchmarks` workflow, which starts Postgres and MySQL service containers, runs everything and uploads `full.json` and `full.md` as an artifact.

To check that the harness works on your machine, run the smoke profile (a few hundred iterations, in memory SQLite only):

```bash
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
nice -n 19 pnpm bench:smoke
```

The exact command the CI job runs:

```bash
pnpm bench:ci
```

That script builds `@glinr/theauth`, runs `node --expose-gc benchmarks/run.mjs --profile full`, then `node benchmarks/report.mjs` to write markdown tables. Output goes to `benchmarks/results/` (git ignored).

## Caveats

- Concurrency numbers are async tasks on one event loop, not threads.
- Postgres and MySQL run on the same machine as the benchmark, so network latency is close to zero.
- Shared CI runners are noisy at the tail. Repeat runs before trusting p99.
- Table sizes grow during a run, which affects operations that scan.

See [scale and architecture notes](https://github.com/glincker/theauth/blob/main/docs/scale-and-architecture.md) for the code paths these scenarios were written to test.

# Performance

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/performance

These numbers come from one laptop, taken while other work was running on it. They show what changed between two builds of the same code. They are not a throughput claim for your deployment, and nothing here compares TheAuth with anything else. The general benchmark harness is described on [Benchmarks](/benchmarks); this page covers the micro benchmarks and the profile driven fixes.

## Where the numbers come from

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Machine | Apple M4 Max, 14 cores, 36 GB, macOS (Darwin 27.2) |
| Node | 22.22.2 |
| Database | SQLite through better-sqlite3 (file and in memory) |
| Load | The load average was about 14 during the runs, so wall clock timings were noisy |
| Before | The source tree as it was before the changes, rebuilt from a copy |
| After | The same entry points built from the current source |

Both sides are bundled with esbuild from source, not from `dist`, so a stale build cannot skew a run. `benchmarks/micro-build.mjs` builds either tree.

### How medians and noise are stated

Each micro benchmark is timed in batches. One run is the median over 9 batches. A result on this page is the median of several runs, with the lowest and highest run in brackets, and the run order alternated between before and after.

Wall clock was too noisy on a busy laptop (the same case moved by 30 to 50 percent between rounds, and some crypto cases swung by more than the change being measured). The micro benchmark tables below therefore use `--clock cpu`, which counts process CPU time (user plus system, all threads). With it the spread between runs was under 10 percent for most cases, and the brackets show it. The database timings are wall clock per operation; their brackets are wider and are shown too.

## What the profiles showed

`node --cpu-prof` on the existing authorize scenario put roughly half of the self time in drizzle query building and the SQLite driver, so the first lever was the number and cost of queries, not the matcher. `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` then showed full table scans on lookups that every authorize and token check makes. In the micro benchmarks, the top self costs were `TextEncoder.encode` (inside the key sort of the approval hash), a fresh `importKey` per call for HMAC secrets, and a fresh JWKS import per device bundle verify.

## Results

### Database paths

SQLite file, 50,000 agents with 4 permissions each, one delegation link each (a third revoked), 7 runs per setting, 3 rounds. Milliseconds per operation, median with the lowest and highest round.

| Operation | Before | After | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `authorize`, direct permission | 4.10 (4.07 to 4.16) | 0.077 (0.075 to 0.077) | 53x |
| `authorize`, three hop delegation chain | 9.88 (9.80 to 9.90) | 0.36 (0.36 to 0.38) | 27x |
| `agent.validateToken` style lookup by token hash | 5.33 (5.30 to 5.35) | 0.12 (0.115 to 0.117) | 46x |
| Admin pending approvals list, 100 quorum requests | 2.29 (2.29 to 2.34) | 0.51 (0.50 to 0.53) | 4.5x |

The wall clock spread inside a round reached 20 to 60 percent for some of these on the loaded machine, but the before and after ranges do not overlap. The cause is the new migration `0014-hot-path-indexes`. Without indexes, SQLite and Postgres scan `theauth_agents` (by `token_hash`), `theauth_permissions` (by `agent_id`), `theauth_delegation_chains` and `theauth_rate_limits` on every call, so the cost grows with table size. MySQL already indexes foreign key columns, so it only gets the composite and `token_hash` indexes. Databases with the MCP module enabled already had the two delegation chain indexes from migration 0007; on a 5,000 row table with MCP on, a direct `authorize` went from 0.52 to 0.076 ms and a three hop chain from 0.86 to 0.36 ms (single round, noisy).

Reproduce with:

```bash
node benchmarks/micro-build.mjs packages/core/.bench/after.mjs
node benchmarks/scale.mjs --entry packages/core/.bench/after.mjs --rows 50000 --runs 7
node benchmarks/scale.mjs --entry packages/core/.bench/after.mjs --rows 50000 --runs 7 --drop-indexes
```

The last command removes the new indexes after boot, which shows what they are worth on the current code.

### The standard harness, small tables

`benchmarks/run.mjs` (profile `smoke`, better-sqlite3 in memory, 3,000 iterations, p50, median of 5 runs). Tables here are small, so the index effect is mostly absent and the gains come from fewer queries.

| Scenario | Before (ms) | After (ms) | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `agent.validateToken` (database lookup and last active write) | 0.448 | 0.097 | 4.6x |
| `agent.rotate` | 0.265 | 0.110 | 2.4x |
| `agent.create`, fresh owner | 0.215 | 0.110 | 2.0x |
| `agent.create`, one owner with a growing agent count | 1.85 | 1.84 | unchanged |
| `authorize`, delegation depth 1, 2, 3 (audit off) | 0.205, 0.282, 0.358 | 0.170, 0.244, 0.315 | 1.14x to 1.21x |
| `authorize`, delegation depth 1, 2, 3 (audit row per call) | 0.252, 0.334, 0.411 | 0.214, 0.290, 0.361 | 1.14x to 1.18x |
| `authorize`, direct permission | 0.067 to 0.115 | 0.067 to 0.114 | unchanged |
| `simulate`, depth 1, 2, 3 | 0.205 to 0.407 | 0.175 to 0.364 | 1.12x to 1.17x |
| JWT `verifySession` (stateless) | 0.022 | 0.022 | unchanged |

The delegation gain comes from reading each agent's inbound links once (the liveness walk used to run one query for the live links and a second one for every link ever received) and from reading an agent and its permissions together.

### CPU hot paths, no database

Nanoseconds per operation (CPU time), median of 3 rounds of 9 batches, lowest and highest round in brackets.

| Case | Before | After | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Colon match, 50 permissions, hit on the last one | 4,350 (4,290 to 4,762) | 1,842 (1,621 to 1,857) | 2.4x |
| Colon match, 50 permissions, no match | 4,330 (4,268 to 4,683) | 1,847 (1,603 to 1,869) | 2.3x |
| Path match, one `*` glob hit | 512 (512 to 515) | 136 (134 to 146) | 3.8x |
| Path match, deep `**` hit | 1,077 (1,074 to 1,079) | 669 (656 to 680) | 1.6x |
| Path match, glob miss | 1,374 (1,372 to 1,386) | 695 (682 to 697) | 2.0x |
| Approval hash canonical JSON, 20 row payload | 38,556 (35,038 to 39,820) | 10,884 (10,740 to 12,374) | 3.5x |
| Device bundle verify (JWKS object) | 92,650 (91,955 to 92,675) | 63,530 (63,205 to 64,405) | 1.5x |
| Device bundle sign | 73,530 (71,510 to 78,040) | 42,560 (40,760 to 43,260) | 1.7x |
| MCP `validateAccessToken`, HS256, offline mode | 24,250 (23,680 to 27,815) | 18,995 (18,455 to 20,300) | 1.3x |
| MCP `validateAccessToken`, HS256, cached mode | 26,155 (24,670 to 27,160) | 20,965 (18,670 to 21,220) | 1.25x |
| MCP `validateAccessToken`, HS256, live mode, 5,000 entry denylist | 26,770 (24,165 to 33,920) | 18,935 (18,240 to 20,130) | 1.4x |
| Stateless session `getSession` | 20,012 (19,992 to 23,261) | 14,145 (13,866 to 15,036) | 1.4x |
| DPoP proof verify (ES256) | 123,155 (119,765 to 126,445) | 120,880 (119,815 to 123,025) | no change |
| Device bundle offline decision | 120 (119 to 122) | 128 (126 to 131) | about 7 percent slower |

Two honest notes. The DPoP proof carries a new public key every time, so there is no key to cache and nothing changed. The offline bundle decision with two permissions got a few nanoseconds slower, because the new colon matcher pays a little more than `split` on very short inputs; it wins as soon as a list has more than a handful of entries.

The MCP validation figures use the HMAC secret path with a fake revocation store holding 5,000 denylist entries. The revocation lookup itself is a set or indexed read and was not the cost in any mode; the key import and JWT parsing were.

## What changed

All of these keep decisions identical. Each fast path has a test that compares it with the code it replaced over a seeded random corpus (`tests/perf-equivalence.test.ts`, `tests/delegation-liveness-queries.test.ts`, `tests/admin-api-list-queries.test.ts`, `tests/migrate-hot-path-0014.test.ts`). No check was removed or reordered.

- **Indexes** (migration `0014-hot-path-indexes`): `theauth_agents(token_hash)`, `theauth_agents(owner_id, status)`, `theauth_permissions(agent_id)`, `theauth_delegation_chains(to_agent_id, status)` and `(from_agent_id, status)`, `theauth_rate_limits(agent_id, resource, window_start)`, `theauth_approval_requests(status, created_at)`. The query plans before and after are asserted in the migration test.
- **HMAC keys**: a string secret is imported once and the non extractable `CryptoKey` is reused (at most 32 secrets, oldest dropped). Used by session cookies, the stateless session ring and MCP HS256 verification.
- **Device bundles**: the JWKS resolver and the signing key are reused while the same JWKS or JWK object keeps the same content. A fingerprint of the content is compared on every call, so a key rotated in place is picked up at once.
- **Resource matching**: the default colon matcher walks both strings with `indexOf` instead of splitting them, and the path matcher skips its table when the pattern has no `**`.
- **Approval hash**: strings that need no escaping skip the character loop, and keys are ordered by byte without encoding two copies per comparison when both are ASCII.
- **Delegation liveness**: one read per agent for inbound links, filtered in memory for the live ones, instead of two reads.
- **Admin API**: the pending approvals list reads quorum approvers for the whole page in one query instead of one per request, and the delegation list without a status filter reads only `limit` rows instead of the 500 row ceiling.

One attempt was dropped. Restricting the delegation impact view's denylist read to the links shown cost more than it saved when the denylist is small, so it is unchanged.

## Not changed on purpose

- DPoP proof keys are not cached: they come from the request.
- Nothing is cached across `authorize` calls. A cached delegation or agent row would delay a revocation, and revocations must take effect on the next call.
- The rate limit counter still does a read then a write per allowed call. Making it atomic is a separate change.

## Run the micro benchmarks yourself

```bash
pnpm --filter @glinr/theauth build   # only needed for benchmarks/run.mjs
node benchmarks/micro-build.mjs packages/core/.bench/micro.mjs
node benchmarks/micro.mjs --entry packages/core/.bench/micro.mjs --runs 9 --clock cpu --out /tmp/micro.json
```

The output file lists, for every case, the median and the lowest and highest run, so you can judge the noise on your own machine before trusting a difference.

# Production security checklist

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/production-checklist

None of these items is exotic. Each one is something that works in development and fails, or worse, silently weakens things, in production. Go through the list once before launch and again after any change to your hosting.

## Secrets

- [ ] **Session secret is 32+ random characters and comes from the environment.** The cookie session manager, the refresher and JWT sessions all reject anything shorter. Generate it with `openssl rand -base64 48`.
- [ ] **Every instance has the same secret.** A mismatch looks like users randomly signed out.
- [ ] **`signingSecret` for MCP is a different value from the session secret.** It does not fall back to any other secret. If you can, publish keys and sign with ES256 or EdDSA instead of a shared HMAC secret ([MCP](/mcp)); generate keys with `generateMcpSigningKey`.
- [ ] **You know how you would rotate them.** theAuth takes one secret at a time, so rotating the session secret signs everyone out. Decide when you would accept that, and write it down.
- [ ] **No secrets in the repository or in client bundles.** OAuth client secrets, database URLs and webhook secrets are server-only.

## Cookies and transport

- [ ] **Everything is served over HTTPS**, including the OAuth callback URL you registered with each provider.
- [ ] **`NODE_ENV=production` is set, or `cookieOptions.secure: true` is.** The cookie session manager picks `Secure` from `NODE_ENV` only ([Cookie options](/cookies)).
- [ ] **`baseUrl` is the public `https://` URL** with the adapter mount path, not the internal address behind your proxy.
- [ ] **`SameSite` is `Lax` or `Strict`** unless you have a measured need for `None`. Cookies are `HttpOnly` by default, keep it that way.
- [ ] **Cross-origin front ends use an explicit CORS allowlist with credentials, never `*`.** Core sends CORS headers only on the MCP endpoints, so the rest is yours to configure ([Troubleshooting](/troubleshooting#cors-and-cross-origin-requests)).
- [ ] **State-changing requests from browsers are checked for origin.** `validateOrigin` and the double-submit helpers are exported for this ([Sessions](/sessions)).

## Proxies and rate limits

- [ ] **`trustedProxy` is set** (`trustedProxyCount` or `trustedHeader`) when you run behind a load balancer or CDN. Without it all clients share one rate-limit bucket. Do not set `trustedHeader` for a header your edge does not overwrite.
- [ ] **The `rateLimit()` plugin is installed** and covers sign-in, sign-up and password reset. Defaults are in [Rate limiting](/rate-limiting).
- [ ] **Rate limit storage is shared between instances**, and exact where it matters. Not memory on multi-instance or serverless, and not Cloudflare KV for limits you rely on ([Which storage should I pick](/choose-storage)).
- [ ] **Device-flow codes live in reliable storage** (`secondaryStorage.deviceCodes`), not in memory that restarts or splits across instances.

## Management routes and sessions

- [ ] **Your framework adapter's `authenticate` resolver matches who should see what.** The default guard accepts any signed-in user, limited to their own agents, delegations and audit rows. A custom resolver is a trust decision and sees everything, so verify admin rights inside it ([Adapters](/adapters)).
- [ ] **`trustedProxy` is set on the adapter** when you use `ipAllowlist`. The adapter ignores forwarded headers for the client IP unless `trustedProxyCount` or `trustedHeader` is configured.
- [ ] **`allowUnauthenticated` is not set anywhere.** Search your code and config.
- [ ] **Email verification is on** for password sign-up if email identity matters to you, and verification and reset links expire.
- [ ] **Compromised-password checking is on.** `createHibpModule` rejects passwords found in breaches using k-anonymity, so the password never leaves your server ([HIBP](/hibp)). Decide whether `onError` should be `'allow'` (default) or `'block'` when the API is down.
- [ ] **Sensitive actions require a fresh session.** Use session freshness so that changing a password or email, or approving a high-risk agent action, asks for a recent sign-in ([Sessions](/sessions)).
- [ ] **Two-factor is available** for accounts that can approve agent actions or manage organizations ([Two-factor](/auth/two-factor)).
- [ ] **You have a plan for imported users.** Hashes in formats other than the PBKDF2 one cannot be verified. Use `force_password_reset` or a lazy rehash ([Migrate from Auth0](/migrate/from-auth0#user-data-migration)).

## Agents and MCP

- [ ] **Agent permissions are narrow.** Grant specific resources and actions rather than wildcards, add `maxCallsPerHour` where an agent could loop, and use `requireApproval` for actions with side effects you cannot undo ([Permissions](/permissions)).
- [ ] **IP allowlists are IPv4 only.** `ipAllowlist` accepts IPv4 addresses and CIDR ranges and denies requests with no known IP. If your traffic arrives over IPv6, the allowlist will block it.
- [ ] **Delegation depth is capped** (`maxDepth`) and delegated permissions are a subset of the delegator's ([Delegation](/delegation)).
- [ ] **Agent token lifetimes are short** and agents are revoked when their owner leaves. Revocation cascades through delegations.
- [ ] **MCP clients register over HTTPS redirect URIs.** Registration rejects plain HTTP except for localhost. If you turn on Client ID Metadata Documents, read the SSRF notes on the [MCP](/mcp) page first.
- [ ] **Refresh-token reuse detection is understood.** Reusing a refresh token revokes the whole family on purpose. Make sure your clients store the newest token.

## Audit, webhooks and data

- [ ] **Audit retention is decided.** Entries are only removed by `audit.cleanup({ retentionDays })`, so choose a value that matches your policy, and ship logs to your SIEM through [event streaming](/event-streaming) if you need them elsewhere.
- [ ] **Webhook receivers verify the signature.** `X-TheAuth-Signature` is `sha256=` plus the HMAC of `<timestamp>.<raw body>`. Verify against the raw body and reject old timestamps ([Webhooks](/webhooks)).
- [ ] **Backups exist and a restore has been tried.** The database is the source of truth for users, sessions, agents and audit. SQLite files need a file-level backup.
- [ ] **Deletion and export paths are wired** if you serve people in the EU ([GDPR](/gdpr)).
- [ ] **Migrations ran on the production database**, and you know whether `skipMigrations` is on.

## Runtime

- [ ] **Clocks are synchronized** on every host that issues or verifies tokens. Verification uses no clock tolerance.
- [ ] **Database connections are pooled** if you are serverless.
- [ ] **Error output does not leak.** Do not log request bodies for sign-in routes, and do not return raw exception messages from your own handlers.
- [ ] **You have run a failed-login and a rate-limit test against production**, from outside your network, and confirmed the 401 and 429 responses look like [Error codes](/errors).

# Troubleshooting

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/troubleshooting

Start with the symptom you see. Each entry says what the cause usually is and what to change. If you have an error code, jump to [Error codes you will meet](#error-codes-you-will-meet). The full list lives in [Error codes](/errors).

## Sign-in works, then the user is signed out

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="The session cookie never reaches the browser">
Open the network tab and look at the `Set-Cookie` header on the sign-in or OAuth callback response. Three things stop a cookie from being stored:

- It is marked `Secure` but the page is served over plain `http://`. Browsers drop it silently. The cookie session manager sets `Secure` only when `NODE_ENV=production`; the OAuth plugin sets it when `baseUrl` starts with `https://`. Behind a TLS-terminating proxy, make sure `baseUrl` is the public `https://` URL, not the internal `http://` one.
- You set `cookieOptions.domain` to a domain the page is not on.
- The response was cached or rewritten by a proxy that strips `Set-Cookie`.

Details and defaults are on [Cookie options](/cookies).
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Everyone is signed out after each deploy">
The session `secret` changed. Session tokens are signed with it, so a new value invalidates every cookie. Keep it in an environment variable that is the same across deploys and across instances. theAuth takes a single secret, not a list, so there is no graceful rotation: plan a rotation as a sign-out of all users. The same applies to `signingSecret` for the MCP module.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Sessions work on one instance and fail on another">
Instances are using different secrets, or something in the session path is in memory. Check that `auth.session.secret` is identical everywhere. If you use the `rateLimit()` plugin or device flow, also check that [secondary storage](/secondary-storage) is not left at the in-memory default.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Signed in on app.example.com, signed out on api.example.com">
Cookies are host-only by default. Set `cookieOptions.domain` to `.example.com` for subdomains. For different registrable domains (`example.com` and `example.org`) cookies cannot be shared at all, use [JWT sessions](/jwt-sessions) with an `Authorization` header.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="The session is fine in the browser but middleware cannot read it">
Edge middleware cannot usually open your database, so it cannot validate a cookie session. Check only that the cookie is present there and validate in server code. See the middleware example in [Migrate from Clerk](/migrate/from-clerk#middleware-ts).
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## CORS and cross-origin requests

theAuth core adds CORS headers only to the MCP endpoints (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, with `WWW-Authenticate` exposed so browser MCP clients can read the challenge). The sign-in, session and management routes send no CORS headers. If your front end is on a different origin from the API, you add the headers yourself in your framework, for example with Hono's `cors()` middleware or Express's `cors` package, and you must allow credentials for cookies:

```ts
import { Hono } from 'hono';
import { cors } from 'hono/cors';
import { theAuthHono } from '@glinr/theauth-hono';

const app = new Hono();

// Register CORS before the auth routes so preflight (OPTIONS) requests are answered.
app.use('/api/theauth/*', cors({
  origin: 'https://app.example.com', // a single origin, not '*', when credentials are on
  credentials: true,
}));
app.route('/api/theauth', theAuthHono(theauth, { authenticate }));
```

On the browser side, send `credentials: 'include'` on `fetch` calls. A wildcard origin together with credentials is rejected by browsers, which shows up as "CORS error" even though the request reached the server.

For a cookie to be sent cross-site at all it needs `SameSite=None; Secure`, and recent browsers also block third-party cookies by default in some modes. If the front end and API can share a registrable domain, do that and keep `SameSite=Lax`. Otherwise use [JWT sessions](/jwt-sessions).

The device approval endpoint is stricter on purpose. `POST /auth/device/authorize` answers `403 access_denied` to a browser `Origin` that is neither the origin of `verificationUri` nor listed in `trustedOrigins`. If your verification page is on another origin, add it to `trustedOrigins` on `deviceAuth()` ([Device authorization](/auth/device)).

## OAuth and redirects

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="redirect_uri_mismatch (reported by Google, GitHub and others)">
The callback URL you registered with the provider must match exactly, character for character. For the `oauth()` plugin it is `{baseUrl}/auth/oauth/callback/{provider}`. Because `baseUrl` includes the adapter mount path, with `baseUrl: 'https://app.example.com/api/theauth'` and Google the URL is `https://app.example.com/api/theauth/auth/oauth/callback/google`. Trailing slashes, `http` versus `https`, and `localhost` versus `127.0.0.1` all count as different. To compute something else, pass `buildRedirectUri` to `oauth()`.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title='"OAuth callback: unknown or already-used state value."'>
The `state` in the callback is not in the database. Common causes: the user pressed back and retried the same callback URL (state is deleted on first use), the callback went to a different deployment with a different database, or the state row was cleaned up. Restart the flow from the authorize URL.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title='"OAuth callback: state has expired. Restart the authorization flow."'>
The user took too long on the provider screen, or a link was opened much later. Send them back to `/auth/oauth/authorize/{provider}`.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title='"OAuth callback: state was issued for provider X, not Y."'>
The authorize step and the callback used different providers. Usually a copy and paste error in the callback URL registered with the provider.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="After sign-in the user lands on a 404">
After a successful OAuth callback the plugin redirects to `{baseUrl}/` with an `auth_user` query parameter. If `baseUrl` includes the mount path (which the callback URL needs), that is a path under your mount. Handle the redirect in your app, or use [`createRedirectChain`](/redirect) to send people to where they were going.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="MCP client says redirect_uri is invalid (INVALID_REDIRECT_URI)">
During dynamic registration, redirect URIs must be HTTPS (or `localhost` for development) and must not contain a fragment. During the authorize and consent steps the `redirect_uri` has to match one registered for the client exactly. See [MCP](/mcp).
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Clock skew

JWT checks use the server's clock. The session and MCP token verification do not add a tolerance, so a server clock that runs ahead can reject a freshly issued token as not yet valid, and one that runs behind keeps expired tokens alive for longer. Run NTP (or your cloud's time sync) on every host that issues or verifies tokens. In containers, the host clock is what counts.

SAML single sign-on is the exception. It allows `clockSkewSeconds` of drift, 120 by default, when checking the assertion's validity window ([SSO](/auth/sso)). If an IdP is rejected with a "not yet valid" or "expired" assertion error, fix the clock first and raise `clockSkewSeconds` only as a stopgap.

Device and one-time codes use expiry timestamps stored by the server, so skew between the device and the server does not matter for them.

## Proxies, load balancers and client IPs

Rate limits are per client IP, and theAuth does not trust `X-Forwarded-For` by default because clients can forge it. When no trusted source is configured the plugin falls back to one shared `"unknown"` bucket. Behind a proxy that means every user shares one limit and a busy site returns `429 RATE_LIMITED` to everyone at once.

Tell theAuth how your edge works, in one of two ways:

```ts
const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  // ...
  // Option A: you run N proxies in front of the app.
  // With "x-forwarded-for: a, b, c" and a count of 1, the client is c.
  trustedProxy: { trustedProxyCount: 1 },

  // Option B: your edge overwrites a single header and the app is only reachable through it.
  // trustedProxy: { trustedHeader: 'cf-connecting-ip' },
});
```

The `rateLimit()` plugin takes the same two options, `trustedProxyCount` and `trustedHeader`. Count from the right: the last entry was added by the proxy closest to you, the leftmost entries were written by the client. Do not set `trustedHeader` unless the app is truly unreachable except through that edge, otherwise anyone can send the header themselves. Standard header names: `cf-connecting-ip` (Cloudflare), `x-real-ip` (nginx), `fly-client-ip` (Fly.io). Values that are not a plain address-like string are discarded.

`withRateLimit` resolves the IP the same way: it ignores forwarded headers unless you pass `trustedProxyCount` or `trustedHeader` (or the instance sets `trustedProxy`). Without one of them every caller shares the `"unknown"` key, so set it when you run behind a proxy, or pass your own `keyExtractor` built on `resolveClientIp` ([Rate limiting](/rate-limiting)).

Also behind a proxy: set `baseUrl` to the public URL with `https://`, or cookies and OAuth callback URLs will be built from the wrong scheme.

## Serverless and edge runtimes

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="Rate limits and device codes behave randomly on Vercel or Workers">
The default [secondary storage](/secondary-storage) is process memory. On serverless each invocation or isolate may have its own, and they are discarded when idle, so counters reset and a device code created in one instance is unknown to the next. Use `"database"`, Redis (Upstash works over HTTP), or on Workers a D1 database. Cloudflare KV is eventually consistent and cannot count atomically, so treat KV limits as soft. See [Which storage should I pick](/choose-storage).
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="SQLite file database on Vercel">
The filesystem of a serverless function is read-only apart from a temporary directory that does not persist. The `sqlite` provider keeps data in memory and rewrites the file, so nothing survives. Use Postgres or MySQL (a serverless-friendly host such as Neon helps with connection counts), or D1 on Cloudflare.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Postgres connection errors under load">
Each cold instance opens its own connections, and a function that scales to hundreds of instances can exhaust the database. Point `database.url` at a pooled connection string (PgBouncer or your provider's pooler) and keep the pool small.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Next.js middleware cannot use theAuth">
Middleware runs on the edge runtime by default. Keep it to a cookie presence check and validate the session in route handlers and server components, which run on Node.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title='Missing package: "TheAuth: provider ... requires the ... package"'>
The `sqlite-native`, `postgres` and `mysql` providers need `better-sqlite3`, `pg` and `mysql2` respectively, installed in your app. The `sqlite` provider uses `sql.js`, which ships with theAuth, and `d1` uses `drizzle-orm/d1`. See [Database setup](/database).
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Cookies are not marked Secure on a platform that does not set NODE_ENV">
The cookie session manager chooses `Secure` from `NODE_ENV`. Set `NODE_ENV=production`, or pass `cookieOptions.secure: true` explicitly.
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Startup errors

| Message | Cause |
|---|---|
| `SessionManager: secret must be at least 32 characters.` | The cookie session secret is short or empty. Same text pattern for `SessionRefresher`. |
| `McpConfig.signingSecret must be at least 32 characters` | The MCP signing secret is short. `createMcpModule` also throws if neither `signingSecret` nor `signing` is set. |
| `theauth-oauth plugin requires auth.session to be configured ...` | You added `oauth()` without `auth.session`. |
| `TheAuth: unsupported database provider "..."` | `database.provider` is not one of `sqlite`, `sqlite-native`, `postgres`, `mysql`, `d1`. |
| `[theauth] <adapter>: the management routes (/agents, /delegations, /audit, /dashboard, /authorize) require authentication, but none is configured.` | The framework adapter has no `authenticate` resolver and `auth.session` is not set. Pass `authenticate`, configure `auth.session`, or for local development only set `allowUnauthenticated: true`. See [Adapters](/adapters). |

## Error codes you will meet

These are returned by the code, not invented for the docs. For the complete list see [Error codes](/errors).

**Email and password** (`@glinr/theauth-email`, JSON body `{ code, message }`):

| Code | HTTP | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| `INVALID_CREDENTIALS` | 401 | Wrong email or password. |
| `EMAIL_NOT_VERIFIED` | 401 | Sign-in blocked until the address is verified. |
| `DUPLICATE_EMAIL` | 409 | An account with that email exists. |
| `USER_NOT_FOUND` | 404 | No such user for the operation. |
| `INVALID_TOKEN`, `TOKEN_EXPIRED` | 400 | The verification or reset token is wrong or old. |
| `INVALID_PASSWORD`, `INVALID_EMAIL`, `WRONG_PASSWORD` | 400 | Validation failed. |

**Username module:** `PASSWORD_RESET_REQUIRED` (403) when the user's `force_password_reset` flag is set, which is how imported users are forced through a reset ([Migrate from Auth0](/migrate/from-auth0#user-data-migration)).

**Passwordless:** magic link answers `401 Invalid or expired magic link`, email OTP answers `401 Invalid or expired OTP code`. Both are deliberately vague about which part failed.

**Rate limits:** `429` with `{ "error": { "code": "RATE_LIMITED", "message": "Too many requests" } }` from `rateLimit()` and `withRateLimit`, with a `Retry-After` header. Plugin endpoints that declare their own limit answer `{ "error": "Rate limit exceeded" }`.

**Session freshness:** `SESSION_NOT_FRESH` when an action needs a recent sign-in. Ask the user to re-authenticate.

**Management routes:** `401 UNAUTHORIZED` "Authentication required" from the adapter guard when the caller is not signed in or `authenticate` returned `null`.

**Device flow** (`/auth/device/token`): `authorization_pending` (keep polling), `slow_down` (the interval grew by 5 seconds, use the new one), `access_denied`, `expired_token`. `/auth/device/authorize` answers `401 login_required`, `403 access_denied`, `400 invalid_request`, `429`.

**MCP and OAuth server:**

| Code | Typical cause |
|---|---|
| `INVALID_CLIENT` | Unknown `client_id`, a disabled client, or a bad `client_secret`. |
| `INVALID_GRANT` | Authorization code unknown, expired or already used; PKCE `code_verifier` failed; `redirect_uri` differs from the authorize request; refresh token expired. |
| `INVALID_GRANT` "Refresh token reuse detected; the grant has been revoked" | An old refresh token was presented again. The whole token family is revoked on purpose. The client must restart authorization. |
| `INVALID_TARGET` | `resource` is missing or is not a known MCP server, or differs from the grant's resource. |
| `INVALID_SCOPE` | A scope that is not supported, or not granted by the original authorization. |
| `LOGIN_REQUIRED` | The authorize request arrived without a signed-in user. |
| `INVALID_AUDIENCE` | The access token has no audience, or the audience is not this resource. |
| `INVALID_TOKEN`, `TOKEN_EXPIRED`, `INVALID_ISSUER` | Bad signature or claims, `exp` in the past, wrong `iss`. A revoked token reports `INVALID_TOKEN`. |
| `INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE` | The token lacks a scope the endpoint requires. The response is a `403` with a step-up challenge. |

**JWT sessions** (`createJwtSessionModule`, returned as `Result` errors): `INVALID_INPUT` for an empty token, `INVALID_TOKEN` for a bad signature, wrong issuer or audience, or a token without `sub`, and `TOKEN_EXPIRED` once `exp` has passed.

# AI coding assistant setup with theAuth docs

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/ai-assistants

Give your assistant the real docs and API. One command sets it up.

```bash title="terminal"
npx @glinr/theauth-cli init --agent
```

It writes these files in your project root:

| Assistant | Files |
|---|---|
| Claude Code | `.claude/skills/theauth/SKILL.md` and `.mcp.json` |
| Cursor | `.cursor/rules/theauth.mdc` and `.cursor/mcp.json` |
| VS Code | `.vscode/mcp.json` |

`--target claude,cursor,vscode` limits the set (default: all three). `--dry-run` writes nothing. `--force` replaces existing files and `theauth` MCP entries.

Existing files are left alone and other MCP servers stay in place. A config that is not plain JSON (for example, one with comments) is skipped and reported. Add the entry by hand:

```json title=".mcp.json"
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "theauth": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@glinr/theauth-cli", "mcp"] }
  }
}
```

VS Code uses `servers` with `"type": "stdio"` instead of `mcpServers`.

## Run the theAuth MCP server

`theauth mcp` is a read-only stdio server.

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `search_docs` | Ranked search over these docs |
| `get_doc` | Full text of one page by slug |
| `add_plugin` | Install command and `plugins` entry. Edits no files. |
| `generate_schema` | SQLite DDL, built in memory. Needs `better-sqlite3`. |
| `inspect` | Setup summary. Env var names, never values. |

## Skill and hosted docs

The skill ([`SKILL.md`](https://github.com/glincker/theauth/blob/main/skills/theauth/SKILL.md)) covers install, plugins, agent identity, delegation and MCP auth. `init --agent` copies it into your project.

The docs site serves a remote MCP server with a search tool over these docs. It needs no install:

```bash title="terminal"
claude mcp add --transport http theauth-docs https://docs.theauth.dev/mcp
```

For Cursor, VS Code, Codex and Gemini CLI, add the same URL as a remote (HTTP) server. Config file names change between releases, so check each tool's MCP docs. The Go docs are not part of this server.

## Rule files

Copy these from [`templates/ai-rules/`](https://github.com/glincker/theauth/tree/main/templates/ai-rules):

| File | Copy to | Tool |
|---|---|---|
| `AGENTS.md` | `AGENTS.md` in your project root | Codex, Cursor, Copilot coding agent, Gemini CLI |
| `.cursor/rules/theauth.mdc` | `.cursor/rules/theauth.mdc` | Cursor |
| `CLAUDE.md` | Append to your `CLAUDE.md` | Claude Code |
| `copilot-instructions.md` | `.github/copilot-instructions.md` | GitHub Copilot |

Gemini CLI reads `GEMINI.md` by default. Copy `AGENTS.md` to `GEMINI.md`, or set `context.fileName` to `AGENTS.md` in `.gemini/settings.json`.

The rules require:

- Never log or commit tokens, secrets or `Authorization` headers.
- Verify delegation with `authorize` or `policy.evaluate`. Never trust a claimed owner.
- Keep policy deny by default. Treat `deny`, `escalate` and errors as do not run.
- Wrap every agent tool with `guardTool` or `guardTools`.
- Use DPoP for MCP tokens that leave your trust boundary.
- Match redirect URIs exactly.
