# Shared Signals (SSF, CAEP, RISC)

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/auth/shared-signals

Shared signals let identity systems tell each other that something security relevant happened: a session was revoked, an account was disabled, a credential changed. theAuth implements the OpenID [Shared Signals Framework 1.0](https://openid.net/specs/openid-sharedsignals-framework-1_0.html) with the CAEP and RISC event types.

One plugin, `sharedSignals()`, can run either or both roles:

- **Transmitter.** Receivers create a stream, choose events and a delivery method, and theAuth sends them signed Security Event Tokens (SETs, RFC 8417).
- **Receiver.** theAuth verifies SETs from a transmitter you trust and runs handlers. By default it revokes local sessions when the transmitter says a session, all sessions, or an account is gone.

Nothing is emitted from your existing sign-in paths unless you wire it in (see [Emit from existing paths](#emit-from-existing-paths)).

## Why you would use it

Without shared signals, a disabled account in one system stays signed in everywhere else until each session expires. With them, the system that knows tells the others in seconds.

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="Revoke everywhere" icon="user-slash">
    Ban a user once and every connected app drops their sessions.
  </Card>
  <Card title="React to risk" icon="shield-exclamation">
    Credential compromise or a device falling out of compliance can force re-authentication.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Standard, not custom" icon="plug">
    Interoperates with any SSF receiver or transmitter, not only theAuth.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Safe by default" icon="lock">
    Signed events, replay protection, SSRF-safe delivery, no events until you opt in.
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

## How it works

## Try it in two steps

<Steps>
  <Step title="Run a transmitter">
    Add `sharedSignals({ transmitter })` and wire `bridge.onAdminAction` (see [Install](#install) and [Emit from existing paths](#emit-from-existing-paths)). Banning a user now emits `account-disabled` and `sessions-revoked`.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Run a receiver">
    In the other app add `sharedSignals({ receiver: { issuer, audience } })` and register a stream with the transmitter pointing at `POST /ssf/receive`. Sessions for the banned user are revoked there with no extra code.
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Install

```ts
import { createTheAuth } from "@glinr/theauth";
import { sharedSignals } from "@glinr/theauth/signals";

const signals = sharedSignals({
  transmitter: {
    issuer: "https://auth.example.com",
    endpointBaseUrl: "https://auth.example.com/api/auth/ssf",
    signingKey: privateKey, // CryptoKey, JWK or Uint8Array
    signingAlgorithm: "ES256",
    keyId: "ssf-1",
    jwksUri: "https://auth.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json",
    authenticate: async (request) => {
      const receiver = await lookupReceiverByBearer(request.headers.get("authorization"));
      return receiver ? { id: receiver.audience } : null;
    },
  },
});

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: "sqlite-native", url: "theauth.db" },
  plugins: [signals],
});
```

The plugin id is `theauth-shared-signals`. When it is present theAuth creates three tables: `theauth_ssf_streams`, `theauth_ssf_subjects` and `theauth_ssf_outbox`.

Publish the public key at `jwksUri` yourself. If you use the [OIDC provider](/auth/oidc-provider) with the same key, its JWKS endpoint already does.

## Transmitter

### Endpoints

Paths are relative to your mount path. `endpointBaseUrl` must be the absolute URL these are served at, because it is advertised in discovery.

| Method and path | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /.well-known/ssf-configuration` | Discovery metadata. Needs your adapter to route the well-known path, as with OIDC discovery. |
| `POST /ssf/stream` | Create a stream. Returns 201. |
| `GET /ssf/stream` | Read one stream (`?stream_id=`) or list the caller's streams. |
| `PATCH /ssf/stream`, `PUT /ssf/stream` | Update or replace a stream. |
| `DELETE /ssf/stream?stream_id=` | Delete a stream. Returns 204. |
| `GET /ssf/status?stream_id=` | Read stream status. |
| `POST /ssf/status` | Set `enabled`, `paused` or `disabled`. |
| `POST /ssf/subjects/add`, `POST /ssf/subjects/remove` | Change the stream's subject list. |
| `POST /ssf/verify` | Ask for a verification event. Returns 204. |
| `POST /ssf/poll/:stream_id` | Poll a stream (RFC 8936). |

Every management and poll endpoint calls your `authenticate` function. A receiver only sees its own streams. Each endpoint declares a rate limit in its metadata.

### Streams

```json
{
  "events_requested": [
    "https://schemas.openid.net/secevent/risc/event-type/sessions-revoked",
    "https://schemas.openid.net/secevent/risc/event-type/account-disabled"
  ],
  "delivery": {
    "method": "urn:ietf:rfc:8935",
    "endpoint_url": "https://rp.example/ssf/receive",
    "authorization_header": "Bearer shared-secret"
  }
}
```

`events_delivered` is the intersection of `events_requested` and the events the transmitter supports. Delivery is `urn:ietf:rfc:8935` (push) or `urn:ietf:rfc:8936` (poll). For poll streams the response carries the poll URL in `delivery.endpoint_url`.

`authorization_header` is stored as given and is never returned.

### Subjects

Subject identifiers follow RFC 9493: `iss_sub`, `email`, `opaque` and `complex` (with `user`, `device`, `session`, `application`, `tenant`, `org_unit` and `group` members).

`defaultSubjects` sets the mode of new streams. With `ALL` (the default) every subject is delivered and `subjects/remove` excludes one. With `NONE` nothing is delivered until `subjects/add` includes a subject. A stream that follows a user also receives events whose complex subject has that user as its `user` member.

### Emitting events

```ts
import { events } from "@glinr/theauth/signals";

await signals.emit({
  ...events.accountDisabled({ reason: "hijacking" }),
  subject: { format: "iss_sub", iss: "https://auth.example.com", sub: userId },
});
```

`emit` signs one SET per matching stream, stores it, and delivers it. Builders exist for every supported event:

| Builder | Event |
| --- | --- |
| `events.sessionRevoked` | CAEP session-revoked |
| `events.credentialChange` | CAEP credential-change |
| `events.tokenClaimsChange` | CAEP token-claims-change |
| `events.assuranceLevelChange` | CAEP assurance-level-change |
| `events.deviceComplianceChange` | CAEP device-compliance-change |
| `events.accountDisabled` | RISC account-disabled |
| `events.accountEnabled` | RISC account-enabled |
| `events.credentialCompromise` | RISC credential-compromise |
| `events.sessionsRevoked` | RISC sessions-revoked |

### Push delivery

SETs are POSTed as `application/secevent+jwt` with the stream's `Authorization` header. A `2xx` marks the SET delivered. `408`, `429`, `5xx` and network errors are retried with exponential backoff (default 1 s doubling to 5 min, up to 5 attempts). Other statuses, including an RFC 8935 `400` error, and redirects fail the SET without retry.

Push URLs go through the same checks as other outbound fetches in theAuth: https only, no credentials, default port, no `localhost` or metadata hostnames, and every resolved address must be public. The check runs when the stream is configured and again before each attempt. Redirects are never followed.

`delivery` options:

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mode` | `background` | `inline` awaits delivery and retries inside `emit`. |
| `maxAttempts` | 5 | Attempts before a SET is marked failed. |
| `baseBackoffMs`, `maxBackoffMs` | 1000, 300000 | Backoff bounds. |
| `timeoutMs` | 5000 | Per request timeout. |
| `fetchImpl`, `resolver` | global fetch, system DNS | Overrides, for example to pin the connection to the validated address. |
| `allowInsecure` | false | Allow http and private hosts. Development only. |

Retries in `background` mode run on in-process timers. If the process exits, pending SETs stay in `theauth_ssf_outbox`; call `signals.transmitter.processDue()` from a scheduled job to resume them. Serverless runtimes that freeze after the response should use `inline` or run `processDue()` on a schedule.

### Poll delivery

`POST /ssf/poll/:stream_id` accepts `maxEvents`, `returnImmediately`, `ack` and `setErrs` and answers `{ "sets": { "<jti>": "<jwt>" }, "moreAvailable": false }`. Unacknowledged SETs are returned again. `returnImmediately: false` waits up to `longPollMs` (default 0, so it answers at once).

## Receiver

```ts
const signals = sharedSignals({
  receiver: {
    issuer: "https://idp.example",
    audience: "https://app.example",
    // keys: discovered from the issuer's ssf-configuration by default
    authorizationHeader: "Bearer shared-secret",
    handlers: {
      "https://schemas.openid.net/secevent/caep/event-type/credential-change": async (event) => {
        await flagForReauth(event.subject);
      },
    },
  },
});
```

The push endpoint is `POST /ssf/receive` (configurable with `path`). Keys come from, in order: `verificationKey`, a static `jwks`, or discovery. Discovery fetches `${issuer}/.well-known/ssf-configuration` (or `configurationUrl`), requires its `issuer` to equal the configured issuer, then fetches `jwks_uri`, all through the SSRF-safe fetcher. An unknown `kid` triggers at most one refetch every 30 seconds.

Checks on every SET: signature, `typ` of `secevent+jwt`, `iss`, `aud`, an `events` object, no `exp`, an `iat` no older than `maxAgeSeconds` (default 3600), and a `jti` not seen before. Replays are acknowledged with `202` and not dispatched again. Failures answer `400` with an RFC 8935 `err` such as `invalid_key`, `invalid_issuer` or `invalid_audience`.

The replay cache is per process memory by default. Pass `replayStorage` (any `SecondaryStorage`) when you run several instances.

### Default session revocation

When the app has a session manager, these events revoke local sessions unless you set `revokeSessions: false`:

| Event | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| session-revoked | Revokes the session when the subject is a `complex` subject with an opaque `session`. Otherwise revokes the user's sessions. |
| sessions-revoked | Revokes all sessions of the user. |
| account-disabled | Revokes all sessions of the user. It does not ban the account. Add a handler for that. |

User mapping: an `iss_sub` from the configured issuer maps `sub` to the local user id, an `email` is looked up in the user table, and an `opaque` id is taken as the user id. Pass `resolveUserId` to replace this. Handlers you supply take precedence over the defaults for the same event type.

## Emit from existing paths

The bridge turns existing callbacks into events. It is opt in: nothing is emitted until you pass the callback.

```ts
const signals = sharedSignals({ transmitter: { /* ... */ } });
const { bridge } = signals;

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  // session.onRevoke: session-revoked per revoked session
  auth: { session: { onRevoke: bridge.onSessionsRevoked } },
  // admin.onAdminAction: ban_user is account-disabled + sessions-revoked, unban_user is account-enabled
  admin: { onAdminAction: bridge.onAdminAction },
  // password reset: credential-change (password, update)
  passwordReset: { /* ... */ onPasswordChanged: bridge.onPasswordChanged },
  // 2FA and passkeys: credential-change create or delete
  totp: { onChange: bridge.onTotpChange },
  passkey: { /* ... */ onCredentialChange: bridge.onPasskeyChange },
  plugins: [signals],
});
```

The callbacks are no-ops until the plugin has initialized, and they swallow errors so a receiver outage never blocks a sign-out or password change. The default subject is `iss_sub` with the transmitter issuer and the user id; pass `subjectForUser` to `sharedSignals` to change it.

## Limits

- Subject formats beyond `iss_sub`, `email`, `opaque` and `complex` (`account`, `phone_number`, `did`, `uri`, and so on) are rejected.
- Per-subject stream status is not supported (`501`). Subject `verified` is stored but not enforced.
- The stream-updated event is not sent.
- Streams are authorized by your `authenticate` function only. There is no built-in OAuth scope model for management calls.
- Delivery is at least once. Receivers should treat `jti` as an idempotency key.
- The platform `fetch` resolves the push hostname again when connecting, so a DNS rebinding attacker with a very short TTL can race the address check. Pass a `fetchImpl` that pins the validated address to close this.
- Database support follows the rest of the SDK: tables use the shared SQLite-style schema definitions.

---

# Agent identity

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/agents

<Columns cols={2}>
<div>
An `AgentIdentity` is the primary entity in theAuth. It represents one AI agent, a process acting on behalf of a human user. Agents are not users. No password, no session, no OAuth flow. Just a token, a set of permissions, and an audit row for every call.

Create one against an existing user ID, hand the token to the agent, and check every action through `authorize()`.
</div>

```ts
const agent = await theauth.agent.create({
  ownerId: user.id,
  name: 'code-reviewer',
  type: 'autonomous',
  permissions: [
    { resource: 'mcp:github:*', actions: ['read'] },
  ],
});

// agent.token is a ta_... bearer, shown once, hashed at rest
console.log(agent.token);
```
</Columns>

## Anatomy

<ParamField path="id" type="string">Stable identifier (a UUID). Never changes.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="token" type="string">Bearer token with a `ta_` prefix (legacy `kv_` tokens are still accepted). Shown once at creation, then SHA-256 hashed. Rotate to replace.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="permissions" type="Permission[]">What this agent is allowed to do. Evaluated at every `authorize()` call.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="status" type="'active' | 'revoked' | 'expired'">Current state. Revocation is permanent.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="ownerId" type="string">The user who owns this agent. Must match an existing row in `theauth_users` (foreign key). Create the row with `theauth.user.create({ id, email })`.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="name" type="string">Human-readable label.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="type" type="'autonomous' | 'delegated' | 'service'">Determines how the agent acquires and uses permissions.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="expiresAt" type="Date" default="now + agents.tokenExpiry (24h)">Optional at creation; when omitted it defaults to `agents.tokenExpiry` from now. Token validation (`authorizeByToken`) rejects an expired agent and flips its `status` to `expired`. `authorize(agentId)` also compares `expiresAt` to the clock, so an elapsed agent is denied with code `agent_expired` (and an audit row) even before its stored `status` flips.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="metadata" type="Record<string, unknown>" default="{}">Arbitrary key/value pairs for your own use.</ParamField>

## Agent types

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="autonomous" icon="robot">
    Acts independently without requiring human approval on each call, unless a permission constraint mandates it. The standard type for background agents, cron jobs, and AI assistants that run unattended.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="delegated" icon="link">
    Receives permissions from another agent via a delegation chain rather than having them declared at creation. Use this for ephemeral sub-agents spun up to complete one task, then discarded.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="service" icon="server">
    Long-lived identity for infrastructure, such as an MCP server or an internal microservice that calls other services on behalf of users. Treat it like a service account.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Lifecycle

<Steps>

<Step title="Create">

```ts
const agent = await theauth.agent.create({
  ownerId: 'user-123',
  name: 'github-reader',
  type: 'autonomous',
  permissions: [
    { resource: 'mcp:github:*', actions: ['read'] },
  ],
  expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 7 * 24 * 3_600_000), // optional, defaults to 24h from now
  metadata: { purpose: 'nightly PR review' },
});

console.log(agent.token); // ta_..., only shown here
```

<Warning>
The token is returned once at creation. theAuth stores only the SHA-256 hash, so the plaintext cannot be recovered later. Save it immediately or rotate to get a new one.
</Warning>

</Step>

<Step title="Authenticate">

Tokens use the `ta_` prefix followed by 32 random bytes encoded as base64url (43 characters, 46 in total). Pass as a Bearer credential:

```http
Authorization: Bearer ta_a3f8c2e1d4b5...
```

<Tip>
Hash-only storage: a full database dump cannot reveal an active token. There are no secrets to rotate after a DB breach, only the tokens themselves.
</Tip>

</Step>

<Step title="Authorize">

When a caller only has the raw token, use `authorizeByToken` in your HTTP middleware:

```ts
const token = request.headers.get('Authorization')?.replace('Bearer ', '');
if (!token) return new Response('Unauthorized', { status: 401 });

const result = await theauth.authorizeByToken(token, {
  action: 'read',
  resource: 'mcp:github:repos',
});

if (!result.allowed) {
  return new Response(result.reason ?? 'Forbidden', { status: 403 });
}
```

The token is hashed and looked up in the database, then permissions are evaluated and the decision is written to the audit log. No JWTs, no network round-trip. This path checks the agent's own permissions only; permissions it holds through delegation are applied by `authorize(agentId, ...)`.

</Step>

<Step title="Rotate">

Rotation issues a new token and immediately invalidates the old one. It is a single update, so there is no window where both are valid. Only active agents can be rotated.

```ts
const rotated = await theauth.agent.rotate(agentId);
// rotated.token is the new plaintext token
```

Rotate on a schedule, or any time you suspect a token has been exposed.

</Step>

<Step title="Update or list">

Permission updates take effect immediately. In-flight requests that already passed authorization are not affected.

```ts
await theauth.agent.update(agentId, {
  name: 'github-reader-v2',
  permissions: [{ resource: 'mcp:github:*', actions: ['read', 'comment'] }],
});

const active = await theauth.agent.list({
  userId: 'user-123',
  status: 'active',
  type: 'autonomous',
});
```

</Step>

<Step title="Revoke">

```ts
await theauth.agent.revoke(agentId);
// All future authorize() calls return allowed: false
// The agent's token is rejected immediately
```

Each attempt by a revoked or expired agent is still written to the audit log as a denied row with the reason `agent_revoked` or `agent_expired`. See [what gets recorded](/audit-trail#what-gets-recorded). `policy.evaluate()` denies a revoked, suspended or expired agent with `POLICY_AGENT_INACTIVE`.

In the TypeScript package, `agent.revoke()` also revokes every active delegation chain the agent gave or received, and the chains downstream of them. The call returns `{ revokedDelegations }` with the chain ids, writes one `agent.cascade.revoked` audit row, and fires `onAgentRevoke`.

<Warning>
Revocation is permanent. There is no un-revoke. To restore access, create a new agent.
</Warning>

</Step>

</Steps>

## Token format

New agent tokens look like `ta_` followed by 43 base64url characters (32 random bytes, 46 characters in total). The first 11 characters are stored as a non-secret lookup prefix; the rest is only ever stored as a SHA-256 hash.

Tokens issued by earlier releases start with `kv_` (the old kavachOS name). They are still accepted everywhere, and their stored rows are not rewritten, so no migration is needed. Nothing new is issued with `kv_`.

To move an agent off a legacy token, rotate it. The old token stops working at once and the new one starts with `ta_`:

```typescript
const rotated = await auth.agent.rotate(agent.id);
console.log(rotated.token); // ta_..., shown once
```

### Secret scanning

Use this regex for GitHub secret scanning custom patterns and gitleaks. It matches both the current and the legacy prefix. The final character is limited to the 16 values a 32 byte base64url string can end with.

```text
\b(?:ta|kv)_[A-Za-z0-9_-]{42}[AEIMQUYcgkosw048]\b
```

A gitleaks rule:

```toml
[[rules]]
id = "theauth-agent-token"
description = "theAuth agent token"
regex = '''\b(?:ta|kv)_[A-Za-z0-9_-]{42}[AEIMQUYcgkosw048]\b'''
keywords = ["ta_", "kv_"]
```

## Limits

The default is 10 active agents per user. Raise at initialization:

```ts
const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite-native', url: 'theauth.db' },
  agents: {
    enabled: true,
    maxPerUser: 50,
  },
});
```

The cap counts active agents. Creating one past it throws a plain `Error` with the message `User <id> has reached the maximum of <n> active agents.` (there is no dedicated error code, and the REST endpoint reports it as `500 INTERNAL_ERROR`).

## What agents aren't

<Info>
An agent is not a user. It has no email, no password, no session, no OAuth account. It has a bearer token and a permission set. If you find yourself reaching for password reset, email verification, or social sign-in on an agent, you want a user, not an agent. Create the user first, then create agents that the user owns.
</Info>

## Next steps

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="Permission engine" icon="shield-halved" href="/permissions">
    Define what agents can and cannot do.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Delegation chains" icon="link" href="/delegation">
    Let agents delegate access to sub-agents.
  </Card>

    Short-lived agents for one-off tasks.
  </Card>

    Use agents in HTTP middleware.
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

# Ephemeral sessions

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/ephemeral-sessions

## What ephemeral sessions are

An ephemeral session is a temporary agent identity that expires on its own. You create one, hand the token to an AI agent, and the token stops working when the TTL runs out or the agent exhausts its action budget, whichever comes first.

The pattern is designed for computer-use agents (Claude computer use, GPT browsing, operator loops) that need just enough access to complete one task without holding persistent credentials across invocations.

Key differences from a regular agent:

| | Regular agent | Ephemeral session |
|---|---|---|
| Lifetime | Indefinite by default | Bounded TTL (default 5 min) |
| Token | Rotatable, persistent | `kveph_` token that stops working at expiry or exhaustion |
| Cleanup | Manual revocation | Marked expired on use, or by `cleanupExpired()` |
| Action budget | None | Optional hard cap |
| Audit | Per-agent | Grouped under one session ID |

## Setup

No extra configuration is needed, ephemeral sessions are part of the `@glinr/theauth` core package and share the same database as the rest of theAuth.

```typescript
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { createEphemeralSessionModule } from '@glinr/theauth/auth';

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite-native', url: 'theauth.db' },
});

const ephemeral = createEphemeralSessionModule({
  db: theauth.db,
  defaultTtlSeconds: 300,   // 5 minutes
  maxTtlSeconds: 3600,      // 1 hour ceiling
  autoRevokeOnExpiry: true, // revoke underlying agent on expiry
  auditGrouping: true,      // group all actions under one audit session ID
});
```

## Creating a session for a computer-use agent

Call `createSession` right before you hand control to the agent. The token is shown exactly once.

```typescript
const result = await ephemeral.createSession({
  ownerId: 'user-abc',          // the human who owns this task
  name: 'fill-checkout-form',   // optional label
  permissions: [
    { resource: 'tool:browser', actions: ['navigate', 'click', 'type'] },
  ],
  ttlSeconds: 120,              // 2 minutes for this particular task
  maxActions: 20,               // hard cap: fail after 20 actions
});

if (!result.success) throw new Error(result.error.message);

const { token, expiresAt, auditGroupId } = result.data;
// Pass `token` to the agent. Never store it or log it.
```

The returned `token` is `kveph_` followed by 64 hex characters, to distinguish it from long-lived agent tokens (`ta_`, or legacy `kv_`). Only its SHA-256 hash is stored. Creating a session also creates a temporary agent (type `autonomous`) that holds the permissions, so `result.data` includes `agentId` as well. `ttlSeconds` above `maxTtlSeconds` returns a `TTL_EXCEEDS_MAX` error, and `permissions` must contain at least one entry.

## Validating a session

Each time the agent makes a request, validate the token before granting access.

```typescript
const check = await ephemeral.validateSession(token);

if (!check.success) {
  // error.code is one of:
  // SESSION_NOT_FOUND, SESSION_EXPIRED, SESSION_EXHAUSTED, SESSION_REVOKED
  return new Response('Unauthorized', { status: 401 });
}

const { sessionId, agentId, remainingActions, expiresIn, auditGroupId } = check.data;
```

`expiresIn` is in seconds. `remainingActions` is `null` when no action cap was set.

## Tracking actions

Call `consumeAction` once per agent action to decrement the budget counter.

```typescript
const consumed = await ephemeral.consumeAction(token);

if (!consumed.success) {
  // SESSION_EXHAUSTED when the budget runs out
  return new Response('Budget exhausted', { status: 429 });
}

const { actionsRemaining } = consumed.data;
// actionsRemaining is null when no maxActions was configured
```

When `actionsRemaining` hits zero, the session transitions to `exhausted`, and the underlying agent is revoked if `autoRevokeOnExpiry` is on (the default). Further calls return `SESSION_EXHAUSTED`. After the session leaves `active`, `consumeAction` returns `SESSION_EXPIRED`, `SESSION_REVOKED` or `SESSION_EXHAUSTED` accordingly.

## Action limits

`maxActions` is a hard cap on how many times `consumeAction` can succeed. It is independent of the TTL, a session can expire by time with actions remaining, or exhaust its action budget before the TTL lapses.

Set a tight budget for tasks with a well-known scope and leave it as `null` for tasks where the step count is unpredictable.

```typescript
// A session with both a time limit and an action cap
await ephemeral.createSession({
  ownerId: userId,
  permissions: [{ resource: 'tool:search', actions: ['query'] }],
  ttlSeconds: 60,
  maxActions: 5,
});
```

## Revoking early

If the agent completes the task before the TTL expires, revoke the session manually.

```typescript
await ephemeral.revokeSession(sessionId);
```

Revocation also revokes the underlying agent. It is idempotent, calling it on an already-revoked session returns success. An unknown session ID returns a `SESSION_NOT_FOUND` error.

## Listing active sessions

Useful for dashboards or for building kill-switch UI.

```typescript
const result = await ephemeral.listActiveSessions('user-abc');

if (result.success) {
  for (const session of result.data) {
    console.log(session.sessionId, session.expiresAt, session.actionsUsed);
  }
}
```

The returned objects have `token` set to `""`, the token is never readable after the initial `createSession` response.

## Cleanup strategies

Two approaches to cleaning up expired sessions:

### Scheduled background job

Run `cleanupExpired()` on a cron schedule, every minute for busy systems, every 5 minutes for lighter loads.

```typescript
// With node:timers/promises or any scheduler
setInterval(async () => {
  const result = await ephemeral.cleanupExpired();
  if (result.success && result.data.count > 0) {
    console.log(`Cleaned up ${result.data.count} expired sessions`);
  }
}, 60_000);
```

### On-demand at validate time

`validateSession` already detects and transitions expired sessions. For low-traffic systems, this is enough, no background job needed.

## Audit grouping

When `auditGrouping: true` (the default), the session gets its own `auditGroupId`. With `auditGrouping: false`, `auditGroupId` is set to the session ID instead. theAuth returns the ID from `validateSession` but does not stamp it onto audit entries for you, so attach it to the entries you record. That makes it straightforward to reconstruct the full activity trace for a single task.

```typescript
const validated = await ephemeral.validateSession(token);
if (validated.success) {
  // Attach to every audit entry for this action
  const { auditGroupId } = validated.data;
}
```

## Session status lifecycle

```
active → exhausted (maxActions reached)
       → expired   (TTL elapsed)
       → revoked   (manual revocation)
```

A session starts as `active`. Once it leaves `active`, it cannot be reactivated. Create a new session for a new task. Expiry is recorded lazily, when the session is next validated, listed, or swept by `cleanupExpired()`.

## Error codes

| Code | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `SESSION_NOT_FOUND` | Token does not match any session |
| `SESSION_EXPIRED` | TTL has elapsed |
| `SESSION_EXHAUSTED` | Action budget is fully consumed |
| `SESSION_REVOKED` | Manually revoked |
| `TTL_EXCEEDS_MAX` | Requested TTL is above `maxTtlSeconds` |
| `VALIDATION_ERROR` | Input failed schema validation (e.g. empty permissions) |

  <Card title="Agent identity" href="/agents" icon="robot">
    Long-lived agent identities that ephemeral sessions are built on top of.

    Hand a subset of permissions to a sub-agent with depth limits.

# Delegation chains

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/delegation

## What is a delegation chain

A delegation chain lets one agent grant a subset of its permissions to another. The delegating agent keeps its own permissions unchanged. The receiving agent gains access only to what was explicitly delegated.

This pattern is most useful when an orchestrator spins up sub-agents for specific tasks. Each sub-agent gets only the access it needs, for only as long as it needs it.

<Info>
The delegating agent must currently hold every permission it is trying to delegate. Attempting to delegate a permission not in the agent's own set throws an `Error` ("Delegated permissions must be a subset of the parent agent's permissions..."). The check runs against the agent's own permissions only, not against permissions it received through other delegations.
</Info>

## Working with delegations

### Creating a delegation

```typescript
const chain = await theauth.delegate({
  fromAgent: orchestrator.id,
  toAgent: subAgent.id,
  permissions: [
    { resource: 'mcp:github:issues', actions: ['read'] },
  ],
  expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 3_600_000), // 1 hour
  maxDepth: 2,
});

console.log(chain.id);        // dlg_...
console.log(chain.depth);     // 1
console.log(chain.expiresAt); // Date
```

<ParamField path="fromAgent" type="string">Agent ID granting the permissions. Must hold every permission being delegated, either as its own permission or through a delegation it received.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="toAgent" type="string">Agent ID receiving the permissions.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="permissions" type="Permission[]">Subset of permissions to delegate. Must not exceed what the fromAgent holds (its own permissions plus the active, unexpired delegations it received).</ParamField>
<ParamField path="expiresAt" type="Date">When the delegation expires. After this point, the chain is no longer valid.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="maxDepth" type="number">Highest chain depth this link and any later link below it may reach. The new link's depth (1 for a first hop, parent depth plus 1 for a re-delegation) must be less than or equal to the effective limit, otherwise the call throws. Default is 3. The limit is inherited: a re-delegation is checked against the smaller of its own `maxDepth` and the `maxDepth` of every active delegation the parent received.</ParamField>

### Permission subset enforcement

The permissions you delegate must be a subset of what the `fromAgent` holds. Narrower resources and fewer actions are allowed. Wider resources or new actions are rejected.

Given an orchestrator with:

```typescript
{ resource: 'mcp:github:*', actions: ['read', 'write', 'comment'] }
```

Valid delegations:

```typescript
{ resource: 'mcp:github:issues', actions: ['read'] }           // narrower resource, fewer actions
{ resource: 'mcp:github:*', actions: ['read'] }                // same resource, fewer actions
{ resource: 'mcp:github:repos', actions: ['read', 'comment'] } // narrower resource, same actions
```

Invalid delegations:

```typescript
{ resource: 'mcp:github:*', actions: ['delete'] }  // action not held by parent
{ resource: 'mcp:slack:*', actions: ['read'] }     // resource not held by parent
```

The subset test is the runtime matcher applied to the child: a parent `mcp:github` does not allow delegating `mcp:github:read`, because `authorize()` would not let the parent use it either. With [path matching](/permissions#path-matching-opt-in), a parent `ros2:/fleet/*` can delegate `ros2:/fleet/r1`.

### Constraints carry over

Constraints on the permissions you delegate are stored on the chain and enforced by `authorize()`, `authorizeByToken()` and `policy.evaluate()`. They are narrowed against the permission the parent holds, so a child can only be tighter:

| Constraint | Result |
|---|---|
| `requireApproval` | True if either side sets it |
| `maxCallsPerHour` | The lower of the two values |
| `allowedArgPatterns`, `ipAllowlist` | The patterns or addresses both sides share. If none are shared, the parent's list stays. |
| `timeWindow` | The overlap of two same-day windows. Otherwise the parent's window stays. |

```typescript
await theauth.delegate({
  fromAgent: orchestrator.id,
  toAgent: worker.id,
  permissions: [
    { resource: 'mcp:payments:refund', actions: ['execute'], constraints: { requireApproval: true } },
  ],
  expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 15 * 60_000),
  maxDepth: 1,
});
```

### Depth limiting

Each link has a depth: 1 for a delegation from an agent that did not itself receive one, otherwise the deepest active chain into the delegating agent plus 1. On every `delegate()` call the code computes an effective limit, the smallest of the `maxDepth` passed on that call (default 3) and the `maxDepth` stored on every active, unexpired delegation into the delegating agent, and throws if the new link's depth is larger. The effective limit is stored on the new link, so a limit set at the top of a chain holds for every hop below it. A later call can lower it, never raise it.

```typescript
// Orchestrator → Sub (depth 1, maxDepth 2): allowed
await theauth.delegate({
  fromAgent: orchestrator.id,
  toAgent: sub.id,
  permissions: [{ resource: 'mcp:github:issues', actions: ['read'] }],
  expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 3_600_000),
  maxDepth: 2,
});

// Sub → SubSub (depth 2, limit min(2, 2) = 2): allowed
await theauth.delegate({
  fromAgent: sub.id,
  toAgent: subSub.id,
  permissions: [{ resource: 'mcp:github:issues', actions: ['read'] }],
  expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 1_800_000),
  maxDepth: 2,
});

// Sub → anyone with maxDepth: 1 is rejected: depth 2 exceeds limit 1
// SubSub → anyone, even with maxDepth: 10, is rejected: depth 3 exceeds the inherited limit 2
```

The default `maxDepth` when not specified is `3`.

<Info>
A delegating agent can re-delegate permissions it received. The subset check runs against the agent's own permissions plus the active delegations into it, so `sub` above, created with `permissions: []`, can pass on what it was given, never more. The new link also cannot outlive the delegation it was derived from: its expiry is capped at the earliest expiry among the delegations into the parent, unless the parent's own permissions already cover the request.
</Info>

### Delegators must be live

A delegation lends authority only while its delegator is live. If a delegating agent is revoked or expired (or any status other than `active`), the links it gave stop counting: the delegate loses the permissions that came through it in `authorize()`, `authorizeByToken()`, `policy.evaluate()`, `explain()`, the simulator and the live MCP check, and the chain passed to `beforeAuthorize` no longer lists it. This applies down the chain, even when no revocation cascade ran. An agent that stands on its own permissions, and a root user as delegator, are not affected, and permissions the delegate holds directly are never touched. The same filter backs token vault consent (a downstream agent cannot use a vault credential through a dead intermediate) and the policy-shrink grant list, so unused-permission suggestions ignore dead links. If a delegator's inbound links are all dead, its onward links still stand when they grant only permissions it holds directly, because that authority never came through the dead chain. Onward links that grant what it received through the dead chain stop.

### Cascading revocation

Revoking a chain marks it revoked and does the same for active chains that start from the receiving agent.

```typescript
await theauth.delegation.revoke(chain.id);
```

If the chain is `orchestrator → sub → subSub`, revoking `orchestrator → sub` also revokes `sub → subSub` immediately. Any agent that relied on the revoked permissions will get `allowed: false` on its next authorization check.

<Warning>
Revocation takes effect on the next `authorize()` call. It does not terminate any in-progress operations.
</Warning>

<Note>
In the TypeScript package, `agent.revoke()` also revokes every active chain where the agent is the source or the target, and the chains downstream of them. It returns their ids as `revokedDelegations` and writes one `agent.cascade.revoked` audit row for the agent. Use `delegation.revoke()` when you want to cut one chain and keep the agent. This `agent.revoke()` cascade is pending in a changeset and is available in the next release after 1.1.2. Before it, revoke the agent's chains with `delegation.revoke()`.
</Note>

<Note>
Tokens minted through MCP token exchange carry their chain in the `act` claim, plus a signed `theauth_dlg` binding to the exact links and agents behind it. With `auth` passed to `createMcpModule`, the resource server checks that binding against the live rows on every request, so revoking a link (and every link below it in the cascade) or revoking an agent makes the next request carrying an affected token fail, on every instance that shares the database. A token never outlives the links and agents it came from. Resource servers that only verify the JWT see the revoke at token expiry. See [MCP token revocation](/mcp-revocation) for the modes and limits. `delegationStore` remains as the opt in check for older tokens that have an `act` claim and no binding.
</Note>

### Effective permissions

To see the full set of permissions an agent has at a given moment, including those received through active chains:

```typescript
const effective = await theauth.delegation.getEffectivePermissions(subAgent.id);
// Returns only the Permission[] received through active, unexpired delegation chains
```

`authorize()` checks the agent's own permissions first and, if they deny, falls back to these delegated permissions. You can call it directly to inspect what an agent has received through delegation.

### Listing chains

```typescript
// All chains originating from the orchestrator (fromAgent === agentId)
const outbound = await theauth.delegation.listChains(orchestrator.id);
```

### DelegationChain type

<ParamField path="id" type="string">Unique chain identifier, prefixed dlg_.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="fromAgent" type="string">Agent ID that created the delegation.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="toAgent" type="string">Agent ID that received the delegation.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="permissions" type="Permission[]">The permissions granted by this chain.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="expiresAt" type="Date">Expiry time for the chain.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="depth" type="number">Current depth of this chain in the delegation tree.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="createdAt" type="Date">When the chain was created.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="rootOwnerId" type="string | undefined">The human who owns the root agent of the chain. If the delegating agent was itself delegated to, the walk continues upward through active, unexpired chains, following the earliest created one when there are several.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="path" type="string[] | undefined">Agent ids from the root delegator down to `toAgent`.</ParamField>

`rootOwnerId` and `path` are returned by `delegate()` (`listChains()` does not include them). `policy.evaluate()` returns the same lineage as `decision.principal`, and each delegation is written to the audit log with the lineage on the row. The audit write is best effort: a failure does not fail the delegation, and it is counted (see [Tamper-evident audit trail](/audit-trail#write-failures)).

## Typical pattern

An orchestrator holds broad permissions, plans a task, and issues short-lived narrow delegations to sub-agents.

<Steps>
  <Step>
    Create the orchestrator with the full permission set it needs.

    ```typescript
    const orchestrator = await theauth.agent.create({
      ownerId: 'user-123',
      name: 'planner',
      type: 'autonomous',
      permissions: [
        { resource: 'mcp:github:*', actions: ['read', 'write', 'comment'] },
        { resource: 'mcp:linear:*', actions: ['read', 'write'] },
      ],
    });
    ```
  </Step>
  <Step>
    Create the sub-agent with no direct permissions.

    ```typescript
    const codeReviewer = await theauth.agent.create({
      ownerId: 'user-123',
      name: 'code-reviewer',
      type: 'delegated',
      permissions: [],
    });
    ```
  </Step>
  <Step>
    Delegate only what the sub-agent needs, with a short expiry and a small `maxDepth` (later hops inherit it, see depth limiting above).

    ```typescript
    await theauth.delegate({
      fromAgent: orchestrator.id,
      toAgent: codeReviewer.id,
      permissions: [
        { resource: 'mcp:github:pulls', actions: ['read', 'comment'] },
      ],
      expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 30 * 60_000), // 30 minutes
      maxDepth: 1,
    });
    ```
  </Step>
</Steps>

# IoT devices

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/iot-devices

A device in theAuth is a principal like an agent. It has an owner, groups, permissions with constraints, delegation from agents, audit rows and revocation. Under the hood each device is backed by an agent row of type `device`, so the permission engine, the delegation chain, the revocation bus and the hash chained audit log all apply without a second rule system.

What a device gets that an agent does not:

- Credentials made for hardware: a pre shared key, a public key that signs short assertions, or a TLS client certificate thumbprint.
- Enrollment by claim code (one device, typed by a person) or bulk token (a factory line, with a use limit).
- An attestation hook for evidence at enrollment, with built in verifiers for Android Key Attestation, Apple App Attest and TPM 2.0 quotes.
- A signed offline policy bundle for devices that cannot call home on every decision.
- Suspend and resume, separate from permanent revoke.

## Turn it on

Devices need `agents`. Add `devices` to your config:

```ts
import { createTheAuth } from "@glinr/theauth";

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: "sqlite", url: "file:./theauth.db" },
  agents: { enabled: true },
  devices: {
    // Optional. Signs offline policy bundles. Use ES256 or EdDSA, keep the private key in your secret store.
    bundleSigning: { alg: "ES256", kid: "bundle-2026-10", privateKey: JSON.parse(process.env.DEVICE_BUNDLE_KEY!) },
  },
  // Assertion replay cache and attestation nonces. Use "database" or Redis with more than one server.
  secondaryStorage: { deviceAuth: "database" },
});
```

Migration `0010-devices` adds three tables (`theauth_devices`, `theauth_device_credentials`, `theauth_device_enrollments`). It runs on the next boot, or apply it with `theauth db up`.

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `maxPerOwner` | 10000 | Devices per owner that are not revoked. Devices do not count against `agents.maxPerUser`. |
| `audience` | `"theauth"` | `aud` a device assertion must carry. |
| `issuer` | `"theauth"` | `iss` of offline bundles. |
| `bundleSigning` | none | `{ alg, kid, privateKey, previous? }`. Without it bundles are refused. |
| `bundleTtlSeconds` | 3600 | Bundle lifetime. Capped at 86400. |
| `attestation` | none | `{ required?, requireNonce?, verify? }`. Evidence without a `verify` function is refused, and so is evidence without a nonce. |
| `revocations` | off | `{ ttlSeconds?, maxEntries? }`. Signs a revocation snapshot next to every bundle. |
| `clientCertThumbprint` | none | `(request) => x5t#S256 or null`, for mTLS terminated at your proxy. |

## A runnable example

```ts
import { createTheAuth, evaluateDeviceBundle, verifyDeviceBundle } from "@glinr/theauth";
import { exportJWK, generateKeyPair } from "jose";

const signing = await generateKeyPair("ES256", { extractable: true });
const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: "sqlite", url: ":memory:" },
  agents: { enabled: true },
  devices: { bundleSigning: { alg: "ES256", kid: "k1", privateKey: await exportJWK(signing.privateKey) } },
});
await theauth.user.create({ id: "owner-1", email: "owner@example.com" });
const devices = theauth.device!;

// Register a thermostat with a pre shared key. The secret is returned once.
const { device, credential } = await devices.register({
  ownerId: "owner-1",
  name: "thermostat-hall",
  kind: "sensor",
  hardwareId: "SN-0042",
  groups: ["hvac"],
  permissions: [
    { resource: "mqtt:sensors:temp:*", actions: ["publish"] },
    { resource: "coap:valve:hall", actions: ["put"], constraints: { requireApproval: true } },
  ],
  credential: { kind: "psk" },
});
console.log("psk", credential?.secret);

// Online decision: same engine as agents, audit row marked theauthPrincipal = { type: "device" }.
console.log(await devices.authorize(device.id, { action: "publish", resource: "mqtt:sensors:temp:hall" }));

// Offline: sign a bundle, verify it on the device side, decide without the server.
const bundle = await devices.issueBundle(device.id);
const checked = await verifyDeviceBundle(bundle.token, { keys: devices.jwks(), deviceId: device.id });
if (checked.ok) {
  console.log(evaluateDeviceBundle(checked.claims, { action: "publish", resource: "mqtt:sensors:temp:hall" }));
  // requireApproval cannot be met offline, so this one is denied.
  console.log(evaluateDeviceBundle(checked.claims, { action: "put", resource: "coap:valve:hall" }));
}

// Kill it. The backing agent is revoked too, which reaches every server through the revocation bus.
await devices.revoke(device.id, "returned to vendor");
```

## Credentials

| Kind | Stored | The device sends |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `psk` | SHA-256 of the secret and a 16 character lookup prefix | `Authorization: Bearer tdk_...` |
| `jwk` | the public key and its RFC 7638 thumbprint | a device assertion JWT as `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` |
| `x509` | the `x5t#S256` thumbprint (RFC 8705 section 3.1) | its TLS client certificate; your proxy passes the thumbprint through `clientCertThumbprint` |

Accepted keys are EC P-256, EC P-384 and Ed25519. A private key or an RSA key is refused at registration. A device can hold several credentials, so rotate by adding the new one and revoking the old one:

```ts
const next = await devices.addCredential(device.id, { kind: "jwk", jwk: newPublicJwk });
await devices.revokeCredential(device.id, oldCredentialId);
```

### Device assertions

A device with a key signs a short JWT for each connection or request. The layout follows RFC 7523 section 3, the replay rules follow DPoP (RFC 9449):

```jsonc
// header
{ "alg": "ES256", "typ": "device-assertion+jwt", "kid": "<RFC 7638 thumbprint of the device key>" }
// payload
{ "iss": "<deviceId>", "sub": "<deviceId>", "aud": "theauth", "iat": 1760000000, "exp": 1760000060, "jti": "<16+ random chars>" }
```

The server checks the signature with the registered key (the algorithm is pinned to the key type), `iss` and `sub` equal the device id, `aud`, a lifetime of at most 300 seconds, `iat` no more than 30 seconds ahead, and a `jti` it has not seen for this device. In Node:

```ts
import { SignJWT, importJWK } from "jose";

const key = await importJWK(devicePrivateJwk, "ES256");
const jwt = await new SignJWT({ jti: crypto.randomUUID() })
  .setProtectedHeader({ alg: "ES256", typ: "device-assertion+jwt", kid: deviceKeyThumbprint })
  .setIssuer(deviceId)
  .setSubject(deviceId)
  .setAudience("theauth")
  .setIssuedAt()
  .setExpirationTime("60s")
  .sign(key);
```

## Enrollment

Ship devices without per device secrets and bind them on first boot.

```ts
// One device, a person types the code from a label or app: XXXXX-XXXXX, 15 minutes, single use.
const claim = await devices.createEnrollmentToken({ ownerId: "owner-1", kind: "claim", groups: ["hvac"] });

// A factory line: long token, use limit, 24 hours by default (30 days max).
const bulk = await devices.createEnrollmentToken({
  ownerId: "owner-1",
  kind: "bulk",
  maxUses: 500,
  permissions: [{ resource: "mqtt:sensors:*", actions: ["publish"] }],
});
```

The device then enrolls itself:

```bash
curl -X POST https://auth.example.com/api/theauth/device/enroll \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"token":"7KQ2M-9XR4T","name":"thermostat-hall","hardwareId":"SN-0042","credential":{"kind":"psk"}}'
```

Codes and tokens are stored as hashes. A use is claimed with one conditional UPDATE, so two devices racing for the last use cannot both win. A bad credential in the request is refused before a use is spent. Each device records the token that created it (`enrollmentId`), so if a bulk token leaks you can list and suspend exactly the devices it made: `devices.list({ enrollmentId })`.

<Warning>
`POST /device/enroll` and `POST /device/attestation-nonce` take no credentials. Keep the adapter rate limiter on for them.
</Warning>

### Attestation

Set `attestation.verify` to check evidence before the device is created. The device first asks for a nonce (`POST /device/attestation-nonce`) and binds it into its evidence, so old evidence cannot be replayed. Evidence that arrives without a nonce is refused unless you set `attestation.requireNonce: false`. The hook receives `{ evidence, nonce, hardwareId, enrollmentId, credentialKind, credentialKeyThumbprint }`, where the last two describe the credential the device is enrolling (`credentialKeyThumbprint` is the RFC 7638 thumbprint of a `jwk` credential).

```ts
devices: {
  attestation: {
    required: true,
    verify: async ({ evidence, nonce, hardwareId }) => {
      const claims = await myEatVerifier(evidence); // your RATS Verifier (RFC 9334)
      if (claims.eat_nonce !== nonce) return { ok: false, reason: "stale evidence" };
      return { ok: true, claims: { ueid: claims.ueid } };
    },
  },
}
```

The built in Android, Apple and TPM verifiers refuse an empty nonce (`""`) as well as a missing one, with the reason "needs the enrollment nonce". Before this, an empty string passed the missing check, and a TPM quote taken with empty qualifying data would have matched it. The Go port (`iot/attest`) already behaved this way. If you write your own `verify`, do the same: evidence that cannot be shown fresh should never be accepted.

A verifier that throws counts as a refusal. The claims you return are stored on the device as `attestation`.

#### Android Key Attestation (built in)

`createAndroidKeyAttestationVerifier` checks the certificate chain that `KeyStore.getCertificateChain` returns for a hardware backed key. It implements Google's published steps: the chain must end at a Google Hardware Attestation root, no certificate may be on Google's revocation list, the key attestation extension must appear once and in the leaf (a later copy could have been added by an attacker), the key and the attestation must meet a minimum security level (TEE or StrongBox), the TEE enforced root of trust must show a locked bootloader and verified boot, the key must have been generated in hardware, and the attestation challenge must equal the enrollment nonce.

```ts
import { createAndroidKeyAttestationVerifier, googleRevocationList } from "@glinr/theauth";

devices: {
  attestation: {
    required: true,
    verify: createAndroidKeyAttestationVerifier({
      revocation: googleRevocationList(), // required choice: a lookup, or "disabled" on purpose
      minSecurityLevel: "trusted_environment", // or "strongbox"
      bootPolicy: "verified", // "verified_or_self_signed" or "any" for development devices
      allowedPackages: ["com.example.robot"], // optional, software enforced
    }),
  },
}
```

On the device, generate an EC P-256 key with `setAttestationChallenge(nonce.getBytes(UTF_8))`, enroll that same public key as a `jwk` credential, and send the chain as evidence: a JSON array of base64 DER certificates, leaf first. By default the verifier requires that the attested key is the enrolled key (`bindKey`), so a genuine device cannot vouch for a key that lives somewhere else. A `psk` or `x509` credential fails that check; set `bindKey: false` if you only want proof that the device is genuine.

Things to know:

- The bundled roots are the two Google roots published at `android.googleapis.com/attestation/root`, copied on 2026-10-18. Pass `roots` to pin a newer list. Anchors are not time checked. Factory chains of the old root (subject serial `f92009e853b6b045`) are accepted after their `notAfter` date, as Google instructs, unless the chain carries the provisioning information extension (Remote Key Provisioning), where validity is enforced.
- `googleRevocationList()` caches the list by its `Cache-Control` header and throws when it cannot fetch it, which refuses the enrollment. Set `staleIfErrorSeconds` to tolerate an outage for a bounded time.
- Not supported: chains that use an attest key to certify another key (the verifier wants the extension in the leaf), the CBOR provisioning information content (only its position is checked), and `attestationIdSerial` or IMEI matching against `hardwareId`.
- `theauth device attest android --evidence chain.json --nonce <n> --revocation google` runs the same verifier from the command line.

**How this verifier was tested.** The test suite uses real attestation chains from Google's own repository, [google/android-key-attestation](https://github.com/google/android-key-attestation/tree/master/src/test/resources) (Apache License 2.0, copied unmodified into `packages/core/tests/fixtures/android-key-attestation.json`): EC and RSA keys, TEE and StrongBox, produced by TestDPC on devices. Three of the four chains verify, and `openssl verify` agrees with us on all four, including that the fourth (EC StrongBox) is not a valid chain: its leaf signature matches neither of the certificates above it. The parsed key description is compared with what `openssl asn1parse` prints for the same bytes. Those devices were unlocked, so the strict boot policy refuses them, which the tests also check. What is not covered: we have no chain from a locked, verified device with a known private key, so key binding is tested with the public key of a fixture leaf, and no chain with the provisioning information extension, so that branch is tested only by reading the specification. Treat the verifier as reviewed against Google's documentation and tested against real fixtures, not as certified by Google.

#### Apple App Attest (built in)

`createAppleAppAttestVerifier` checks the attestation object that `DCAppAttestService.attestKey` returns, following Apple's [Attestation Object Validation Guide](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/devicecheck/attestation-object-validation-guide): the CBOR object has format `apple-appattest`, its `x5c` holds the credential and intermediate certificates and the chain must end at the Apple App Attestation Root CA, the credential certificate's nonce extension (OID 1.2.840.113635.100.8.2) must equal SHA-256 of `authData` followed by the client data hash, the key identifier must be SHA-256 of the certificate's public key point and equal the credential id, `rpIdHash` must be SHA-256 of an App ID you allow, the counter must be 0, and the AAGUID must match the environment you expect.

```ts
import { createAppleAppAttestVerifier } from "@glinr/theauth";

devices: {
  attestation: {
    required: true,
    verify: createAppleAppAttestVerifier({
      appIds: ["ABCDE12345.com.example.robot"], // TeamID.BundleID, required
      environment: "production", // "development" for sandbox builds, "any" for both
      allowedValidationCategories: [1], // optional, see below
    }),
  },
}
```

On the device, generate a key with `generateKey`, enroll your own credential as a `jwk` credential, and attest with client data that names that credential. By default (`bind: "client-data"`) the verifier expects the client data to be the UTF-8 text `<nonce>:<RFC 7638 thumbprint of the enrolled key>`, hashed with SHA-256:

```swift
let clientData = Data("\(nonce):\(thumbprint)".utf8)
let hash = Data(SHA256.hash(data: clientData))
let attestation = try await DCAppAttestService.shared.attestKey(keyId, clientDataHash: hash)
// evidence: {"attestation": attestation.base64EncodedString(), "keyId": keyId}
```

Apple's certificate then vouches for that exact pairing of nonce and enrolled key. App Attest keys cannot be exported or used as a signing credential for your own tokens, which is why the enrolled key is a separate one. `bind: "attested-key"` instead demands that the enrolled key is the App Attest key itself, and `bind: "none"` checks the nonce only.

Things to know:

- The bundled root was downloaded over HTTPS from `apple.com/certificateauthority/Apple_App_Attestation_Root_CA.pem` on 2026-10-18. Apple publishes no fingerprint for it, so the evidence that it is the right root is that the intermediate certificates in real attestations verify against it. Pass `roots` to pin your own.
- The credential certificate is valid for about three days. Verify at enrollment, not later. There is no revocation list for App Attest, so no revocation option exists.
- Two extensions in `authData` are returned as claims when present: `apple_validation_category_01` (Apple's guide shows 1 for an OS distributed app, a development signed build on an iPhone reported 3) and `apple_bundle_version_01`. Apple's own 2026 sample sets only the attested credential flag yet carries the extension map, so the verifier reads the map whenever bytes follow the key, and the map is covered by the certificate's nonce.
- Not built: verifying the fraud metric receipt (a PKCS#7 object from Apple, outside the signed data), verifying assertions from `generateAssertion` and tracking their counters, and any macOS specific checks.
- `theauth device attest apple --evidence att.json --nonce <n> --app-id <TeamID.BundleID>` runs the same verifier from the command line.

**How this verifier was tested.** Three real attestation objects, copied unmodified into `packages/core/tests/fixtures/apple-app-attest.json`: the sample in Apple's validation guide (fetched from developer.apple.com on 2026-10-18, example app `com.example.myapp`), a recording from a physical iPhone on iOS 14.4 in the development environment from [veehaitch/devicecheck-appattest](https://github.com/veehaitch/devicecheck-appattest/blob/main/src/test/resources/ios-14.4.yaml) (Apache License 2.0), and a recording from an iPhone on iOS 27.0.1 in the production environment from [jewei/app-attest-php](https://github.com/jewei/app-attest-php/blob/main/spec/termakan-ios27-attestation.json) (MIT). All three verify against the bundled root with the clock set inside their three day window, which also shows the chain, the nonce and the key id logic match what Apple's service produces. The tests refuse a different nonce, another App ID, the wrong environment, a wrong key id, a changed `authData`, an expired certificate and a foreign root. Limits of that evidence: the tests do not bind with real keys, because those devices never saw our client data format. The `client-data` path is run on real data by reading the iOS 27 recording's challenge (which contains colons) as `<nonce>:<thumbprint>`, which exercises the code but is not a recording of a device doing it. Nothing here covers attestation objects from macOS, Mac Catalyst or visionOS. Treat the verifier as reviewed against Apple's documentation and tested against real fixtures, not as certified by Apple.

#### TPM 2.0 quotes (built in)

`createTpm2QuoteVerifier` checks a TPM2_Quote against the TCG TPM 2.0 Library specification. The attestation key must be a restricted signing key that cannot leave its TPM (`restricted`, `sign`, `fixedTPM`, `fixedParent`, not `decrypt`), because only a restricted key signs nothing but structures the TPM built, which is what gives the `TPM_GENERATED` magic its meaning. The quote must be a TPM_ST_ATTEST_QUOTE, its qualifying data must equal the enrollment nonce, its signature must verify under that key (RSASSA or ECDSA, SHA-256 or stronger), its clock must be marked safe, and the PCR values in the evidence must hash to the signed digest. With `roots`, the evidence must also carry a certificate chain from the attestation key to a root you trust.

```ts
import { createTpm2QuoteVerifier } from "@glinr/theauth";

devices: {
  attestation: {
    required: true,
    verify: createTpm2QuoteVerifier({
      roots: [vendorRootPem], // trust anchor for the attestation key certificate
      challengeEncoding: "hex", // how the nonce string maps to the qualifying data
      expectedPcrs: { sha256: { 7: "<hex of the secure boot PCR you expect>" } },
    }),
  },
}
```

The evidence is JSON: `akPublic` (TPMT_PUBLIC or TPM2B_PUBLIC, base64), `quote` (the TPMS_ATTEST message, base64), `signature` (TPMT_SIGNATURE, base64), `pcrs` (hex values by bank and index, for example `{"sha256": {"0": "...", "7": "..."}}`, covering every PCR the quote selected) and `akCertificates` (base64 DER, leaf first). With tpm2-tools these are what `tpm2_quote` writes with `-m` and `-s` plus the values from `tpm2_pcrread`. We did not run tpm2-tools while building this, so check the flags and the output format against your version.

Things to know:

- There is no bundled root. TPM vendors and clouds each run their own, so you pass the one you trust. Without `roots` you must pass `allowUnverifiedAk: true`, and the claims then say `akVerified: false`: the quote proves someone holding that key signed a TPM shaped structure, not that a TPM exists.
- This verifier does not run the TPM2_MakeCredential and TPM2_ActivateCredential handshake that proves an attestation key shares a TPM with an endorsement key, and it does not check TPM2_Certify of the enrolled device key. A genuine TPM therefore vouches for the nonce, but the quote does not prove that the enrolled credential lives in that TPM. If that matters, make the attestation key the device identity or add the handshake on your server.
- The event log, RSA-PSS signatures and ECDAA are not supported. PCR values are reported in the claims, and `expectedPcrs` compares chosen ones.
- `theauth device attest tpm --evidence quote.json --nonce <n> --root vendor-root.pem` runs the same verifier from the command line.

**How this verifier was tested.** The fixture is a real attestation from a Google Compute Engine Shielded VM (virtual TPM) in [google/go-tpm-tools](https://github.com/google/go-tpm-tools/blob/7350267efdfa67fc62be505004fd61d7d05e5288/internal/test/attestations/gce-cos-85-nonce9009.pb) (Apache License 2.0): three quotes of the same machine (SHA-1, SHA-256 and SHA-384 PCR banks, signed RSASSA-2048 with SHA-256), a second file with quotes taken without a nonce, and the key certificate from the same file. Google's published [intermediate](https://pki.goog/cloud_integrity/tpm_ek_intermediate_2.crt) and [root](https://pki.goog/cloud_integrity/tpm_ek_root_1.crt) were fetched on 2026-10-18 to complete the chain. `openssl verify` accepts that chain, and `openssl dgst -verify` accepts all six quote signatures and finds each PCR digest in its quote, which agrees with this verifier. The tests also refuse another nonce, a quote taken without one, changed PCR values, a changed quote or signature, a key that is not restricted, a foreign root and an expired chain. Limits: it is one vendor and one virtual TPM, so physical TPMs from Infineon, STMicro, Nuvoton or Intel and Windows platform keys are untested. In this fixture the certified key carries the endorsement key certificate usage, which is how that cloud issues it. The ECDSA branch is covered only by keys generated inside the test, which shows the code path works and nothing about any device.

## Authorization, delegation and revocation

- `devices.authorize(id, request)` checks the device state first (`device_suspended`, `device_revoked`, `device_expired`, `device_not_found`), then runs the same pipeline as agents: `beforeAuthorize` hooks, own and delegated permissions, constraints, approvals and audit.
- Every audit row for a device has `parameters.theauthPrincipal = { type: "device", id }`. Keys starting with `theauth` are reserved, so a device cannot plant that marker through arguments.
- `devices.delegate({ fromAgent, deviceId, permissions, expiresAt })` lets an agent hand a subset of its permissions to a device. Revoking the agent revokes the chain.
- `devices.suspend(id)` is reversible. `devices.revoke(id)` is permanent, revokes the backing agent and cascades its delegations.
- Device backing agents are hidden from `agent.list()` unless you pass `type: "device"`, and their bearer token can never be used or rotated.

## Offline policy bundles

A bundle is a compact JWS with `typ: device-policy+jwt`, signed with `bundleSigning`:

```json
{
  "iss": "theauth", "sub": "<deviceId>", "aud": "<deviceId>",
  "iat": 1760000000, "nbf": 1760000000, "exp": 1760003600, "jti": "...",
  "seq": 1760000000123, "owner": "owner-1", "groups": ["hvac"],
  "perms": [{ "resource": "mqtt:sensors:temp:*", "actions": ["publish"] }]
}
```

Rules on the device, as implemented by `verifyDeviceBundle` and `evaluateDeviceBundle`:

1. Verify the signature against `GET /device/jwks`, `typ`, `iss`, and that `sub` and `aud` are this device. Respect `nbf` and `exp` with 30 seconds of skew.
2. Keep the highest `seq` accepted and refuse a lower one, so an old and wider bundle cannot be replayed.
3. Match permissions the same way the server does.
4. `requireApproval` always denies offline. `maxCallsPerHour` denies unless you pass the local call count. Time windows use the device clock.

`perms` is the device's own permissions plus active delegations at issue time. A revocation reaches online checks at once but reaches an offline device only when its bundle expires, so pick the TTL as the longest stale window you accept. One hour is the default.

### Signed revocation snapshots

A revoked device keeps working offline until its bundle expires. If a robot talks to other devices while disconnected, or you want a device to notice its own revocation without a round trip, turn on snapshots:

```ts
devices: {
  bundleSigning: { alg: "ES256", kid: "bundle-2026-10", privateKey },
  revocations: { ttlSeconds: 3600 }, // opt in; needs bundleSigning
}
```

`issueBundle` then returns `revocations: { token, claims }` next to the bundle (and `GET /device/bundle` includes it). The token is a compact JWS (`typ: device-revocations+jwt`, same key and JWKS as bundles) that lists the revoked and suspended devices of the bundle's owner: claims `iss`, `sub` (the owner), `iat`, `nbf`, `exp`, `jti`, `seq` (issue time in ms), `n` (entry count), `h` (`sha256-64`) and `ids`. Each entry is the first 8 bytes of the SHA-256 of the device id, sorted, concatenated and base64url encoded, so a device costs 11 characters and the list is exact for practical purposes (a false match needs a 64 bit collision). A Bloom filter would be smaller, but its false positives would lock healthy devices out, so we did not use one. `maxEntries` (default 50000) caps the list, and the server refuses to sign a truncated one.

The device opts in to checking it when it verifies the bundle:

```ts
const res = await verifyDeviceBundle(bundle.token, {
  keys: jwks,
  deviceId,
  revocations: { token: bundle.revocations?.token, maxAgeSeconds: 900, lastSeq: savedSnapshotSeq },
});
if (!res.ok) {
  // "revoked": this device is on the list
  // "stale_revocations": snapshot missing, expired or older than maxAgeSeconds (fail closed)
  // "rollback": an older snapshot than one already accepted
}
```

`maxAgeSeconds` is measured from the snapshot's `iat`, so a device can demand fresher data than the snapshot's own `exp`. Without the `revocations` option nothing changes. To ask whether a peer is revoked, call `verifyRevocationSnapshot(token, { keys, maxAgeSeconds, owner })` and then `result.has(peerId)`. The Go package `iot/device` has the same checks (`VerifyBundle` with `Revocations`, `VerifyRevocations`, `RevocationSnapshot.Contains`) and runs against shared vectors generated from the TypeScript code. One note on timing: suspension is reversible, and a resumed device stays on a snapshot until that snapshot expires, so pick a short `ttlSeconds` if you suspend often.

## HTTP routes

Management routes need a signed in owner and only show that owner's devices:

| Method | Path | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GET | `/devices` | list (`ownerId`, `status`, `group`, `enrollmentId`, `limit`, `offset`) |
| POST | `/devices` | register |
| GET, PATCH, DELETE | `/devices/:id` | get with credentials, update, revoke |
| POST | `/devices/:id/suspend`, `/devices/:id/resume` | pause and resume |
| POST, DELETE | `/devices/:id/credentials[/:credentialId]` | add, revoke a credential |
| POST | `/devices/:id/bundle` | issue a bundle |
| GET, POST | `/devices/enrollment-tokens` | list, create an enrollment token |
| DELETE | `/devices/enrollment-tokens/:id` | revoke an enrollment token |

`GET /devices/enrollment-tokens` takes `ownerId`, `limit` and `offset`. Each row has `id`, `kind`, `ownerId`, `maxUses`, `uses`, `groups`, `status` (`active`, `expired`, `revoked` or `used_up`) and the dates. It never returns the plaintext token or its hash, so a lost token cannot be recovered from the list: revoke it and create another.

```ts
const res = await fetch(`${base}/devices/enrollment-tokens?limit=20`, {
  headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${sessionToken}` },
});
const { data } = await res.json();
for (const t of data) console.log(t.id, t.status, `${t.uses}/${t.maxUses}`);
```

Device facing routes (turn them off with `routes: { devices: false }`):

| Method | Path | Auth |
| --- | --- | --- |
| POST | `/device/enroll` | enrollment token in the body |
| POST | `/device/attestation-nonce` | none |
| POST | `/device/authorize` | device credential; 401 bad credential, 403 denied |
| GET | `/device/bundle` | device credential |
| GET | `/device/jwks` | none |

With `devices.spiffe` set the handler also serves `POST /device/spiffe/verify`, and the admin routes `POST /devices/spiffe/verify`, `POST /devices/spiffe/token` and `POST /devices/:id/spiffe`. See [SPIFFE workload identity](/spiffe).

To exercise bundles, snapshots, offline use, clock skew and revocation against a fleet of simulated devices, see the [device conformance kit](/device-conformance-kit).

`/auth/device/*` is a different thing: the RFC 8628 flow where a person signs in on a TV or CLI.

## Resource names for device protocols

Resources are colon separated, and `*` matches the rest:

- MQTT topic `sensors/temp/42` is `mqtt:sensors:temp:42`, actions `publish` and `subscribe`. The filter `sensors/#` is `mqtt:sensors:*`. `+` has no direct equivalent, so a broker plugin should expand or deny it.
- CoAP `/actuators/valve` is `coap:actuators:valve`, actions `get`, `put`, `post`, `delete`, `observe`.
- ROS 2 topics follow [Robotics and ROS 2](/robotics-ros2).

## CLI

```bash
theauth device register --config ./theauth.config.mjs --owner owner-1 --name gw-1 --psk \
  --perm "mqtt:sensors:*=publish" --group yard
theauth device list --config ./theauth.config.mjs --status active
theauth device enroll-token --config ./theauth.config.mjs --owner owner-1 --kind bulk --max-uses 200
theauth device suspend <deviceId> --config ./theauth.config.mjs --reason "battery swap"
theauth device revoke <deviceId> --config ./theauth.config.mjs
theauth device attest android --evidence chain.json --nonce <nonce> --revocation google
theauth device attest apple --evidence att.json --nonce <nonce> --app-id ABCDE12345.com.example.robot
theauth device attest tpm --evidence quote.json --nonce <nonce> --challenge hex --root vendor-root.pem
theauth device spiffe verify-x509 --cert leaf.pem --root ca.pem
theauth device spiffe link <deviceId> spiffe://example.org/ns/yard/sa/robot-7 --config ./theauth.config.mjs
```

SPIFFE SVIDs as device credentials are covered in [SPIFFE workload identity](/spiffe).

## What is not here yet

CWT and COSE encoding of bundles for very small devices, a built in verifier for EAT, App Attest assertions and the TPM credential activation handshake, uploading decisions a device made offline into the audit chain, and a dashboard page.
