# Input provenance

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/input-provenance

## The threat

Prompt injection works because the model cannot tell an instruction from the user apart from text it read on a web page or in a file. [OWASP LLM01](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/) lists segregating and marking external content as a mitigation, and notes there is no complete prevention. So some injections will get through. When one does, you need to answer three questions fast: which document carried it, which calls did it influence, and which of those did damage.

Input provenance is the record that answers them. Each audit row can list the inputs the caller says were in context: a kind, an optional id and a hash of the content. The content is never stored. Given a suspect document, you hash it, search the audit log, and get every call that had it in context.

This is evidence for investigation, not a guard. The server records what the caller declares and does not check that a source is real or complete. For blocking calls based on where arguments came from, see the [taint guard](/taint-guard).

## What is recorded

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `kind` | `user_message`, `tool_output`, `retrieved_document` or `agent` |
| `id` | Optional identifier you choose, such as a message id, a URL or a tool call id |
| `hash` | 64 hex characters, computed from the content |
| `hv` | `2` for the keyed hash. Absent on rows written before the keyed hash |

The kinds map onto the provenance model in [W3C PROV](https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-overview/): an input is an entity, the call is an activity that used it. The same idea appears in the [OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions](https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai), which keep message content off by default because it often holds personal data. Here the default is the same: hash, never content.

## The hash is keyed

A plain SHA-256 of a short message can be confirmed by anyone who reads the audit table and guesses the text. So the stored hash is an HMAC-SHA-256 under a subkey derived with HKDF ([RFC 5869](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5869)) from the audit key (`audit.hmacKey`, or the installation secret when you set none). The chain key itself is never used to hash content.

Because the hash is keyed, a client cannot compute it. To look something up, send the content to the server and let it hash with its key. The query API, the HTTP route and the CLI all take `content` for this reason. Rows written before the keyed hash keep their plain hash (no `hv`), and a content query matches both forms.

## Record inputs in code

```ts
await theauth.authorize(
  agent.id,
  { action: "execute", resource: "mcp:github:create_issue" },
  {
    inputs: [
      { kind: "user_message", id: "msg_123", content: userText },
      { kind: "retrieved_document", id: "https://example.org/page", content: pageText },
    ],
  },
);
```

For guarded tools, pass `inputs` to `guardTool`. Find every call that had a document in context:

```ts
const rows = await theauth.audit.query({
  provenance: { kind: "retrieved_document", content: pageText },
});
for (const row of rows) console.log(row.timestamp, row.agentId, row.resource, row.inputs);
```

## Send inputs over HTTP

`POST /authorize` and `POST /authorize/token` accept an `inputs` array in the body, with the same fields as above. A header form exists for proxies and gateways that cannot rewrite bodies: `TheAuth-Inputs` holds the base64url encoding of the same JSON array, up to 8192 characters and 32 inputs. Prefer entries with a `hash` over `content` in a header, since proxies log headers. A malformed header is ignored and never blocks the request. When both are present, the body wins.

```ts
import { encodeInputsHeader } from "@glinr/theauth";

await fetch(`${base}/authorize/token`, {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    authorization: `Bearer ${agentToken}`,
    "content-type": "application/json",
    "theauth-inputs": encodeInputsHeader([{ kind: "tool_output", id: "call_7", content: toolResult }]),
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({ action: "read", resource: "mcp:github:issues" }),
});
```

Query the audit log with `GET /audit?provenanceKind=retrieved_document&provenanceContent=...`. `provenanceHash` takes a stored hash. Each entry carries `inputs` (kind, id, hash, hv).

## Gateway

The [gateway](/gateway) reads `TheAuth-Inputs` on each request and records it on the permission check and the audit entry, then removes the header before forwarding to your upstream. An agent framework that fetches through the gateway can attach the documents it has in context without touching the upstream service.

## Admin MCP server

Clients of the admin MCP server pass inputs in the tool call `_meta`, under the key `io.theauth/inputs` (MCP reserves unprefixed names, so the key carries a reverse DNS prefix):

```json
{
  "name": "revoke_agent",
  "arguments": { "id": "agent_1", "reason": "suspected injection" },
  "_meta": {
    "io.theauth/inputs": [{ "kind": "user_message", "id": "ticket-88", "content": "Please revoke agent_1" }]
  }
}
```

The server writes them into the audit event for that call. `query_audit` takes `provenanceKind`, `provenanceContent` and `provenanceHash`.

## CLI

```bash
# every call that had this page in context
theauth audit query --input-content "$(cat suspect.html)" --provenance retrieved_document

# every call with any retrieved document, last 100
theauth audit query --provenance retrieved_document --limit 100

# by stored hash, from a row you already looked at
theauth audit query --provenance retrieved_document:3f2a...c9
```

Set `THEAUTH_AUDIT_HMAC_KEY` if your app runs with `audit.hmacKey`, or the CLI cannot reproduce the keyed hash.

## Dashboard

The audit page shows an Inputs column with one chip per recorded input: the kind, then the id or the first eight hash characters. Retrieved documents are amber, since they are the usual injection carrier. A filter narrows the page to one kind.

## Hold risky calls after untrusted input

With `policy.taint.inputLabels` on, the kinds in `context.inputs` become call level labels named `input:<kind>`, and a [taint rule](/taint-guard) can forbid them. This holds `tool:exec` for human approval whenever a retrieved document was in context:

```ts
const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  // ...
  policy: {
    taint: {
      inputLabels: true,
      rules: [{ resource: "tool:exec", forbid: ["input:retrieved_document"] }],
    },
  },
});
```

The effect defaults to `escalate`, which opens an approval request. After a person approves it, the retry with the `approvalId` passes. Use `effect: "deny"` to refuse outright. The option is off by default, so existing rules see the same labels as before. It rests on the caller declaring its inputs, so it reduces risk and is not a boundary against a caller that hides a document.

## What it does not do

- It does not verify the claim. A caller that leaves out a poisoned document leaves it out of the record.
- It does not follow data through the model. It says what was in context, not what the model used.
- A caller supplied `hash` is stored as given and is only as private as the caller's hashing. Use `content` where you can.
- Rows from before the keyed hash can have their short content guessed by someone who reads the table. Newer rows cannot, without the key.

---

# Audit receipts and chain vectors

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/audit-receipts

## What interoperates and what does not

The TypeScript library (`@glinr/theauth`) and the Go library (`theauth-go`) each keep their own tamper evident audit log. The two logs are different formats. Only the layer on top of them is shared.

| Layer | Shared between the libraries | Notes |
|-------|------------------------------|-------|
| Receipt, leaf encoding, field commitments | Yes | Same bytes, tested in both CI pipelines |
| Merkle tree (RFC 6962) and inclusion or consistency proofs | Yes | Same algorithm and same digests |
| Signed checkpoint (Ed25519) | Yes | Same signed message |
| Row hash chain | No | Different payloads, scope, timestamps and digests |
| Database tables | No | `theauth_audit_logs` here, `audit_events` (or `theauth_audit_events` on SQLite) in Go |

The claim this page supports, and no stronger one: **receipts and signed checkpoints interoperate; the chains are not interchangeable.** A receipt issued by either library verifies with the other. A chain written by one library cannot be verified, extended or read in place by the other, and one database cannot hold a single log written by both.

| | TypeScript | Go |
|---|---|---|
| Chain scope | One chain per agent, unique `(agent_id, chain_seq)` | One chain per organization, unique `(chain_key, chain_seq)` |
| Hash payload | `canonicalJson({v, seq, prev, row})`, keys sorted | `json.Marshal` of a struct, struct field order |
| Timestamp hashed | Milliseconds, truncated to whole seconds | Microseconds |
| Digest | SHA-256, or HMAC-SHA256 when `audit.hmacKey` is set | SHA-256 |
| Hash versions | 1 (raw ids), 2 (pseudonyms) | 1, called 101 in the receipt layer |

A receipt proves that one row, as disclosed, is a leaf of the log a checkpoint signed. It does not prove the log holds every event for an agent. See [Audit checkpoints and receipts](/audit-checkpoints) for what a receipt proves and what it does not.

## What a receipt is

A receipt is one JSON object that a counterparty can verify offline with the checkpoint public key:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "decision": {
    "rowId": "r2",
    "rowHash": "hex64",
    "hashVersion": 2,
    "revealed": { "action": { "value": "execute", "salt": "hex64" } },
    "commitments": { "resource": "hex64" }
  },
  "proof": { "version": 1, "rowId": "r2", "leafIndex": 1, "treeSize": 3, "leafHash": "hex64", "path": ["hex64"] },
  "checkpoint": { "version": 1, "alg": "Ed25519", "keyId": "k1", "size": 3, "rootHash": "hex64", "timestamp": 1790985600000, "since": null, "until": null, "signature": "base64url" }
}
```

Every field of the row that the receipt layer knows about is either revealed (value plus salt) or hidden (commitment only). The verifier recomputes the commitments for revealed fields, rebuilds the leaf, checks the leaf is in the tree, and checks the checkpoint signature.

## Leaf encoding

For each field name in the field set of the row's hash version:

```text
salt       = hex(HMAC-SHA256(auditKey, "theauth.audit.receipt.salt.v1" 0x00 rowHash 0x00 field))
commitment = hex(SHA-256("theauth.audit.receipt.field.v1" 0x00 field 0x00 salt 0x00 canonicalJson(value)))
preimage   = canonicalJson({ v: 1, rowId, rowHash, hashVersion, fields: { field: commitment, ... } })
leafHash   = SHA-256(0x00 || utf8(preimage))
```

`0x00` is a single zero byte. `canonicalJson` writes object keys sorted by UTF-16 code unit at every depth, no whitespace, strings escaped like JavaScript `JSON.stringify`, and `null` for absent values. `auditKey` is `audit.hmacKey` when set, otherwise the per-installation audit secret (as UTF-8 bytes of its hex string in TypeScript, as raw bytes in Go). Salts are derived, never stored, and a receipt reveals a salt only for a revealed field.

Field sets, in the order the library lists them:

| Hash version | Fields |
|---|---|
| 1 (TypeScript) | `id`, `action`, `resource`, `parameters`, `result`, `reason`, `durationMs`, `tokensCost`, `ip`, `userAgent`, `cacheHit`, `timestamp`, `agentId`, `userId` |
| 2 (TypeScript) | `id`, `action`, `resource`, `parameters`, `result`, `reason`, `durationMs`, `tokensCost`, `ip`, `userAgent`, `cacheHit`, `timestamp`, `policyVersion`, `delegationChain`, `inputProvenance`, `idPseudonyms` |
| 101 (Go) | `id`, `organizationId`, `action`, `targetType`, `targetId`, `metadata`, `ip`, `userAgent`, `createdAtMicro`, `policyVersion`, `delegationChain`, `inputProvenance`, `chainSeq`, `prevHash` |

Version 2 and 101 leave the personal ids out so erasure does not break a receipt. The row hash still covers them through their pseudonyms (version 2) or their stored form (Go).

## Tree construction

Leaves are every chained row, sorted ascending by row timestamp in milliseconds, then by row id. The tree is the RFC 6962 Merkle tree:

```text
leaf hash   = SHA-256(0x00 || leaf bytes)
node hash   = SHA-256(0x01 || left || right)
empty tree  = SHA-256("")
```

The tree splits at the largest power of two below the leaf count, so an odd node at the end of a level is carried up unchanged. Inclusion and consistency proofs follow RFC 9162 section 2.1.

A checkpoint signs `{version, alg, keyId, size, rootHash, timestamp, since, until}`. The signed bytes are the string `theauth.audit.checkpoint.v1` followed by a newline and the canonical JSON of that object. The signature is Ed25519, 64 bytes, encoded as base64url without padding. Any other `alg` is rejected, and the `keyId` must match one of the keys you pass in.

## Verify with the TypeScript library

```ts
import { verifyReceipt } from "@glinr/theauth";

// publicKeys: [{ keyId, publicKey: JsonWebKey }, ...]
const verdict = await verifyReceipt(receipt, publicKeys);
if (!verdict.valid) throw new Error(`receipt rejected: ${verdict.reason}`);
```

`verifyInclusionProof`, `verifyConsistencyProof` and `verifyCheckpoint` work the same way. Reasons include `malformed`, `unknown_key`, `bad_signature`, `leaf_mismatch`, `bad_proof` and `bad_commitment`.

## Verify with the Go library

```go
import "github.com/glincker/theauth-go/v2/audit/checkpoint"

// keys: []checkpoint.PublicKey{{KeyID: "k1", PublicKey: jwk}}
out := checkpoint.VerifyReceipt(receipt, keys...)
if !out.Valid {
	return fmt.Errorf("receipt rejected: %s", out.Reason)
}
```

`checkpoint.VerifyInclusionProof`, `VerifyConsistencyProof` and `VerifyCheckpoint` mirror the TypeScript functions and return the same reason strings.

## How interoperation is tested

- The Go repository writes `go-fixture.json` (checkpoints, inclusion and consistency proofs, receipts and tamper cases). This repository vendors a byte-identical copy in `packages/core/tests/fixtures/receipts/` and `tests/audit-receipt-go-fixture.test.ts` verifies it with the TypeScript verifiers in the normal test run. Refresh the copy with `node scripts/refresh-go-receipt-fixture.mjs` when the Go checkout sits next to this one. CI never needs the Go checkout.
- The TypeScript side writes `ts-fixture.json` and Merkle vectors that the Go CI verifies and rebuilds byte for byte.
- A drift in either direction fails a test in one of the two repositories.

## Chain test vectors (TypeScript row hashes)

`packages/core/tests/fixtures/audit-chain-vectors.json` lets an outside verifier recompute TypeScript row hashes without this library. It is generated by `npx tsx scripts/gen-audit-chain-vectors.mjs`, and a test regenerates it in memory and fails if the committed file differs. Go has its own, separate chain format; these vectors say nothing about it.

Format (`formatVersion` 1; any incompatible change bumps the number):

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `format` | `"theauth.audit.chain-vectors"` |
| `formatVersion` | `1` |
| `chains[]` | Chains. Each has `name`, `hashFormat` (`ts-v1` or `ts-v2`), `agentId`, `hashVersion`, `hmacKey` (string or `null`), `pseudonymKey` (string or `null`), `rows` |
| `chains[].rows[]` | `seq`, `prev` (`null` at seq 1), `input` (every column of the row), `payload` (the exact string that is hashed), `hash`. Version 2 chains also carry `erasedInput` on the last row: the same row with the raw id columns blanked, which must hash identically |
| `negative[]` | `name`, `chain`, `failsAtRow` (index in the chain after the mutation), `mutate`, `expect` |

To verify a row: build `payload` as `canonicalJson({v: hashVersion, seq, prev, row})` where `row` holds the version's hashed fields, then `hash = hex(HMAC-SHA256(hmacKey, utf8(payload)))` when `hmacKey` is set (key as UTF-8 text) or `hex(SHA-256(utf8(payload)))` when it is `null`. Hashed fields:

- Version 1: `id`, `action`, `resource`, `parameters`, `result`, `reason`, `durationMs`, `tokensCost`, `ip`, `userAgent`, `cacheHit`, `timestamp` (milliseconds), `agentId`, `userId`.
- Version 2: the same twelve common fields plus `policyVersion`, `delegationChain`, `inputProvenance` and `idPseudonyms`. The raw id columns are not hashed.

Absent values hash as `null`. `idPseudonyms[field] = hex(HMAC-SHA256(pseudonymKey, "theauth.audit.pseudonym.v1:" + id))` for `userId`, `agentId`, `subjectId`, `actorId` and `approverId`, where `pseudonymKey` is `audit.hmacKey` when set and the per-installation secret otherwise.

Check order for a chain: `prev` equals the previous row's `hash` (`null` for the first row), then the recomputed hash equals `hash`, then, for version 2, every raw id still present and not starting with `[deleted-` matches its pseudonym. The negative vectors carry the reason each mutation must produce:

| `mutate.kind` | Effect | `expect` |
|---|---|---|
| `set_input` | Replace one input field | `hash_mismatch`, or `pseudonym_mismatch` for a raw id that the version 2 hash does not cover |
| `set_payload` | Hash a different string (reordered keys, pretty printed) | `hash_mismatch` |
| `set_key` | Use another HMAC key, or none | `hash_mismatch` |
| `set_seq` | Hash with a different sequence number | `hash_mismatch` |
| `drop_row` | Remove a row (truncation in the middle or at the start) | `prev_hash_mismatch` |

A chain cut off at its tail still verifies row by row. Detecting that needs a signed checkpoint or an `expectedHeads` anchor, which is why checkpoints exist.

The vectors above test the row hash only. `verifyAuditChain` on a live database also checks where each chain starts. The oldest remaining row must be seq 1 with `prev = null`, or be explained by an `audit.checkpoint` row: either the one retention cleanup writes (`throughSeq` and `lastHash` match the first row's link) or the anchor `theauth.audit.checkpoint()` writes (`firstSeq`, `firstId` and `firstHash` name the first row). Both are chained rows and carry a `mac`: `hex(HMAC-SHA256(key, "theauth.audit.anchor.v1:" + canonicalJson(fields)))`, with the same key as the pseudonyms. Otherwise the result is `truncated_prefix`. `checkpoint()` also returns the anchors and heads, so you can keep them outside the database and pass them back as `anchors` and `expectedHeads`; a pinned anchor whose row is gone gives `truncated_prefix`, one whose hash differs gives `anchor_mismatch`. It anchors chains as they are when called, so verify first. `allowUnanchoredPrefix: true` turns the start check off.

`audit.erasure` records follow the same rule. They are chained rows, and each entry is MACed under `"theauth.audit.erasure.v1:"` over the erased row's id, agent, seq, hash, `prevHash`, `hashVersion`, reason (`anonymized` or `deleted`) and, for an anonymized version 1 row, the hash of the row as erasure left it. A record that is not on a chain gives `erasure_unchained`, an entry with a bad MAC gives `erasure_forged`, and a row whose `hash_version` went back to 1 (or NULL) gives `version_downgrade`.

## Verifying a Go export from TypeScript

`verifyGoAuditChain(rows, options?)` recomputes the hash chain of rows exported by theauth-go. It is a separate verifier from `verifyAuditChain`, because the Go chain is a different format (see the table at the top). It is pure and runs on Web Crypto only, so it works in a browser, a worker or Node.

```ts
import { verifyGoAuditChain } from "@glinr/theauth";

const result = await verifyGoAuditChain(rows, { pseudonymSecret: secretHex });
if (!result.ok) console.error(result.firstFailure); // { reason, chainKey, rowId, seq, index }
```

From a shell: `theauth audit verify-go export.json [--secret-hex <hex>] [--partial] [--json]` (a JSON array, `{"rows": [...]}` or NDJSON). It reads the file and nothing else.

Rows use the JSON of Go's `models.AuditEvent` (`id`, `organizationId`, `action`, `createdAt`, `chainSeq`, `prevHash`, `hash`, and so on). The four hashed pseudonyms are not part of that struct, so the export must add `actorUserPseudonym`, `subjectPseudonym`, `actorPseudonym` and `approverPseudonym` (empty or absent for ids that were never set). Without them you must pass `pseudonymSecret` (the 32 raw bytes as `Uint8Array`, or hex), and erased rows can then not be verified.

What is checked, per chain key (the organization id, or `""` for global events), in this order, stopping at the first failure:

| Check | Reason on failure |
|---|---|
| Row shape (`id`, `action`, `createdAt` as RFC 3339, `chainSeq` >= 1, `hash`) | `malformed_row` |
| `hashVersion` absent or `1` | `unsupported_hash_version` |
| `chainSeq` continues from 1 without a repeat or gap, rows in order | `seq_duplicate`, `seq_gap` |
| `prevHash` equals the previous row's `hash` (empty at seq 1) | `prev_hash_mismatch` |
| SHA-256 of the rebuilt `json.Marshal` bytes equals `hash` | `hash_mismatch` |
| Pseudonym inputs are present | `missing_pseudonym_input` |
| With `pseudonymSecret`: each raw id still present matches its pseudonym | `pseudonym_mismatch` |

Erasure works as in Go: a row whose raw id is blank while its pseudonym is set counts as erased and still verifies through the pseudonym. Rows with no hash are skipped and counted as `unchained`. Interleaved chains are fine. `allowPartialStart` trusts the first row of each chain, for an export window.

What is not checked:

- **Truncation by the chain check alone.** A chain cut at its tail still verifies, since every remaining row links to the one before it. Pair it with a signed head checkpoint, described next.
- **Keys.** The Go chain is plain SHA-256, with no HMAC mode, so anyone who can write the table can rewrite a suffix and recompute every hash. This verifier cannot change that, and it has no HMAC support because there is nothing to support. Without `pseudonymSecret` the pseudonyms are trusted as exported (`pseudonymsUnchecked` counts those rows).
- **Fields outside the hash.** `event`, `recordedAtUs` and the native columns of a database are not hashed.
- **Numbers beyond 2^53** inside `metadata` or `inputProvenance`: JavaScript parses them as floats, so the rebuilt text can differ from Go's. Metadata with such values reports `hash_mismatch`.
- **Storage.** It checks an export, not that the export matches the database.

### Rotating pseudonyms

When theauth-go runs with audit pseudonym rotation, a row's pseudonyms look like `r1:<period>:<hex>` instead of plain hex. The period is a whole number of days since the Unix epoch, and the hex is `HMAC-SHA256(periodSecret, "theauth.audit.pseudonym.v2:p<period>:" + id)`. The chain hash covers the stored text, so the hash check needs no secret. To also compare the raw ids still on a row with their pseudonyms, pass the secret of each period:

```ts
const result = await verifyGoAuditChain(rows, {
  pseudonymSecret: stableSecretHex,
  periodSecrets: { "20370": hexOfPeriod20370, "20371": hexOfPeriod20371 },
});
```

`periodSecrets` is an object or a `Map` keyed by period number, with raw bytes or hex values. A rotated pseudonym is never compared under `pseudonymSecret`. If its period has no entry (the secret was shredded, or you did not export it) the pseudonym is trusted as stored and the row is counted in `pseudonymsUnchecked`, the same as Go's own check. A raw id on a row of a shredded period can therefore be edited without detection. Older rows with plain hex pseudonyms keep using `pseudonymSecret`, and both forms verify in one export. From a shell: `--period-secrets periods.json` with `{"20370": "<hex>", ...}`. The fixture `tests/fixtures/go-e2e-head-vectors.json` was written by the real Go code and covers stable rows, rotated rows, an erased row and a shredded period.

### Catching tail truncation with a head checkpoint

theauth-go can sign the last position of every chain: `checkpoint.CreateHeadCheckpoint` writes `{version, alg, keyId, timestamp, heads: [{chainKey, seq, hash}], signature}`, signed with Ed25519 (RFC 8032). Keep that file somewhere the log's writer cannot rewrite. `verifyGoHeadCheckpoint` checks the signature and then asks whether each signed chain still reaches its signed `seq` with the signed hash. It is the same idea as a Certificate Transparency monitor holding a signed tree head (RFC 6962 section 3.5) and checking the log against it.

```ts
import { verifyGoAuditChain, verifyGoHeadCheckpoint } from "@glinr/theauth";

const chain = await verifyGoAuditChain(rows, { pseudonymSecret: secretHex });
const head = await verifyGoHeadCheckpoint(headCheckpoint, [publicKey], rows);
if (!chain.ok || !head.valid) console.error(chain.firstFailure, head);
// head: { valid: true } or { valid: false, reason, chainKey? }
```

`publicKey` is `{ keyId, publicKey: { kty: "OKP", crv: "Ed25519", x } }`, the same shape as for Merkle checkpoints, and you can pass several keys for rotation. Leave `rows` out to check the signature alone (`verifyGoHeadSignature` does the same).

| Reason | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `malformed` | Wrong version, unsorted or repeated `chainKey`, a `seq` below 1, a hash that is not 64 lowercase hex characters |
| `unsupported_alg` | `alg` is not `Ed25519`, or the key is not an Ed25519 OKP key |
| `unknown_key` | No supplied key carries the head's `keyId` |
| `bad_signature` | The signature does not verify, or is not strict unpadded base64url |
| `chain_truncated` | A signed chain is missing from the rows or ends below its signed `seq` (`chainKey` names it) |
| `head_mismatch` | The row at the signed `seq` has another hash, is absent, or two rows claim that `seq` with different hashes |

Rows and chains added after the head was signed are fine. The check looks only at the signed positions, so run `verifyGoAuditChain` on the same rows too, and give it every chain from the signed `seq` up: an export window that stops early reports `chain_truncated`. The signed bytes are the domain string `theauth.audit.head.v1` and a newline, followed by the canonical JSON of the other fields. Chain keys are ordered by UTF-8 bytes, as Go orders them, not by JavaScript string order.

From a shell:

```sh
theauth audit verify-go export.json --head head.json --head-key public-key.json
```

`public-key.json` holds one key object, a list of them, or `{"keys": [...]}`. The command prints one line for the chain and one for the head, and exits 1 if either fails (2 if a file cannot be read). With `--json` the head result is added under `head`.

The head vectors are `packages/core/tests/fixtures/go-head-checkpoint-vectors.json`. Go wrote and signed every case (with the RFC 8032 section 7.1 test 1 key) and the expected result of each case comes from the Go verifier, so the TypeScript tests fail if the two ever disagree. The generator and the steps to rerun it are in `scripts/go-head-vectors/`.

The conformance vectors are `packages/core/tests/fixtures/go-audit-chain-vectors.json`, produced by running the real Go hashing code. The generator source and the steps to rerun it are in `scripts/go-chain-vectors/`.

## Running both libraries

Do not point both libraries at one database or schema. Both create a table named `theauth_audit_secrets`, with incompatible layouts:

| Library | `id` | `secret` |
|---|---|---|
| TypeScript | `TEXT`, value `audit-pseudonym-v1` | `TEXT`, 64 hex characters |
| Go | `smallint` or `INTEGER`, always `1` | `bytea` or `BLOB`, raw bytes |

The TypeScript library checks the table before it migrates and again on every start with `skipMigrations`. If the table exists with a layout it did not create, it throws:

```text
AUDIT_SECRETS_LAYOUT_MISMATCH: table theauth_audit_secrets already exists with a different layout (...)
```

The error has `code === "AUDIT_SECRETS_LAYOUT_MISMATCH"` and a `found` string listing the column types it saw. Nothing is renamed or altered. Give each library its own database or schema. To check by hand, list the column types of `theauth_audit_secrets` (`pragma_table_info` on SQLite, `information_schema.columns` on Postgres and MySQL): a TypeScript table has text `id` and `secret` columns. If you see an integer `id` and a binary `secret`, the Go library created it.

---

# Audit checkpoints and receipts

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/audit-checkpoints

## Overview

The [hash chain](/audit-trail) lets you check your own log. It does not let someone else check it without database access, and it does not show that the log was left alone after a given date. Checkpoints add that.

A checkpoint is a signed tree head, the same idea Certificate Transparency uses ([RFC 6962](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6962), since obsoleted by [RFC 9162](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9162)). TheAuth builds a Merkle tree over every chained audit row and signs `{size, rootHash, timestamp, keyId}` with Ed25519. From there:

- An **inclusion proof** shows one row is a leaf of the tree the checkpoint committed to.
- A **consistency proof** shows a newer checkpoint extends an older one, with no earlier row changed.
- A **receipt** bundles a decision, an inclusion proof and the checkpoint into one JSON object.

All verification functions run offline and need only the public key.

## Sign a checkpoint

```ts
import {
  createCheckpoint,
  generateCheckpointKeyPair,
  createMemoryCheckpointStore,
} from "@glinr/theauth";

const keys = await generateCheckpointKeyPair("audit-2026-10");
// Keep keys.privateKeyJwk in your secret store. Publish keys.publicKey.

const store = createMemoryCheckpointStore();
const result = await createCheckpoint(db, { signer: keys.signer, store });
if (!result.success) throw new Error(result.error.message);
const checkpoint = result.data; // { size, rootHash, timestamp, keyId, signature, ... }
```

`signer` is any object with a `keyId` and an async `sign(bytes)`, so the private key can live in a KMS. `createEd25519Signer(privateKeyJwk, keyId)` covers the in-process case. Pass `since` or `until` to cover only a time range; both bounds are signed into the checkpoint.

An empty log gives a size 0 checkpoint.

## Mint and verify a receipt

```ts
import { createReceipt, verifyReceipt } from "@glinr/theauth";

const made = await createReceipt(db, rowId, checkpoint, {
  reveal: ["action", "resource", "result", "timestamp"],
});
if (!made.success) throw new Error(made.error.message);
const json = JSON.stringify(made.data); // send this

// Counterparty, no database:
const verdict = await verifyReceipt(JSON.parse(json), publicKey);
// { valid: true } or { valid: false, reason: "bad_signature" | "leaf_mismatch" | ... }
```

Consistency between two checkpoints:

```ts
const proof = await createConsistencyProof(db, older, newer);
if (proof.success) {
  const ok = await verifyConsistencyProof(proof.data, older, newer, publicKey);
}
```

`createConsistencyProof` takes the database because a checkpoint holds only the root, not the tree.

## What a receipt proves

- The operator signed a log head with that key at that time.
- A row with the revealed values was a leaf of that log, bound to the row's chain hash.
- If you hold two checkpoints and a consistency proof, the newer log kept every row of the older one unchanged and in place.

## What it does not prove

- **That the log is complete.** A row that was never written, or was left out of a checkpoint, is invisible. Checkpoints cover rows that exist at signing time.
- **That the operator showed everyone the same log.** A signer could sign two different heads for two parties. Catching that needs the checkpoint published somewhere many parties read, and someone comparing what they saw.
- **That a hidden field is what the operator says.** A hidden field is only a commitment. Reveal it with its salt to prove it.
- **That the decision was right.** It proves the record, not the judgment behind it.
- **Time precision.** The checkpoint timestamp is the signer's clock. It is not an independent time stamp.
- **Who a pseudonym is.** Version 2 rows commit to keyed pseudonyms of user, agent and approver ids, not raw ids. Revealing `idPseudonyms` shows the pseudonyms. Someone holding the audit key can confirm an id matches one; a counterparty without it cannot.

## Redaction and its limits

Each hashed field of a row gets a commitment: SHA-256 over the field name, a per-field salt and the canonical JSON value. The salt is derived from the audit key and the row hash, so the operator can rebuild it any time and stores nothing extra. A receipt includes the salt only for fields you reveal, plus the commitments for the rest.

- Hidden fields stay hidden as long as the audit key stays secret. Anyone with the key can recompute salts and test guesses.
- Revealing a field reveals exactly that value. There is no partial reveal inside `parameters`; reveal it whole or not at all.
- The set of field names, the row id, the row's chain hash and its position in the log are visible in every receipt.

## Keep checkpoints where a counterparty trusts them

A checkpoint you alone hold is a claim you can quietly replace. Publish each one somewhere the counterparty already trusts and that keeps history, such as a public repository, a transparency feed, an append-only bucket, or a message to the counterparty's own system. Verifiers should keep the checkpoints they have seen and ask for a consistency proof when a new one arrives.

## Key rotation

Every checkpoint names its `keyId`. Verification functions accept one public key or an array, and pick the key by `keyId`; a checkpoint whose `keyId` is not in the set, or whose `alg` is anything other than `Ed25519`, is rejected.

To rotate: create a new key pair under a new id, publish the new public key next to the old ones, and sign new checkpoints with the new key. Keep the old public keys published so older receipts still verify. A consistency proof can join checkpoints signed by different keys if you pass both public keys.

If a private key leaks, checkpoints signed after the leak cannot be trusted from that key. Publish a revocation note with the last good checkpoint, and move on to a new key.

## Operating notes

- **Log order.** Leaves are ordered by row timestamp (whole seconds), then row id, across all agents. Rows written later with an earlier or equal timestamp can sort before rows an older checkpoint already covered; then proofs against that checkpoint fail with `LOG_MISMATCH`, an alarm and not a missed tamper. Use `until` to checkpoint only rows old enough to be settled.
- **Unchained rows** (written before `tamperEvident` was on) are not in the tree.
- **Cleanup and key changes.** Deleting old rows with retention cleanup changes the tree, so older checkpoints can no longer be proved against the live database; keep the receipts you issued. Changing `audit.hmacKey` changes every salt, which changes the tree the same way.
- **Cost.** Building a checkpoint or proof reads and hashes every row in range. Run it on a schedule, not per request. Leaf hashes are cached in process per database and reused for rows whose content has not changed (a row is re-hashed whenever any covered field differs), so repeated proofs and receipts cost a read of the range, not a full re-hash. `createCheckpoint` returns `INVALID_RANGE` for a `since` or `until` that is not a valid date.
- **Storage.** `CheckpointStore` is an interface with an in-memory implementation. There is no database-backed store yet.

# Observability

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/observability

The audit table answers "what happened to this agent". Observability answers "how many denials per code in the last hour, and is a guard slow". theAuth emits one structured event per authorization decision and lets you forward it to the telemetry you already run.

## Decision events

Set `observability.onDecision` when you create the instance. It fires once per decision from `authorize`, `authorizeByToken` and `policy.evaluate`.

```ts
const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: "sqlite", url: "theauth.db" },
  observability: {
    onDecision: (event) => {
      metrics.increment("authz", { code: event.code, decision: event.decision });
    },
    // Optional: hide identifiers before they reach the listener.
    redactResource: (resource) => resource.replace(/\/users\/[^/]+/, "/users/:id"),
  },
});
```

### Event fields

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `source` | `authorize`, `authorizeByToken` or `policy.evaluate` |
| `agentId`, `ownerId` | Who acted and who owns the agent. `agentId` is missing for user subjects and unknown tokens |
| `action`, `resource` | What was asked. `resource` has been through `redactResource` |
| `allowed`, `decision` | `allow`, `deny` or `escalate` |
| `code` | The [decision code](/errors), for example `no_permission` or `hook_timeout` |
| `durationMs` | Wall time of the whole decision, hook included |
| `cacheHit` | True when `policy.evaluate` answered from its cache |
| `delegationDepth` | Hops from the agent to the root owner. See the note below |
| `hookOutcome`, `hookMs`, `guard` | How `beforeAuthorize` ended (`allow`, `deny`, `escalate`, `timeout`, `error`, `fail_open`), how long it took, and the guard that answered |
| `auditId`, `at` | The audit row id (empty when none was written) and the decision time |

The event never carries tokens or the raw `arguments` of the call. Tool arguments stay in the audit row, where your retention rules apply.

<Note>
`delegationDepth` costs a lineage lookup, so it is resolved only when a delegated grant took part in the decision or a hook already loaded the lineage. An agent allowed by its own permissions reports 0, even if it also holds delegations.
</Note>

### Delivery guarantees

- The listener runs in a queued microtask after the decision is made. `authorize` never waits for it, and the decision cannot change because of it.
- A throw, or a returned promise that rejects, is swallowed, counted, and logged at `warn`. It never reaches the caller.
- A listener that runs longer than `slowListenerMs` (default 5, env `THEAUTH_OBSERVABILITY_SLOW_MS`) is counted as slow. The call itself is not interrupted, so keep the listener cheap: push the event onto a queue or a metrics client and return.
- Events from different calls can arrive out of order. Sort on `at` if you need order.
- Without a listener, nothing is built or queued. With one, the cost on the request path is a closure and a `queueMicrotask`. In a local micro benchmark (in-memory SQLite, 3000 sequential `authorize` calls) the difference was within noise, about 105 microseconds per call either way.

Read the counters at runtime:

```ts
theauth.observability.stats(); // { emitted, errors, slow }
```

## Logger

Pass a `logger` to receive the SDK's diagnostics. The default is a no-op, so the library never writes to your console on its own.

```ts
import pino from "pino";

const log = pino();
const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  // ...
  logger: {
    debug: (msg, fields) => log.debug(fields, msg),
    info: (msg, fields) => log.info(fields, msg),
    warn: (msg, fields) => log.warn(fields, msg),
    error: (msg, fields) => log.error(fields, msg),
  },
});
```

Today the SDK logs a warning when a `beforeAuthorize` hook times out or fails, and when an `onDecision` listener throws or runs slow. A logger that throws is ignored.

## OpenTelemetry

`@glinr/theauth-plugin-telemetry` maps decision events to spans and metrics. It uses structural types, so it adds no `@opentelemetry` dependency: pass the tracer and meter you already have.

```ts
import { metrics, trace } from "@opentelemetry/api";
import { theauthOtel } from "@glinr/theauth-plugin-telemetry";

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: "sqlite", url: "theauth.db" },
  ...theauthOtel({
    tracer: trace.getTracer("theauth"),
    meter: metrics.getMeter("theauth"),
  }),
});
```

There is no standard semantic convention for authorization decisions yet, so the names live under `theauth.`.

**Metrics**

| Name | Type | Attributes |
|---|---|---|
| `theauth.decisions` | Counter, unit `{decision}` | `theauth.decision`, `theauth.decision.code`, `theauth.source` |
| `theauth.decision.duration` | Histogram, unit `ms` | same |

Metric attributes stay low cardinality on purpose: no agent id, no resource, no action.

**Spans**

One span per decision, backdated to cover it: `theauth.authorize`, or `theauth.policy.evaluate` for `policy.evaluate`. Attributes: `theauth.decision`, `theauth.decision.code`, `theauth.agent.id`, `theauth.owner.id`, `theauth.delegation.depth`, `theauth.guard.name`, `theauth.source`, `theauth.action`, `theauth.resource`, `theauth.cache_hit`, `theauth.audit.id`, `theauth.hook.outcome`, `theauth.hook.duration` (ms). Set `includeResource: false` to drop the resource, or use `redactResource` in core.

Span events `theauth.hook.timeout`, `theauth.hook.error` and `theauth.hook.fail_open` mark a hook that did not finish. Timeouts and errors also set the span status to ERROR. A plain deny does not: a denial is a correct answer, not a fault.

Useful queries: denials by code (`sum by (theauth_decision_code) (rate(theauth_decisions[5m]))`), p99 of `theauth.decision.duration` split by `theauth.source`, and spans with a `theauth.hook.timeout` event to find a slow guard.

## Dashboard

The audit page has a Code column and a code filter. Each row has a "Why" button that opens a drawer calling `POST /explain` on the [HTTP handler](/dashboard) for that agent, action and resource at the row's time. It shows the code, the matched grant, each constraint, the hook outcome and the closest grants that missed. The explanation is a fresh read-only evaluation against today's rules, so it can differ from the recorded decision if permissions changed since.

The code filter is sent as a `codes` query parameter and applied again to the loaded page, so it works even when your audit endpoint ignores `codes`.

## Related

- [Lifecycle hooks](/hooks) for `beforeAuthorize`, timeouts and the fail-closed policy that produce `hook_timeout` and `hook_error`.
- [Audit trail](/audit) for the stored record behind each `auditId`.

# Database hooks

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/database-hooks

`databaseHooks` lets you run your own code around the rows theAuth writes for `user`, `session` and `account`. The shape follows Better Auth's `databaseHooks`, so a hook you wrote there moves over with small changes.

```ts
import { createTheAuth } from "@glinr/theauth";

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: "sqlite", url: "theauth.db" },
  auth: { session: { secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET! } },
  databaseHooks: {
    user: {
      create: {
        // Runs before the row is written.
        before: async (user) => {
          if (!user.email.endsWith("@example.com")) return false; // abort
          return { data: { name: user.name ?? "New user" } }; // replace fields
        },
        // Runs after the row is committed.
        after: async (user) => {
          await sendWelcomeEmail(user.email);
        },
      },
    },
    session: {
      create: {
        before: async (session) => ({
          data: { expiresAt: new Date(session.expiresAt.getTime() - 60_000) },
        }),
      },
    },
  },
});
```

## What a hook can return

A `before` hook returns one of three things.

| Return | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `undefined` | The write goes ahead unchanged. |
| `false` | The write is stopped. The caller gets a `DatabaseHookError` with code `DATABASE_HOOK_ABORTED`. |
| `{ data }` | The listed fields replace the ones about to be written. |

Only some fields can be replaced. Anything else in `data` (including `id`) stops the write with `DATABASE_HOOK_INVALID_PAYLOAD`.

| Model | Fields you can replace |
| --- | --- |
| `user` | `email` (lowercased and checked again), `name`, `metadata` |
| `session` | `expiresAt`, `metadata` |
| `account` | `expiresAt` |

Hooks never see OAuth access or refresh tokens. Session metadata keys that theAuth owns (the auth event history, the idle activity stamp and the remember me flag) are kept as computed, so a hook cannot forge a stronger login.

## Where hooks fire

| Model | Create | Update |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `user` | `theauth.user.create`, magic link, email OTP, phone and OAuth sign-up | Not wired yet |
| `session` | `sessions.create`, including the new session of a refresh | `recordAuth` (step-up) |
| `account` | `linkAccount` when a provider account is linked | Token refresh on a repeat sign-in, and a repeat `linkAccount` |

Writes that are internal bookkeeping do not fire hooks: the idle activity stamp on a session, a pending OAuth row that has no user yet, and revocation deletes. Other user creation paths (anonymous, username, one tap, SCIM, importers) do not fire user hooks yet.

## Failure behavior

`before` hooks fail closed. A throw, a timeout or a malformed return value stops the write with a `DatabaseHookError` (`DATABASE_HOOK_FAILED`, `DATABASE_HOOK_TIMEOUT` or `DATABASE_HOOK_INVALID_PAYLOAD`), whatever `hookSafety.onError` is set to. The error message is generic, so it does not leak what your hook checked.

`after` hooks run once the row exists, so they cannot undo it. A throw or timeout is logged through `logger.warn` and swallowed.

The timeout comes from `hookSafety.timeoutMs` or `THEAUTH_HOOK_TIMEOUT_MS` (default 2000 ms). Each hook gets an `AbortSignal` in `ctx.signal` that fires when it runs out of time.

Hooks receive a copy of the data. Changing the argument does not change what is stored, return `{ data }` instead.

## Single-use claims stay atomic

Magic link tokens, OTP codes, OAuth state and refresh rotation all consume something with one conditional statement so that only one concurrent caller wins. Hooks never run inside that statement.

- A `before` hook runs ahead of the write it guards. If it aborts, nothing else was changed: a session `before` abort does not evict another session when `maxConcurrent` is set, and a refresh that is aborted leaves the old session usable.
- An `after` hook fires only for the caller that won. A refresh fires `session.create.after` once the old session has been claimed, so a refresh that loses the race fires nothing.
- A `before` hook that aborts a sign-up that already consumed a code (for example an OTP verify that creates the user) leaves that code consumed. The user retries with a new code.

Run slow work (email, webhooks, analytics) in `after`, and keep `before` to quick checks.

## Handling an abort

```ts
import { DatabaseHookError } from "@glinr/theauth";

try {
  await theauth.user.create({ email: "someone@other.test" });
} catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof DatabaseHookError && err.code === "DATABASE_HOOK_ABORTED") {
    // err.model is "user", err.operation is "create"
  }
}
```

The OAuth callback turns a `DatabaseHookError` into a 403 response.

# ID generation

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/id-generation

By default theAuth gives every new user, session and OAuth account a random UUID (v4). `advanced.database.generateId` changes that for those three tables.

```ts
import { createTheAuth } from "@glinr/theauth";

const auth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: "postgres", url: process.env.DATABASE_URL! },
  advanced: { database: { generateId: "uuidv7" } },
});
```

## Options

| Value | Result |
|---|---|
| `"uuid"` (default) | Random v4 UUID. |
| `"uuidv7"` | Time ordered UUID v7, [RFC 9562 section 5.7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9562#name-uuid-version-7). |
| `({ model }) => string` | Your own id. `model` is `"user"`, `"session"` or `"account"`. |

A function can return a different shape per table:

```ts
import { createTheAuth } from "@glinr/theauth";
import { ulid } from "ulid";

const auth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: "postgres", url: process.env.DATABASE_URL! },
  advanced: {
    database: {
      generateId: ({ model }) => (model === "user" ? `usr_${ulid()}` : crypto.randomUUID()),
    },
  },
});
```

The function must be synchronous and return a new id on every call. theAuth checks each result: 1 to 191 characters from `A-Z a-z 0-9 _ - .`. Anything else throws `THEAUTH_ID_INVALID` before the insert. The 191 limit is the longest key MySQL indexes with `utf8mb4`, and the same limit is applied on every dialect so a database move does not break ids.

## Why UUID v7

Random UUIDs scatter inserts across the primary key index. A v7 id starts with a millisecond timestamp, so new rows land at the end of the index, which keeps pages full on Postgres and MySQL and makes `ORDER BY id` match creation order. theAuth's generator also keeps ids made in one millisecond in order (a 12 bit counter, RFC 9562 section 6.2 method 1) and never goes backwards when the clock steps back.

A v7 id exposes the creation time of the row. Session ids are not secrets (the cookie is a signed JWT whose `sub` is the id), but if user creation times are sensitive in your product, keep `"uuid"` for users:

```ts
generateId: ({ model }) => (model === "user" ? crypto.randomUUID() : generateUuidV7())
```

`generateUuidV7` is exported from `@glinr/theauth`.

## Database generated ids are refused

Better Auth accepts `generateId: false` and `"serial"` to let the database assign ids. theAuth throws `THEAUTH_ID_UNSUPPORTED` at startup for both. The id columns are `TEXT` and every table that points at a user or session (agents, audit rows, organization members, tokens) stores the id as text, and theAuth must know an id before it writes the row that references it. Integer ids would need a different schema for every table. If you want ids you control, return them from a function.

## Where it applies

The option is used wherever theAuth creates a user, session or OAuth account row: `user.create`, sessions from every sign in path, anonymous users, username sign up, magic link, email OTP, phone, Google One Tap and OAuth sign up and account linking. An explicit `id` passed to `user.create` is kept as given.

It does not change:

- Rows whose id is a prefixed or derived value on purpose, such as SCIM users (`u_scim_...`), SSO providers (`sso_...`), importers and the GDPR erasure tombstone.
- Agents, delegations, tokens, audit rows and the other tables, which keep random UUIDs.

## Changing it on a live database

Nothing is rewritten. Existing ids stay as they are, and only rows created after the change use the new generator, so a table can hold v4 ids, v7 ids and custom ids at once. All three fit the same `TEXT` column and compare as plain strings. Sorting by `id` is only creation order among rows made with `"uuidv7"`.

If you also need old rows to carry the new shape, that is an application level migration: update the primary key and every referencing column in one transaction, with foreign key checks deferred. theAuth does not provide it, because the referencing tables depend on which plugins you enabled.

## Errors

| Code | When |
|---|---|
| `THEAUTH_ID_UNSUPPORTED` | `false`, `"serial"` or an unknown value. Thrown by `createTheAuth`. |
| `THEAUTH_ID_INVALID` | A custom function returned a bad id. Thrown at the insert, before any row is written. |

Both are `IdGenerationError` (exported from `@glinr/theauth`) with a `code` property.

# Policy shrink

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/policy-shrink

## What it does

Agents tend to be granted more than they need, because it is easier to widen a grant than to work out the narrow one. Policy shrink goes the other way. It reads the authorization decisions recorded for an agent over a window, works out which grants were never used, and proposes a smaller permission set that still reproduces every call that was allowed.

Nothing is changed for you. The functions read audit rows and return a report. You decide whether to apply it.

## How it works

1. `analyzeUsage` loads the agent's effective permissions (its own, plus permissions delegated to it through active chains that have not expired) and splits them to one action each. It then reads the audit rows in the window and attributes every allowed call to the grant that authorized it, using the same `matchResource` and `matchAction` the engine uses, trying own permissions before delegated ones.
2. `suggestShrink` turns that analysis into `keep`, `remove` and `rewrites`.
3. `verifyShrink` replays the recorded rows against the proposal and reports what would flip. `previewPolicyChange` does the same by reading the rows itself, and works for any proposed change, not just a shrink.

Only allowed rows count as use. A call denied for another reason (rate limit, time window, approval, revoked agent) is not treated as proof that a grant is idle. If such a call matched a grant, that grant lands in `attemptedOnly` and stays in `keep`.

## Run it

```ts
import { analyzeUsage, previewPolicyChange, suggestShrink } from "@glinr/theauth";

const since = new Date(Date.now() - 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000);

const analysis = await analyzeUsage(theauth.db, agentId, { since });
const plan = suggestShrink(analysis, { minObservations: 5 });
const report = await previewPolicyChange(theauth.db, agentId, plan.keep, { since });

console.log(plan.remove, report.newlyDenied);
```

`analyzeUsage` returns `granted`, `used` (permission, count, `firstSeen`, `lastSeen`, and `via` with the delegation chain ids involved), `unused`, and an `evidence` block with row counts. Rows are read in pages of 1000 with a keyset cursor, so a long window does not load into memory at once. Set `pageSize` to change that.

### Options for suggestShrink

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `minObservations` | `1` | Allowed calls a permission needs to be kept. |
| `generalize` | `false` | Merge observed sibling resources into `parent:*`. |
| `generalizeMin` | `3` | Distinct observed siblings needed before a merge. |

A non-finite number (for example `NaN` from an unset environment variable) in any numeric option, or in `maxExamples` and `pageSize`, is ignored and the default is used.

Output is deterministic and follows the order of the granted list.

### Generalizing

With `generalize` on, `mcp:github:issues`, `mcp:github:pulls` and `mcp:github:repos` can become `mcp:github:*`. A merge happens only when every merged resource was used, when one of the agent's existing grants already covers the wildcard (the result is never broader than what the agent has today), and when the wildcard matches no resource that was denied for lack of a grant. Even so, the wildcard admits siblings nobody has called yet, so each merge is listed in `rewrites` with its `from` permissions. Leave it off if you want the result to match observed use exactly.

A `*` segment in a resource pattern matches that segment and everything after it, at any depth, and also the parent itself (`tool:*` matches `tool`, `tool:a` and `tool:a:b`). Replay uses the same matching as `authorize()`.

## Example output

This comes from `examples/policy-shrink`, an agent with seven grants (ten once split by action) and 498 recorded calls:

```text
granted (one entry per action): 10
used:
  mcp:github:repos read  x212
  mcp:github:issues read  x148
  mcp:github:issues write  x37
  tool:db:orders query  x96
  tool:db:users query  x3
never used:
  mcp:github:repos write
  mcp:github:pulls read
  tool:db:users delete
  tool:mail send
  tool:billing *

replayed allows: 496
still allowed:   493
newly denied:    3
  query tool:db:users
  query tool:db:users
  query tool:db:users
newly allowed (was denied for lack of a grant): 0
```

The run used `minObservations: 5`, so `tool:db:users query`, called three times, was dropped and shows up as newly denied. That is the report doing its job: it is the line you read before deciding. With the default of `1` every historical allow is kept.

## Reading the report

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `replayedAllows` | Historical allowed calls replayed. |
| `stillAllowed` | Of those, how many the proposal still allows. |
| `newlyDeniedCount`, `newlyDenied` | Allowed calls the proposal would deny. The list is capped at `maxExamples` (default 1000), the count is exact. |
| `wouldAlsoAllowCount`, `wouldAlsoAllowPreviouslyDenied` | Calls denied for lack of a grant that the proposal would allow. Expect this to be non-empty when you widen. |
| `ignoredRows` | Denials for other causes and bookkeeping rows, left out of the comparison. |
| `perPermission` | Allows attributed to each proposed permission. |

Allowed calls that no current grant covers (an expired delegation, a removed permission) cannot be reproduced by a set built from today's grants. They are listed in `analysis.uncovered`.

## Delegated permissions

Delegated permissions are part of the agent's effective set. When a call is attributed to a delegated grant, the chain id is recorded in `via`, so you can see which delegation to narrow instead of editing the agent. Expired and revoked chains are not part of the granted set.

## Limits

- It proves past behaviour only. It cannot know about calls the agent will make next month.
- A rare but legitimate call (a quarterly job, an incident runbook) may fall outside the window and be proposed for removal. Review the `remove` list and the window before applying it, and widen `since` for agents with long cycles.
- Matching covers action and resource. Constraints (rate limits, time windows, IP allowlists, approvals) depend on live state, so they are carried over on kept permissions but not re-evaluated in the replay.
- Reading is bounded by the audit retention you configured. Rows already deleted are not evidence.
- Overlapping grants are attributed the way `authorize()` picks them, first match wins. A broad grant listed before a narrow one gets the credit, and the narrow one shows as unused.
- Audit rows only exist for decisions that were recorded. Check that `auditAll` was on for the window.

## Related

- [Tutorial: find and remove unused agent permissions](/tutorials/remove-unused-agent-permissions)
- [Agent accountability](/accountability): where permissions, approvals and audit fit together.
- [Tamper evident audit trail](/audit-trail): the decision rows that `analyzeUsage` reads.
- [Delegation](/delegation): delegated permissions count as granted.
- [Taint aware tool guard](/taint-guard): limit what a call can do once the permission is kept.

# Privilege analyzer

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/analyzer

The privilege analyzer scans agent permissions to find over-privileged agents, unused permissions, and potential security issues.

## Usage

```ts
const analysis = await theauth.analyzer.analyzeAgent(agentId);

console.log(analysis.score);           // "minimal" | "appropriate" | "over-permissioned" | "wildcard-heavy"
console.log(analysis.findings);        // PrivilegeFinding[]
console.log(analysis.recommendations); // suggested permission changes (string[])
```

`analyzeAgent(agentId, { since })` compares the agent's permissions against audit log entries since `since` (default: the last 30 days). If the agent does not exist, it returns an `"appropriate"` result with `agentName: "unknown"` and no findings.

## Analyze all agents

```ts
const analyses = await theauth.analyzer.analyzeAll();

for (const analysis of analyses) {
  for (const finding of analysis.findings) {
    console.log(`${analysis.agentId}: ${finding.type} (${finding.severity}) - ${finding.description}`);
  }
}

const summary = await theauth.analyzer.getSummary();
// { total, byScore: Record<string, number>, criticalFindings }
```

`analyzeAll` covers agents whose status is `active`. There is no `scanAll` method.

## Finding types

| Type | Severity | Description |
|------|----------|-------------|
| `wildcard_permission` | critical | The resource is `*` or ends in `:*` or `/*`, or the actions include `*` |
| `unused_permission` | warning | The resource does not appear in the audit log within the lookback window |
| `overly_broad` | warning | A namespace permission where only one or two specific sub-resources were used |
| `no_constraints` | info | No `maxCallsPerHour`, `timeWindow`, `requireApproval`, or `ipAllowlist` on the permission |
| `no_expiry` | info | The agent has no expiration date set |

## Score

| Score | When |
|-------|------|
| `wildcard-heavy` | Any critical finding, or two or more wildcard findings |
| `over-permissioned` | One wildcard finding, or two or more warnings |
| `minimal` | No findings |
| `appropriate` | Only info-level findings, or a single warning |

## Configuration

The analyzer has no configuration options. The lookback window is 30 days by default and can be overridden per call with `since`.

<Warning>
The analyzer reads from the audit trail. Keep `agents.auditAll` enabled (the default) so that permission usage is recorded; otherwise every permission looks unused.
</Warning>

# Trust scoring

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/trust

## What trust scores are

A trust score is a 0 to 100 number that reflects how much an agent has earned autonomous operation. New agents start with a baseline of 50. Over time, successful calls raise the score; denied requests, permission violations, and anomalous patterns lower it.

The score maps to one of five named levels that your application can use to gate behavior, requiring human approval for low-trust agents, unlocking faster paths for high-trust ones.

Scores are computed from the audit log, not guessed. An agent cannot self-report a high score.

## TrustScore fields

<ParamField path="agentId" type="string">The agent this score belongs to.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="score" type="number">Numeric value from 0 to 100.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="level" type="'untrusted' | 'limited' | 'standard' | 'trusted' | 'elevated'">Named trust level derived from the score.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="factors.successRate" type="number">Percentage of all calls that were allowed.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="factors.denialRate" type="number">Percentage of all calls that were denied.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="factors.ageInDays" type="number">Days since the agent was created.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="factors.totalCalls" type="number">Total authorization calls in the audit log.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="factors.anomalyCount" type="number">Denied calls whose reason contains `INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS`, `privilege`, or `escalation`. Built-in denial reasons do not contain these words, so this stays 0 unless your hooks produce them (see [Anomaly detection](/anomaly)).</ParamField>
<ParamField path="factors.lastViolation" type="string | undefined">ISO timestamp of the most recent denied call.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="computedAt" type="string">ISO timestamp of when this score was last computed.</ParamField>

## How scores are computed

The formula starts at 50 and applies adjustments:

```
score = 50
score += min(25, floor(allowedCalls / 100))   // +1 per 100 successful calls, capped at +25
score -= deniedCalls × 5                       // -5 per denial
score -= anomalyCount × 10                     // -10 per counted anomaly (a denial whose reason matches, see anomalyCount)
score += 10 if ageInDays > 30                  // bonus for established agents
score += 5  if ageInDays > 7                   // smaller bonus for recent agents
score = clamp(score, 0, 100)
```

An agent with 200 successful calls, no denials, and 40 days of history scores: `50 + 2 + 10 = 62`, landing in the `standard` level (60 to 79). Note that a brand-new agent with no history sits at the baseline of 50, which is `limited`.

## Trust levels

| Level | Default threshold | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `untrusted` | score < 40 | Misbehaving or heavily denied. Approve all sensitive actions manually. |
| `limited` | 40 to 59 | Early history (a new agent starts here at 50). Apply stricter rate limits. |
| `standard` | 60 to 79 | Baseline autonomous operation. |
| `trusted` | 80 to 94 | Established track record. Fewer restrictions warranted. |
| `elevated` | 95 to 100 | Long-running, clean history. Maximum autonomy. |

The thresholds are lower bounds hardcoded in the core (`createTheAuth` passes an empty trust config), so they cannot be changed through `createTheAuth` today. Use `score.score` in your own logic if you need different cut-offs.

## Code examples

### Compute a score on demand

```typescript
const score = await theauth.trust.computeScore('agt_abc123');

console.log(score.score);           // 72
console.log(score.level);           // 'standard'
console.log(score.factors.denialRate); // 1.4
```

`computeScore` always reads live audit data and writes the result to the `trust_scores` table. Call it whenever you need a fresh value.

### Read the last computed score

```typescript
const score = await theauth.trust.getScore('agt_abc123');

if (!score) {
  // Score has never been computed for this agent
  console.log('No score yet, call computeScore first');
}
```

`getScore` returns the cached row from the database without recomputing. It returns `null` for agents that have never been scored.

### Recompute scores for all active agents

```typescript
const scores = await theauth.trust.computeAll();

for (const score of scores) {
  console.log(`${score.agentId}: ${score.level} (${score.score})`);
}
```

Useful for a scheduled job that refreshes scores nightly or after a batch of activity.

### Filter agents by trust level

```typescript
// All agents currently in the 'untrusted' band
const untrusted = await theauth.trust.getScores({ level: 'untrusted' });

// Agents with a score of at least 80
const highTrust = await theauth.trust.getScores({ minScore: 80 });
```

`getScores` reads from the `trust_scores` table. Agents that have not been scored yet do not appear in results.

### Gate sensitive operations by trust level

```typescript
const score = await theauth.trust.computeScore(agentId);

if (score.level === 'untrusted' || score.level === 'limited') {
  // Require manual approval before proceeding
  await theauth.approval.request({
    agentId,
    userId: agent.ownerId,
    action: 'delete',
    resource: 'file:prod-data/*',
  });
  return { queued: true };
}

// Proceed autonomously for trusted agents
await deleteFiles(agentId);
```

<Info>
  Scores are recomputed on demand. theAuth does not maintain a background scorer. Call `computeScore` or `computeAll` on a schedule that fits your use case, every request, every few minutes, or nightly.
</Info>

# Anomaly detection

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/anomaly

## What exists today

theAuth does not ship an anomaly detector. There is no `scan()` function and no anomaly finding type. Three small pieces exist, and everything else on this page is something you build on top of the audit log.

| Piece | What it does |
|---|---|
| Trust score `anomalyCount` | `theauth.trust.computeScore()` counts denied audit entries whose `reason` contains `INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS`, `privilege`, or `escalation` (case-insensitive for the last two). Each counted entry lowers the score by 10, on top of 5 for the denial itself. |
| `onViolation` hook | A lifecycle hook that fires on every denied `authorize()` call, with a coarse `type`: `permission_denied`, `rate_limited`, `ip_blocked`, `time_restricted`, or `approval_required`. |
| `anomaly.detected` event type | A name reserved in the event stream's `EventType` list. Nothing in the library emits it. You can emit it yourself with the stream's `emit()`. |

<Warning>
  The built-in denial reasons are plain sentences such as `No permission grants agent "x" access to "write" on "y"`. They do not contain `INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS`, `privilege`, or `escalation`, so `anomalyCount` stays at 0 unless a `beforeAuthorize` hook or your own wrapper produces a reason with one of those words. Do not rely on `anomalyCount` as a privilege escalation detector without that.
</Warning>

### Not implemented

These were described on earlier versions of this page and are not in the TypeScript package: a `scan()` API, the finding types `privilege_escalation`, `high_denial_rate`, `rapid_fire`, `unusual_resource_access`, and `off_hours_activity`, the `AnomalyConfig` options (`since`, `until`, `minDenialRate`, `rapidFireThreshold`, `agentId`), and finding objects with `severity`, `evidence`, and `detectedAt`. If you want these signals, compute them from the audit log as shown below.

## Code examples

### Find denied calls for an agent

```typescript
const denied = await theauth.audit.query({
  agentId: 'agt_abc123',
  result: 'denied',
  since: new Date(Date.now() - 24 * 3_600_000),
});

console.log(`${denied.length} denied call(s) in the last 24 hours`);
```

### Compute a denial rate per agent

```typescript
const since = new Date(Date.now() - 24 * 3_600_000);

const logs = await theauth.audit.query({ since, limit: 5000 });

const byAgent: Record<string, { total: number; denied: number }> = {};

for (const entry of logs) {
  const bucket = (byAgent[entry.agentId] ??= { total: 0, denied: 0 });
  bucket.total++;
  if (entry.result === 'denied') bucket.denied++;
}

const highDenialAgents = Object.entries(byAgent)
  .filter(([, { total, denied }]) => total > 0 && denied / total > 0.2)
  .map(([agentId, { total, denied }]) => ({
    agentId,
    denialRate: (denied / total) * 100,
  }));

console.log('Agents with >20% denial rate:', highDenialAgents);
```

### React to denials with the `onViolation` hook

```typescript
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';

const violations = new Map<string, number>();

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite-native', url: 'theauth.db' },
  hooks: {
    onViolation: async ({ agentId, type, resource, reason }) => {
      const count = (violations.get(agentId) ?? 0) + 1;
      violations.set(agentId, count);
      console.warn(`[violation] ${agentId} ${type} on ${resource}: ${reason}`);
    },
  },
});
```

The hook is called without being awaited, so a slow handler does not delay the `authorize()` result. Keep counters in a durable store if you need them to survive restarts.

### Pause an agent after repeated denials

```typescript
const denied = await theauth.audit.query({
  agentId: 'agt_abc123',
  result: 'denied',
  since: new Date(Date.now() - 3_600_000),
});

if (denied.length >= 3) {
  await theauth.agent.revoke('agt_abc123');
  console.log('Agent revoked after repeated denials.');
}
```

<Warning>
  `agent.revoke()` is permanent. If you want to temporarily suspend an agent and restore it later, create a new agent with the same configuration instead of revoking.
</Warning>

### Read the trust score factors

```typescript
const score = await theauth.trust.computeScore('agt_abc123');

console.log(score.score, score.level);
console.log(score.factors.denialRate, score.factors.anomalyCount);
if (score.factors.lastViolation) {
  console.warn(`Last denial: ${score.factors.lastViolation}`);
}
```

`lastViolation` is the timestamp of the most recent denied call of any kind. Computing a score also stores it.
