# MCP server grants

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/mcp-grants

The MCP authorization server issues tokens for the authorization code flow by default. Four more ways to get a token are available, and all four are off until you configure them:

- `client_credentials`: a confidential client gets a token for itself, with no user involved.
- Token exchange (RFC 8693): trade an access token this server issued for a narrower one, optionally for another resource.
- `jwt-bearer` (RFC 7523): redeem an Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) signed by an identity provider you trust.
- `private_key_jwt`: authenticate a client with a signed assertion instead of a shared secret.

Everything here goes in the `config` object you pass to `createMcpModule`. See [MCP OAuth 2.1](/mcp) for the base setup.

## What changes in the metadata

Each enabled grant is added to `grant_types_supported` in the authorization server metadata. `private_key_jwt` and its algorithm list (`token_endpoint_auth_signing_alg_values_supported`) are always advertised. A grant that is not enabled answers `unsupported_grant_type`.

## Register the client for the grant

A client can only use a grant it is registered for. Through dynamic registration, list the grant type in `grant_types`:

| Grant | `grant_types` value |
| --- | --- |
| Client credentials | `client_credentials` |
| Token exchange | `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange` |
| jwt-bearer | `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer` |

Registration refuses a grant type that is not enabled on the server, and refuses `client_credentials` for a client with `token_endpoint_auth_method: "none"`. For clients you pre-register in config, set `grantTypes` on the entry in `preRegisteredClients`. The default there is `authorization_code` and `refresh_token` only.

<Warning>
  Open dynamic registration lets any caller create a client that lists these grants. The grants still need a `resolvePrincipal` mapping (client credentials), a trusted issuer (jwt-bearer) or a valid subject token (exchange), so registration alone gets nobody a token. If you do not want self-registered clients to be eligible at all, restrict `/mcp/register` or use pre-registered clients.
</Warning>

All three grants require a `resource` (RFC 8707) unless [`lenientClients.optionalResource`](/mcp-client-compat) is on and exactly one resource is configured. None of them issues a refresh token, and `offline_access` is never granted.

## client_credentials

```ts
import { createMcpModule } from "@glinr/theauth/mcp";

const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    // ...issuer, baseUrl, signingSecret, resource
    clientCredentials: {
      enabled: true,
      resolvePrincipal: async (client) => {
        const service = await db.findServiceByClientId(client.clientId);
        if (!service) return null; // refuse
        return {
          subject: `svc:${service.id}`, // becomes the token sub
          agentId: service.agentId,     // emitted as agent_id when set
          agentType: "autonomous",
          trustTier: "standard",
          scopes: ["mcp:read"],         // upper bound for this principal
        };
      },
    },
  },
  // ...your storage callbacks
});
```

`resolvePrincipal` is required. Without it no client can obtain a token, so a client created through open registration is not enough on its own.

The token request:

```http
POST /api/auth/mcp/token
Authorization: Basic base64(client_id:client_secret)
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=client_credentials&scope=mcp:read&resource=https://mcp.example.com
```

Rules:

- The client must be confidential: a secret (`client_secret_basic` or `client_secret_post`) or `private_key_jwt`.
- The token `sub` is the principal's `subject`, never a user.
- Scopes are bounded by `principal.scopes`, falling back to the client's registered `scope`. With neither, the request fails with `invalid_scope`. A request can narrow within that bound, never widen.
- No refresh token is issued. Send a DPoP proof and the token is bound to that key (`token_type: "DPoP"`).

## Token exchange (RFC 8693)

```ts
import { createInMemoryJtiDenylist } from "@glinr/theauth/mcp";

const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    // ...
    jtiDenylist: createInMemoryJtiDenylist(), // required with tokenExchange
    tokenExchange: {
      enabled: true,
      maxChainDepth: 3, // default
      authorize: async ({ client, subject, scopes, resource }) => {
        return client.clientId === "orchestrator" && scopes.every((s) => s.startsWith("mcp:"));
      },
    },
  },
  // ...
});
```

Clients that authenticate with `private_key_jwt` can also revoke tokens through `mcp.revoke(request)`. The framework adapters do not serve `/mcp/revoke` themselves, so mount a `POST` route in your host that calls `mcp.revoke(request)` (see [MCP](/mcp)); metadata advertises `<baseUrl>/mcp/revoke`, so mount it there. The assertion audience must be the revoke endpoint URL or the issuer, an assertion addressed to the token endpoint is refused there, and the `jti` store is shared with the token endpoint. An assertion combined with basic auth or `client_secret` is rejected.

`createMcpModule` throws at startup if `tokenExchange.enabled` is set without `jtiDenylist`, unless you pass `auth`, which supplies the shared database denylist. The denylist is what makes a revoked subject token fail the exchange. See the multi-instance note below.

The request carries a `subject_token` (and optionally an `actor_token`), both with `..._token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token`. Only access tokens issued by this server are accepted. Other token types are rejected with `invalid_request`.

```http
grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange
&subject_token=eyJ...
&subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token
&scope=mcp:read
&resource=https://tools.example.com
```

What the server enforces:

| Rule | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Subject and actor tokens | Must verify, be unexpired and not be on the denylist. |
| Scope | Narrow only. Anything outside the subject token's scopes is `invalid_scope`. |
| Audience | Unchanged, or another configured resource (`resource` or `audience`). Otherwise `invalid_target`. |
| Lifetime | The new token never outlives the subject token. |
| DPoP | A bound subject token needs a proof from the same key, and the new token carries that binding. |
| Delegation chain | The new token gets a nested `act` claim, capped at `maxChainDepth` hops (default 3). |
| Policy | `authorize` returning `false` refuses with `access_denied`. |

The `act` claim names the actor: the actor token's user and client when you send one, otherwise the exchanging client. Earlier hops are nested inside it, and resource servers see them as `principal.delegationChain` (see [DPoP and requireMcpAuth](/dpop)). The response includes `issued_token_type`.

## jwt-bearer and ID-JAG (RFC 7523)

An enterprise identity provider signs an assertion that says "this user may use this client at this resource". The client redeems it at the token endpoint.

```ts
const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    // ...
    jwtBearer: {
      enabled: true,
      trustedIssuers: [
        {
          issuer: "https://idp.corp.example",
          jwksUri: "https://idp.corp.example/.well-known/jwks.json",
        },
      ],
      mapSubject: async ({ issuer, subject, clientId, scopes }) => {
        const user = await db.findUserByEmail(subject);
        return user?.id ?? null; // null refuses the grant
      },
      // algs: ["ES256", "ES384", "EdDSA", "PS256", "RS256"], // default
      // maxLifetimeSeconds: 300,                              // default
      // clockSkewSeconds: 30,                                 // default
    },
  },
  // ...
});
```

`trustedIssuers` must have at least one entry and `mapSubject` is required, or startup throws. Each issuer takes `jwksUri` (HTTPS, fetched through the SSRF-safe fetcher), static `jwks`, or both. Static keys are tried first, and a `jwksUri` is consulted when no static key matches. Fetched key sets are cached in process for five minutes, and an unknown `kid` triggers at most one refetch every 30 seconds. If a refetch fails, the stale copy is used for up to 30 minutes.

The assertion must have JOSE header `typ: oauth-id-jag+jwt` and claims `iss`, `sub`, `aud`, `exp`, `iat`, `jti` and `client_id`. The checks:

- `iss` is one of the trusted issuers, and the signature verifies against its keys.
- `aud` equals this server's `issuer`.
- `client_id` equals the authenticated client.
- `exp - iat` is at most `maxLifetimeSeconds`.
- `jti` has not been seen from that issuer. Replays are tracked in `assertionStorage`.
- An optional `scope` claim bounds the scopes (default `openid`), and an optional `resource` claim must agree with the request.

```http
grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer
&assertion=eyJ...
&resource=https://mcp.example.com
```

## private_key_jwt client authentication

Register the client with public keys instead of a secret:

```json
{
  "redirect_uris": [],
  "grant_types": ["client_credentials"],
  "token_endpoint_auth_method": "private_key_jwt",
  "jwks_uri": "https://agent.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json"
}
```

Give exactly one of `jwks` (public keys only, private members are refused) or `jwks_uri` (public HTTPS). Client ID Metadata Documents can declare `private_key_jwt` too. No secret is generated for these clients.

At the token endpoint the client sends `client_assertion_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer` and a `client_assertion`. The assertion must have:

- `iss` and `sub` both equal to the `client_id`.
- `aud` equal to the token endpoint URL (`dpop.tokenEndpointUrl`, else `<baseUrl>/mcp/token`) or the issuer.
- `exp` no more than 300 seconds out (30 seconds of skew allowed), and a `jti`.
- A signature in ES256, ES384, EdDSA, PS256 or RS256. HMAC and `none` are never accepted.

Each `jti` works once per client. Do not send a `client_secret` or Basic header alongside an assertion: the request is refused.

## Multi-instance deployments

Two stores default to process memory and break down behind a load balancer.

**`jtiDenylist`.** `createInMemoryJtiDenylist()` is per process. A token revoked through `mcp.revoke` on one instance still exchanges on another. With `auth` the default is already the shared database store (see [MCP token revocation](/mcp-revocation)). Otherwise pass your own `McpJtiDenylist` (`revoke(jti, expiresAt)` and `isRevoked(jti)`) backed by Redis or your database.

**`assertionStorage`.** The replay cache for `private_key_jwt` assertions and jwt-bearer `jti` values defaults to an in-process store. With several instances an assertion can be replayed once per instance. Give every instance the same shared store:

```ts
const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  // ...
  secondaryStorage: "database", // or a Redis storage
});

const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    // ...
    assertionStorage: theauth.secondaryStorage.for("nonces"),
  },
  // ...
});
```

Replay protection is only as strict as the store's `incr`. Cloudflare KV is not atomic (`atomicIncr` is `false`), so two simultaneous replays can both pass there.

# MCP token revocation

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/mcp-revocation

An MCP access token is a signed JWT. A resource server can check the signature and `exp` and never talk to theAuth again, which is fast and also means a token outlives the thing that justified it. This page explains how theAuth closes that gap, how to choose a freshness mode, and what it does not cover.

The short version: with a database and the default settings, revoking a delegation link, an agent, a single token or a refresh token family makes the next MCP request that carries an affected token fail on every theAuth instance that shares the database. Signing a user out everywhere, banning, deleting or erasing a user, and deprovisioning through SCIM do the same for that user's tokens, and the token endpoint refuses to mint new ones from refresh tokens or authorization codes issued before the revoke. Some paths are not covered, and the Limits section lists them. A request that already passed validation finishes.

## What a token carries

A token minted by [token exchange](/mcp-grants) keeps the RFC 8693 `act` claim, nested with the current actor outermost. It also carries a private claim, `theauth_dlg`, that ties the token to the exact records its authority rests on:

```json
{
  "act": { "sub": "agent-b", "act": { "sub": "agent-a" } },
  "agent_id": "agent-b",
  "theauth_dlg": { "v": 1, "agt": ["agent-a", "agent-b"], "lnk": ["chain_01H..."] },
  "theauth_pjti": ["jti-of-the-subject-token"]
}
```

- `agt` lists the agent ids on the authority path, root first. Every one must stay `active` and unexpired.
- `lnk` lists the delegation link id for each consecutive pair in `agt`.
- `agent_id` (and `principal.agent`) is the acting agent, the last entry of `agt`. A bound token whose `agent_id` is not in `agt` is invalid.
- `theauth_pjti` (exchanged tokens only) lists the jtis of the subject token lineage, root first. Revoking any of those tokens, or the refresh family behind one, revokes this token too: on the next live call, within the poll window in cached mode, and on the next `revalidate()` in offline mode.
- Exchange refuses (`invalid_grant`) a child naming an agent the subject user neither owns nor reaches over live delegation links from an agent they own.

The claim is signed, so a resource server can trust it only after verifying the signature. It holds ids and nothing else: no permissions, no names.

Tokens are bound when their authority resolves to agent rows: token exchange, and authorization code, refresh, client credentials and jwt-bearer tokens that carry `agent_id`. An ordinary token gets the agent's live inbound path up to its root, `agt: [root, ..., agentId]` with one `lnk` per hop, or `agt: [agentId]` and an empty `lnk` when nobody delegated to it. The path is capped at 8 hops above the agent, and the validator still checks the root's own inbound link live. Because every link is in the claim, revoking a delegation above the agent is seen in cached mode and on `revalidate()` in offline mode, not only in live mode. A token with no agent behind it, such as a plain user to service token, is unbound. Only token, subject and client revocation apply to it, because there is no delegation record to revoke.

A token also never outlives its sources. At mint time `exp` is the earliest of the configured lifetime, the subject and actor token expiry, every link's expiry and every agent's expiry on the path. That is a cap on `exp`, so it applies whatever freshness mode you run. It is not a revocation: revoking the parent token is a separate rule, covered by `theauth_pjti` above.

## Freshness modes

The mode decides what a resource server validation reads. Set it in the `revocation` block of the MCP config:

```ts
const mcp = createMcpModule({
  auth: theauth,
  config: {
    // ...issuer, baseUrl, signingSecret, resource
    revocation: {
      mode: "live", // "live" | "cached" | "offline"
    },
  },
});
```

| Mode | What validation reads | Staleness after a revoke | Cost per request |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `live` | The revocation table and the binding check (one read per agent and link on the path, plus the walk up from the root) | None on any instance sharing the database | A few indexed reads. There is no fixed bound: it grows with the path length |
| `cached` | A per process cache keyed by `jti` | None on the instance that performs the revoke, which clears its cache when it pushes. Other instances usually within `pollIntervalMs`, never longer than `maxStalenessMs` | One small query per instance per `pollIntervalMs`, plus a live read on a cache miss |
| `offline` | Signature, `exp` and the `jtiDenylist` read for the token's own `jti` | Up to the token's `exp`. A revoked parent token, link, agent or user is not seen until you call `revalidate()` | One read of the denylist when one is configured (it is by default with `auth`), none otherwise |

The default is `live` when you pass `auth` to `createMcpModule` (a shared database), and `offline` when you pass your own stores, because there is nothing shared to read. The environment variable `THEAUTH_MCP_REVOCATION_MODE` sets the mode when the config does not.

Three things hold in every mode. The token endpoint checks live for the refresh token and authorization code grants: a refresh token or code whose `jti`, subject (sign out everywhere, ban, delete), client (CIMD block) or bound agent was revoked is refused with `invalid_grant`, and a store error fails closed with `server_error`. Token exchange validates the subject and actor tokens live. Introspection always checks live. Expiry is always honored at mint time. The `client_credentials` and `jwt-bearer` grants do not read the revocation table before they mint (see Limits).

Live mode costs a handful of primary key or indexed lookups on requests that are usually tool calls, so most deployments should leave it on. Move to `cached` above roughly a thousand validations per second per instance:

```ts
revocation: {
  mode: "cached",
  maxStalenessMs: 5000, // hard upper bound, default 5000
  pollIntervalMs: 1000, // how often an instance checks for new revocations, default 1000
  cacheMax: 10000,      // entries per process, default 10000
}
```

| Option | Env var | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mode` | `THEAUTH_MCP_REVOCATION_MODE` | `live` with `auth`, else `offline` |
| `maxStalenessMs` | `THEAUTH_MCP_REVOCATION_MAX_STALENESS_MS` | 5000 |
| `pollIntervalMs` | `THEAUTH_MCP_REVOCATION_POLL_MS` | 1000 |
| `cacheMax` | `THEAUTH_MCP_REVOCATION_CACHE_MAX` | 10000 |
| `revokeOnSignOutEverywhere` | none | `true` |
| `requireBoundChain` | none | `false` |
| `clockSkewMs` | `THEAUTH_MCP_REVOCATION_SKEW_MS` | 0 (opt in) |
| `pruneIntervalMs` | `THEAUTH_MCP_REVOCATION_PRUNE_INTERVAL_MS` | 60000 |
| `onRevoked` | none | none |

`revokeOnSignOutEverywhere`, `clockSkewMs` and `onRevoked` are read from the `mcp` config you pass to `createTheAuth`, because the revocation bus and the database store are built there. If you pass `mcp` only to `createMcpModule`, no `sub` rows are written and sign out everywhere does nothing for MCP tokens. Pass the same config object to both, as the [MCP page](/mcp) does.

`clockSkewMs` widens the `sub` and `client` watermark by that many milliseconds, so a revoker whose clock lags still kills tokens minted just before the revoke. The cost is that a token minted within that window after a revoke is also refused. It defaults to 0, which assumes your instances keep NTP time. Set it (2000 is a reasonable value) if they do not.

In cached mode a process that performs the revoke clears its cache at once. Other instances compare a fingerprint of the revocation table (the newest `revoked_at_ms` and the number of rows near it) on each poll and clear when it changes. If a revocation row failed to write, or an agent expiry was shortened by hand, the cache entry still dies at `maxStalenessMs`.

In offline mode, shorten `accessTokenTtl` (300 seconds is a reasonable start). Exchanged tokens cannot be refreshed, so the lifetime is the whole bound.

A store error during a live or cached check rejects the token with a server error. It never falls back to offline.

## The shared denylist and migration 0007

Revocations are rows in `theauth_mcp_revocations`, created by migration `0007`. The same migration adds indexes on `theauth_delegation_chains` for `from_agent_id` and `to_agent_id`, which the delegation liveness walk needed. Run `theauth db up` (or let the instance migrate on start). With `skipMigrations: true`, generate the SQL with `theauth db sql --from 0007`. See [Database](/database).

| `kind` | Denies | Row removed after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `jti` | One token | The token's `exp` |
| `dlg` | Every token bound to that delegation link | The link's expiry |
| `agent` | Every token bound to that agent | The agent's expiry, or 7 days when it has none |
| `sub` | Every token of a user minted at or before the revoke | 7 days |
| `client` | Every token of a client minted at or before the revoke | `accessTokenTtl` plus 60 seconds for a CIMD block |

A row never expires less than 60 seconds after it is written, so a row for an already expired link outlives clock skew. Rows for things with no expiry last 7 days unless `THEAUTH_MCP_REVOCATION_RETENTION_MS` sets another value. A `jti` row is skipped when the token expired more than a minute ago.

`sub` and `client` rows are watermarks on `iat`. Validation reads both kinds (a hit reports `client_revoked`). `mcp.cimd.block` writes a `client` row for the blocked client when the denylist is the shared store, so its tokens are refused at once in live mode on every instance (see [Client ID Metadata Documents](/mcp-client-id-metadata)). You can also write one yourself through the store. A token minted in the same second as the revoke also dies, which fails closed. Expired rows are pruned after writes, in batches of 500 and at most four batches per run, and at most once per `pruneIntervalMs` per instance (60 seconds by default). There are no timers, so pruning only happens on an instance that writes. For a cron job or a read only instance, call `auth.revocations.prune()`, which deletes expired rows now and resolves to the number deleted. The delegation and agent tables stay the source of truth for live checks. The rows exist to speed up the fail path and to drive cache invalidation across instances.

With `auth`, `config.jtiDenylist` defaults to this shared store, so a token revoked on one instance is refused on all of them. An explicit `jtiDenylist` always wins. With `createInMemoryJtiDenylist()` the denylist is per process.

## What pushes a revocation

| Trigger | Rows written |
| --- | --- |
| `auth.delegation.revoke(id)`, including every link in the cascade | `dlg` for each revoked link |
| `auth.agent.revoke(id)` | `agent` for the agent, `dlg` for the links it cut |
| `session.revokeAll(userId)` (sign out everywhere) | `sub`, unless `revokeOnSignOutEverywhere: false` |
| `admin.banUser`, `admin.deleteUser`, `gdpr.deleteUser`, SCIM deactivation or deprovisioning | `sub` for the user and `agent` for each agent they own |
| `POST /mcp/revoke` (RFC 7009) of an access token | `jti` for that token |
| `POST /mcp/revoke` of a refresh token, and refresh token reuse detection | `jti` for the token and for each live access token of the refresh token family |

The `sub` row is a watermark on `iat`. `admin.unbanUser` does not bring back tokens issued before the ban, and the owner's agents stay revoked.

Revoking a single session does not touch MCP tokens, because they are not tied to a session. Signing out does not delete refresh token families either. The live check at the token endpoint is what stops a refresh token after a sign out everywhere.

A push is retried once. If the retry also fails, the failure is logged with the revoked ids (never a token) and counted: `auth.revocations.stats()` reports `pushFailures` for pushes that failed after the retry and `attemptFailures` for every failed attempt. The revoke itself continues: the link or agent row is already revoked, so live mode still sees it and cached mode falls back to its staleness bound. The instance clears its own cache before it writes and again after. If the row for an explicit token revoke fails to write, the revoke call fails (the HTTP route answers 503 `temporarily_unavailable`, described below) instead of reporting success, because that row is the only record. Pushes work on runtimes without `process`, such as Cloudflare Workers without `nodejs_compat` and Deno.

An agent whose `expiresAt` passes is not pushed. Expiry is read from the agent row on live checks and capped into `exp` at mint.

## Introspection and revocation endpoints

`POST /mcp/revoke` is RFC 7009. A client may revoke its own tokens, and a `client_id` mismatch answers 200 without doing anything, as the RFC asks. An unknown token also answers 200. When the revocation store cannot record the revoke, the endpoint answers 503 with `Retry-After` and `{ "error": "temporarily_unavailable" }` (RFC 7009 section 2.2.1) instead of a 500. This instance still treats the token as revoked locally (its freshness cache is dropped), but other instances learn about it only after a successful retry, so the client should retry.

`POST /mcp/introspect` is RFC 7662, for resource servers that cannot or should not trust the JWT alone. It is off until you enable it:

```ts
introspection: {
  enabled: true,
  resourceServers: [
    { clientId: "orders-api", audiences: ["https://orders.example.com/mcp"] },
  ],
  maxRequestsPerMinute: 600, // per client, per instance, env THEAUTH_MCP_INTROSPECT_RPM
}
```

When enabled and mounted, the metadata advertises `introspection_endpoint`. The route is mounted by default and answers 404 until `enabled` is true. If you mount a subset with `routes: { mcp: { ... } }`, include `introspect: true`.

The caller must be a confidential client and authenticate with `client_secret_basic`, `client_secret_post` or `private_key_jwt`. Public clients are refused with 401 `invalid_client`. No token parsing happens before that check.

The answer is always live. Only access tokens are introspectable, and refresh tokens report `active: false`. A `token` longer than 8192 characters is inactive without any cryptography. Responses carry `Cache-Control: no-store`.

Who sees what:

- Active token, entitled caller: `scope`, `client_id`, `sub`, `exp`, `iat`, `aud`, `iss`, `jti`, `token_type`, and when present `cnf`, `act`, `agent_id` and `theauth_dlg`.
- Inactive token, entitled caller: `{ "active": false, "theauth_inactive_reason": "delegation_revoked" }`. The reasons are `expired`, `revoked`, `subject_revoked`, `client_revoked`, `delegation_revoked`, `delegation_expired`, `agent_revoked`, `agent_expired` and `invalid`.
- Any other caller: exactly `{ "active": false }`.

A caller is entitled when it is the token's own `client_id`, or a `resourceServers` entry whose `audiences` include the token's `aud`. A resource server that is not listed learns nothing about why a token is dead, and cannot tell a revoked token from one it was never entitled to see.

There is no default audit row. Pass `introspectionAudit` to `createMcpModule` to receive the caller client, the `jti`, the result and the reason after each decision of an authenticated caller. The token is never passed to it.

## Shared Signals events

Pass `onRevoked` in the `mcp.revocation` config of `createTheAuth` to forward revocations to a Shared Signals transmitter:

```ts
revocation: {
  onRevoked: (event) => signals.bridge.onMcpRevocation(event),
}
```

Here `signals` is the result of `sharedSignals(...)`. `dlg`, `agent` and `sub` revocations with a known user become CAEP `session-revoked` events, with the revoke reason in `reason_admin` and a session id of the form `<kind>:<id>`. A `jti` revocation sends nothing, because there is no user worth naming. Delivery is asynchronous and errors are swallowed. This is event emission, not a CAEP or SSF conformance claim. See [Standards](/standards).

## Tightening exchange

By default a token exchange whose actors resolve to no agent row mints an unbound token (`act` only). Set `requireBoundChain: true` to refuse it with `invalid_grant`, so every delegated token is revocable through its delegation:

```ts
revocation: { requireBoundChain: true }
```

When a binding store is attached (the default with `auth`), exchange also refuses a chain where two consecutive agent actors have no live delegation link between them, whatever this setting says. With custom stores and no binding store, nothing is checked.

Exchange also checks ownership. Every agent the child token names must be one the subject user owns, or one reached over live delegation links from an agent they own. Otherwise exchange answers `invalid_grant` and writes a denied `mcp.token_exchange` audit row under the refused agent.

## Long running handlers

Validation happens once, before the handler runs. A tool call that takes minutes, or an SSE stream, would otherwise outlive a revoke. `requireMcpAuth` hands the handler a session whose `revalidate()` repeats the revocation and binding checks live:

```ts
const handler = mcp.requireMcpAuth(
  async (request, principal) => {
    for (const step of steps) {
      const alive = await principal.session?.revalidate?.();
      if (alive && !alive.success) return new Response("revoked", { status: 401 });
      await runStep(step);
    }
    return Response.json({ ok: true });
  },
  { requiredScopes: ["mcp:write"], revalidateEveryMs: 5000 },
);
```

`revalidateEveryMs` throttles the store reads: a call within that window of the last check returns success without querying. It is off by default, and without it `revalidate()` always checks.

## Limits

These are the places revocation does not reach. Plan around them.

- **Offline resource servers.** A server that verifies the JWT itself, or that caches introspection answers, sees a revoke when its cache ends or the token expires. Only live validation and uncached introspection are immediate.
- **Calls in progress.** A request validated before the revoke commits completes. Streams and long handlers are cut off only if they call `revalidate()`.
- **Offline and cached freshness.** Offline mode trusts the token until `exp`, apart from a `jti` row in the denylist. It does not see a revoked parent token, link, agent or user until you call `revalidate()`. Cached mode has the poll delay described above.
- **Sign out and refresh tokens.** Signing out does not delete refresh token families. The live check at the token endpoint refuses the refresh, but the family rows stay until they expire.
- **client_credentials and jwt-bearer.** These grants mint without reading the revocation table. A `sub` or `client` watermark kills tokens minted before it, and does not stop these grants minting a new token afterward. An agent bound client is still refused once its agent is revoked or expired.
- **Authorization code and another user's agent.** The authorization code path refuses a revoked or expired agent, but it does not yet refuse a client that an admin bound to another user's agent. This is an open policy decision.
- **Unbound tokens.** A token whose actors are not theAuth agents has no delegation to revoke. Use `requireBoundChain` if that is not acceptable.
- **Tokens minted before the upgrade.** They carry no `theauth_dlg`. With `act` and no `delegationStore` they are trusted until `exp`; tokens with an `agent_id` get a single agent status check. Exchanged tokens cannot refresh, so the gap closes within `accessTokenTtl`, one hour by default.
- **HS256 shares the secret.** With `signingSecret`, any resource server that holds the secret can sign a token, including one with a forged `theauth_dlg` or none. Use RS256 or ES256 signing keys (see the MCP page) for resource servers you do not fully control, and give them the public key only. Setting signing keys is not enough: a server that still has `signingSecret` configured accepts HS256 tokens, so remove it from those servers.
- **No push on expiry.** A shortened expiry is seen by live and cached modes and not by offline. Nothing is pushed when an agent simply expires.
- **Replicas lag.** Live checks must read the primary. Pointing them at a lagging read replica adds the lag to every bound above.
- **Custom stores.** With your own stores and no database, or with the in-memory denylist, there is no cross instance freshness.
- **Replay.** Binding does not stop a stolen live token being used. [DPoP](/dpop) does. The two are independent: the binding says the authority is alive, `cnf.jkt` says the caller is the holder.

# MCP client compatibility

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/mcp-client-compat

Some MCP clients do not follow the strict shape the authorization server enforces by default. They leave out `resource`, ask for vendor scopes the server has never heard of, redirect to a loopback address on a random port, or name a sub-path of your MCP server as the audience. By default every one of those is an error.

`lenientClients` turns individual relaxations on, one at a time. Every option is off unless you set it, which is the strict behavior described in [MCP OAuth 2.1](/mcp).

```ts
import { createMcpModule } from "@glinr/theauth/mcp";

const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    // ...issuer, baseUrl, signingSecret, resource
    lenientClients: {
      optionalResource: true,
      pathAudience: true,
      dropUnknownScopes: true,
      loopbackAnyPort: true,
    },
  },
  // ...your storage callbacks
});
```

## Options

| Option | Relaxes | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `optionalResource` | A missing `resource` parameter | off |
| `dropUnknownScopes` | Rejecting scopes the server does not support | off |
| `loopbackAnyPort` | Exact match of loopback redirect URIs | off |
| `loopbackAllowLocalhost` | Adds `http://localhost` to `loopbackAnyPort` | off |
| `pathAudience` | Exact match of the `resource` value | off |

### optionalResource

When `resource` is missing at the authorize endpoint or in an authorization code exchange, it defaults to the one configured resource (`allowedResources` when set, otherwise `resource`). With zero or several configured resources, a missing value is still `invalid_target`. A `resource` that is present but not allowed is always `invalid_target`. It also lets the non-interactive grants (client credentials, jwt-bearer) fall back to the same single resource.

Tradeoff: low. The audience can only ever be a resource you configured, and with a single one there is nothing to be ambiguous about.

### dropUnknownScopes

A requested scope the server does not support is dropped instead of failing the request. The supported set is the defaults (`openid`, `profile`, `email`, `offline_access`) plus `config.scopes`. The granted scope comes back in the token response, and the request only fails with `invalid_scope` when scopes were requested and none are left. On a refresh, scopes outside the original grant are dropped the same way, so a refresh cannot widen.

Tradeoff: medium. A client no longer finds out from an error that it asked for something wrong, and it may receive less than it expected. It can never receive more than the server supports and its registration allows. Clients must read the returned `scope` instead of assuming.

### loopbackAnyPort

RFC 8252 section 7.3. When a registered redirect URI is `http://127.0.0.1` or `http://[::1]`, a request matches if scheme, host, path and query are identical and only the port differs. `127.0.0.1` and `[::1]` do not match each other, and URIs with a fragment or userinfo never match. `localhost` is excluded unless `loopbackAllowLocalhost` is also set.

Tradeoff: higher. Any process on the user's machine can listen on a port and receive the redirect. PKCE S256 is what stops that process from redeeming the code, and this server requires PKCE for every client. Do not enable this for a client that cannot do S256. It only affects clients that registered a loopback URI.

### pathAudience

A requested `resource` matches a configured one when the two are equal apart from a trailing slash, or when the configured value is a path prefix of the request on a `/` boundary. `https://api.example.com/mcp/sse` matches `https://api.example.com/mcp`, and `https://api.example.com/mcp-admin` does not. Requests carrying a query or fragment never match. When several configured resources match, the longest wins. The issued token's `aud` is always the configured resource, never the sub-path.

Tradeoff: low to medium. A client can get a token for the whole configured resource while naming one sub-path, so do not rely on the sub-path to narrow what the token allows.

## Recommended profile

For a single-resource MCP server that public clients (Client ID Metadata Documents or dynamic registration) connect to:

```ts
lenientClients: {
  optionalResource: true,   // many clients omit resource
  pathAudience: true,       // clients address /mcp/sse or /mcp/messages
  dropUnknownScopes: true,  // vendor scopes the server does not list
  loopbackAnyPort: true,    // native clients use ephemeral ports
},
clientIdMetadataDocuments: {
  enabled: true,
  allowedHosts: ["clients.example.com"], // hosts whose client metadata you accept
},
```

Leave `loopbackAllowLocalhost` off unless a client you must support registers `http://localhost/...`. If you only serve clients that behave, enable none of these. The strict defaults are the safer ones, and each switch is easy to add later when a specific client needs it.

## Differences from the Go library

The Go library has the same five switches as `ClientCompat` (`OptionalResource`, `DropUnknownScopes`, `LoopbackAnyPort`, `LoopbackAllowLocalhost`, `PathAudience`). See [Client compatibility profile](/go/guides/client-compat) for its documentation. The meaning matches, with these differences:

- **Scope source.** Go keeps a scope only if it is in the resource catalog and in the client's registered scope. The TypeScript server checks the server's supported set (defaults plus `config.scopes`) at the authorize endpoint. Grants that are bounded by a registered scope or principal still enforce that bound.
- **Path audience strictness.** Go also refuses userinfo, dot segments and percent-encoded dots or slashes in the requested resource. The TypeScript check compares origin and path after URL parsing and refuses a query or fragment.
- **jwt-bearer.** Go compares the raw `resource` of an ID-JAG assertion and does not accept sub-paths there. TypeScript canonicalizes both the claim and the request value.
- **No PAR.** The TypeScript server has no pushed authorization requests, so `optionalResource` applies at authorize and token only.

Clients that identify themselves with an `https://` client ID document are covered in [Client ID metadata documents](/mcp-client-id-metadata).

  <Card title="Go: client compatibility" href="/go/guides/client-compat" icon="plug">

# Client ID metadata documents

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/mcp-client-id-metadata

A client ID metadata document lets an MCP client identify itself with a URL instead of a pre-registered ID or a dynamic registration call. The client's `client_id` is an `https://` URL that points at a JSON document. theAuth fetches that document when the client first asks for authorization and reads the client's settings from it.

This page covers how that works, how to turn it on, and what your application has to do to use it safely.

## How it works

The `client_id` is an `https` URL with a path, for example `https://app.example.com/oauth/client.json`. It has no query, no fragment, no credentials and no port.

When an authorization request names a client ID that is not already stored, theAuth fetches the URL. The response must be a `200` JSON document, and the document must name itself: its `client_id` field must equal the URL it was fetched from. A document that names a different URL, or that leaves the field out, is rejected.

The document can set the client's redirect URIs, whether the client is public or uses `private_key_jwt`, the grant types and scopes it may request, and display fields. It cannot set a shared secret, and it cannot name an agent. Any field that breaks a rule rejects the whole document. Unknown `theauth_*` fields are rejected as well.

After a successful fetch, theAuth stores the client and reuses the stored copy until the cache expires. See [Caching and refresh](#caching-and-refresh).

## Enabling it

Turn the feature on in the MCP module config. `consentPage` is required. Without it, `createMcpModule` throws at startup, because any host can publish a client document, so every authorization has to be approved by a user.

```ts
import { createMcpModule } from "@glinr/theauth/mcp";

const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    // ...issuer, baseUrl, signingSecret, resource
    consentPage: "https://app.example.com/consent",
    clientIdMetadataDocuments: {
      enabled: true,
      resolver: "auto",
      // Optional. Exact hosts or "*.example.com" (subdomains only).
      // When set, nothing outside this list is fetched.
      allowedHosts: ["*.example.com"],
      // Optional. Same syntax, checked before allowedHosts.
      deniedHosts: ["bad.example.com"],
    },
  },
  // ...your storage callbacks
});
```

Choose `resolver` by runtime:

| Runtime | Value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Node | `"auto"` | Uses `node:dns` to check the addresses a name resolves to. |
| Bun | `"auto"` | Same as Node. |
| Deno | `"auto"` | Same as Node. |
| Cloudflare Workers | `createDohResolver()` | Resolves names over DNS over HTTPS, because `node:dns` is not available. |
| Cloudflare Workers | `"none"` | Checks host names only, with no address check. Pair it with `allowedHosts`. |

On a runtime without `node:dns`, `"auto"` fails every fetch closed (no address check means no fetch), so set the resolver explicitly. The one exception is a configured `allowedHosts` list: the hosts are then vetted by name, fetches go ahead, and theAuth logs a warning once through the module logger that no address check is running.

### Options

Every option except `enabled` is optional. Numbers outside the range are clamped, not rejected.

| Option | Default | Range or note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `resolver` | `"auto"` | `"auto"`, `"none"`, or a resolver such as `createDohResolver()`. |
| `fetchImpl` | global `fetch` | Override, for example to pin the connection to the resolved address. |
| `allowedHosts`, `deniedHosts` | none | Exact hosts or `*.example.com`. Denied is checked first. |
| `maxBytes` | 5120 | 1024 to 16384. |
| `timeoutMs` | 5000 | 500 to 10000. Covers headers and body. |
| `minCacheSeconds` | 60 | Floor 30. |
| `maxCacheSeconds` | 86400 | Ceiling 604800. |
| `defaultCacheSeconds` | 3600 | Used when the response has no `max-age`. |
| `negativeCacheSeconds` | 30 | 0 to 300. 0 turns the failed-fetch memory off. |
| `onBoundClientChange` | `"disable"` | `"disable"` or `"allow"`. |
| `maxFetchesPerHostPerMinute` | 30 | 1 to 100000. Admin `refresh` is excluded. |
| `maxUnconsentedClients` | 1000 | Needs a store that implements `countUnconsentedCimdClients`. |
| `unconsentedRetentionSeconds` | 86400 | How long an unconsented row is kept before a sweep may delete it. |
| `onEvent` | none | Receives `cimd.fetched`, `cimd.rejected`, `cimd.changed` and `cimd.blocked`. |

## Turning off dynamic registration

Clients that use a metadata document do not need dynamic registration. If you only serve metadata document clients and pre-registered clients, turn registration off:

```ts
registration: { enabled: false }
```

With this set, `POST /mcp/register` answers 404, `registration_endpoint` is left out of the metadata document, and `registerClient` returns `REGISTRATION_DISABLED`. Clients that were registered earlier keep working.

## Building the consent screen

theAuth does not render the consent screen. Your consent page does, and it gets the facts from `mcp.describeClient(clientId, redirectUri?, { firstUse? })`. Without `redirectUri` it describes the client's first registered redirect URI. A URI the client did not register fails with `INVALID_REDIRECT_URI`, and a blocked, disabled or unknown client fails with `INVALID_CLIENT`. Control and bidirectional override characters are stripped from `clientName`, and a `logoUri` that is not http or https is dropped. The result is a `Result`, and its data includes these fields:

- `verifiedHost`: the host name of the `client_id`. Show this as the headline, for example "app.example.com wants access".
- `clientName`: the name the client wrote in its document. Show it under the host with the wording "calls itself ...". Never show it alone, and never use it to decide who the client is.
- `logoUri`: the logo the client wrote. The browser loads it, and theAuth does not fetch it.
- `redirectUri` and `redirectHost`: where the approval sends the user. Always show the redirect host.
- `source`: `"cimd"`, `"dcr"` or `"preregistered"`. `verifiedHost` is `null` unless the source is `cimd`.
- `agentId`: the agent an admin bound the client to, or `null`.
- `warnings`: a list of codes. Render every one of them.

The warning codes:

| Code | Meaning | What to show |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `redirect_host_differs` | The redirect host is not the client host or a subdomain of it. | A visible caution that approval sends the user to a different site. |
| `localhost_redirect` | The redirect URI is on loopback. Any program on the user's machine can listen there and receive the code. | A visible caution that a local program may be the one asking. |
| `idn_host` | The host contains an `xn--` label. | The name in its ASCII form, and a note that it may look like another name. |
| `name_mentions_other_host` | `clientName` contains a domain name that is not the client host. | A note that the name points at another site. |
| `client_uri_host_differs` | The client's home page is on a different host. | A note with both hosts. |
| `http_redirect` | The redirect URI uses plain http. | A caution that the code travels unencrypted. |
| `bound_to_agent` | An admin bound this client to an agent. | Say that approving lets the client act as that agent. |
| `recently_changed` | The stored document was re-read and updated in the last 24 hours. | A note that the client's settings changed lately. |
| `first_use` | The user has not approved this client before. Your app sets this flag by passing `{ firstUse: true }`. | Extra text on the first approval. |

Show the host first. The client's own name, logo and description are the client author's words, and the author can write anything in them.

## Binding a client to an agent

A client can be bound to an agent so its tokens act as that agent. Only an admin can do this, through the module API:

```ts
await mcp.clients.bindAgent(clientId, agentId);
```

`bindAgent` fetches and stores a client that was never used before it writes the binding, and it throws when the document cannot be fetched, is invalid or is blocked. The document cannot name an agent. A document with an `agent_id` field or a `theauth_*` field is rejected.

After a client is bound, its document can still change. If its `redirect_uris` or `token_endpoint_auth_method` change, the default `onBoundClientChange: "disable"` turns the client off with the reason `cimd_changed_while_bound`. An admin turns it back on with `mcp.cimd.enable(clientId)`. Changes to the keys (`jwks` or `jwks_uri`) do not disable the client. The purpose of this rule is that a takeover of the client's domain does not silently keep the agent's identity.

## Blocking a client

Block a single client by its URL, or every client on a host:

```ts
await mcp.cimd.block({ kind: "url", value: "https://app.example.com/oauth/client.json", reason: "abuse report" });
await mcp.cimd.block({ kind: "host", value: "example.net", reason: "domain sold" });
```

A URL block must be the canonical `client_id`. A host block takes a bare host name (a leading `*.` is accepted and means the same thing) and covers subdomains.

The two kinds behave differently. A URL block stops new authorizations, deletes the client's stored tokens so refresh stops, adds its access token ids to `jtiDenylist` when one is set, writes a `client` row to the shared revocation store (so every token the client holds is refused at once in live mode, and in cached mode within `maxStalenessMs`), and marks the stored client as disabled (reason `blocked`). A host block is checked on every authorize and token call, so clients on that host stop working at once. It does not disable their stored rows. When the store can list CIMD clients it also deletes their tokens and writes a `client` revocation row for each, so unblocking the host later does not bring old tokens back. Unblocking never turns a disabled client back on: run `mcp.cimd.enable(clientId)` for that. Remove a block with `mcp.cimd.unblock(id)`, list blocks with `mcp.cimd.listBlocks()`, and read a stored client with its document snapshot through `mcp.cimd.inspect(clientId)`.

Blocking needs a block store. Pass `auth` to `createMcpModule`, or a `blocks` store, or `block` throws.

Blocks are stored in the `theauth_mcp_client_blocks` table on database stores. The in-memory store keeps them only for the life of the process.

## Caching and refresh

The cache lifetime comes from the `Cache-Control: max-age` header on the document:

- A `max-age` value is used, clamped to between 60 seconds and 24 hours.
- `no-store`, `no-cache` and `max-age=0` give the 60 second minimum.
- A response without `max-age` gets the default of 1 hour.
- Failed fetches and invalid documents are never stored. A failed URL is remembered for `negativeCacheSeconds` (30 by default), so an unreachable host does not get a request on every authorization.

The expiry is stored with the client, so every instance agrees on when to fetch again. When the cache expires, the next authorization or token refresh fetches the document again. If the document has been deleted or no longer names itself correctly, the fetch fails and refresh stops working for that client. Deleting the document is the way a client owner revokes it. A timeout, network error or DNS failure is treated as transient instead: the stored copy keeps serving until `maxCacheSeconds` after it was fetched, then the client fails closed.

To fetch right away, for example after you change a document, run `mcp.cimd.refresh(clientId)`. It ignores the stored expiry and the retry delay.

A few limits keep anonymous traffic from costing you anything. An unauthenticated `/authorize` request for a metadata document client is answered with a login redirect and neither fetches nor stores anything; the document is fetched once the user is logged in. Fetches are rate limited per registrable domain, taken as the last two labels of the host so random subdomains share one budget (`maxFetchesPerHostPerMinute`, default 30). Over the limit, a client with a stored copy keeps using it for transient cases and a new client is refused (`cimd.rejected` with reason `rate_limited`). When the store can report it, the number of stored clients nobody has consented to is capped (`maxUnconsentedClients`, default 1000; a new client over the cap is refused with reason `capacity`) and stale ones are swept (`unconsentedRetentionSeconds`, default one day). DNS lookups, the JWKS cache (256 entries, 20 keys, 16 KB each) and the failed-fetch memory are all bounded. `onEvent` runs in a microtask and its errors, including a rejected promise from an async hook, are swallowed.

Setting `enabled: false` is a kill switch: stored metadata document clients stop resolving too, so their refresh tokens stop working.

The cache limits are the four `*CacheSeconds` options in the table above.

## What is and is not protected

**What theAuth checks.** A client_id must be a canonical https URL on port 443 with a path, no query, no fragment and no credentials. Before fetching, theAuth refuses IP addresses, single label names, local and internal suffixes, and wildcard DNS services such as nip.io and sslip.io. With a resolver it also refuses names that resolve to loopback, private, link-local, carrier-grade NAT, unique-local or cloud metadata addresses. It never follows redirects, reads at most 5 KB, requires a 200 JSON response, gives up after 5 seconds, and fails closed. The document must repeat its own URL as client_id, cannot use shared secrets, and cannot name an agent. Redirect URIs are matched exactly.

**What is closed on Node and Bun.** When the runtime lets theAuth control the connection, the request goes through `node:https` instead of `fetch`, pinned to the addresses it just vetted. The connection's `lookup` never asks DNS again: it hands back only those addresses, checks each one again at connect, and refuses the whole answer if any is loopback, private, link-local, carrier-grade NAT, unique-local, multicast or a cloud metadata address (IPv4-mapped IPv6 included). A multi-address answer is checked in full, none skipped. A rebinding DNS server therefore cannot steer the connection, because there is no second lookup to win. TLS still validates the certificate against the original hostname, keep-alive is off, a fresh agent is used per request, and one deadline covers DNS, connect, headers and body. Same rules as before: exact 200, no redirects, 5 KB cap. Pinned requests ignore `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY` and `NO_PROXY` on purpose, so an unvetted proxy cannot carry the request. If you need an egress proxy, enforce it at the network level. The Node and Bun path is on by default and is skipped when you pass your own `fetchImpl` or set `pinnedConnect: "off"`.

**What theAuth cannot check.** On Cloudflare Workers and Deno, and whenever you pass `fetchImpl`, `pinnedConnect: "off"` or `resolver: "none"`, theAuth checks a hostname and then lets the runtime's fetch connect, and the runtime resolves the name again. A DNS server built to answer differently each time (DNS rebinding) can make that second lookup point at a private address. With `resolver: "none"` there is no address check at all, only the name rules. DNS over HTTPS answers from public DNS, which can differ from what a server inside your network sees.

**What to do about it.** If you know your clients, set `allowedHosts`: that is the only setting that fully closes the gap on every runtime. It also covers a document's `jwks_uri`, which must be on an allowed host. On Deno, block private address ranges for outbound traffic from the auth server at the network level. On Cloudflare Workers outbound requests leave from Cloudflare's network, not yours, so a rebinding attack cannot reach your private network from there.

**About names and logos.** client_name and logo_uri are whatever the client's author wrote. Show the client_id hostname as the identity. A redirect URI on localhost means any program on the user's machine can complete the flow as that client, so show the warning theAuth gives you.

**Revocation.** Blocking a client stops new authorizations and refresh tokens at once. Access tokens it already holds stay valid until they expire unless a shared revocation store is configured, which then refuses them through the `client` row (with `auth`, the shared revocation store is the default; see [MCP token revocation](/mcp-revocation)).

# OAuth 2.1 and MCP conformance test

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/conformance

Black-box checks for any OAuth 2.1 authorization server or MCP resource server. Each check passes, fails or skips. No secrets needed.

```bash
npx @glinr/theauth-conformance https://auth.example.com
```

## Conformance command options

```text
theauth-conformance <url> [options]

  --json                 Print the report as JSON
  --badge <file>         Write a shields.io endpoint badge JSON file
  --resource <url>       Protected MCP endpoint to probe for the 401 challenge
  --client-id <id>       Use this client instead of registering one through DCR
  --redirect-uri <uri>   Redirect URI registered for --client-id
  --token <token>        Access token, only read to inspect its audience
  --refresh-token <tok>  Refresh token for the rotation check (it gets consumed)
  --timeout <ms>         Per-request timeout, default 10000
  --verbose              Include evidence in the human report
  --strict               Exit 1 on any failed check, not only MUST failures
```

The tool checks the `/.well-known` metadata paths for authorization servers and protected resources. Set `THEAUTH_CONFORMANCE_TOKEN` and `THEAUTH_CONFORMANCE_REFRESH_TOKEN` to keep tokens out of shell history.

| Exit code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | No MUST check failed |
| `1` | A MUST check failed (any failed check with `--strict`) |
| `2` | Usage error |

## Checks

Severity follows RFC 2119. A failed MUST turns the badge red. A failed SHOULD or MAY turns it yellow.

| Check id | Severity | Spec | Verifies |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `as-metadata` | must | RFC 8414 | Issuer matches, endpoints https |
| `rs-metadata` | should | RFC 9728 | Names an authorization server |
| `metadata-consistency` | must | RFC 9728, RFC 8414 | Issuer and scopes agree |
| `pkce-s256-advertised` | must | OAuth 2.1, RFC 7636 | `S256` advertised, `plain` not |
| `pkce-required` | must | OAuth 2.1, RFC 9700 | No `code_challenge` is refused |
| `pkce-plain-rejected` | must | OAuth 2.1, RFC 7636 | `plain` method is refused |
| `redirect-exact-match` | must | OAuth 2.1, RFC 9700 | Altered or foreign URI never followed |
| `dcr-registration` | should | RFC 7591 | Public client registers (201) |
| `dcr-validation` | must | RFC 7591 | Plain http and `javascript:` refused |
| `refresh-garbage-rejected` | must | RFC 6749, OAuth 2.1 | Made-up refresh token refused |
| `refresh-rotation` | must | OAuth 2.1, RFC 9700 | Rotates, old token refused, replay revokes |
| `resource-indicator-audience` | must | RFC 8707 | JWT `aud` matches resource |
| `token-exchange-rejects-garbage` | must | RFC 8693 | Made-up subject token refused |
| `token-exchange-act-chain` | should | RFC 8693 | Nested `act` claims. Always skipped. |
| `introspection-inactive` | must | RFC 7662 | Garbage token gives `active=false` |
| `dpop-advertised` | may | RFC 9449 | Asymmetric algorithms only |
| `dpop-enforced` | must | RFC 9449 | Garbage proof gets 401 |
| `www-authenticate-resource-metadata` | must | RFC 9728, RFC 6750 | 401 has working `resource_metadata` |

Skips are never faked into passes, and each one says why.

## Skipped checks

- Not advertised: DCR, token exchange, introspection, DPoP.
- `refresh-rotation`: needs `--refresh-token` and `--client-id`. The test consumes the token.
- `resource-indicator-audience`: needs `--token` (a JWT).
- `token-exchange-act-chain`: needs a valid subject token and client credentials.
- Introspection behind client authentication (401 or 403).
- Negative authorize probes: the server never accepts a valid request, or shows a login page for the bad one. Skipped if the control request is rejected.

## Badge

`--badge out.json` writes a [shields.io endpoint](https://shields.io/badges/endpoint-badge):

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "label": "agent-auth",
  "message": "13/13 passed, 5 skipped",
  "color": "brightgreen"
}
```

Host the JSON at a stable public URL and point shields at it:

```markdown
[![agent-auth conformance](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https%3A%2F%2Fexample.com%2Fagent-auth-badge.json)](https://docs.theauth.dev/conformance)
```

Refresh it in CI with `npx @glinr/theauth-conformance https://auth.example.com --badge badge.json`.

Only checks that ran count toward the message. Green: nothing failed. Yellow: only SHOULD or MAY failed. Red: a MUST failed. Grey (`not tested`): nothing could run.

## Use in code

```ts
import { buildBadge, runSuite } from "@glinr/theauth-conformance";

const report = await runSuite({ target: "https://auth.example.com", timeoutMs: 10000 });
const badge = buildBadge(report);
```

## Guard conformance

A guard vendor can check an HTTPS endpoint against the [remote guard protocol](/guards):

```bash
npx @glinr/theauth-conformance guard https://guard.example.com/theauth --secret "$GUARD_SECRET"
```

The secret can also come from `THEAUTH_GUARD_SECRET`. It signs the probes and is never printed. Twelve checks run:

| Check | Severity | What it proves |
|---|---|---|
| `guard-rejects-unsigned` | MUST | A request without signature headers is refused (4xx or deny) |
| `guard-rejects-bad-signature` | MUST | A wrong secret is refused |
| `guard-rejects-stale` | MUST | A correctly signed request one hour old is refused |
| `guard-canary-allow` | MUST | Resource `conformance:canary:allow` returns a valid allow verdict |
| `guard-canary-deny` | MUST | Resource `conformance:canary:deny` returns a valid deny verdict with a reason |
| `guard-malformed-input` | MUST | A signed body that is not JSON, or lacks `input`, is never allowed |
| `guard-no-redirect` | MUST | The endpoint answers directly |
| `guard-dry-run` | SHOULD | A `dryRun: true` canary still gets a valid verdict |
| `guard-response-signed` | MUST | A verdict carries `x-theauth-response-signature` and `x-theauth-response-timestamp` |
| `guard-response-signature` | MUST | The signature covers `<requestId>.<timestamp>.<body>` with the shared secret |
| `guard-response-fresh` | MUST | The response timestamp is within 300 seconds |
| `guard-latency` | SHOULD | The slowest of 3 canaries answers within 2000 ms |

The package ships a reference guard, `startGuardReference({ secret })`, that passes all twelve. Its tests also run deliberately flawed variants to prove each check catches its flaw. In code: `runSuite({ target, timeoutMs: 10000, mode: "guard", guardSecret })`.

## Tested against theAuth

The package test runs the suite against the real MCP OAuth module from `@glinr/theauth` on a Node `http` server. Pinned result: 13 pass, 0 fail, 5 skipped (refresh rotation, audience, token exchange twice, introspection). A lax stub server must fail the checks.

## Limits

- A green badge means the server behaved correctly on these probes. It is not an audit.
- Skips never count as passes.
