# Admin MCP server for theAuth deployments

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/admin-mcp

The `@glinr/theauth-mcp` server is read-only by default. Add `--allow-writes` (or set `THEAUTH_ALLOW_WRITES=1`) to register four write tools. Each write needs human approval.

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "theauth-admin": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@glinr/theauth-mcp", "--allow-writes"],
      "env": {
        "THEAUTH_API_URL": "https://auth.example.com/api",
        "THEAUTH_API_KEY": "...",
        "THEAUTH_MCP_ACTOR": "ops-bot@example.com"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

## Embed as a library

Host the server in your own process instead of spawning the CLI. Import from `@glinr/theauth-mcp`.

```ts
import { ApiClient, createLogger, createServer, loadConfig } from "@glinr/theauth-mcp";
import { StdioServerTransport } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/stdio.js";

const client = new ApiClient(loadConfig(process.env));
const server = createServer(client, createLogger(), "1.0.0", { actor: "ops-bot@example.com" });
await server.connect(new StdioServerTransport());
```

## Read tools

Always registered: `list_agents`, `get_agent`, `list_delegations`, `list_sessions`, `query_audit`, `check_permission`, `inspect_token`, `doctor` and `get_approval_status`. Tokens and secret-looking fields are redacted.

## Write tools

| Tool | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `revoke_agent` | Revoke an agent identity |
| `revoke_delegation` | Revoke a delegation chain |
| `rotate_key` | Rotate an agent credential. The new token is not shown to the client. |
| `disable_user` | Disable a user and end its sessions |

## Approval flow

Writes use the [approval flow](/approval). No write runs on the first call.

<Steps>

<Step>

### Request

The client calls the tool with the target `id`. The server logs the request, opens an approval (for example `admin:revoke_agent` on `agent:abc`) and returns `{ "status": "pending", "approvalId": "..." }`.

</Step>

<Step>

### Approve

A human approves or denies through your normal approval channel.

</Step>

<Step>

### Retry

The client polls `get_approval_status`, or calls the same tool again with `approvalId`.

</Step>

<Step>

### Run

If the approval is approved and unexpired, the server spends it and runs the change. Otherwise nothing runs.

</Step>

</Steps>

## Audit

With `THEAUTH_MCP_ACTOR` set (default `theauth-mcp`), every call is logged as `admin_mcp.<tool>` with that actor. Writes log each step: requested, pending, executed, denied or failed.

## Deployment routes

Core ships these routes as an opt-in plugin, `adminApi`. It is off unless `enabled` is exactly `true`. When it is off, every route answers 404.

```ts
import { adminApi, createTheAuth } from "@glinr/theauth";

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  // ...
  plugins: [
    adminApi({
      enabled: true,
      adminUserIds: ["user_ops"],
      systemAgentId: "agent_admin_mcp",
      rateLimit: { max: 60, window: 60 },
    }),
  ],
});
```

| Route | Backed by |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /delegations` | Delegation chains, filtered by `agentId` and `status` |
| `DELETE /delegations/{id}` | `revokeDelegation` (cascades to child chains) |
| `GET /sessions` | Sessions as one-way `ref`s, never ids or tokens |
| `POST /users/{id}/disable` | Admin `banUser` (ends sessions, revokes agent tokens) |
| `POST /approvals` | `approval.request` |
| `GET /approvals?status=pending` | Pending, unexpired requests, newest first. `limit` up to 100. Arguments come back as JSON text cut at 2 KB. |
| `GET /approvals/{id}` | `approval.get` |
| `POST /approvals/{id}/approve` | Human decision. 403 `SELF_APPROVAL` for the opener, 409 if not pending or expired. |
| `POST /approvals/{id}/deny` | Same rules as approve. |
| `POST /approvals/{id}/consume` | `consumeApproval`. A replay or race is refused with 409. |
| `POST /audit/events` | `recordAuditEvent`, secret-looking params redacted |

## Limits

- Calls need an `Authorization: Bearer` credential for a user in `adminUserIds`. Bad credentials get 401, other users get 403, and an empty list refuses everyone. Cookie-only requests are refused.
- `systemAgentId` must be an existing agent. The `agentId` and `userId` the MCP server sends are labels and are ignored. The approval belongs to the calling admin.
- Approval actions must look like `admin:<name>`. Only the admin who opened an approval can consume it. Approving is four-eyes: the admin who opened a request cannot approve or deny it (403 `SELF_APPROVAL`) unless `allowSelfApproval: true`. Each decision writes an `admin_api.approval.approve` or `.deny` audit event.
- The dashboard Approvals page calls these routes, so it needs an app that serves `/api/approvals` with the signed-in admin's Bearer token. The `theauth dashboard` CLI server signs in with one shared secret, has no admin identity, and cannot use the page. A decision is audited after it is applied, so a failed audit write does not undo it.
- An approval is single use and tied to one action and one resource.
- If the audit write for a new request fails, the request is not opened.
- Admins cannot disable themselves or other configured admins, unless `allowDisablingAdmins` is set.
- Requests are rate limited per admin user. Ids, enums and body sizes are validated.

---

# DPoP and requireMcpAuth

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/dpop

A bearer token works for whoever holds it. (Agent tokens, the `ta_` strings, can be bound too: see [sender constrained agent tokens](/dpop-agent-tokens).) If an agent's token leaks from a log or a proxy, the thief can call your tools. DPoP closes that gap: the token carries the thumbprint of a key the client holds, and every request has to include a short-lived proof signed with that key.

DPoP is opt-in. Without `dpop` in your MCP config nothing changes.

## Turn it on

```ts
import { createMcpModule } from "@glinr/theauth/mcp";

const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    enabled: true,
    issuer: "https://auth.example.com",
    baseUrl: "https://auth.example.com/api/auth",
    signingSecret: process.env.MCP_SIGNING_SECRET!,
    resource: "https://mcp.example.com",
    dpop: {
      // required: true,        // refuse unbound tokens everywhere
      // requireNonce: true,    // server nonces (RFC 9449 section 8 and 9)
      storage: theauth.secondaryStorage.for("nonces"), // shared replay cache
    },
  },
  // ...your storage callbacks
});
```

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `algs` | ES256, ES384, EdDSA, PS256 | Accepted proof algorithms. |
| `required` | false | Every token request needs a proof, and resources refuse unbound tokens. |
| `proofMaxAgeSeconds` | 300 | Oldest accepted `iat`. |
| `clockSkewSeconds` | 30 | Allowed skew in both directions. |
| `requireNonce` | false | Proofs must carry a server nonce. |
| `nonceTtlSeconds` | 300 | Nonce lifetime. |
| `storage` | in-process memory | Replay cache and nonces. Use a shared store with more than one instance. |
| `tokenEndpointUrl` | `<baseUrl>/mcp/token` | The `htu` clients sign for the token endpoint. |

Both metadata documents then list `dpop_signing_alg_values_supported`. The protected resource document also sets `dpop_bound_access_tokens_required` when `required` is on.

## What the token endpoint does

When a request carries a `DPoP` header, the endpoint verifies the proof (`typ`, algorithm, public `jwk`, signature, `htm`, `htu`, `iat`, `jti` replay) and issues an access token with `cnf: { jkt }` and `token_type: "DPoP"`. Without a header you get a normal bearer token, unless `required` is set. The non-interactive grants (client credentials, token exchange, jwt-bearer) honor the proof the same way. See [MCP server grants](/mcp-grants).

The proof is checked before the authorization code is consumed. When `requireNonce` is on and the proof has no valid nonce, the endpoint answers `400 use_dpop_nonce` with a `DPoP-Nonce` header and leaves the code alone, so the client retries with the same code and a fresh proof.

Refresh tokens inherit the binding. A refresh request signed by a different key is refused before the token rotates, so a thief cannot burn the real client's token. Your `storeToken` callback should persist `dpopJkt` from the stored record, otherwise the binding is lost on refresh.

The built-in `createMcpResponseHelpers(...).tokenResponse` and every framework adapter copy the nonce into the `DPoP-Nonce` header. If you write your own token route, read `result.error.details?.dpopNonce`.

## Protect a handler

`requireMcpAuth` wraps any `(Request) => Response` function. It accepts `Authorization: Bearer` and, with DPoP enabled, `Authorization: DPoP`.

```ts
// Resource server
const tools = mcp.requireMcpAuth(
  async (request, principal) => {
    return Response.json({
      user: principal.userId,
      agent: principal.agent?.id ?? null,
      chain: principal.delegationChain,
      scheme: principal.scheme,
    });
  },
  { requiredScopes: ["mcp:read"] },
);

// Works anywhere that speaks Web Request/Response, for example Hono:
// app.all("/tools", (c) => tools(c.req.raw));
```

The client sends `Authorization: DPoP <token>` plus `DPoP: <proof>` where the proof is signed for the exact method and URL and includes `ath`, the base64url SHA-256 of the token. Use a new `jti` every time. The [client helper](#client-helper) below does all of that for you.

### What gets checked

- Token: signature, issuer, expiry, audience against `expectedAudience` or `McpConfig.resource`, then revocation (the jti denylist and, for delegated tokens, the live delegation binding, depending on the [freshness mode](/mcp-revocation)).
- Proof: `htm`, `htu` (query and fragment ignored), `iat` window, `ath`, nonce, `jti` not seen before, and the proof key matching `cnf.jkt`.
- Bearer downgrade: a bound token sent as `Bearer` is refused. This also covers `validateToken`, `middleware`, `withMcpAuth` and `requireScopes`.
- A `DPoP` scheme request carrying an unbound token is refused.
- Scopes: a shortfall returns 403 `insufficient_scope`.

DPoP and revocation answer different questions. The `cnf.jkt` match says the caller holds the key the token was issued to. The revocation check says the authority behind the token is still alive. Both run, and the proof checks run first because they need no database read, so a request with a bad proof never reaches the revocation store. Revocation sits before the scope check, so a revoked token gets 401, never a 403 step up. An exchanged token is bound to the key of the exchange request, and a DPoP bound subject token needs a proof from the same key.

[Introspection](/mcp-revocation#introspection-and-revocation-endpoints) reports `cnf.jkt` and `token_type: "DPoP"`, but it does not see your request. A resource server that introspects must still verify the proof itself. Replay protection for proof `jti` values is per process unless you set a shared `storage` in the DPoP config, which matters with more than one instance.

Options: `requiredScopes`, `expectedAudience`, `resourceUrl` (the public URL clients sign, for proxies), `resourceMetadataUrl`, `requireDpop`, `requireNonce`.

### Challenges

With no credentials the response is 401 with `Bearer resource_metadata="..."` and, if DPoP is on, a second `DPoP algs="ES256 ...", resource_metadata="..."` header. Bad tokens return `error="invalid_token"`, bad proofs `error="invalid_dpop_proof"`, and a missing nonce `error="use_dpop_nonce"` with a `DPoP-Nonce` header. The `resource_metadata` URL points at the RFC 9728 document so MCP clients can find your authorization server.

### The principal

| Field | Source |
| --- | --- |
| `userId`, `clientId`, `scopes`, `resource`, `tokenId`, `expiresAt` | Token claims |
| `agent` | `agent_id`, `agent_type`, `trust_tier` (needs `emitAgenticJwtClaims`) |
| `delegationChain` | Nested RFC 8693 `act` claims, current actor first |
| `scheme`, `dpopJkt` | How the caller authenticated |

## Client helper

`@glinr/theauth-client` ships `createDPoPClient` and `createDPoPProver`. They use WebCrypto only, so they run in browsers, Node, Bun, Deno and edge runtimes. Both sign with ES256.

```ts
import { createDPoPClient } from "@glinr/theauth-client";

const dpop = await createDPoPClient(); // generates a P-256 key pair

// 1. Token endpoint. The helper adds the DPoP header and handles the nonce challenge.
const tokenRes = await dpop.fetch("https://auth.example.com/api/auth/mcp/token", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" },
  body: new URLSearchParams({
    grant_type: "authorization_code",
    code,
    code_verifier: verifier,
    client_id: clientId,
    redirect_uri: redirectUri,
    resource: "https://mcp.example.com",
  }),
});
const { access_token } = await tokenRes.json();

// 2. Resource request. Sends `Authorization: DPoP <token>` and a proof with `ath`.
const res = await dpop.fetch(
  "https://mcp.example.com/tools",
  { method: "POST", body: JSON.stringify({ tool: "list_repos" }) },
  { accessToken: access_token },
);
```

What it does on each call:

- Builds a proof with `htm`, a normalized `htu` (scheme, host and path, query and fragment dropped), `iat`, a fresh `jti`, `ath` when there is an access token, and `nonce` when one is cached for the origin.
- Sets `Authorization: DPoP <token>` when an access token is given, per request through the third argument or as the `accessToken` option (a string or a function).
- Reads `DPoP-Nonce` from every response and caches it per origin.
- On a `use_dpop_nonce` challenge (a 400 or 401 with a `DPoP-Nonce` header) it retries once with the new nonce and a new proof.

### Nonce flow

With `dpop.requireNonce` on the server, the first request has no nonce:

1. The client sends a proof without a nonce.
2. The server answers `400 use_dpop_nonce` (token endpoint) or `401` with `WWW-Authenticate: DPoP error="use_dpop_nonce"` (resource), plus a `DPoP-Nonce` header. The authorization code is not consumed.
3. The helper stores the nonce, signs a new proof that carries it, and retries once.
4. Later requests to the same origin send the cached nonce. When the server rotates it, the same challenge repeats.

The retry happens once per call. If the second attempt is also a challenge, the response is returned to you.

### Keys

The generated private key is non-extractable and lives only as long as the object. A token is bound to that key, so keep using the same one for refresh. To persist it, pass your own key pair, for example one you store in IndexedDB:

```ts
const dpop = await createDPoPClient({ keyPair: storedKeyPair }); // ECDSA P-256 CryptoKeyPair
const jkt = await dpop.thumbprint(); // the cnf.jkt value the server binds to
```

Use `createDPoPProver` when you only need proofs and want to send the request yourself. It exposes `createProof({ method, url, accessToken?, nonce? })`, `thumbprint()`, `publicJwk`, `getNonce(url)` and `setNonce(url, nonce)`. Share one prover between a token client and a resource client with `createDPoPClient({ prover })` so both use the same key and nonce cache.

## Adapters and CORS

The token endpoint returns the nonce in `error.details.dpopNonce`. All ten framework adapters (Express, Fastify, Hono, NestJS, Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, SolidStart, TanStack and Astro) copy it into the `DPoP-Nonce` response header on `/mcp/token` errors, so the retry works through any of them. Before this, only the Hono and Express adapters did.

The adapters' MCP CORS headers also allow the `DPoP` request header and expose `DPoP-Nonce` and `WWW-Authenticate`, which a browser client needs to read the challenge. If you serve the token endpoint some other way, set the same headers yourself.

## Limits

- The replay cache is only as strict as its store. Cloudflare KV is not atomic, so two simultaneous replays can both pass. Use Redis or the database store when that matters.
- The `dpop_jkt` authorization request parameter (binding the code to a key up front) is not implemented. The binding starts at the token request.
- Unbound refresh tokens issued before you enabled DPoP are bound to whatever key first refreshes them. Rotate them out by setting `required` after a refresh cycle.

---

# Sender constrained agent tokens

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/dpop-agent-tokens

An agent token (`ta_...`) is a bearer credential. Whoever holds the string can use it. Binding it to a key fixes that: the token stores the thumbprint of a key the agent holds, and every request must carry a short-lived proof signed with that key. A token copied out of a log file stops working.

This page covers the REST authorize route and `requireAgent`. For tokens issued by the MCP OAuth server, see [DPoP and requireMcpAuth](/dpop). Both use the same proof format and the same `cnf` claim ([RFC 7800](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7800)).

Binding is opt-in per agent. A token without a binding behaves exactly as before.

## Turn it on

```ts
import { createTheAuth } from "@glinr/theauth";

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: "postgres", url: process.env.DATABASE_URL! },
  agents: {
    enabled: true,
    confirmation: {
      dpop: {
        // requireNonce: true,   // server nonces (RFC 9449 section 8 and 9)
        // resourceUrl: (req) => `https://api.example.com${new URL(req.url).pathname}`,
      },
      // required: true,         // refuse agent tokens that are not bound
    },
  },
  secondaryStorage: "database", // shared replay cache and nonces across instances
});
```

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `dpop.algs` | ES256, ES384, EdDSA, PS256 | Accepted proof algorithms. |
| `dpop.proofMaxAgeSeconds` | 300 | Oldest accepted proof `iat`. |
| `dpop.clockSkewSeconds` | 30 | Skew allowed in either direction. |
| `dpop.requireNonce` | false | Proofs must carry a server nonce. |
| `dpop.nonceTtlSeconds` | 300 | Nonce lifetime. |
| `dpop.storage` | the `nonces` secondary storage | Replay cache and nonces. |
| `dpop.resourceUrl` | `request.url` | The URL clients sign as `htu`. Set it behind a proxy. |
| `methods` | none | Extra proofs of possession, such as a certificate thumbprint. See below. |
| `required` | false | Refuse agent tokens that carry no binding. |

With more than one instance, point `secondaryStorage` at the database or Redis. Otherwise the replay cache lives in each process and a proof could be replayed against another instance.

## Bind a token to a key

Pass `cnf` when you create the agent. The value is the RFC 7638 thumbprint of the agent's public key:

```ts
import { createDPoPClient } from "@glinr/theauth-client";

const dpop = await createDPoPClient(); // P-256 key pair in WebCrypto
const jkt = await dpop.thumbprint();

const agent = await theauth.agent.create({
  ownerId: user.id,
  name: "invoice-bot",
  type: "autonomous",
  permissions: [{ resource: "invoices", actions: ["read"] }],
  cnf: { jkt },
});
// agent.token is bound to that key.
```

Over HTTP, send the same member in the body of `POST /agents`:

```json
{ "ownerId": "user_1", "name": "invoice-bot", "type": "autonomous",
  "permissions": [{ "resource": "invoices", "actions": ["read"] }],
  "cnf": { "jkt": "NzbLsXh8uDCcd-6MNwXF4W_7noWXFZAfHkxZsRGC9Xs" } }
```

The agent identity returned by `agent.get` and `agent.list` shows `cnf`. It is part of the public identity, not a secret.

Rotating a token keeps its binding by default, so a leaked token is replaced by one the thief cannot use either. To move the agent to a new key, or drop the binding:

```ts
await theauth.agent.rotate(agent.id);                      // same key
await theauth.agent.rotate(agent.id, { cnf: { jkt: next } }); // new key
await theauth.agent.rotate(agent.id, { cnf: null });          // plain bearer token again
```

`POST /agents/:id/rotate` takes the same `cnf` in an optional JSON body. `PATCH /agents/:id` does not change a binding.

## Call with a proof

The agent sends `Authorization: DPoP <token>` and a `DPoP` header. The client helper does both and retries once when the server asks for a nonce:

```ts
const res = await dpop.fetch(
  "https://api.example.com/api/theauth/authorize/token",
  {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ action: "read", resource: "invoices" }),
  },
  { accessToken: agent.token },
);
```

In your own routes, `requireAgent` does the same checks:

```ts
import { requireAgent } from "@glinr/theauth/http";

export async function handler(request: Request): Promise<Response> {
  const result = await requireAgent(theauth, request, { action: "read", resource: "invoices" });
  if (!result.ok) return result.response;
  return Response.json({ agent: result.agent.id });
}
```

### What gets checked

- The proof: `typ` is `dpop+jwt`, the algorithm is on the allow list, the header holds a public `jwk`, the signature verifies, `htm` and `htu` match the request (query and fragment ignored), `iat` is inside the window, `ath` is the SHA-256 of the token, and the `jti` has not been seen before.
- The binding: the thumbprint of the proof key equals `cnf.jkt` on the agent.
- A bound token sent as `Bearer` with no proof is refused. A bound token is never usable as a plain bearer token.
- A token with no binding ignores any proof header and works as before (unless `required` is set).

The binding check also sits inside `authorizeByToken`, not only in the HTTP layer. A caller who skips the HTTP handler and calls `theauth.authorizeByToken(token, request)` on a bound token gets `confirmation_required`. Pass the proofs your own transport verified through the context:

```ts
await theauth.authorizeByToken(token, { action: "read", resource: "invoices" }, {
  confirmation: { jkt: verifiedThumbprint },
});
```

Only set `confirmation` from data you verified yourself.

### Errors

| Situation | Status | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bound token, no proof | 401, code `confirmation_required` | `WWW-Authenticate: DPoP error="invalid_token", algs="..."` |
| Proof is valid but for another key | 401, code `confirmation_failed` | same challenge |
| Proof is malformed, stale, replayed, wrong `htm`, `htu` or `ath` | 401, `error: "invalid_dpop_proof"` | `WWW-Authenticate: DPoP error="invalid_dpop_proof"` |
| `DPoP` scheme without a proof header | 401, `invalid_dpop_proof` | same |
| Nonce missing or stale | 401, `use_dpop_nonce` | `DPoP-Nonce` header carries the new value |
| `required` is on and the token is not bound | 401, code `confirmation_required` | |

Refused bound tokens are written to the audit log with the decision code, so a pattern of stolen-token attempts is visible.

## Introspection

`POST /agents/introspect` with `{ "token": "ta_..." }` answers in the shape of RFC 7662 and includes `cnf`, so a resource server that checks tokens itself can verify the proof:

```json
{ "data": { "active": true, "token_type": "DPoP", "sub": "user_1",
  "agent_id": "ag_123", "agent_type": "autonomous", "exp": 1800086400, "iat": 1800000000,
  "cnf": { "jkt": "NzbLsXh8uDCcd-6MNwXF4W_7noWXFZAfHkxZsRGC9Xs" } } }
```

The route needs a signed-in caller and only reveals agents inside that caller's scope. A token that is unknown, revoked, expired or out of scope answers `{ "active": false }`. In code: `await theauth.agent.introspect(token)`. Introspection does not see your request, so the resource server still has to verify the proof itself.

## Client certificates and other proofs

The binding is a map. `jkt` is the DPoP member. `x5t#S256` is the member for mutual TLS (RFC 8705): the thumbprint of the client certificate. theAuth does not terminate TLS, so you tell it how to read the proof from a request. Typically your proxy forwards the verified certificate thumbprint in a header:

```ts
const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  // ...
  agents: {
    enabled: true,
    confirmation: {
      methods: {
        // Your reverse proxy sets this header after it verified the client certificate.
        // Strip it from incoming requests at the edge, or anyone can forge it.
        "x5t#S256": (request) => request.headers.get("x-client-cert-sha256"),
      },
    },
  },
});

await theauth.agent.create({
  // ...
  cnf: { "x5t#S256": certificateThumbprint },
});
```

- When a token is bound to several members, every one must match. A token with `jkt` and `x5t#S256` needs both a DPoP proof and the certificate.
- A token bound to a member that has no extractor is always refused.
- An extractor that throws counts as proof of nothing.
- A damaged `cnf` value in the database is treated as a binding nobody can satisfy. It never turns into an unbound token.

This is also the hook the device features use for IoT clients: a device that holds a certificate or a key can be bound the same way.

## Limits

- DPoP protects against a copied token. It does not help if the attacker can run code inside the agent process and use the key through it (RFC 9449 section 11).
- Without nonces, a stolen key can pre-sign proofs with future `iat` values inside the skew window. Use `requireNonce` and short token lifetimes if that is in your threat model.
- FAPI 2.0 asks authorization servers to issue only sender constrained tokens and offers DPoP or mutual TLS for it. `required: true` plus either method gives you that property for agent tokens. It does not by itself make a deployment FAPI conformant.

---

# Reverse proxy gateway for AI agent auth

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/gateway

```bash
npx @glinr/theauth-gateway --config gateway.json --database ./theauth.db --port 3000
```

Needs Node 20 or newer. For MCP servers, use [Gateway for MCP servers](/gateway-mcp).

<Steps>
<Step>

### Create an agent

Create it in the gateway's SQLite file. Keep `agent.token`.

```typescript
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite-native', url: './theauth.db' },
  agents: { enabled: true },
});

const agent = await theauth.agent.create({
  ownerId: 'user-1', // must be an existing user id
  name: 'support-bot',
  type: 'autonomous',
  permissions: [{ resource: 'api', actions: ['read'] }],
});
console.log(agent.token);
```

</Step>
<Step>

### Write gateway.json

```json
{
  "upstream": "http://localhost:8080",
  "policies": [
    { "path": "/health", "public": true },
    {
      "path": "/api/**",
      "method": "GET",
      "requiredPermissions": [{ "resource": "api", "actions": ["read"] }]
    },
    {
      "path": "/api/**",
      "requiredPermissions": [{ "resource": "api", "actions": ["write"] }]
    }
  ],
  "rateLimit": { "windowMs": 60000, "max": 100 }
}
```

</Step>
<Step>

### Start and call

Run the command at the top, then:

```bash
curl http://localhost:3000/api/items                                         # 401
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $AGENT_TOKEN" http://localhost:3000/api/items # proxied
```

</Step>
</Steps>

<Warning>
The default `--database` is `:memory:`, so protected requests get 401. The CLI is SQLite only.
</Warning>

## Request order

The first matching policy wins.

| Step | Check | On failure |
|------|-------|------------|
| 1 | `/_theauth/health`, then CORS preflight | None |
| 2 | First policy matching path glob and method | Still needs a token, but no permission check or route limit |
| 3 | Agent token, unless `public` or `requireAuth: false` | 401, `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` |
| 4 | Global and policy rate limits | 429, `Retry-After` |
| 5 | Every `requiredPermissions` pair | 403 |
| 6 | Forward, then audit | None |

Error codes: `UNAUTHORIZED`, `FORBIDDEN`, `RATE_LIMITED`, `PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE`, `BAD_GATEWAY`, `GATEWAY_TIMEOUT`.

## Always on

| Behavior | Detail |
|----------|--------|
| Fixed upstream | Clients cannot pick a host. Only `http` and `https`, no embedded credentials. |
| Tokens stripped (breaking) | `Authorization` and `DPoP` are removed. Keep them with `--forward-auth` or `stripAuthHeader: false`. |
| Headers | Client `Forwarded`, `X-Forwarded-*` and `X-Real-IP` are dropped. `X-Forwarded-For` comes only from `trustedProxy`. |
| Redirects | Not followed. Upstream `Location` is rewritten to the gateway. |
| Body and timeout | Over `maxBodyBytes` gets 413. No headers within `upstreamTimeoutMs` gets 504. |
| Streaming | SSE and streamable HTTP pass through. A disconnect cancels the upstream. |
| 502 | Says only that the upstream is unreachable. |

## CLI flags

| Flag | Default | Purpose |
|------|---------|---------|
| `--upstream`, `-u` | required | Upstream URL |
| `--port`, `-p` | `3000` | Listen port |
| `--database`, `-d` | `:memory:` | SQLite path |
| `--config`, `-c` | none | `gateway.json` path |
| `--forward-auth` | off | Send `Authorization` upstream |
| `--no-audit` | off | Audit off |
| `--max-body-bytes` | `10485760` | Body cap, 10 MiB |
| `--trusted-proxy-count` | `0` | Proxies in front |
| `--trusted-header` | none | Edge header, such as `cf-connecting-ip` |
| `--mcp-resource`, `--mcp-issuer`, `--mcp-scope` | none | [MCP mode](/gateway-mcp) |

`--strip-auth` is still accepted and does nothing.

## gateway.json

```jsonc
{
  "upstream": "http://localhost:8080",         // required, http or https only
  "audit": true,
  "stripAuthHeader": true,                     // false keeps Authorization upstream
  "maxBodyBytes": 5242880,                     // default 10485760 (10 MiB)
  "upstreamTimeoutMs": 15000,                  // default 30000 (30 s for headers)
  "cors": { "origins": ["https://app.example.com"], "credentials": true }, // unlisted callers never get the first origin
  "rateLimit": { "windowMs": 60000, "max": 100 }, // per agent, or per client on anonymous routes
  "trustedProxy": { "trustedProxyCount": 1 },
  // "mcp" turns on MCP mode. "basePath" is accepted but has no effect on routing.
  "policies": [
    { "path": "/health", "public": true },     // micromatch: /api/* one level, /api/** any depth
    {
      "path": "/api/**",
      // requiredPermissions checks the agent's own permissions only, not delegated ones
      "requiredPermissions": [{ "resource": "api", "actions": ["read", "write"] }],
      "rateLimit": { "windowMs": 60000, "max": 20 }
    }
  ]
}
```

Policy fields: `path`, `method`, `public`, `requireAuth`, `requiredPermissions`, `requiredScopes` (MCP only), `rateLimit`. Validated on start.

## Embedded mode

Pass a `createTheAuth()` instance as `theauth`. For Postgres or MySQL, use this mode.

```typescript
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { createGateway } from '@glinr/theauth-gateway';

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite-native', url: 'theauth.db' },
  agents: { enabled: true },
});

const gateway = createGateway({
  upstream: 'http://localhost:8080',
  theauth,
  policies: [
    { path: '/health', public: true },
    { path: '/api/**', requiredPermissions: [{ resource: 'api', actions: ['read'] }] },
  ],
});

await gateway.listen(3000);

// Or mount it in your own server: Web Request in, Response out.
const response = await gateway.handleRequest(request);
```

## Docker and Kubernetes

Run the gateway as a sidecar. Expose only its port.

```dockerfile
CMD ["npx", "@glinr/theauth-gateway", "--config", "/etc/gateway.json", "--database", "/data/theauth.db", "--port", "3000"]
```

## Limits

- **Direct upstream access bypasses it.** Bind the upstream to a private network.
- **No body inspection.** Policies match method and path only.
- **Paths match as the gateway sees them.** Test encoded paths such as `%2F`.
- **HTTP only.** No TLS or WebSocket. Put a TLS proxy in front.
- **Rate limits are in memory, per process.**
- **Audit is not an access log.** It records a permission check, not the decision.
- **Agent revocation is immediate.** MCP OAuth limits: [MCP page](/gateway-mcp#limits).

# MCP server gateway with OAuth 2.1 and RFC 9728

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/gateway-mcp

```bash
export THEAUTH_MCP_SIGNING_SECRET='the same 32+ character secret as your authorization server'

npx @glinr/theauth-gateway \
  --upstream http://127.0.0.1:3001 \
  --mcp-resource https://mcp.example.com/mcp \
  --mcp-issuer https://auth.example.com \
  --mcp-scope mcp:read \
  --port 3000
```

Needs an [MCP OAuth 2.1](/mcp) authorization server. The upstream never sees a client token.

<Steps>
<Step>

### Set the signing secret

Must match your authorization server's `signingSecret`. Pass it by environment variable, not on the command line.

</Step>
<Step>

### Start the gateway

`--mcp-resource` is the token audience: your authorization server must set it as `aud`. Terminate TLS in front and route the public URL to port 3000.

</Step>
<Step>

### Check the challenge

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/mcp -d '{}'
# HTTP/1.1 401
# WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://mcp.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp"

curl http://localhost:3000/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp
```

Clients then follow the challenge on their own.

</Step>
</Steps>

## What MCP mode does

| Feature | Behavior |
|---------|----------|
| Protected resource metadata | RFC 9728 at the well-known path and its path suffixed form. `resource` is the public MCP URL, `authorization_servers` your issuer. |
| Token checks | Signature, issuer, expiry, audience (RFC 8707). Tokens for other resources are refused. DPoP-bound tokens work if your auth module has `dpop` enabled. |
| Challenges | `WWW-Authenticate` carries `resource_metadata` and `error`. Scope shortfalls get `403 insufficient_scope`. |
| Scopes | `requiredScopes`, gateway wide or per route. |
| Agent policy | `requiredPermissions` for tokens with an `agent_id` claim. |
| Origin check | Foreign `Origin` rejected (DNS rebinding protection). |
| Streaming | SSE and streamable HTTP both ways, unbuffered. The client token is never forwarded upstream. |

## Per route scopes and agent policy

```json
{
  "upstream": "http://127.0.0.1:3001",
  "mcp": {
    "resource": "https://mcp.example.com/mcp",
    "issuer": "https://auth.example.com",
    "requiredScopes": ["mcp:read"]
  },
  "cors": { "origins": ["https://app.example.com"] },
  "policies": [
    { "path": "/mcp/admin/**", "requiredScopes": ["mcp:write"] },
    {
      "path": "/mcp",
      "method": "POST",
      "requiredPermissions": [{ "resource": "tools", "actions": ["call"] }],
      "rateLimit": { "windowMs": 60000, "max": 120 }
    }
  ]
}
```

```bash
npx @glinr/theauth-gateway --config gateway.json --port 3000
```

`requiredPermissions` checks the agent in the `agent_id` claim, against the gateway's TheAuth database. No `agent_id` means 403. Use `requiredScopes` for tokens not tied to an agent.

## Embedded mode

For a same-process authorization server or a revocation list, pass the real module.

```typescript
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { createMcpModule, createInMemoryJtiDenylist } from '@glinr/theauth/mcp';
import { createGateway } from '@glinr/theauth-gateway';

const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    enabled: true,
    issuer: 'https://auth.example.com',
    baseUrl: 'https://auth.example.com/api/auth',
    signingSecret: process.env.MCP_SIGNING_SECRET!,
    jtiDenylist: createInMemoryJtiDenylist(),
  },
  // storage callbacks, see the MCP OAuth page
});

const gateway = createGateway({
  upstream: 'http://127.0.0.1:3001',
  theauth,
  mcp: { auth: mcp, resource: 'https://mcp.example.com/mcp', requiredScopes: ['mcp:read'] },
});
await gateway.listen(3000);
```

Only `requireMcpAuth` and `getProtectedResourceMetadata` are used, so a shared-key validation module is enough. The CLI does this.

## Limits

- **Path level only.** Tool names sit in the unparsed JSON-RPC body. Enforce per tool rules upstream or split routes.
- **The CLI cannot see revocations.** Tokens stay valid until `exp`. Use short lifetimes, or embedded mode with a shared `jtiDenylist`.
- **HS256 shared secret.** Anyone holding it can mint tokens. The CLI does not fetch JWKS.
- **Not an authorization server.** Registration, login, consent and issuing stay upstream.
- **Well-known paths are shadowed.** Upstream `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` routes never run.
- **Sessions are not bound to tokens.** `Mcp-Session-Id` passes through, and a second authenticated client that learns an ID could use it. Treat IDs as secrets.
- **Audit only with `agent_id`.** Other OAuth tokens are enforced but not logged.
- **Rate limits are in memory, per process.**
- **HTTP only.** No TLS or WebSocket. The legacy stdio transport is out of scope.
- **Not tested with a real MCP client.** Unit and local socket tests only. Add headers missing from the default list to `cors.headers`.

---

# Robotics and ROS 2 authorization

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/robotics-ros2

A robot is an agent in theAuth. Its permissions say which topics it may publish and subscribe to, which services it may call or answer, and which actions it may send or execute. theAuth uses that one list in two places:

1. **The DDS layer.** `theauth ros2 export` writes the files SROS2 and DDS Security read, so the middleware refuses what the policy refuses.
2. **A gate node.** For things DDS cannot express (human approval, step up, rate limits, time windows, argument checks) a node asks theAuth before it publishes the command.

theAuth is not a safety system and nothing here makes a machine compliant with ISO 10218, ISO/TS 15066 or IEC 62443. An emergency stop must be a hardware or safety controller function that works with the network down. See [Safety stops](#safety-stops).

## Resource names

| Resource | Meaning | Actions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ros2:/cmd_vel` | topic | `publish`, `subscribe` |
| `ros2:srv:/reset` | service | `call` (the client), `reply` (the server) |
| `ros2:action:/navigate_to_pose` | action | `call` (the client), `execute` (the server) |
| `ros2:*` or `*` | every topic, service and action | any |
| `ros2:srv:*`, `ros2:action:*` | every service, every action | any |

The action `*` means every verb of that kind. Names must be absolute (`/scan`, not `scan` or `~/scan`) and made of letters, digits and underscores.

With the default matching, a `*` works only as a whole colon segment. `ros2:/fleet/*` is not a pattern: theAuth's policy engine would never match it at runtime, so the exporter lists it as skipped instead of writing a DDS rule the runtime check disagrees with. List exact names, or turn on [path matching](/permissions#path-matching-opt-in) (`resourceMatching: "path"` on the server, `--resource-matching path` on the export):

- `ros2:/fleet/**` exports as the DDS glob `rt/fleet/*`.
- `ros2:/fleet/*` (exactly one level) is skipped. A DDS permissions topic is an fnmatch pattern whose `*` also crosses `/`, so the grant would reach `/fleet/a/b` while theAuth denies it. This was checked against Fast DDS, see [the glob result](#verified-on-ros-2-humble). Use `**`, list exact names, or pass `--single-level widen` to export the wider DDS grant on purpose. The runtime gate still enforces one level.

```typescript
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { ros2Action, ros2Service, ros2Topic } from '@glinr/theauth/robotics';

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite-native', url: './theauth.db' },
  agents: { enabled: true },
});

const robot = await theauth.agent.create({
  ownerId: 'user-1',
  name: 'robot1-nav',
  type: 'autonomous',
  permissions: [
    { resource: ros2Topic('/scan'), actions: ['subscribe'] },
    { resource: ros2Topic('/odom'), actions: ['publish'] },
    { resource: ros2Service('/reset_costmap'), actions: ['call'] },
    { resource: ros2Action('/navigate_to_pose'), actions: ['execute'] },
    // Hazardous: a person approves each use.
    {
      resource: ros2Topic('/cmd_vel'),
      actions: ['publish'],
      constraints: { requireApproval: true },
    },
  ],
});
```

## Export to SROS2 and DDS Security

```bash
theauth ros2 export \
  --robot <agent-id> --server https://auth.example.com/api/auth \
  --enclave /fleet/robot1/nav --out ./robot1-nav
```

You need to be logged in as an admin (`theauth login`). To work offline, pass `--permissions perms.json` (an array of permissions, or an object with a `permissions` array) instead of `--robot`.

Four files are written:

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `policy.xml` | SROS2 policy format 0.2.0. Input for `ros2 security create_permission`. |
| `permissions.xml` | DDS Security 1.1 permissions grant, unsigned. |
| `governance.xml` | DDS Security 1.1 domain governance, unsigned. Encrypted discovery and data, unauthenticated participants refused. |
| `theauth-export.json` | Rules written, permissions gated, permissions skipped and why. |

The output is deterministic: sorted, no timestamps except the validity window you pass. Re-export after a policy change and `git diff` shows what moved.

### How permissions map to DDS

The mapping is the one SROS2 uses in its `permissions.xsl`. A topic `/cmd_vel` becomes the DDS topic `rt/cmd_vel`. A service client publishes `rq/<name>Request` and subscribes to `rr/<name>Reply`, and the server does the reverse. An action client publishes the three `_action` request topics and subscribes to the three replies plus `feedback` and `status`. The grant ends in `<default>DENY</default>`, so anything not listed is refused.

DDS Security evaluates rules in document order and the first match wins. The exporter writes allow rules only, so order never changes the outcome.

### The node baseline

A ROS 2 node opens a few endpoints of its own before your code runs: it publishes `/rosout`, publishes and subscribes `/parameter_events`, and answers six parameter services under its own name (`describe_parameters`, `get_parameter_types`, `get_parameters`, `list_parameters`, `set_parameters`, `set_parameters_atomically`). SROS2's `create_permission` does not add these, and under `Enforce` a node missing any of them fails at startup (see [what was verified](#verified-on-ros-2-humble)). So the exporter adds them by default, for the node named by `--node` (default: the last token of the enclave path) in the namespace given by `--namespace` (default `/`).

The name must be the real ROS node name, because the parameter services are named after it. If the last enclave token is not a valid node name (for example `robot-1`, since node names cannot contain a hyphen) and you did not pass `--node`, the baseline is skipped and `theauth-export.json` says so. Pass `--no-node-baseline` to leave it out. Whether a node started with rosout logging and parameter services turned off still needs them was not tried.

### Gated permissions

A permission with any constraint (`requireApproval`, `requireAcr`, `maxCallsPerHour`, `timeWindow`, `ipAllowlist`, `allowedArgPatterns`) cannot be written into a static DDS grant. Exporting it as a plain allow would drop the constraint without a word. So by default the exporter leaves it out and reports it under `gated`. The robot's own enclave then cannot publish `/cmd_vel` at all.

That is the intended shape. Give the grant to the gate node instead, whose enclave is exported with `--gated include`, and let nothing else publish to the actuation topic:

```bash
# Planner and drivers: gated permissions left out (default).
theauth ros2 export --robot <planner-agent> --enclave /fleet/robot1/planner --out ./planner

# The gate: gated permissions granted, because the gate is where they are enforced.
theauth ros2 export --robot <gate-agent> --enclave /fleet/robot1/gate --gated include --out ./gate
```

`--gated include` on a normal participant is a weaker setup: anything holding that enclave's key can publish without the runtime check. Use it only for the gate.

### Sign and install

theAuth never sees your permissions CA key, so signing is yours. The usual route uses the ROS tooling, which also validates the policy against the schema:

```bash
export ROS_SECURITY_KEYSTORE=~/keystore
ros2 security create_keystore "$ROS_SECURITY_KEYSTORE"          # once
ros2 security create_enclave "$ROS_SECURITY_KEYSTORE" /fleet/robot1/nav
ros2 security create_permission "$ROS_SECURITY_KEYSTORE" /fleet/robot1/nav ./robot1-nav/policy.xml
```

Run `create_enclave` first: `create_permission` reads the enclave certificate to set the validity window. The result is `permissions.xml` and `permissions.p7s` in the enclave directory. Note that this regenerates `permissions.xml` from `policy.xml`. The exported `permissions.xml` is the same content for a DDS stack without the ROS tooling, and it uses the validity window you gave to `theauth ros2 export` (`--not-before`, `--not-after`, default one year). Keep that window inside the enclave certificate's.

To sign `permissions.xml` and `governance.xml` yourself, with OpenSSL (detached S/MIME, SHA-256, the same form `ros2 security` writes):

```bash
openssl smime -sign -text -in permissions.xml -out permissions.p7s \
  -signer permissions_ca.cert.pem -inkey permissions_ca.key.pem -md sha256
openssl smime -sign -text -in governance.xml -out governance.p7s \
  -signer permissions_ca.cert.pem -inkey permissions_ca.key.pem -md sha256

# Check a signature:
openssl smime -verify -in permissions.p7s -CAfile permissions_ca.cert.pem -out /dev/null
```

Then run the robot with security enforced:

```bash
export ROS_SECURITY_ENABLE=true
export ROS_SECURITY_STRATEGY=Enforce
export ROS_SECURITY_KEYSTORE=~/keystore
ros2 run my_pkg nav_node --ros-args --enclave /fleet/robot1/nav
```

Without `Enforce`, ROS 2 falls back to permissive mode and an unlisted participant still starts. Each process needs its own enclave, because DDS Security grants are per participant.

The subject in `permissions.xml` has to equal the enclave certificate's subject exactly, otherwise DDS ignores the grant. `ros2 security create_enclave` issues `CN=<enclave path>`, which is the default here. Pass `--subject` if yours differs.

## Gate hazardous commands at runtime

The gate sits between whatever decides to move and the topic that moves the machine. It calls `POST /authorize/token` with the robot's agent token and publishes only on an explicit `allowed: true`.

```typescript
import { guardRobotCommand, ros2Topic } from '@glinr/theauth/robotics';

const options = {
  baseUrl: 'https://auth.example.com/api/auth',
  token: () => process.env.THEAUTH_ROBOT_TOKEN ?? '',
  timeoutMs: 1000,
  // Exact resources that run without asking. Software stop commands only.
  safetyStops: [ros2Topic('/e_stop')],
};

const result = await guardRobotCommand(
  options,
  { action: 'publish', resource: ros2Topic('/cmd_vel') },
  () => publishVelocity(0.4),
);

if (!result.ok) {
  // result.code: no_permission, approval_required, step_up_required, guard_error, ...
  // result.approvalRequired is true when a person (or a step up) would let it through.
  logRefusal(result.code, result.reason);
}
```

It fails closed. A timeout, a refused connection, a 500, a body that is not JSON, or anything other than `allowed: true` returns `{ ok: false }` and the command does not run. Errors thrown by your own command function are not caught.

When the answer is `approval_required`, create the approval as described in [Approvals](/approval), and pass the granted id as `approvalId` on the retry.

### Two person rule for dangerous commands

Some commands should need two people, for example releasing a brake, moving an arm near a person or driving above a speed limit. Open the approval with a quorum, and the gate keeps answering `approval_pending` until two different operators have approved.

```typescript
const req = await theauth.approval.request({
  agentId: robot.id,
  userId: fleetOwnerId,
  action: "publish",
  resource: "ros2:/arm/cmd_vel",
  arguments: { linear: 0.4 },
  requiredApprovals: 2,
});

await theauth.approval.approve(req.id, "operator-a"); // still pending
await theauth.approval.approve(req.id, "operator-b"); // approved

// The gate passes the id on the retry. It works once, for these arguments only.
const result = await theauth.authorize(robot.id, {
  action: "publish",
  resource: "ros2:/arm/cmd_vel",
  arguments: { linear: 0.4 },
  approvalId: req.id,
});
```

The person who opened the request cannot be one of the two, and the same operator cannot approve twice. A single denial cancels it, and if the second operator does not act before `ttl` runs out, the request expires and the first approval is discarded. Keep `ttl` short for robot commands so an old approval cannot be reused later. See [Approvals](/approval) for the full rules.

### rclpy: a gate node

This node listens on `/cmd_vel_request`, asks theAuth, and republishes to `/cmd_vel`. Give the planner an enclave that may publish `/cmd_vel_request` only, and give this node the only grant for `/cmd_vel`. It uses only the Python standard library for HTTP.

```python
import json
import os
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request

import rclpy
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist
from rclpy.callback_groups import ReentrantCallbackGroup
from rclpy.executors import MultiThreadedExecutor
from rclpy.node import Node

AUTHORIZE_URL = os.environ["THEAUTH_URL"].rstrip("/") + "/authorize/token"
TOKEN = os.environ["THEAUTH_ROBOT_TOKEN"]
TIMEOUT_S = float(os.environ.get("THEAUTH_TIMEOUT_S", "1.0"))
# How long an "allowed" answer is reused. 0 asks every time. A revoked robot keeps moving
# for up to this long, so keep it short.
ALLOW_TTL_S = float(os.environ.get("THEAUTH_ALLOW_TTL_S", "0.5"))

def authorize(action, resource):
    """Return (allowed, code). Any failure is a refusal."""
    body = json.dumps({"action": action, "resource": resource}).encode()
    request = urllib.request.Request(
        AUTHORIZE_URL,
        data=body,
        method="POST",
        headers={"content-type": "application/json", "authorization": "Bearer " + TOKEN},
    )
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=TIMEOUT_S) as response:
            data = json.load(response).get("data", {})
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as err:
        try:
            data = json.load(err).get("data", {})
        except ValueError:
            data = {}
    except Exception:
        return False, "guard_error"
    return data.get("allowed") is True, data.get("code", "guard_error")

def is_stop(msg):
    """A command that only asks for zero motion needs no permission."""
    return all(v == 0.0 for v in (
        msg.linear.x, msg.linear.y, msg.linear.z,
        msg.angular.x, msg.angular.y, msg.angular.z,
    ))

class CommandGate(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__("command_gate")
        group = ReentrantCallbackGroup()
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, "/cmd_vel", 10)
        self.sub = self.create_subscription(
            Twist, "/cmd_vel_request", self.on_request, 10, callback_group=group
        )
        self.allowed_until = 0.0

    def on_request(self, msg):
        if is_stop(msg):
            self.pub.publish(msg)
            return
        now = time.monotonic()
        if now >= self.allowed_until:
            allowed, code = authorize("publish", "ros2:/cmd_vel")
            if not allowed:
                self.get_logger().warn("cmd_vel refused: " + code)
                return
            self.allowed_until = now + ALLOW_TTL_S
        self.pub.publish(msg)

def main():
    rclpy.init()
    node = CommandGate()
    executor = MultiThreadedExecutor()
    executor.add_node(node)
    executor.spin()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Put a watchdog on the actuation side too: if `/cmd_vel` stops arriving, the motor controller should drop to zero velocity. Then a dead gate stops the robot instead of leaving the last command running.

### rclcpp: the same idea, as a sketch

This is a sketch, not a tested package. `http_post_json` stands for whichever HTTP client you already link (libcurl, cpp-httplib). Run it off the executor thread, and treat every failure as a refusal.

```cpp
#include <chrono>
#include <geometry_msgs/msg/twist.hpp>
#include <rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp>

// Returns true only for HTTP 200 with {"data":{"allowed":true}}.
// Returns false on timeout, transport error, bad JSON, or any other status.
bool theauth_allows(const std::string &action, const std::string &resource);

class CommandGate : public rclcpp::Node {
 public:
  CommandGate() : Node("command_gate") {
    pub_ = create_publisher<geometry_msgs::msg::Twist>("/cmd_vel", 10);
    sub_ = create_subscription<geometry_msgs::msg::Twist>(
        "/cmd_vel_request", 10,
        [this](geometry_msgs::msg::Twist::ConstSharedPtr msg) { on_request(*msg); });
  }

 private:
  static bool is_stop(const geometry_msgs::msg::Twist &m) {
    return m.linear.x == 0 && m.linear.y == 0 && m.linear.z == 0 &&
           m.angular.x == 0 && m.angular.y == 0 && m.angular.z == 0;
  }

  void on_request(const geometry_msgs::msg::Twist &msg) {
    if (!is_stop(msg) && !theauth_allows("publish", "ros2:/cmd_vel")) {
      RCLCPP_WARN(get_logger(), "cmd_vel refused");
      return;
    }
    pub_->publish(msg);
  }

  rclcpp::Publisher<geometry_msgs::msg::Twist>::SharedPtr pub_;
  rclcpp::Subscription<geometry_msgs::msg::Twist>::SharedPtr sub_;
};
```

## Safety stops

An emergency stop must not wait for a network, a DDS graph, a process or theAuth. That belongs in hardware or a certified safety controller, under the standards for your machine (ISO 13850 covers emergency stop principles).

`safetyStops` in `guardRobotCommand` exists for a narrower reason: a software stop command should not become slower, or refusable, because the auth server is down. Listed resources run immediately with no request. Matching is exact on purpose. `ros2:*`, a prefix, or a typo will not match, so the bypass cannot widen by accident. Keep the list to commands that only stop motion. Pass `onSafetyStop` to record that a bypass happened. It is never awaited and errors in it are swallowed.

Revocation shortens how long a stolen robot token or enclave key keeps working. It does not stop a robot that is already moving.

## Compare two policies

```bash
theauth ros2 diff before.json after.json
```

Prints the DDS topics that would be added or removed and the permissions that became or stopped being gated. Exit code 0 means no change, 2 means the exported policy differs, 1 is an error. Use it in review before rolling a policy change to a fleet.

## Verified on ROS 2 Humble

Everything in this section was run, in Docker, on 2026-10-18. The setup: image `ros:humble` (digest `sha256:566b87e6dfc4...`, aarch64), `ros-humble-sros2` 0.10.9, `ros-humble-rmw-fastrtps-cpp` 6.2.10, Fast DDS 2.6.12, `rclpy` publisher and subscriber scripts on `std_msgs/String`, one enclave per process, `ROS_SECURITY_ENABLE=true ROS_SECURITY_STRATEGY=Enforce`. The exporter ran on the host and the XML was mounted into the container.

What this does not cover: only Humble and only `rmw_fastrtps_cpp` (no Jazzy, no Cyclone DDS, no Connext, no Zenoh). Only `rclpy` nodes, no `rclcpp`. Only topics. Services and actions were not exercised end to end, apart from the parameter services every node serves. Certificate expiry and key revocation were not tried. The gate node of this page was not run: the "gate" below is just an enclave exported with `--gated include`.

### Export, then build the keystore

```bash
# Host. perms: /chatter publish plus a gated /cmd_vel (requireApproval) for the talker.
theauth ros2 export --permissions talker.json --enclave /w11/talker --out out-talker
#   9 rules exported, 1 gated, 0 skipped.
#     gated  ros2:/cmd_vel [publish] left out: requireApproval
theauth ros2 export --permissions listener.json --enclave /w11/listener --out out-listener
theauth ros2 export --permissions driver.json   --enclave /w11/driver   --out out-driver   # subscribes /cmd_vel
theauth ros2 export --permissions gate.json     --enclave /w11/gate     --out out-gate --gated include

# Container.
ros2 security create_keystore "$ROS_SECURITY_KEYSTORE"
for e in talker listener gate driver; do
  ros2 security create_enclave   "$ROS_SECURITY_KEYSTORE" /w11/$e
  ros2 security create_permission "$ROS_SECURITY_KEYSTORE" /w11/$e /work/out-$e/policy.xml
done
export ROS_SECURITY_ENABLE=true ROS_SECURITY_STRATEGY=Enforce
```

`create_permission` accepted every exported `policy.xml`.

### What flowed and what was refused

Each row starts the subscriber, waits three seconds, then runs the publisher for twelve seconds at 2 Hz.

| Publisher enclave and topic | Subscriber enclave and topic | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| talker, `/chatter` | listener, `/chatter` | Both created. The listener received 13 messages. |
| talker, `/secret` (not in any policy) | listener, `/secret` | Publisher refused: `create_publisher() could not create data writer`. Subscriber refused with `rt/secret topic not found in allow rule`, and the `rclpy` process then crashed with a segmentation fault instead of raising. |
| talker, `/cmd_vel` (gated, left out) | driver, `/cmd_vel` | Publisher refused. The driver subscribed and received 0 messages. |
| gate (exported with `--gated include`), `/cmd_vel` | driver, `/cmd_vel` | Both created. The driver received 13 messages. |
| listener, `/chatter` (only has subscribe) | listener, `/chatter` | Publisher refused. |

The refusal text from Fast DDS, as printed:

```text
[SECURITY Error] rt/secret topic not found in allow rule. (./src/cpp/security/accesscontrol/Permissions.cpp:1245) -> Function check_create_datareader
```

Two more checks. With security switched off (`ROS_SECURITY_ENABLE=false`) the same `/secret` publisher and subscriber exchanged messages (14 and 15 received in two runs), so the refusals above come from the permissions and not from the test scripts. And a publisher with security off talking to an `Enforce` subscriber on `/chatter` delivered 0 messages: the governance's refusal of unauthenticated participants held.

### Signing your own XML

The exported `permissions.xml` and `governance.xml` were also signed with the OpenSSL commands from [Sign and install](#sign-and-install) (using `public/permissions_ca.cert.pem` and `private/permissions_ca.key.pem` from the keystore), copied over the enclave's `permissions.*` and `governance.*`, and `openssl smime -verify` printed `Verification successful` for all four. The talker and listener then behaved as in the first two table rows. `openssl x509 -subject` printed `subject=CN = /w11/talker`, and DDS accepted the exporter's `CN=/w11/talker` as equal.

### The node baseline is needed

With only the application topics in `policy.xml`, a node under `Enforce` does not start. Observed in order, each one fixed by adding that item:

```text
rt/rosout topic not found in allow rule ... check_create_datawriter
rq/talker/describe_parametersRequest topic not found in allow rule ... check_create_datareader
rt/parameter_events topic not found in allow rule ... check_create_datawriter
```

That is why [the node baseline](#the-node-baseline) exists. Exporting `/rosout`, six parameter services and `/parameter_events` made the first table row work.

### Globs

Enclave `globss` was exported from `ros2:/fleet/**` with `--resource-matching path` (DDS topic `rt/fleet/*`). Enclave `glob1` was exported from `ros2:/fleet/*` with `--resource-matching path --single-level widen`, which writes the same `rt/fleet/*`. Both enclaves, creating publishers:

```text
/fleet        refused
/fleet/a      allowed
/fleet/a/b    allowed
/fleet/a/b/c  allowed
/other        refused
```

So in Fast DDS the `*` of a permissions topic does cross `/`, as this page says: the one level `/fleet/*` cannot be written as a DDS glob, and `--single-level widen` really does grant the deeper names. A glob does not match its own prefix (`/fleet`).

## What is not covered

- **Zenoh.** There is no Zenoh `access_control` exporter. rmw_zenoh's key expressions carry more than the topic name, and a config that looks right but matches nothing is worse than none. The `zenoh_security_tools` package from the rmw_zenoh repository generates Zenoh access control from an SROS2 policy file, so feed it the exported `policy.xml`.
- **micro-ROS.** A microcontroller does not run a full DDS participant. Check eProsima's documentation for how the Micro XRCE-DDS agent and its client link are secured, and treat the agent as the trust boundary.
- **Delegated permissions.** `--robot` exports the robot's own permissions and the live permissions delegated to it (`GET /agents/:id?include=delegated`).
- **Certificate lifetimes.** DDS Security validity windows are absolute dates. Pass `--enclave-cert <pem>` and the grant window defaults to the certificate's own window; a `--not-before` or `--not-after` outside it is refused. Re-export and re-sign on a schedule shorter than the window.
- **Per node policy inside one process.** DDS Security grants apply per participant, and ROS 2 uses one participant per process, so two composed nodes share one grant.

## Sources

- OMG DDS Security 1.1 (formal/18-04-01), permissions and governance documents.
- SROS2 source and schemas, `github.com/ros2/sros2` (`permissions.xsl`, `policy.xsd`, default governance).
- ROS 2 design article, "ROS 2 DDS-Security integration".
- Zenoh manual, access control.

# Overview

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/adapters/index

## How adapters work

The `@glinr/theauth` package has zero framework dependencies. It operates entirely on the Web platform `Request`/`Response` API. Adapter packages wrap the core and expose framework-idiomatic handlers for authentication, authorization, and MCP OAuth routes.

Because the core uses only Web platform APIs, theAuth runs on edge runtimes without modification: Next.js Edge Runtime, Cloudflare Workers, Deno Deploy, Vercel Edge Functions, and Bun. The Hono and SvelteKit adapters are fully edge-compatible out of the box. The Next.js adapter works on edge when you use `export const runtime = 'edge'` in your route file.

Each adapter follows the same pattern: accept a `theauth` instance, optionally accept a config object, and return something your framework knows how to mount.

```typescript
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { createMcpModule } from '@glinr/theauth/mcp';
import { mcpStore } from './mcp-store.js'; // storage callbacks, see the MCP page

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite-native', url: 'theauth.db' },
  baseUrl: 'https://auth.yourapp.com',
});

// optional, enables MCP OAuth endpoints
const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    enabled: true,
    issuer: 'https://auth.yourapp.com',
    baseUrl: 'https://auth.yourapp.com/api/theauth', // origin plus the mount path
    signingSecret: process.env.MCP_SIGNING_SECRET!, // at least 32 characters
  },
  ...mcpStore,
});
```

Pass `mcp` to the adapter to enable the MCP OAuth 2.1 endpoints under the same mount path. `createMcpModule` comes from `@glinr/theauth/mcp` and takes a config object plus storage callbacks, see [MCP](/mcp).

## Authenticate the management routes

The agent, delegation, audit and dashboard routes (`/agents`, `/delegations`, `/audit`, `/dashboard`, and `POST /authorize`) manage your whole agent fleet, so every adapter requires an authenticated caller. `/authorize/token` (agent bearer token), the MCP endpoints, password reset, email verification and plugin routes are not affected; they carry their own checks.

Pass an `authenticate` function. It receives the standard `Request` and returns `{ id }` for an allowed caller or `null` to reject with 401:

```ts
const authenticate = async (request: Request) => {
  const user = await theauth.auth.resolveUser(request);
  return user?.id === process.env.ADMIN_USER_ID ? { id: user.id } : null;
};

app.route('/api/theauth', theAuthHono(theauth, { authenticate }));
```

`theauth.auth.resolveUser` only consults the `auth.adapter` you configured. If you rely on `auth.session` alone, skip `authenticate` (see next paragraph) or validate the token yourself with `theauth.auth.session.validate(token)`.

If you leave `authenticate` out and `auth.session` is configured on `createTheAuth`, the adapter accepts any valid session (cookie or `Authorization: Bearer <session token>`). That admits every signed-in user, but each one only sees and acts on their own agents, delegations and audit rows. Write your own resolver when admins or service tokens need to reach everything; whatever a custom resolver accepts is unrestricted. If neither is configured, the adapter throws when you create it:

```
[theauth] theAuthHono: the management routes (/agents, /delegations, /audit, /dashboard, /authorize) require authentication, but none is configured.
```

For a local demo you can opt out with `allowUnauthenticated: true`. A warning is logged on startup. Do not ship it.

### Rate limiting and cross-site writes

Every adapter refuses abusive traffic before authentication runs.

- **Rate limits** are per client, in three tiers: token, registration and authorize routes (30 per minute), other writes (120 per minute) and reads (300 per minute). Exceeding one returns `429` with `Retry-After`.
- **Cookie sessions** cannot be used for cross-site writes. A `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE` that carries a cookie and no `Authorization` header must come from the adapter's own origin or one listed in `trustedOrigins`. Bearer callers are not affected.

```typescript
app.use("/api/theauth", theAuthExpress(theauth, {
  trustedProxy: { trustedProxyCount: 1 },
  trustedOrigins: ["https://app.example.com"],
  rateLimit: { read: { max: 600, window: 60 } },
}));
```

Two hooks cover the cases the defaults miss. `skip` leaves a request out of rate limiting (health checks, your own network) and `key` replaces the client key, for example to count per tenant:

```typescript
rateLimit: {
  skip: (request, path) => path === "/health",
  key: (request) => request.headers.get("x-tenant"), // null falls back to the client IP
}
```

Set `trustedProxy` so limits apply per client IP. Without it the IP is unknown and callers are split by their credential instead. Counts are kept in the `rateLimit` [secondary storage](/configuration). With the default in-process store each instance counts alone; configure `secondaryStorage: "database"` or a Redis style store and one limit holds across instances. If the store errors, the request is let through so an outage there does not take sign-in down. Use `rateLimit: false` or `csrf: false` to switch either check off.

### Upgrading

Earlier versions mounted these routes with no authentication. After upgrading, pass `authenticate` (or configure `auth.session`) to each adapter call, or add `allowUnauthenticated: true` while you work on it locally.

## Headers and CORS

Every response is `Cache-Control: no-store` by default. Security headers (`securityHeaders`) and an exact-origin CORS allowlist (`cors`) are opt-in. See [Routes](/adapters/routes#security-headers).

## Endpoints registered

All adapters register the same set of REST routes under `basePath` (default `/api/theauth`):

| Path | Methods | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `/agents` | `GET`, `POST` | List and create agents |
| `/agents/:id` | `GET`, `PATCH`, `DELETE` | Get, update, revoke an agent |
| `/agents/:id/rotate` | `POST` | Rotate an agent's token |
| `/authorize` | `POST` | Authorize an action by agent ID |
| `/authorize/token` | `POST` | Authorize an action by bearer token |
| `/delegations` | `POST` | Create a delegation chain |
| `/delegations/:id` | `DELETE` | Revoke a delegation |
| `/delegations/:agentId` | `GET` | List delegation chains for an agent |
| `/audit` | `GET` | Query audit logs |
| `/audit/export` | `GET` | Export audit logs as JSON or CSV |

When `mcp` is passed, additional endpoints are registered:

| Path | Methods | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` | `GET` | OAuth 2.1 server metadata (RFC 8414) |
| `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` | `GET` | Protected resource metadata (RFC 9728) |
| `/mcp/register` | `POST` | Dynamic client registration (RFC 7591) |
| `/mcp/authorize` | `GET` | Authorization endpoint (PKCE + S256) |
| `/mcp/token` | `POST` | Token endpoint |

<Warning>
  These paths are relative to the mount point, but MCP clients look for the `/.well-known/*` documents at the root of your origin. When you mount the adapter under a prefix such as `/api/theauth`, also serve `mcp.getMetadata()` and `mcp.getProtectedResourceMetadata()` from root-level `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` and `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` routes. See [MCP](/mcp).
</Warning>

## Using without an adapter

If your framework is not listed, call the module methods directly from any server that handles standard `Request` objects. The `mcp` module from `createMcpModule` does not route URLs for you: you map paths to its methods yourself.

```typescript
import { mcp } from './lib/theauth.js';

async function handler(request: Request): Promise<Response> {
  const url = new URL(request.url);

  if (url.pathname === '/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server') {
    return Response.json(mcp.getMetadata());
  }
  if (url.pathname === '/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource') {
    return Response.json(mcp.getProtectedResourceMetadata());
  }

  // Protect everything else: 401 or 403 responses are built for you
  const check = await mcp.requireScopes(request, ['mcp:read']);
  if (!check.authorized) return check.response;

  return Response.json({ tools: [] });
}
```

You would also route `/mcp/register`, `/mcp/authorize`, and `/mcp/token` to `mcp.registerClient(body)`, `mcp.authorize(request)`, and `mcp.token(request)`, which return a `Result` you turn into a `Response`. The adapters in this table already do that, and the agent REST routes are only available through an adapter.
