# Multi-session

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/multi-session

By default, theAuth allows unlimited concurrent sessions per user. The multi-session module adds a cap with a configurable overflow strategy, plus functions for listing and revoking sessions, useful for building an "active devices" settings page.

It is a plain module exported from `@glinr/theauth`, not a plugin. It registers no HTTP routes and does not hook into sign-in on its own: you call `enforceSessionLimit` before creating a session, and you expose the list and revoke operations from your own routes.

## Setup

```typescript title="lib/theauth.ts"
import { createTheAuth, createMultiSessionModule } from '@glinr/theauth'; // [!code highlight]

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'postgres', url: process.env.DATABASE_URL! },
  auth: { session: { secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET! } },
});

export const multiSession = createMultiSessionModule( // [!code highlight]
  {
    maxSessions: 5, // [!code highlight]
    overflowStrategy: 'evict-oldest', // [!code highlight]
  },
  theauth.db,
  theauth.auth.session!, // [!code highlight]
);
```

The third argument is the low-level session manager (`theauth.auth.session`, or `cookieSessionManager.raw` if you use `createCookieSessionManager`).

## Enforcing the cap

Call `enforceSessionLimit` before you create a session, and use `buildSessionMetadata` to record device and IP:

```typescript title="Sign-in handler"
import { buildSessionMetadata, MultiSessionLimitError } from '@glinr/theauth';

try {
  await multiSession.enforceSessionLimit(userId);
} catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof MultiSessionLimitError) {
    return new Response(JSON.stringify({ error: err.code }), { status: 429 });
  }
  throw err;
}

const { token } = await theauth.auth.session!.create(userId, buildSessionMetadata(request));
```

## Overflow strategies

| Strategy | Behavior |
|----------|----------|
| `evict-oldest` | Revokes the oldest sessions (by creation time) until there is room for the new one |
| `reject` | Throws `MultiSessionLimitError` with code `SESSION_LIMIT_REACHED`. Turning that into an HTTP status is up to your handler |

## List sessions

`listSessions(userId)` returns all non-expired sessions for a user, newest first. Wire it to your own route to build an "active devices" UI.

```typescript title="List sessions (server)"
const sessions = await multiSession.listSessions(userId);
```

**Result shape**

```json
[
  {
    "id": "5f0c2d1e-...",
    "createdAt": "2026-06-01T10:00:00.000Z",
    "expiresAt": "2026-06-08T10:00:00.000Z",
    "device": "Chrome on macOS",
    "ip": "203.0.113.1"
  }
]
```

`device` and `ip` are only present when the session was created with metadata from `buildSessionMetadata` (or your own metadata with those keys). `device` is a short string parsed from the `User-Agent` header, such as `Chrome on macOS`. IP addresses are stored as-is, apply your own masking if required. Any other metadata keys appear under `metadata`. The result has no `current` flag, compare `id` with the caller's session ID yourself.

## Revoke a session

```typescript title="Revoke session (server)"
await multiSession.revokeSession(sessionId);
```

`revokeSession` deletes the session by ID. It does not check who owns it, so verify that the session belongs to the signed-in user before calling it.

## Revoke all other sessions

```typescript title="Sign out all other devices (server)"
const revoked = await multiSession.revokeOtherSessions(userId, currentSessionId);
```

Revokes every non-expired session for the user except `currentSessionId` and returns the number revoked. `getSessionCount(userId)` returns the number of active sessions.

## Configuration reference

<ParamField path="maxSessions" type="number" default="10">Maximum concurrent sessions per user.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="overflowStrategy" type="'evict-oldest' | 'reject'" default="'evict-oldest'">What to do when a new sign-in would exceed maxSessions.</ParamField>

# OWASP agentic AI top 10 mapped to theAuth

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/owasp-agentic-mapping

<Note>
  Risk names follow a secondary reading of the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026 (OWASP GenAI Security Project), without its numeric identifiers. Check the wording against the OWASP publication before you cite it in an audit. Feature links point to the TypeScript SDK docs. The Go threat model ([/go/security/threat-model](/go/security/threat-model)) uses its own categories and does not map to this list.
</Note>

| # | Risk | theAuth feature | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Agent Goal Hijack | [Taint-aware tool guard](/taint-guard), [approval flows](/approval) | Tracks where an argument came from, not whether the plan is malicious |
| 2 | Tool Misuse and Exploitation | [Permissions](/permissions), [rate limiting](/rate-limiting), MCP `requiredScopes` | Only tools you register are gated |
| 3 | Identity and Privilege Abuse | [Agent identity](/agents), [token vault](/token-vault), [DPoP](/dpop), RFC 8707 audience checks | Unbound bearer tokens work for any holder; offline checks miss revocation |
| 4 | Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities | jwt-bearer accepts listed issuers only, [MCP registry](/publishing), lenient client options off by default | Third-party MCP servers and their code are not scanned |
| 5 | Unexpected Code Execution | None. Withhold code-execution tools via [permissions](/permissions) | Does not inspect or sandbox code |
| 6 | Memory and Context Poisoning | Taint labels, [audit trail](/audit) | Memory stores are yours; not scanned |
| 7 | Insecure Inter-Agent Communication | Token exchange (RFC 8693) with an `act` chain, [delegation chains](/delegation) | Messages outside the token flow are not covered |
| 8 | Cascading Failures | [Rate limiting](/rate-limiting), delegation depth limits, cascading revocation | Limits are per agent and per IP, not fleet-wide |
| 9 | Human-Agent Trust Exploitation | [Approval flows](/approval), MCP `consentPage` | Cannot tell whether approval was informed; design the prompt yourself |
| 10 | Rogue Agents | Revocation, [trust scoring](/trust), [anomaly detection](/anomaly) | Anomaly detection is limited; the page lists what is missing |

# Security doctor

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/security-doctor

`theauth doctor --security` reads a theauth config file and reports unsafe settings. It does not open a database or call a server, so it runs in CI before deploy. For the setup and live server checks, see [CLI tools](/cli-tools).

```sh
theauth doctor --security
theauth doctor --security --config ./config/theauth.json --json --fail-on high
```

## Options

| Option | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--config <file>` | JSON or ES module config. Default: `theauth.config.mjs`, `.js` or `.json` in `--cwd`. |
| `--cwd <dir>` | Directory to look in. |
| `--json` | Print `{ ok, failOn, findings }`. |
| `--fail-on <level>` | Lowest severity that exits 1: `high` (default), `medium` or `low`. |

Exit codes: 0 no finding at or above the threshold, 1 at least one, 2 usage error or a config that cannot be loaded.

## Output

```json
{
  "ok": false,
  "failOn": "high",
  "findings": [
    {
      "id": "sec.lockout.off",
      "severity": "high",
      "message": "Login lockout is turned off, so one account can be guessed without limit",
      "fix": "Add rateLimit() to plugins, or confirm the handler or a gateway in front enforces limits.",
      "docs": "/security-doctor#sec-lockout-off"
    }
  ]
}
```

Finding ids never change once released, so you can suppress or alert on them. Findings are sorted high first.

## Findings

The linter reads the real `createTheAuth` config (`TheAuthConfig`). Settings that live outside that object cannot be read, so they are not linted: the `createTheAuthHandler` options (`cors`, `rateLimit`, `trustedOrigins`), the cookie flags of the session cookie, the options a plugin factory such as `rateLimit()` closes over, the `resolveUser` dependency of a handler, a stateless session manager, and the audit anchors you store outside the database.

<a id="sec-session-secret-weak"></a>
### sec.session.secret_weak (high)
`secret`, `auth.session.secret`, `mcp.signingSecret` (or `THEAUTH_SECRET`) is under 32 characters, repeats few distinct characters, or contains a word such as `secret`, `password`, `example` or `changeme`. Generate one with `theauth secret`.

<a id="sec-cookie-secure-off"></a>
### sec.cookie.secure_off (high)
`redirects.cookie.secure` is `false` while `baseUrl` is not localhost. The redirect chain cookie is the only cookie whose flags `TheAuthConfig` carries. The session cookie is `Secure` by default on every runtime (it no longer depends on `NODE_ENV`), and its flags are not config options.

<a id="sec-cookie-samesite-none"></a>
### sec.cookie.samesite_none (high)
`redirects.cookie.sameSite` is `none`. Use `lax` or `strict` unless you embed the app cross-site on purpose.

<a id="sec-cookie-host-prefix-missing"></a>
### sec.cookie.host_prefix_missing (low)
`auth.session` is set, `baseUrl` is not localhost, and `auth.session.cookieName` (default `theauth_session`) does not start with `__Host-`. The prefix stops a sibling subdomain from overwriting the cookie. Fires on the default name.

<a id="sec-password-pbkdf2-low"></a>
### sec.password.pbkdf2_low (high)
`username.pbkdf2Iterations`, `passwordReset.pbkdf2Iterations` or `THEAUTH_PBKDF2_ITERATIONS` resolves below 600000 (the core default) for a flow that is configured.

<a id="sec-rate-limit-off"></a>
### sec.rate_limit.off (medium)
`username`, `passwordReset`, `magicLink`, `emailOtp` or `phone` is configured and `plugins` has no `rateLimit()` plugin (id `theauth-rate-limit`). A limit you disable inside `rateLimit()` is not visible to the linter, and neither are the `createTheAuthHandler` limits, so this checks that the plugin is registered. Ignore it when the handler or a gateway enforces limits.

<a id="sec-lockout-off"></a>
### sec.lockout.off (high)
`username.lockout` is `false`, or `THEAUTH_LOGIN_LOCKOUT_DISABLED` is `1` or `true`, while `username` is configured. One account can then be guessed without limit.

<a id="sec-hosts-wildcard"></a>
### sec.hosts.wildcard (high)
`allowedHosts` contains a bare `*` or `**` (optionally with a scheme), so any `Host` header is accepted when building callback and magic link URLs. Use exact hosts or a suffix pattern such as `*.example.com`. This replaces the earlier `sec.cors.wildcard`, which read options that are not part of the config.

<a id="sec-redirect-allowlist-empty"></a>
### sec.redirect.allowlist_empty (medium)
`redirects` is set but `redirects.allowedOrigins` is empty or missing, so only same-origin return URLs work.

<a id="sec-mcp-revocation-offline"></a>
### sec.mcp.revocation_offline (medium)
`mcp.enabled` with `mcp.revocation.mode` `offline` (or `THEAUTH_MCP_REVOCATION_MODE=offline`). Revoked tokens then stay valid until they expire. Use `live` or `cached`. When neither the config nor the env sets a mode, core picks `live` if the module has a database, so the linter stays quiet.

<a id="sec-org-no-auth"></a>
### sec.org.no_auth (high)
`org.trustedServerUse` is `true`. The org `handleRequest` then acts on ids in the request without resolving a caller. Pass a `resolveUser` dependency and remove the flag, unless your own code authorizes every call first.

<a id="sec-api-keys-no-auth"></a>
### sec.api_keys.no_auth (high)
`apiKeys.trustedServerUse` is `true`. Same risk and fix as the org handler.

<a id="sec-api-keys-no-scope-resolver"></a>
### sec.api_keys.no_scope_resolver (low)
`apiKeys` is set without `grantablePermissions` and there is no `org` module. Self service creation then fails closed and can only mint keys with an empty permission list. With the org module present, core defaults the cap to the creator's org roles (see below), so the linter stays quiet. A resolver is a function, so a JSON config can never carry one: lint the `.mjs` config for this rule.

<a id="sec-device-path-matching-off"></a>
### sec.device.path_matching_off (medium)
`devices` is set, `resourceMatching` is not `path`, and a key of `permissions` contains `/` plus a `*`, `**`, `+` or `#` segment. In the default mode `*` counts only as a whole `:` segment, so `mqtt:fleet/*/temp` is plain text and never matches a real topic. Set `resourceMatching: "path"`.

<a id="sec-device-mid-wildcard"></a>
### sec.device.mid_wildcard (medium)
`devices` is set and a `permissions` resource has a wildcard before its last segment. In the default mode a mid `*` or `**` grants more than it reads. In every mode `#` must be the last level of a topic filter (MQTT 5, section 4.7.1.2).

<a id="sec-device-bundle-ttl-long"></a>
### sec.device.bundle_ttl_long (medium)
`devices.bundleTtlSeconds` is above 3600. An offline policy bundle cannot be revoked once issued, so a revoked device keeps its permissions until the bundle expires.

<a id="sec-device-no-attestation"></a>
### sec.device.no_attestation (medium)
`devices` is set without `attestation.verify`. Enrollment tokens can then be issued, and whoever holds one can register any hardware. The verifier is a function, so a JSON config always fires this rule.

<a id="sec-approval-no-step-up"></a>
### sec.approval.no_step_up (medium)
`approval` is set with no `requireAcr`, `maxAuthAge` or `stepUp`. A `requireApproval` permission can then be approved from any signed in session, with no proof of a strong or recent login. A rule passed per request to `approval.request()` is not visible to the linter.

<a id="sec-agent-dpop-not-required"></a>
### sec.agent.dpop_not_required (medium)
`agents.enabled` with `agents.confirmation.required` off, while a `permissions` catalog action or an `agents.defaultPermissions` entry is a write action (`write`, `create`, `update`, `delete`, `admin`, `manage`, `publish`, `execute`, `send` or `*`). A leaked token then works as a bearer token. Require a bound token (RFC 9449 DPoP or RFC 8705 mutual TLS).

## API key scope default

When `apiKeys` has no `grantablePermissions` and the `org` module is on, a self service key can carry a permission only if `org.hasPermission` allows it for the creator in at least one org they belong to. Owners pass for everything, a user with no org membership holds nothing, and a failing lookup denies. The match is exact: a role entry such as `agents:*` does not cover `agents:read`, so use an explicit `grantablePermissions` when your roles use patterns. An explicit `grantablePermissions` still wins, and trusted server code calling `create()` is not capped.

## Dropped checks

- `sec.session.stateless_no_ban_check`: the stateless session manager is created in code, not in `TheAuthConfig`, and its ban check (`db` or `isBanned`) cannot be read from a config file.
- `sec.audit.anchors_missing`: anchors come from `audit.checkpoint()` and are stored outside the config, so no option says whether they exist. See [audit checkpoints](/audit-checkpoints).
- `sec.cors.wildcard`: replaced by `sec.hosts.wildcard`. CORS is an option of `createTheAuthHandler`, not of the config.

## CI

```yaml
- run: npx theauth doctor --security --fail-on high
```

The linter reads only the `TheAuthConfig` fields named above. A field it does not know is ignored, and a rule fires only on the unsafe value, so an unset optional field stays quiet unless the table says it fires when missing.

---

# Protect an MCP server with OAuth 2.1

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/use-cases/mcp-server-behind-oauth

Every MCP request carries a token issued for this server and checked for audience and scope. theAuth issues the token and the MCP endpoint checks it, in one process.

<Steps>

<Step>

### Create the authorization module

Storage is passed as callbacks. The in-memory maps are for illustration; back them with your own database.

```typescript title="auth.ts"
import { createTheAuth } from "@glinr/theauth";
import { createMcpModule } from "@glinr/theauth/mcp";
import type { McpAccessToken, McpAuthorizationCode, McpClient } from "@glinr/theauth/mcp";

const clients = new Map<string, McpClient>();
const codes = new Map<string, McpAuthorizationCode>();
const tokens = new Map<string, McpAccessToken>();
const byRefreshToken = new Map<string, string>();

const mcpStore = {
  storeClient: async (client: McpClient) => {
    clients.set(client.clientId, client);
  },
  findClient: async (clientId: string) => clients.get(clientId) ?? null,
  storeAuthorizationCode: async (code: McpAuthorizationCode) => {
    codes.set(code.code, code);
  },
  consumeAuthorizationCode: async (code: string) => {
    const found = codes.get(code) ?? null;
    if (found) codes.delete(code); // single use
    return found;
  },
  storeToken: async (token: McpAccessToken) => {
    tokens.set(token.accessToken, token);
    if (token.refreshToken) byRefreshToken.set(token.refreshToken, token.accessToken);
  },
  findTokenByRefreshToken: async (refreshToken: string) => {
    const accessToken = byRefreshToken.get(refreshToken);
    return accessToken ? (tokens.get(accessToken) ?? null) : null;
  },
  revokeToken: async (accessToken: string) => {
    tokens.delete(accessToken);
  },
  // Return the signed-in user id from your session, or null to send them to loginPage
  resolveUserId: async (_request: Request) => null as string | null,
};

export const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: "sqlite-native", url: "theauth.db" },
  baseUrl: "https://auth.yourapp.com",
  mcp: { enabled: true },
});

export const mcp = createMcpModule({
  config: {
    enabled: true,
    issuer: "https://auth.yourapp.com",
    baseUrl: "https://auth.yourapp.com/api/theauth",
    signingSecret: process.env.MCP_SIGNING_SECRET!, // at least 32 characters
    resource: "https://mcp.yourapp.com/mcp", // this server's canonical URI (RFC 8707)
    scopes: ["mcp:read", "mcp:execute"],
    accessTokenTtl: 3600,
    loginPage: "https://auth.yourapp.com/login",
    allowedResources: ["https://mcp.yourapp.com/mcp"],
  },
  ...mcpStore,
});
```

</Step>

<Step>

### Mount the OAuth endpoints

The adapter serves the metadata routes, `POST /mcp/register`, `GET /mcp/authorize` and `POST /mcp/token`. The client then exchanges its code with the PKCE verifier and the resource. The full endpoint table is in [MCP OAuth 2.1](/mcp).

```typescript title="server.ts"
import { Hono } from "hono";
import { theAuthHono } from "@glinr/theauth-hono";

const app = new Hono();
app.route("/api", theAuthHono(theauth, { mcp }));
```

```http
POST /api/theauth/mcp/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=authorization_code
&code=<code from the redirect>
&code_verifier=<PKCE verifier>
&redirect_uri=http://127.0.0.1:8976/callback
&client_id=<client id>
&resource=https://mcp.yourapp.com/mcp
```

</Step>

<Step>

### Wrap the MCP routes

`requireMcpAuth` checks the signature, issuer, expiry and audience, then the scopes you name. It runs your handler only when all of those pass, and passes in the verified principal.

```typescript title="server.ts"
const listTools = mcp.requireMcpAuth(
  async (_request, principal) => {
    return Response.json({
      tools: [{ name: "search_docs" }],
      user: principal.userId,
      client: principal.clientId,
      scopes: principal.scopes,
    });
  },
  { requiredScopes: ["mcp:read"] },
);

const callTool = mcp.requireMcpAuth(
  async (request, principal) => {
    const body = (await request.json()) as { name: string };
    return Response.json({ ok: true, tool: body.name, by: principal.userId });
  },
  { requiredScopes: ["mcp:execute"] },
);

app.get("/mcp/tools", (c) => listTools(c.req.raw));
app.post("/mcp/tools/call", (c) => callTool(c.req.raw));
```

The principal has `userId`, `clientId`, `agent`, `delegationChain`, `scopes`, `resource`, `tokenId` and `expiresAt`. Use `principal.userId` for ownership checks. Do not trust a user id from the request body.

</Step>

<Step>

### Mount revocation

The TypeScript adapters do not serve `/mcp/revoke` by default, so pass the request to `mcp.revoke` yourself.

```typescript title="server.ts"
app.post("/api/theauth/mcp/revoke", async (c) => {
  await mcp.revoke(c.req.raw);
  return c.body(null, 200);
});
```

</Step>

<Step>

### Check the result

A request with no token gets a 401 and a `WWW-Authenticate` challenge that points at the protected resource metadata. A valid token runs the handler.

```bash
curl -i https://mcp.yourapp.com/mcp/tools
# HTTP/1.1 401
# WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://mcp.yourapp.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource", ...

curl -i -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" https://mcp.yourapp.com/mcp/tools
# HTTP/1.1 200
```

</Step>

</Steps>

## What is enforced

| Enforced | Not enforced |
| --- | --- |
| Signature, issuer, expiry and audience on every request | Revocation for locally validated JWTs, until the token expires |
| Scopes per route (`requiredScopes`), 403 `insufficient_scope` on a miss | `/mcp/revoke` and `/mcp/jwks` are not served by default |
| `resource` required by `middleware`, `validateToken` and `requireScopes` | A client that omits `resource` gets a token not bound to your server |
| Token requests for resources outside `allowedResources` refused | Dynamic client registration is a compatibility path; the spec prefers [Client ID Metadata Documents](/mcp-client-compat) |
| Optional DPoP binding (`dpop` config, see [DPoP](/dpop)) | `examples/mcp-server` uses `validateToken`, not `requireMcpAuth` |

For agent tokens, set `tokenExchange` and `jtiDenylist` in the MCP config. See [MCP server grants](/mcp-grants). The Go version of this flow on SQLite is [OAuth 2.1 on SQLite](/use-cases/sqlite-oauth-server), which is Go only.

# GitHub Actions OIDC for CI agents (Go only)

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/use-cases/github-actions-oidc

A GitHub Actions job exchanges its OIDC token for a short-lived theAuth access token, with no stored client secret.

<Warning>
  Go only. The TypeScript package has no GitHub helper, and its `jwtBearer` grant expects an ID-JAG assertion (`typ: oauth-id-jag+jwt`, a `client_id` claim and `aud` equal to the issuer). A raw GitHub OIDC token is refused. The full Go write-up is in [`go/docs/github-actions-oidc.md`](https://github.com/glincker/theauth/blob/main/go/docs/github-actions-oidc.md).
</Warning>

<Steps>

<Step>

### Request the job's OIDC token

Grant `id-token: write` and request a token for your audience. GitHub signs claims that name the repository, branch, environment and workflow.

```yaml title=".github/workflows/deploy.yml"
name: deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  id-token: write   # lets the job request an OIDC token
  contents: read

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - name: Get a GitHub OIDC token
        run: |
          AUD="https://auth.example.com/gh"
          GH_TOKEN=$(curl -sS \
            -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN" \
            "$ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL&audience=$AUD" | jq -r .value)
          echo "::add-mask::$GH_TOKEN"
          echo "GH_TOKEN=$GH_TOKEN" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
```

</Step>

<Step>

### Exchange it for an access token

Post the token to the theAuth token endpoint with the RFC 7523 `jwt-bearer` grant. Add `client_id=<agent client id>` to make the token act as an agent, so the agent's policy and rate limit apply.

```bash
ACCESS=$(curl -sS https://auth.example.com/oauth/token \
  -d grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer \
  --data-urlencode "assertion=$GH_TOKEN" \
  -d resource=https://api.example.com/mcp \
  -d scope=api.read | jq -r .access_token)
echo "::add-mask::$ACCESS"
echo "ACCESS_TOKEN=$ACCESS" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
```

</Step>

<Step>

### Restrict the issuer (Go)

`GitHubActionsIssuer` refuses to build an issuer with no restriction. Each of `Repository`, `RepositoryOwner`, `Refs` and `Environment` adds a matcher, and all matchers must pass. `SubjectMapper` maps GitHub's `sub` to a local user, because the built-in mapper expects a ULID.

```go
iss, err := theauth.GitHubActionsIssuer(theauth.GitHubActionsOptions{
    Repository:    "acme/app",                  // exact owner/name
    Refs:          []string{"refs/heads/main"}, // or one glob: "refs/heads/release/*"
    Environment:   "production",
    Audience:      "https://auth.example.com/gh",
    SubjectMapper: myWorkflowMapper{},          // GitHub's sub is not a ULID
})
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

cfg.AuthorizationServer = &theauth.AuthorizationServerConfig{
    Issuer:    "https://auth.example.com",
    Resources: resources,
    JWTBearer: &theauth.JWTBearerConfig{TrustedJWTIssuers: []theauth.TrustedJWTIssuer{iss}},
}
```

If `Audience` is empty, the required `aud` is your authorization server issuer URL.

</Step>

<Step>

### Check a denial

A workflow that fails any matcher gets `invalid_grant` with the same description every time. Test it by running the workflow from a branch other than `main`. The operator sees the failed claim names in the audit log:

```json
{"action": "jwt_bearer.claims_denied",
 "targetType": "jwt_issuer", "targetId": "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com",
 "metadata": {"issuer": "...", "failed_claims": ["repository", "ref"], "agent_id": "...", "agent_name": "..."}}
```

</Step>

</Steps>

## What is enforced

| Enforced | Not enforced |
| --- | --- |
| Every matcher must pass | Tests sign with a local key. The GitHub request flow has not run against GitHub from the repository, so check it in your pipeline first. |
| Constructor refuses an issuer with no restriction | Hand-built issuers: add the matchers yourself, or any public repository's workflow can log in |
| Denial text never names the failed claim | Long jobs: compare duration with `AssertionMaxAge` (default 300 seconds) |
| Audit event lists failed claim names only | Scope limits come from `scope` and `resource` on the exchange |
| GitHub's environment protection rules (such as reviewers) run before the job, so the token is issued after approval | No TypeScript path |

Claim names come from GitHub's live discovery document.

# OAuth 2.1 server on SQLite in one Go binary

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/use-cases/sqlite-oauth-server

One Go binary and one SQLite file run an OAuth 2.1 authorization server that issues tokens for an MCP server.

<Note>
  Go library only. The TypeScript OAuth 2.1 server (`createMcpModule`) takes storage callbacks you write, see [MCP OAuth 2.1](/mcp). The full Go guide is [`go/docs/mcp-oauth-sqlite.md`](https://github.com/glincker/theauth/blob/main/go/docs/mcp-oauth-sqlite.md), and the store is documented in [SQLite storage](/go/guides/sqlite-storage).
</Note>

<Steps>

<Step>

### Register a public client

Registration is closed unless configured. The client sends the user to `/oauth/authorize` with `code_challenge_method=S256` and `resource`, then exchanges the code at `/oauth/token`.

```json
{
  "client_name": "Claude Code (e2e)",
  "redirect_uris": ["http://127.0.0.1:8976/callback"],
  "grant_types": ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"],
  "response_types": ["code"],
  "token_endpoint_auth_method": "none"
}
```

</Step>

<Step>

### Open the database and build the server

You own the `*sql.DB`, so set the pragmas. `New` refuses a database without foreign keys. The busy timeout and immediate transactions make concurrent token requests wait, not fail with `database is locked`.

```go
db, err := sql.Open("sqlite",
	"file:auth.db?_pragma=foreign_keys(1)&_pragma=busy_timeout(10000)&_pragma=journal_mode(WAL)&_txlock=immediate")
if err != nil {
	log.Fatal(err)
}
if err := sqlitestore.Migrate(ctx, db); err != nil { // applies every pending migration
	log.Fatal(err)
}
store, err := sqlitestore.New(db)
if err != nil {
	log.Fatal(err)
}

a, err := theauth.New(theauth.Config{
	Storage:       store,
	BaseURL:       "https://auth.example.com",
	EncryptionKey: key, // 32 bytes, seals the JWKS private keys
	AuthorizationServer: &theauth.AuthorizationServerConfig{
		Issuer: "https://auth.example.com",
		Resources: []theauth.ProtectedResource{{
			Identifier: "https://mcp.example.com/mcp",
			Scopes:     []string{"files.read", "files.write"},
		}},
		RegistrationTokens:    []string{initialAccessToken},
		AccessTokenRevocation: true,
	},
})
if err != nil {
	log.Fatal(err)
}
```

`Migrate` applies migrations 0001 to 0034. The OAuth tables start at 0020.

</Step>

<Step>

### Protect the MCP routes

`mcpresource` checks the bearer token on each request against the endpoints above. A request without a token gets a 401 that names the protected resource metadata URL. A token without the scope gets a 403 `insufficient_scope`.

```go
v := mcpresource.New("https://mcp.example.com/mcp",
	mcpresource.WithJWKS("https://auth.example.com/oauth/jwks"),
	mcpresource.WithIntrospection("https://auth.example.com/oauth/introspect", rsID, rsSecret),
)
mux.Handle("/mcp", v.Middleware(handler))
mux.Handle("/write", v.Middleware(v.RequireScope("files.write")(writeHandler)))
```

</Step>

<Step>

### Serve the well-known paths

The OAuth routes sit at the root of the handler you mount. If the issuer has a path, RFC 8414 and RFC 9728 clients request the well-known document under the origin root. Forward `/.well-known/` as well, or those URLs return 404.

```go
const prefix = "/api/v1/auth-lib"

h := a.Handler() // build once: each call mounts new routes and rate-limit buckets
mux := http.NewServeMux()
mux.Handle(prefix+"/", http.StripPrefix(prefix, h))
mux.Handle("/.well-known/", h) // no StripPrefix: the library matches the issuer path
```

</Step>

</Steps>

## What is enforced

| Enforced | Not enforced |
| --- | --- |
| PKCE with S256, the only method the server accepts | A JWKS-only resource server accepts a revoked token until it expires. Use introspection or a revocation checker. |
| Registration closed unless configured | One writer per file. Run one process per database file, and use Postgres or MySQL for several replicas. |
| `New` refuses a database without foreign keys | Rate limiter, replay cache and CIMD cache live in process memory, so sharing one file across app servers is not supported. |
| Signing keys sealed with `EncryptionKey` | A changed `EncryptionKey` makes stored keys unreadable, so existing tokens stop verifying. Back up the file and the key together. |
| Restart keeps key IDs, active and revoked tokens, refresh tokens and unredeemed codes (tested) | Your code must call `a.Close()` on shutdown so the audit writer drains. |

`mcpresource` is a separate module and can run in another process. Check module versions in the Go docs before you copy imports.

# Lifecycle hooks

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/hooks

## What hooks are

Hooks are async callbacks you register at startup. theAuth calls them at specific points in the authorization and agent lifecycle. They let you add custom logic without patching the SDK: log denials to Slack, block agents from running in unsandboxed environments, fire webhooks, or update your own database.

<Warning>
  Hooks are async. `beforeAuthorize` and `beforeAgentCreate` are awaited, run under a timeout, and can block requests by returning `{ allow: false }`. A timeout, a throw or a malformed verdict in `beforeAuthorize` denies the call by default (see [Hook safety](#hook-safety-timeout-and-fail-closed)). All other hooks (`afterAuthorize`, `afterAgentCreate`, `onAgentRevoke`, `onViolation`) are fire-and-forget: theAuth does not await them and does not catch their errors, so a throw becomes an unhandled promise rejection (which can terminate a Node.js process). Wrap their bodies in `try/catch`.
</Warning>

`beforeAuthorize` runs for `theauth.authorize()`, `theauth.authorizeByToken()` and `theauth.policy.evaluate()` when the subject is an agent. It runs after the agent is resolved and known to be active, and before any permission is evaluated. It does not run for an unknown agent id, an invalid token, or a revoked or expired agent: those deny first. A `policy.evaluate()` call for a user-only subject (no `agentId`) has no agent, no delegation chain and no audit row, so the hook does not run. `afterAuthorize` and `onViolation` fire for `authorize()` and `authorizeByToken()`, and receive a `source` field naming the entry point.

## Available hooks

<ParamField path="beforeAuthorize" type={`(context: BeforeAuthorizeContext) => Promise<{ allow: boolean; reason?: string } | { decision: "allow" | "deny" | "escalate"; reason?: string; guard?: string; ruleId?: string; metadata?: Record<string, string | number | boolean> } | void>`}>Fires before permission evaluation for an agent that can act. Return nothing or `{ allow: true }` to proceed. Return `{ allow: false, reason }` (or `{ decision: "deny" }`) to block with code `hook_denied`. Return `{ decision: "escalate" }` to require human approval: `authorize()` returns `allowed: false` with code `approval_required`, and `policy.evaluate()` returns `decision: "escalate"` with `escalation.tier` set to `"hook"`. A hook can only narrow access: an allow never overrides a denial from the agent's own permissions.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="afterAuthorize" type={`(context: { agentId, action, resource, source, result }) => Promise<void>`}>Fires after authorize() or authorizeByToken() completes with the final result (`{ allowed, reason?, auditId, code? }`). It does not fire when `beforeAuthorize` blocked the call or when the agent was not found or is not active.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="beforeAgentCreate" type={`(input: CreateAgentInput) => Promise<{ allow: boolean; reason?: string } | void>`}>Fires before `theauth.agent.create()`. Return `{ allow: false }` to reject the creation; `create()` then throws a `HookBlockedError` carrying your reason. It runs under the same timeout as `beforeAuthorize`, but a timeout or a throw makes `create()` throw by default, so creation never proceeds on a broken hook unless you set `onTimeout` or `onError` to `"allow"`.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="afterAgentCreate" type={`(agent: AgentIdentity) => Promise<void>`}>Fires after an agent is successfully created.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="onAgentRevoke" type={`(agentId: string) => Promise<void>`}>Fires after `theauth.agent.revoke()` succeeds.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="onViolation" type={`(violation: { type, code, agentId, action, resource, reason, source }) => Promise<void>`}>Fires when `theauth.authorize()` or `theauth.authorizeByToken()` returns a denial (including a `beforeAuthorize` block). `code` is the machine-readable denial code and `type` is its coarse grouping. Budget policies are not part of `authorize()`, so they do not trigger it.</ParamField>

## The beforeAuthorize context

The hook receives the old fields (`agentId`, `action`, `resource`, `arguments`) plus the resolved agent and the delegation chain behind it, so a guard can decide on who the call is really for.

```typescript
hooks: {
  async beforeAuthorize({ agent, delegation, source, context, dryRun, signal, action, resource }) {
    // agent: the resolved agent, token omitted (id, ownerId, tenantId, name, type, permissions, status)
    // delegation.rootOwnerId: the human accountable for the root of the chain
    // delegation.path: agent ids from the root agent down to this agent
    // delegation.links: the grant between each pair on the path, with its permissions, constraints, depth and expiry
    // delegation.inbound: every active grant into this agent (authorize merges all of them)
    // source: "authorize" | "authorizeByToken" | "policy.evaluate" | "explain"
    // context: { ip?, userAgent? } when the caller passed them
    // dryRun: true when the call comes from explain(); do not cause side effects
    // signal: aborted when the hook times out; pass it to fetch()
    const res = await fetch(guardUrl, { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify({ action, resource, root: delegation.rootOwnerId }), signal });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error('guard unavailable'); // denies with code hook_error by default
    const verdict = await res.json();
    return verdict.ok ? undefined : { decision: 'deny', reason: 'Blocked by guard' };
  },
}
```

`delegation.path` has one element when the agent is not delegated. When an agent has several inbound grants, `path` and `links` follow the oldest one, and `inbound` lists all of them. Revoked and expired grants never appear. The chain is loaded only when a `beforeAuthorize` hook is configured, so integrations without one pay nothing. A hook verdict is never cached: `policy.evaluate()` asks the hook on every call, even when the permission decision itself comes from the cache.

The `reason` you return is shown to the calling agent. Do not put secrets in it.

## Hook safety: timeout and fail-closed

A hook that hangs would hang every authorization, and a hook that throws should not silently open the door. `beforeAuthorize` therefore runs under a timeout and denies by default when it fails.

```typescript
const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database,
  hooks: { beforeAuthorize },
  hookSafety: {
    timeoutMs: 1500,                       // default 2000, 0 disables, clamped to 60000
    onTimeout: 'deny',                     // 'deny' | 'allow' | 'throw'
    onError: 'deny',                       // thrown error or malformed verdict
    beforeAgentCreate: { onTimeout: 'throw' },
    onHookError: ({ hook, kind, error, elapsedMs, agentId }) => metrics.increment(`hook.${hook}.${kind}`),
  },
});
```

| Situation | Result | Code | Reason returned to the caller |
|-----------|--------|------|-------------------------------|
| Hook returns deny | Denied | `hook_denied` | Your reason, else `Blocked by beforeAuthorize hook` |
| Hook returns escalate | Denied, needs approval | `approval_required` | Your reason, else `beforeAuthorize hook requires approval` |
| Timeout, mode `deny` | Denied | `hook_timeout` | `beforeAuthorize hook timed out after <n>ms` |
| Error or malformed verdict, mode `deny` | Denied | `hook_error` | `beforeAuthorize hook failed` (the error text is not returned) |
| Timeout or error, mode `allow` | Evaluation continues | Final code of the evaluation | Final reason. The audit row carries `theauthHook.outcome: "fail_open"` |
| Mode `throw` | The call rejects | | `HookTimeoutError` (code `HOOK_TIMEOUT`) or your original error |

Each setting resolves from the per-hook option (`hookSafety.beforeAuthorize`), then the top-level `hookSafety` option, then an environment variable, then the built-in default. Invalid environment values are ignored.

| Setting | Environment variable | Default |
|---------|----------------------|---------|
| `timeoutMs` | `THEAUTH_HOOK_TIMEOUT_MS` | `2000` |
| `onTimeout` | `THEAUTH_HOOK_ON_TIMEOUT` | `deny` for `beforeAuthorize`, `throw` for `beforeAgentCreate` |
| `onError` | `THEAUTH_HOOK_ON_ERROR` | `deny` for `beforeAuthorize`, `throw` for `beforeAgentCreate` |

For `beforeAgentCreate`, `deny` and `throw` both make `create()` throw: `deny` throws a `HookBlockedError` with the code, `throw` rethrows the original error.

`onHookError` is called on every timeout and error whatever the mode. It must not throw (a throw is swallowed) and cannot change the outcome. Setting a mode to `allow` is a deliberate fail-open: every such bypass is marked in the audit row and reported to `onHookError`, so it stays visible.

On a timeout the `signal` passed to the hook is aborted, so a hook that forwards it to `fetch()` stops its request. A late result from an abandoned hook is ignored.

## What a block leaves in the audit log

A `beforeAuthorize` block has an agent and an owner, so it writes a normal audit row in the agent's hash chain and returns that row's id as `auditId` (an empty string when `agents.auditAll` is `false`). A call for an unknown agent id or unknown token still writes nothing.

| Column | Value |
|--------|-------|
| `result` | `denied`, or `escalated` for an escalate verdict |
| `decision_code` | `hook_denied`, `hook_timeout`, `hook_error` or `approval_required` |
| `reason` | The reason returned to the caller |
| `parameters` | The call arguments plus `theauthHook: { hook, outcome, guard?, ruleId?, metadata?, elapsedMs }` |
| `duration_ms` | How long the hook ran |
| `subject_id`, `actor_id`, `delegation_chain` | Root owner, the agent, and the path when delegated |

`outcome` is `deny`, `escalate`, `timeout`, `error` or `fail_open`. The `theauthHook` key is set by theAuth and overrides a tool argument with the same name. `metadata` is capped at 16 scalar keys with values cut to 256 characters. Query these rows with `theauth.audit.query({ codes: ['hook_denied', 'hook_timeout', 'hook_error'] })`.

### Violation codes and types

Every denial carries a `code` from a closed set. `onViolation` receives it as `code`, `authorize()` and `authorizeByToken()` return it as `result.code`, and `policy.evaluate()` returns it as `decision.code`. Branch on `code`, not on the `reason` text.

```typescript
import { DECISION_CODES, violationTypeOf } from '@glinr/theauth';

hooks: {
  async onViolation({ code, agentId }) {
    if (code === DECISION_CODES.RATE_LIMITED) await alerts.warn(agentId);
    // violationTypeOf(code) gives the coarse type
  },
},
```

`type` stays available and keeps the same five values. It is derived from `code` with `violationTypeOf`:

| Type | Codes that map to it |
|------|----------------------|
| `rate_limited` | `rate_limited` |
| `ip_blocked` | `ip_not_allowed` (the request IP is missing or not in the permission's `ipAllowlist`) |
| `time_restricted` | `time_restricted` (outside the permission's `timeWindow`) |
| `approval_required` | `approval_required` and every `approval_*` denial |
| `permission_denied` | every other code |

A `beforeAuthorize` deny reports code `hook_denied`, so its `type` is `permission_denied` whatever the reason text says. A timeout reports `hook_timeout` and an error `hook_error`, also `permission_denied`. An escalate verdict reports `approval_required`. See [Errors](/errors#decision-codes) for the full list of codes.

<Note>
  `classifyViolation(reason)` is still exported but deprecated. It matches substrings of the reason text, so a reason that merely contains "rate" or "time" is misclassified. Use `code` and `violationTypeOf` instead.
</Note>

## Registering hooks

Pass a `hooks` object to `createTheAuth`:

```typescript
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite-native', url: 'theauth.db' },
  hooks: {
    async beforeAuthorize({ agentId, action, resource }) {
      // Example: block calls outside business hours
      const hour = new Date().getUTCHours();
      if (hour < 8 || hour >= 20) {
        return {
          allow: false,
          reason: `Agent ${agentId} cannot run outside business hours (08:00 to 20:00 UTC)`,
        };
      }
      // Return nothing (or { allow: true }) to let the request proceed
    },

    async afterAuthorize({ agentId, action, resource, result }) {
      if (!result.allowed) {
        console.warn(`[theauth] Denied: agent=${agentId} action=${action} resource=${resource} reason=${result.reason}`);
      }
    },
  },
});
```

## Logging every denial

```typescript
const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite-native', url: 'theauth.db' },
  hooks: {
    async afterAuthorize({ agentId, action, resource, result }) {
      if (!result.allowed) {
        await logger.warn('Authorization denied', {
          agentId,
          action,
          resource,
          reason: result.reason,
          auditId: result.auditId,
        });
      }
    },
  },
});
```

The `result.auditId` links this log line to the audit entry, so you can correlate your own logs with the theAuth audit trail. When `agents.auditAll` is `false`, the permission engine returns an `auditId` but does not write a row for it. Unknown-agent denials return an empty `auditId`. Denials for a revoked or expired agent, and calls blocked by a `beforeAuthorize` hook, return the id of the row that was written.

## Enforcing a sandbox check

```typescript
const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite-native', url: 'theauth.db' },
  hooks: {
    async beforeAgentCreate(input) {
      // Require sandbox metadata on all autonomous agents
      if (input.type === 'autonomous' && !input.metadata?.sandboxId) {
        return {
          allow: false,
          reason: 'Autonomous agents must declare a sandboxId in metadata',
        };
      }
    },
  },
});
```

Returning `{ allow: false }` from `beforeAgentCreate` causes the `theauth.agent.create()` call to throw a `HookBlockedError` (an `Error`) whose message is the reason you provided.

## Reacting to violations

The `onViolation` hook fires for every denial returned by `theauth.authorize()` or `theauth.authorizeByToken()`, with the `code` and `type` described above. Use it to send alerts or update your observability platform.

```typescript
const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite-native', url: 'theauth.db' },
  hooks: {
    async onViolation({ type, agentId, action, resource, reason }) {
      // Send to your alerting system
      await alerts.send({
        severity: type === 'rate_limited' ? 'warning' : 'error',
        title: `TheAuth violation: ${type}`,
        fields: { agentId, action, resource, reason },
      });

      // For repeat offenders, you could revoke here
      if (type === 'ip_blocked') {
        await theauth.agent.revoke(agentId);
      }
    },
  },
});
```

## Cleaning up after revocation

```typescript
import { createDiscoveryModule } from '@glinr/theauth-plugin-discovery';

// Create it once, after the instance exists, using the same database
let discovery: ReturnType<typeof createDiscoveryModule>;

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite-native', url: 'theauth.db' },
  hooks: {
    async onAgentRevoke(agentId) {
      // Remove the agent's discovery card. The discovery module is the separate
      // @glinr/theauth-plugin-discovery package; it is not on the theauth instance.
      await discovery.removeCard(agentId);

      // Notify your own systems
      await internalApi.notifyAgentRevoked(agentId);
    },
  },
});

discovery = createDiscoveryModule(theauth.db);
```

## External guards

An external guard is a policy service that decides whether an agent may act, for example HOL Guard. It plugs in through `beforeAuthorize`. `guardHook` adapts a guard to that hook, so the guard only implements `check`. Timeout, default deny and audit fields come from the hook runner.

```ts
import { createTheAuth, guardHook, type ExternalGuard } from "@glinr/theauth";

const holGuard: ExternalGuard = {
  name: "hol-guard",
  version: "1.0.0",
  async check(input, signal) {
    const res = await fetch("https://guard.example.com/check", {
      method: "POST",
      body: JSON.stringify(input),
      signal,
    });
    return res.json(); // { decision: "allow" | "deny" | "escalate", reason?, ruleId?, metadata? }
  },
};

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database,
  hooks: { beforeAuthorize: guardHook(holGuard) },
  hookSafety: { beforeAuthorize: { timeoutMs: 1500 } },
});
```

For a vendor endpoint over HTTPS, use `httpGuard` instead of writing the `fetch` yourself. It signs the request, requires a signed response, validates the verdict strictly and refuses redirects. See [remote guards](/guards).

### What the guard receives

`check(input, signal)` gets the agent (id, owner, tenant, type, name, never the token), the request (`action`, `resource`, `arguments`), the full delegation chain from the root human (`rootOwnerId`, `path`, `links` with each grant's permissions, `inbound`), the entry point (`source`), the client `ip` when known, and `dryRun`. `dryRun` is true from `explain()`, so the guard should not count or log it as a real call. The `signal` aborts at the hook timeout, so pass it to `fetch`.

### Verdicts

The guard returns `{ decision: "allow" | "deny" | "escalate", reason?, guard?, ruleId?, metadata? }`. `guardHook` fills `guard` with `guard.name` when the guard leaves it empty. `reason` is returned to the calling agent, so keep secrets out of it. `guard`, `ruleId` and `metadata` are written to the audit row under `parameters.theauthHook`. A guard can only narrow access: an allow never overrides theAuth's own permission checks.

### Default deny

A throw, a rejected promise or a malformed verdict denies with code `hook_error`. No answer within `timeoutMs` (default 2000) aborts the signal and denies with code `hook_timeout`. Failing open is possible only by setting `onTimeout: "allow"` or `onError: "allow"` in `hookSafety`, and each fail-open is recorded on the audit row.

### Composing guards

`composeBeforeAuthorize` runs several hooks in order with deny-overrides. The first deny short-circuits, an escalate beats allow, and a throw from any hook propagates so the whole check denies.

```ts
import { composeBeforeAuthorize, guardHook } from "@glinr/theauth";

hooks: { beforeAuthorize: composeBeforeAuthorize(guardHook(holGuard), guardHook(internalRules)) }
```

---

# Community integrations

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/community-integrations

A community integration is a package written by someone outside the theAuth maintainers that connects theAuth to another tool. Typical examples are a policy service that decides `beforeAuthorize`, an alerting bridge that reacts to `onViolation`, or an audit exporter that forwards `afterAuthorize` results.

Integrations use the public hook API from [Lifecycle hooks](/hooks). They do not patch the SDK, and they do not need access to the theAuth database.

## Build one from the template

The repository ships a minimal skeleton at `templates/integration-adapter/`. It contains:

- `package.json` with `@glinr/theauth` as a peer dependency, so your package uses the host application's copy.
- `src/index.ts` with a `createBeforeAuthorizeHook` factory and a placeholder `evaluate(context)` function.
- `src/index.test.ts`, a vitest suite covering allow, deny, thrown errors, and timeouts.
- `README.md` with registration steps.

Copy the directory, rename the package, and replace `evaluate()` with your own check. Keep the factory shape so hosts can pass options such as `timeoutMs` and an injected evaluator for tests.

```typescript
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { createBeforeAuthorizeHook } from 'your-integration';

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite-native', url: 'theauth.db' },
  hooks: {
    beforeAuthorize: createBeforeAuthorizeHook({ timeoutMs: 2000 }),
  },
});
```

### Framework adapters

If you are building an adapter for a web framework instead of a hook, do not re-implement the routes. Wrap the handler from core: `createTheAuthHandler(theauth, options)` from `@glinr/theauth/http` takes a web `Request` and returns a `Response`, and `listRoutes()` describes everything it serves. Your adapter only translates the framework's request and response types (Node frameworks can use `toWebRequest` and `sendWebResponse`) and exports a `requireScope` wrapper around `requireAgent`. See the [route reference](/adapters/routes).

## The contract

### Hook input

`beforeAuthorize` receives one object per `theauth.authorize()` call:

| Field | Type | Notes |
|-------|------|-------|
| `agentId` | `string` | The agent making the call. |
| `action` | `string` | The action being requested. |
| `resource` | `string` | The resource the action targets. |
| `arguments` | `object`, optional | Extra call arguments, when the caller provides them. |

`beforeAuthorize` does not run for `theauth.authorizeByToken()` or `theauth.policy.evaluate()`.

### Hook output

Return one of the following:

- `{ allow: true }` or nothing: the call proceeds.
- `{ allow: false, reason: string }`: the call is blocked. theAuth returns `{ allowed: false, reason, auditId: "" }` and writes no audit row.

### Failure behavior

Integrations must deny by default. If your code throws, rejects, or does not settle within the host's time budget, return `{ allow: false, reason }` with a short explanation. Do not return `{ allow: true }` from a catch block.

theAuth awaits `beforeAuthorize`, and an exception thrown inside it propagates to the caller. A fail-open integration can therefore turn a backend outage into unrestricted agent access. The template enforces a timeout and converts errors into denials for this reason.

Other hooks (`afterAuthorize`, `onViolation`, and the rest) are fire-and-forget. Wrap their bodies in `try/catch`, because an unhandled rejection can terminate a Node.js process.

## Get listed

Maintainers review listings. To request one:

1. Open a Discussion in [glincker/theauth](https://github.com/glincker/theauth/discussions) with the spec and fixture described below.
2. Include a short spec: what the integration does, which hooks it uses, its failure behavior, and the package name and version.
3. Attach a test fixture: a small script or vitest file that shows an allow case, a deny case, and an error case against your package.
4. A maintainer reviews the spec and fixture. Accepted integrations are added to the table below.

Listing does not mean theAuth maintains or audits the package. Review the code before you depend on it.

## List your guard

A guard vendor does not need a package. Expose an HTTPS endpoint that follows the [remote guard protocol](/guards), run `npx @glinr/theauth-conformance guard <url> --secret <s>`, and attach the JSON report (`--json`) to your Discussion. Customers then wire it with `httpGuard`.

| Name | Maintainer | Package | Status |
|------|------------|---------|--------|
| _No integrations listed yet._ | | | |

# requireScope

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/require-scope

`requireScope(theauth, { action, resource })` guards a route so only agents holding that permission reach your handler. It reads `Authorization: Bearer ta_...`, calls `authorizeByToken`, and either answers the request itself or continues with the agent identity attached.

## Behavior

| Situation | Response |
| --- | --- |
| No bearer token | 401 `UNAUTHORIZED` |
| Unknown, revoked, or expired token | 401 `UNAUTHORIZED` |
| Valid token, scope not granted | 403 `FORBIDDEN` with the denial reason in `error.message` |
| Allowed | Handler runs with the agent identity |

Errors use the same `{ "error": { "code", "message" } }` shape as the rest of the adapters. Every check is recorded in the audit trail like any other authorization.

## Hono

```ts
import { Hono } from "hono";
import { requireScope, type AgentEnv } from "@glinr/theauth-hono";

const app = new Hono<AgentEnv>();

app.get("/invoices", requireScope(theauth, { action: "read", resource: "invoices" }), (c) => {
  const agent = c.get("agent");
  return c.json({ agentId: agent.id });
});
```

## Next.js

The guard wraps a route handler. The handler receives the agent as its second argument and the route context as its third.

```ts
import { requireScope } from "@glinr/theauth-nextjs";

export const GET = requireScope(theauth, { action: "read", resource: "invoices" })(
  async (_req, agent) => Response.json({ agentId: agent.id }),
);
```

## Express

```ts
import { getAgent, requireScope } from "@glinr/theauth-express";

app.get("/invoices", requireScope(theauth, { action: "read", resource: "invoices" }), (_req, res) => {
  res.json({ agentId: getAgent(res)?.id });
});
```

## Options

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `action` | Action the agent must be allowed to perform. |
| `resource` | Resource the action applies to. |
| `clientIp` | Optional `(request) => string \| undefined`. Supplies the caller IP for `ipAllowlist` constraints and audit rows. Behind a proxy, resolve it from a header you trust. |

`requireScope` is separate from `theAuthHono`, `theAuthNextjs`, and `theAuthExpress`. It does not need the management routes or an `authenticate` resolver.

# Webhooks

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/webhooks

## What webhooks do

Webhooks push signed HTTP POST requests to a URL you control. Use them to sync user records, trigger onboarding flows, alert on suspicious logins, or feed events into your analytics pipeline.

<Warning>
  Webhooks are a delivery mechanism, not an event source. The theAuth core does not call `emit` for you when a user signs up or an agent is created. Your code (or a lifecycle hook) calls `theauth.webhooks?.emit(event, payload)` at the points where you want a delivery to happen.
</Warning>

## Setup

Pass an array of endpoints as `webhooks` to `createTheAuth`. Each endpoint has its own URL, secret, and event list. The instance then exposes `theauth.webhooks` (`null` when no endpoints were configured).

```typescript
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite-native', url: 'theauth.db' },
  webhooks: [
    {
      url: 'https://myapp.com/webhooks/theauth',
      secret: process.env.THEAUTH_WEBHOOK_SECRET!,
      events: ['user.created', 'agent.created'],
    },
  ],
});

// Emit from anywhere in your app. Delivery is fire-and-forget.
theauth.webhooks?.emit('user.created', { userId: 'user_123' });
```

<Warning>
  Store the webhook secret in an environment variable, not in source code. theAuth uses it to sign every request with HMAC-SHA256.
</Warning>

### Endpoint options

<ParamField path="url" type="string">Destination URL for the POST request.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="secret" type={`string | Array<string | { id: string; secret: string }>`}>Signing secret used for the HMAC-SHA256 signature. Pass an array, `[current, ...previous]`, to rotate: the first entry signs. Array entries must be at least 32 bytes, empty and duplicate entries are rejected when `webhooks()` is created. A plain string keeps working as before.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="events" type="WebhookEvent[]">Event types this endpoint receives. There is no `'*'` wildcard: list every event you want.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="retries" type="number">Retry attempts after the first failed delivery. Defaults to 3.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="timeout" type="number">Per-request timeout in milliseconds. Defaults to 10000.</ParamField>

You can add endpoints at runtime with `theauth.webhooks?.addEndpoint({ ... })` and read them back with `listEndpoints()`.

## Event reference

These are the event names accepted by `emit` and by an endpoint's `events` list:

| Event | Intended meaning |
|-------|-----------|
| `user.created` | A new human user registers |
| `user.updated` | A user account changes |
| `user.deleted` | A user account is deleted |
| `session.created` | A session is created |
| `session.revoked` | A session is revoked |
| `agent.created` | A new agent identity is created |
| `agent.revoked` | An agent is revoked |
| `agent.rotated` | An agent token is rotated |
| `auth.sign-in` | A user signs in |
| `auth.sign-up` | A user signs up |
| `auth.password-reset` | A password is reset |
| `auth.email-verified` | An email address is verified |

The meaning column describes what you would emit the event for. The library does not emit these automatically. Delegation and approval events are not part of this list.

## Payload

The request body is JSON:

```json
{
  "event": "user.created",
  "timestamp": "1767225600",
  "data": { "userId": "user_123" }
}
```

`timestamp` is Unix time in seconds, as a string, and `data` is the payload you passed to `emit`.

## Request headers

Every webhook delivery includes these headers:

| Header | Value |
|--------|-------|
| `X-TheAuth-Signature` | `sha256=<hex>`, the HMAC-SHA256 of `<timestamp>.<raw body>` using your secret |
| `X-TheAuth-Event` | Event type, e.g. `user.created` |
| `X-TheAuth-Timestamp` | Unix timestamp (seconds) of delivery, the same value as `timestamp` in the body |
| `X-TheAuth-Key-Id` | Only sent when the current signing secret was configured as `{ id, secret }`. Receivers try the key with this id first |

## Verifying signatures

The signature covers the timestamp and the raw body joined by a dot, not the body alone. Always verify it before trusting the payload, and reject old timestamps to limit replays.

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Node">
```typescript
import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto';

function verifyWebhook(
  rawBody: Buffer,
  timestamp: string,
  signature: string,
  secret: string,
): boolean {
  const expected =
    'sha256=' + createHmac('sha256', secret).update(`${timestamp}.${rawBody.toString('utf8')}`).digest('hex');
  const a = Buffer.from(expected);
  const b = Buffer.from(signature);
  return a.length === b.length && timingSafeEqual(a, b);
}

// Express handler
app.post('/webhooks/theauth', express.raw({ type: 'application/json' }), (req, res) => {
  const sig = req.headers['x-theauth-signature'] as string;
  const ts = req.headers['x-theauth-timestamp'] as string;
  if (!verifyWebhook(req.body, ts, sig, process.env.THEAUTH_WEBHOOK_SECRET!)) {
    return res.status(401).send('Invalid signature');
  }
  const event = JSON.parse(req.body.toString());
  // handle event...
  res.sendStatus(200);
});
```
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Edge (Web Crypto)">
```typescript
async function verifyWebhook(
  rawBody: string,
  timestamp: string,
  signature: string,
  secret: string,
): Promise<boolean> {
  const key = await crypto.subtle.importKey(
    'raw',
    new TextEncoder().encode(secret),
    { name: 'HMAC', hash: 'SHA-256' },
    false,
    ['sign'],
  );
  const mac = await crypto.subtle.sign('HMAC', key, new TextEncoder().encode(`${timestamp}.${rawBody}`));
  const expected = 'sha256=' + Array.from(new Uint8Array(mac)).map(b => b.toString(16).padStart(2, '0')).join('');
  return expected === signature;
}
```
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Rotating the signing secret

Each delivery is signed with one key, the first entry of `secret`. Receivers rotate by accepting both keys for a while. Add the new key first, deploy, then remove the old one, so no delivery is ever rejected.

1. Generate a new secret (`openssl rand -base64 32`) and add it to the receivers: `secret: [oldSecret, newSecret]`. Deploy the receivers. Nothing changes yet, because the sender still signs with the old key.
2. Switch the sender to sign with the new key and keep the old one: `secret: [newSecret, oldSecret]`. Deploy. Deliveries now carry the new signature, and in-flight retries signed earlier still verify.
3. After the retry window and your timestamp tolerance have passed, remove the old key from the receivers and the sender: `secret: [newSecret]`.

The `verify` helper from `@glinr/theauth/webhook` accepts the same list. It checks every key and does not stop at the first match, so timing does not reveal which key signed.

```typescript
import { verify } from '@glinr/theauth/webhook';

const ok = await verify({
  secret: [
    { id: '2026-10', secret: process.env.WEBHOOK_SECRET_NEW! },
    { id: '2026-04', secret: process.env.WEBHOOK_SECRET_OLD! },
  ],
  rawBody: await request.text(),
  signature: request.headers.get('X-TheAuth-Signature') ?? '',
  timestamp: request.headers.get('X-TheAuth-Timestamp') ?? '',
  keyId: request.headers.get('X-TheAuth-Key-Id') ?? undefined,
});
```

Key ids (letters, digits, `_` and `-`, up to 32 characters) are optional labels. They only choose which key is tried first. The secrets are never logged or included in error messages.

## Retry behavior

If your endpoint returns a non-2xx status, errors, or times out, theAuth retries up to `retries` times (default 3) after the first attempt, with exponential backoff:

| Retry | Delay before it |
|---------|-------|
| 1 | 1 second |
| 2 | 2 seconds |
| 3 | 4 seconds |

After the last retry the delivery is dropped silently. There is no persisted delivery record, no `failed` state, and no replay: retries run in memory in the same process, so a restart loses pending retries.

## Standalone subscription module

`@glinr/theauth` also exports a separate `createWebhookModule({ secret, maxRetries?, timeoutMs? })` with runtime subscriptions kept in memory: `subscribe(url, events)`, `unsubscribe(id)`, `list()`, `dispatch(event, payload)`, and `test(subscriptionId)`. It is independent of `theauth.webhooks`, signs the raw body only (`X-TheAuth-Signature: sha256=<hex>` of the body, plus `X-TheAuth-Delivery` and an ISO `X-TheAuth-Timestamp`), tries up to `maxRetries` attempts in total, and accepts a different event list that includes `delegation.created`, `delegation.revoked`, `auth.login`, `auth.logout`, `auth.failed`, and `org.*` events. Verify its deliveries with the exported `verifyWebhookSignature(secret, rawBody, signature)`. Subscriptions are lost on restart.

```typescript
import { createWebhookModule } from '@glinr/theauth';

const webhooks = createWebhookModule({ secret: process.env.THEAUTH_WEBHOOK_SECRET! });
const sub = await webhooks.subscribe('https://myapp.com/webhooks/theauth', ['agent.created']);

webhooks.dispatch('agent.created', { agentId: 'agt_123' });
const ping = await webhooks.test(sub.id); // { success, statusCode?, error? }
```

# Event streaming

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/event-streaming

## What event streaming is

Event streaming gives you a persistent, real-time connection to theAuth events via [Server-Sent Events (SSE)](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Server-sent_events). Whenever your code calls `stream.emit()` (an agent is revoked, a budget is exceeded, and so on), connected clients receive it, no polling required.

Events are also persisted to the database so you can replay anything you missed.

## Streaming vs webhooks

Webhooks and SSE are separate mechanisms with separate event sets: the webhook module delivers the events you pass to `theauth.webhooks.emit()`, and the stream delivers the events you pass to `stream.emit()`. You can emit the same occurrence to both.

| | Webhooks | Event streaming |
|---|---|---|
| Transport | HTTP POST to your server | Persistent HTTP connection to your browser or service |
| Latency | Network latency plus retries | Near-instant |
| Auth | Signed with an HMAC signature header | Bearer token |
| Missed events | Retried up to 3 times by default, then dropped | Replay via the `since` timestamp |
| Best for | Backend integrations, data pipelines | Dashboards, SOC tooling, live monitoring |

Use webhooks when you need durable delivery to an external service. Use event streaming when you need a live view, a security dashboard, an admin feed, or a CI script watching for `budget.exceeded`.

## Setup

```typescript
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { createEventStreamModule } from '@glinr/theauth/auth';

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite-native', url: 'theauth.db' },
});

const stream = createEventStreamModule({
  db: theauth.db,
  requireAuth: true,
  validateToken: async (token) => {
    // Return a subscriber ID (userId or agentId) on success, null on failure.
    // Here: a TheAuth-managed session (requires `auth.session` in the config).
    const session = await theauth.auth.session?.validate(token);
    return session?.userId ?? null;
  },
});

// Mount in a Web-standard (Request/Response) handler, for example a Next.js route
export async function GET(request: Request): Promise<Response> {
  return stream.handleRequest(request) ?? new Response('Not found', { status: 404 });
}

// Emit from anywhere in your application
stream.emit({
  id: crypto.randomUUID(),
  type: 'agent.created',
  timestamp: new Date(),
  data: { agentId: agent.id, name: agent.name },
});
```

<Note>
  `handleRequest` takes a Web `Request` and returns a Web `Response`, or `null` for any request that is not an SSE request: the method must be GET, the path must end in `/events/stream`, and the `Accept` header must include `text/event-stream`. This makes it safe to call inside a catch-all handler. Node `(req, res)` handlers such as Express need a small adapter to convert to and from `Request` and `Response`.
</Note>

## Connecting from a browser

The browser's built-in `EventSource` API handles reconnection automatically.

```typescript
const source = new EventSource(
  '/api/theauth/events/stream?token=your-bearer-token',
);

// Each message is named by its type and carries { id, type, timestamp, data, agentId?, userId? }
source.addEventListener('agent.created', (event) => {
  const payload = JSON.parse((event as MessageEvent).data);
  console.log('New agent:', payload.data.agentId);
});

source.addEventListener('budget.exceeded', (event) => {
  const payload = JSON.parse((event as MessageEvent).data);
  console.warn('Budget exceeded:', payload.data);
});

source.addEventListener('error', (event) => {
  // Server-sent error events carry JSON; connection errors have no data
  const raw = (event as MessageEvent).data;
  if (typeof raw === 'string') {
    console.error('Stream error:', JSON.parse(raw).code);
  }
});

// Clean up
source.close();
```

If you pass the token via the `Authorization` header instead, use the `eventsource` package or a fetch-based polyfill, since the native `EventSource` does not support custom headers.

## Connecting from Node.js

```typescript
import { EventSource } from 'eventsource';

const source = new EventSource('https://your-app.com/api/theauth/events/stream', {
  headers: {
    Authorization: 'Bearer your-bearer-token',
  },
});

// Messages are named events, so onmessage never fires. Listen per type.
source.addEventListener('agent.revoked', (event) => {
  const payload = JSON.parse(event.data);
  console.log('Event:', payload.type, payload.data);
});

source.onerror = () => {
  console.error('Connection lost, reconnecting...');
};
```

## Event types

<Warning>
  The stream module is standalone. The theAuth core does not call `stream.emit()` for you, so none of these events fire automatically: you emit the ones you need from your own code, hooks, or webhook handlers. `anomaly.detected` is only a reserved type name, since theAuth has no anomaly detector.
</Warning>

The type column below describes the intended meaning of each type.

| Type | When it fires |
|---|---|
| `audit` | Any agent action logged to the audit trail |
| `agent.created` | A new agent identity is registered |
| `agent.revoked` | An agent is permanently revoked |
| `agent.rotated` | An agent token is rotated |
| `auth.signin` | A user signs in |
| `auth.signout` | A user signs out |
| `auth.failed` | A sign-in attempt fails |
| `delegation.created` | A new delegation chain is created |
| `delegation.revoked` | A delegation is revoked |
| `budget.exceeded` | An agent exceeds its cost budget |
| `anomaly.detected` | Reserved name. theAuth has no anomaly detector, so this only appears if your own code emits it |
| `cost.recorded` | A cost event is attributed to an agent |

## Filtering events

Pass a `types` query parameter with a comma-separated list to receive only the events you care about.

```
GET /api/theauth/events/stream?types=agent.revoked,budget.exceeded
```

```typescript
// From a browser
const source = new EventSource(
  '/api/theauth/events/stream?token=tok&types=agent.created,agent.revoked',
);
```

Unknown type names in `types` are ignored; if none are valid, the connection receives all types. You can also restrict the types at the module level, which filters live delivery.

```typescript
const stream = createEventStreamModule({
  db: theauth.db,
  requireAuth: true,
  validateToken,
  eventTypes: ['audit', 'budget.exceeded'], // only these types are delivered live
});
```

## Replay and cursor

Events passed to `emit()` are persisted in the `theauth_stream_events` table (a failed write is ignored). If a client disconnects and reconnects, pass `since` to receive everything it missed, oldest first, after the `connected` event. `since` must be an ISO 8601 timestamp with an offset or `Z`; anything else is rejected with a 400.

```
GET /api/theauth/events/stream?since=2026-01-15T10:00:00Z
```

The module also reads the `Last-Event-ID` header as a fallback cursor, but it parses the value as a date. Each SSE message uses your event `id` as its `id:` field, so the header only works for replay if your event IDs are timestamps (for example ISO strings). With UUID IDs, as in the examples here, an automatic browser reconnect replays nothing, so track the last timestamp yourself and pass `since`.

Replay applies the connection's `types` filter, or the module-level `eventTypes` if the client sent none. A client that passes its own `types` can replay types outside the module-level list, and the programmatic `replay()` method does not apply the module-level list at all.

```typescript
// Programmatic replay without an open connection
const result = await stream.replay(new Date('2026-01-15T10:00:00Z'), ['audit', 'auth.failed']);
if (result.success) {
  for (const event of result.data) {
    console.log(event.type, event.data);
  }
}
```

`replay` returns up to 1000 events in descending order (newest first). Apply your own pagination on top if you need to page through large windows.

## Auth requirements

By default `requireAuth: true`. Every connection must present a Bearer token, either in the `Authorization` header or as the `token` query parameter.

```
Authorization: Bearer <token>
GET /api/theauth/events/stream?token=<token>
```

When the token is missing or `validateToken` returns `null`, the stream sends a single `error` event and closes (the HTTP status is still 200).

```json
{ "code": "UNAUTHORIZED", "message": "Invalid token" }
```

<Warning>
  If you set `requireAuth: true` but do not provide `validateToken`, any non-empty token is accepted. Always supply `validateToken` in production.
</Warning>

To disable auth for local development or internal-only deployments:

```typescript
const stream = createEventStreamModule({
  db: theauth.db,
  requireAuth: false,
});
```

<Warning>
  Never disable auth in production. The stream exposes audit events and agent lifecycle data.
</Warning>

## Configuration

```typescript
interface EventStreamConfig {
  db: Database;

  // Maximum concurrent connections. Returns 503 when exceeded (default: 100).
  maxConnections?: number;

  // Interval between heartbeat comments in ms (default: 30000)
  heartbeatIntervalMs?: number;

  // Module-level event type allow-list. Clients cannot exceed this (default: all).
  eventTypes?: EventType[];

  // Require a Bearer token to connect (default: true)
  requireAuth?: boolean;

  // Validate the token and return a subscriber ID (userId or agentId), or null.
  // If omitted while requireAuth is true, any non-empty token is accepted.
  validateToken?: (token: string) => Promise<string | null>;
}
```

## Connection limits

The stream rejects connections beyond `maxConnections` with a `503 Too many connections` response. Size this based on your deployment: a single process can comfortably handle hundreds of concurrent SSE connections; above that, consider a pub/sub layer (Redis, NATS) in front of the module.

## Heartbeat

The server sends `: heartbeat` comments on the configured interval (default 30 seconds) to keep load balancers and proxies from closing idle connections. No action is required on the client side, `EventSource` ignores comment lines.

## Emitting events from plugins

Any part of your application can emit to the stream.

```typescript
// After revoking an agent
await theauth.agent.revoke(agentId);

stream.emit({
  id: crypto.randomUUID(),
  type: 'agent.revoked',
  timestamp: new Date(),
  data: { agentId, reason: 'manual-revocation' },
  agentId,
  userId: currentUser.id,
});
```

Integrate with the [webhooks](/webhooks) module to fire both a webhook and a stream event from the same action.

## Module API

```typescript
interface EventStreamModule {
  // Emit an event to all connected clients and persist for replay
  emit(event: StreamEvent): void;

  // Handle an SSE connection request. Returns a Response or null.
  handleRequest(request: Request): Response | null;

  // Number of currently active connections
  getConnectionCount(): number;

  // Replay persisted events since a date, optionally filtered by type.
  // Up to 1000 events, newest first.
  replay(since: Date, types?: EventType[]): Promise<Result<StreamEvent[]>>;

  // Close all connections and stop the heartbeat timer
  close(): void;
}
```
