# OpenAPI spec

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/openapi

`generateOpenAPISpec` returns an OpenAPI 3.1 document describing the REST endpoints `createTheAuthHandler` serves. It is generated from the handler's route table and the typed result shapes in core, so it cannot lag behind the routes. The same document is checked in as `sdks/openapi.json`, and a test fails when the two differ. Feed it to a code generator to produce a client for Python, Java, Rust or any other language.

```ts title="openapi.ts"
import { generateOpenAPISpec } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { writeFileSync } from 'node:fs';

const spec = generateOpenAPISpec({
  baseUrl: 'https://auth.example.com', // origin, default http://localhost:3000
  basePath: '/api/theauth',            // where the handler is mounted, default /api/theauth
  version: '2.0.0',                    // contract version, default 2.0.0
});

writeFileSync('theauth-openapi.json', JSON.stringify(spec, null, 2));
```

Then generate a client, for example:

```bash
npx @openapitools/openapi-generator-cli generate -i theauth-openapi.json -g python -o ./theauth-client
```

## Serving it

The function is pure, so you can expose it from any route:

```ts
app.get('/openapi.json', (c) => c.json(generateOpenAPISpec({ baseUrl: new URL(c.req.url).origin })));
```

## Options

| Option | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `baseUrl` | `http://localhost:3000` | Origin in `servers[0].url` |
| `basePath` | `/api/theauth` | Mount path appended to `baseUrl` |
| `version` | `2.0.0` | `info.version` |
| `handler` | all routes | Pass your `TheAuthHandlerOptions`, and routes the handler would not serve (`routes.explain: false`, `routes.mcp: false`) are left out |
| `adminApi` | `true` | Include the approval routes of the admin API plugin |

## What it covers

Every route in the handler's route table: agents, `/authorize` and `/authorize/token`, `/explain`, delegations, audit, dashboard aggregates and the MCP OAuth endpoints (including `/mcp/introspect`). The admin API approval routes (`/approvals`) are added unless you set `adminApi: false`.

`AuthorizeResult` carries `code`, one of the decision codes, and a denied call (403, or 401 for an identity failure) returns the same `{ data }` result as an allowed one. `ExplainResult` includes the delegation chain (`delegation.path`, `links`, `inbound`), the constraint checks and near misses.

## Regenerating `sdks/openapi.json`

```bash
pnpm --filter @glinr/theauth exec jiti scripts/generate-openapi.ts          # write
pnpm --filter @glinr/theauth exec jiti scripts/generate-openapi.ts check  # exit 1 when stale
```

Requests authenticate with a bearer token (`BearerAuth` for signed-in callers, `AgentToken` for `/authorize/token`, `ClientBasic` for OAuth client endpoints). Endpoints that other plugins register (email, OAuth, passkeys and so on) are not included; see [Writing plugins](/plugins) for how those are mounted.

---

# Writing plugins

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/plugins

A plugin is a plain object with an `id`, an optional `init` function and optional `hooks`. `@glinr/theauth-email`, the discovery plugin and the telemetry plugin are built this way. You pass plugins to `createTheAuth({ plugins: [...] })`.

## A complete plugin

```ts title="ping-plugin.ts"
import { createTheAuth, type TheAuthPlugin } from '@glinr/theauth';

const json = (body: unknown, status = 200) =>
  new Response(JSON.stringify(body), { status, headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });

export function ping(): TheAuthPlugin {
  return {
    id: 'example-ping',
    async init(ctx) {
      ctx.addMigration(
        'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS example_pings (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, at INTEGER NOT NULL)',
      );
      ctx.addEndpoint({
        method: 'GET',
        path: '/ping/:name',
        metadata: { description: 'Say hello', rateLimit: { window: 60, max: 30 }, requireAuth: false },
        async handler(request) {
          const name = new URL(request.url).searchParams.get('_param_name');
          return json({ hello: name });
        },
      });
      return { context: { pingVersion: 1 } };
    },
  };
}

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite', url: ':memory:' },
  plugins: [ping()],
});

const res = await theauth.plugins.handleRequest(new Request('http://localhost/ping/ada'));
console.log(await res?.json()); // { hello: 'ada' }
```

## The context passed to `init`

| Member | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `db` | The Drizzle database handle. |
| `config` | The resolved `createTheAuth` config. |
| `addEndpoint(endpoint)` | Register an HTTP endpoint (below). |
| `addMigration(sql)` | Queue a `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` statement. Migrations run after all plugins initialize, so keep each statement idempotent. |
| `sessionManager` | The shared session manager, or `null` when `auth.session` is not configured. |

`init` may return `{ context }`; those values are merged into `theauth.plugins.getContext()`.

## Endpoints

An endpoint has a `method`, a `path` relative to the mount point, a `handler(request, ctx)` that takes a Web `Request` and returns a `Response`, and optional `metadata`:

- `rateLimit: { window, max }`: `window` is in seconds. Counted per client IP, in memory, per process. Over the limit the router returns 429.
- `requireAuth`: when true, the router calls `getUser` first and returns 401 if there is no session.
- `description`: used for documentation.

Paths support `:param` segments. The router copies captured values into the request URL as `_param_<name>` query parameters, as shown above. The handler `ctx` also gives you `db`, `getUser(request)` and `getSession(token)`.

The JSON, body-parsing and cookie helpers that built-in plugins use are internal, so write small equivalents in your own plugin (the `json` function above is one).

## Typed endpoints

`defineEndpoint` validates path parameters, the query string and the JSON body with zod before your handler runs, and records the shapes so a browser or mobile client can call the route with full type inference. It returns a normal endpoint, so `ctx.addEndpoint` takes it.

```typescript
import { defineEndpoint, type ApiOf } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { z } from 'zod';

export const invite = defineEndpoint({
  method: 'POST',
  path: '/team/:teamId/invite',
  params: z.object({ teamId: z.string().min(1) }),
  query: z.object({ notify: z.enum(['yes', 'no']).default('yes') }),
  body: z.object({ email: z.string().email() }),
  response: z.object({ invited: z.string() }),
  async handler({ params, query, body }, ctx) {
    const user = await ctx.getUser(ctx.request);
    if (!user) return new Response('Unauthorized', { status: 401 });
    return { invited: `${body.email}@${params.teamId}` };
  },
});

export const endpoints = [invite] as const;
export type TeamApi = ApiOf<typeof endpoints>;
```

Input that does not match the schemas returns `400` with `{ error: { code: 'INVALID_INPUT', issues } }`. Return a plain value for a JSON `200`, or a `Response` to control the status yourself. A `response` schema, when given, is checked before sending and a mismatch returns `500` instead of leaking an unexpected shape.

Call it from the client without importing any server code:

```typescript
import { createEndpointClient } from '@glinr/theauth-client';
import type { TeamApi } from './server/endpoints'; // type only

const api = createEndpointClient<TeamApi>({ baseUrl: '/api/theauth' });
const out = await api.call('POST /team/:teamId/invite', {
  params: { teamId: 't1' },
  body: { email: 'a@b.co' },
});
if (out.ok) console.log(out.data.invited);
else console.log(out.error.code, out.error.issues);
```

The route key, input and result are all inferred, and a route with no required input takes no argument. Cookies are sent by default (`credentials: 'include'`); pass `headers` for bearer tokens.

## Lifecycle hooks

```ts
hooks: {
  onRequest: async (request) => undefined,        // return a Request to replace it, or a Response to short-circuit
  onAuthenticate: async (user, session) => {},    // after a successful sign-in
  onSessionCreate: async (userId) => ({ source: 'my-plugin' }), // return metadata to attach
  onSessionRevoke: async (sessionId) => {},
}
```

## Serving plugin endpoints

`theauth.plugins.handleRequest(request, basePath?)` returns a `Response`, or `null` when no endpoint matches, so you can fall through to the rest of your app. `theauth.plugins.getEndpoints()` lists every registered endpoint, which is what the [framework adapters](/adapters) use to mount routes. Strip your mount prefix by passing it as `basePath`.

```ts
const response = await theauth.plugins.handleRequest(request, '/api/theauth');
return response ?? new Response('Not found', { status: 404 });
```

## Notes

- `schema` on a plugin is for Drizzle type safety only. Tables are created by `addMigration`.
- `AuthPlugin` is a deprecated alias of `TheAuthPlugin`.
- Plugin rate limits are per process. Behind several instances, enforce limits at your gateway as well.

---

# Redirect chains

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/redirect

`createRedirectChain` remembers the page a user wanted before they were sent to sign in, lets you queue extra steps (verify email, onboarding), and tells you where to send them next. State lives in one short-lived cookie, so it works on any runtime that has Web `Request` and `Response`.

```ts title="redirects.ts"
import { createRedirectChain } from '@glinr/theauth/redirect';

const redirects = createRedirectChain({ defaultPath: '/dashboard' });

// 1. Auth middleware: not signed in. Remember where they were headed.
function requireSignIn(request: Request): Response {
  return new Response(null, {
    status: 302,
    headers: { Location: '/sign-in', 'Set-Cookie': redirects.capture(request) },
  });
}

// 2. After sign-up: add steps that must happen first.
const c1 = redirects.push('/verify-email', { label: 'verify' });

// 3. As each step finishes, pop the next destination.
function next(request: Request): Response {
  const { url, done, clearCookie } = redirects.pop(request);
  const headers = new Headers({ Location: url });
  if (done && clearCookie) headers.append('Set-Cookie', clearCookie);
  return new Response(null, { status: 302, headers });
}
```

`push` returns a `Set-Cookie` value, so send it on the response that moves the user to the next step. The same helpers are also exported from `@glinr/theauth`.

## API

| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| `capture(request)` | `Set-Cookie` that stores the request URL as the origin. Keeps an existing origin if the user reloads the sign-in page. |
| `push(path, { label?, query? })` | `Set-Cookie` with a step added. Steps pop last-in, first-out, then the origin. |
| `pop(request)` | `{ url, done, clearCookie }`. `done` is true once the origin has been returned. |
| `peek(request)` | `{ url, remaining }` without consuming, or `null`. |
| `getOrigin(request)`, `parse(request)` | The origin entry or full chain state, or `null` if absent or expired. |
| `clear()` | `Set-Cookie` that deletes the chain. |
| `buildUrl(entry)`, `createEntry(url, label?)` | Helpers for entries. |

## Options

| Option | Default |
|---|---|
| `cookieName` | `theauth_redirect` |
| `maxAge` (seconds) | `600` |
| `defaultPath` | `/` |
| `excludePaths` | `/sign-in`, `/sign-up`, `/forgot-password`, `/reset-password`, `/verify-email`, `/api/` |
| `preserveQuery`, `preserveHash` | `true` |
| `maxDepth` | `10` |
| `cookie` | `httpOnly`, `secure`, `sameSite: "lax"`, `path: "/"` |

If the captured page is in `excludePaths`, the chain falls back to `defaultPath`, so users never bounce back to the sign-in page.

## Return URL allow list

Any `redirectTo`, `returnTo` or `callbackURL` value that comes from a request is untrusted. Pass it through `redirects.sanitize()` (or `resolveRedirectTarget`) before you redirect after sign-in, sign-out or email verification:

```ts
const redirects = createRedirectChain({
  defaultPath: '/dashboard',
  allowedOrigins: ['https://app.example.com'],
});

const next = redirects.sanitize(url.searchParams.get('returnTo')); // safe path, allowed URL, or '/dashboard'
```

A target passes only if it is a same-origin path (one leading `/`) or an absolute http(s) URL whose origin exactly matches `allowedOrigins`. These are refused and replaced by `defaultPath`:

- protocol-relative `//host` and `///host`, and `/.//host`
- backslashes (`/\host`), control characters, tabs, newlines and Unicode whitespace
- percent-encoded forms of the above, decoded up to three times (`/%2F%2Fhost`, `/%5Chost`, `/%252F%252Fhost`)
- `javascript:`, `data:`, `vbscript:`, `file:`, `blob:` and every other scheme
- userinfo tricks (`https://app.example.com@evil.com`) and scheme forms without `//` (`https:evil.com`)
- bare words (`evil.com`, `dashboard`) and anything over 2048 characters

The chain applies the same check when it builds a URL, so a forged or tampered `theauth_redirect` cookie, or a request path that starts with `//`, cannot send a user off site. The OAuth module takes an `allowedRedirectUris` list for the `redirectUri` it sends to providers: a value that is not an exact entry throws before state is stored and again on callback.

## Security notes

Entries created from a URL keep only its path, query and hash, never the origin. The cookie itself is base64url JSON and is **not signed**, so a user can edit it. Before you redirect to the `url` that `pop` or `peek` returns, check that it starts with a single `/` (and not `//` or `/\`), and validate any `redirectTo` value you accept from users before passing it to `createEntry` or `push`.

```ts
const safe = (u: string) => u.startsWith('/') && !u.startsWith('//') && !u.startsWith('/\\');
```

# Error codes

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/errors

theAuth returns structured errors in the following shape:

```typescript
interface TheAuthError {
  code: string;    // machine-readable error code
  message: string; // human-readable description
  details?: Record<string, unknown>; // additional context
}
```

All SDK functions that can fail return a `Result<T>` discriminated union rather than throwing:

```typescript
const result = await theauth.authorize(agentId, { action: 'write', resource: 'mcp:github:*' });

if (!result.allowed) {
  console.log(result.reason); // e.g. 'Rate limit exceeded: 20/20 calls per hour for resource "mcp:deploy:staging"'
}
```

For REST API calls, errors are returned as JSON with the corresponding HTTP status code:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "FORBIDDEN",
    "message": "Admin access required"
  }
}
```

## Decision codes

`authorize()`, `authorizeByToken()` and `policy.evaluate()` return a machine-readable `code` next to the free-form `reason`. The set is closed: `DECISION_CODES` is exported from `@glinr/theauth`, with the `DecisionCode` type, `isDecisionCode()` and `violationTypeOf()`. Branch on `code`, never on `reason` text.

| Code | Meaning | `onViolation.type` |
|------|---------|--------------------|
| `allowed` | The call is allowed. | none |
| `approval_consumed` | The call is allowed and spent a single-use approval. | none |
| `no_permission` | No permission grants the action on the resource. | `permission_denied` |
| `rate_limited` | `maxCallsPerHour` is used up. | `rate_limited` |
| `ip_not_allowed` | The IP is missing or not in `ipAllowlist`. | `ip_blocked` |
| `time_restricted` | Outside the permission's `timeWindow`. | `time_restricted` |
| `argument_rejected` | An argument failed `allowedArgPatterns`, or a pattern is not a valid regex. | `permission_denied` |
| `approval_required` | The permission has `requireApproval` and no approval id was given, or a `beforeAuthorize` hook returned `escalate`. | `approval_required` |
| `approval_not_found` | No approval request has this id. | `approval_required` |
| `approval_pending` | The approval request has no answer yet. | `approval_required` |
| `approval_denied` | A human denied the approval request. | `approval_required` |
| `approval_expired` | The approval request passed its `expiresAt`. | `approval_required` |
| `approval_already_used` | The approval was already spent. | `approval_required` |
| `approval_mismatch` | The approval is for another agent, action or resource. | `approval_required` |
| `approval_arguments_mismatch` | The arguments differ from the ones the human approved. | `approval_required` |
| `approval_granted` | Lifecycle event only: a human approved a request. Never returned by `authorize()`. | none |
| `agent_not_found` | No agent with that id. | `permission_denied` |
| `agent_revoked` | The agent is revoked. | `permission_denied` |
| `agent_expired` | The agent is expired. | `permission_denied` |
| `invalid_token` | `authorizeByToken` got an unknown, revoked or expired token. | `permission_denied` |
| `owner_mismatch` | `policy.evaluate` was given an owner that does not own the agent. | `permission_denied` |
| `hook_denied` | A `beforeAuthorize` hook blocked the call. | `permission_denied` |
| `hook_timeout` | A `beforeAuthorize` hook timed out and the default `deny` mode blocked the call. | `permission_denied` |
| `hook_error` | A `beforeAuthorize` hook threw or returned a malformed verdict and the default `deny` mode blocked the call. | `permission_denied` |
| `taint_violation` | A taint rule matched the call's input provenance. | `permission_denied` |
| `risk_escalation` | A risk tier requires approval or step up. | `permission_denied` |
| `policy_indeterminate` | The policy engine could not decide (invalid input, graph error). It denies. | `permission_denied` |

`code` is optional on the `AuthorizeResult` type so results you build by hand still compile, but core always sets it. `PolicyDecision.code` is always present.

## Error code reference

<Warning>
`theauth.authorize()` does not return HTTP-style codes. It returns `{ allowed, reason, auditId, code }` where `code` is one of the lowercase decision codes above and `reason` is free-form text. Agent calls such as `agent.create()` (at the `maxPerUser` limit), `agent.update()`, `agent.revoke()` and `agent.rotate()` throw a plain `Error` with a descriptive message, so there are no `AGENT_*` or `PERMISSION_*` REST codes to branch on. Use the decision codes for authorization outcomes. The tables below list the uppercase codes that core, the adapters and the gateway really emit.
</Warning>

REST errors from the adapters and the gateway use `{ "error": { "code", "message" } }`. MCP OAuth endpoints use the RFC 6749 wire shape `{ "error": "invalid_grant", "error_description": "..." }`, with the code lowercased.

### Delegation errors

`theauth.delegate()` throws a `DelegationError` (a typed `Error` with a `code`). The framework adapters map it to HTTP 400 and send `code` through as the REST error code.

| Code | HTTP status | Description |
|------|-------------|-------------|
| `DELEGATION_PERMISSION_SUBSET` | 400 | The delegating agent is trying to grant a permission it does not hold, or a wider one. |
| `DELEGATION_DEPTH_EXCEEDED` | 400 | The delegation would exceed the `maxDepth` limit. |
| `DELEGATION_PARENT_REVOKED` | 400 | The parent delegation in the chain has been revoked. |

### User errors

`theauth.user.create()` throws a `UserError`. Branch on `code`.

| Code | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `USER_INVALID_INPUT` | The input failed schema validation. The message lists the failing fields. |
| `USER_EMAIL_CONFLICT` | The email is already registered under a different user id than the one you passed. |
| `USER_ID_CONFLICT` | The id is already in use by another email. |

### Hook errors

| Code | Where | Description |
|------|-------|-------------|
| `hook_timeout`, `hook_error` | `HookBlockedError.code` | A `beforeAgentCreate` hook timed out or failed and the mode was `deny`. For `beforeAuthorize` the same strings come back as decision codes. |
| `HOOK_TIMEOUT` | `HookTimeoutError.code` | A hook timed out and the mode was `throw`. |

### Agent tool errors

| Code | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `TOOL_APPROVAL_REQUIRED` | A guarded tool needs human approval or step up. Do not retry until it is granted. |
| `TOOL_GUARD_FAILED` | The policy check for a guarded tool could not complete, so the tool was blocked. |

### Token errors

Returned by the MCP token validator as `Result` errors, and by `mcp.requireScopes` as a typed denial (`status`, `error.code`, `error.message`, and `rejected` for a token whose signature verified). Over HTTP they are a 401 with a `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token", error_description="...", resource_metadata="..."` challenge (a request with no token gets the same header without `error`). The 401 body is a JSON-RPC error with code `-32001` and the reason in `error.data.code`.

| Code | HTTP status | Description |
|------|-------------|-------------|
| `INVALID_TOKEN` | 401 | The token cannot be verified, has been revoked, or is malformed. For a revoked token `details.revocation` holds `{ reason, id }` on the server side only, never in the 401 body. See [MCP token revocation](/mcp-revocation). |
| `TOKEN_EXPIRED` | 401 | The token's `exp` claim is in the past. |
| `INVALID_AUDIENCE` | 401 | The token's `aud` does not match this resource. |
| `INVALID_ISSUER` | 401 | The token's `iss` does not match this server. |
| `DELEGATION_REVOKED` | 401 | A delegation link or agent behind the token (its `theauth_dlg` binding, or its `act` chain with `delegationStore`) is revoked, expired or missing. Reported by `requireScopes`; `validateToken` reports `INVALID_TOKEN` with the reason in the message. |
| `DPOP_REQUIRED` | 401 | The token is bound to a DPoP key but was presented without a DPoP proof. Reported by `requireScopes`. |

### MCP and OAuth errors

The MCP module returns `Result` errors with these codes. The token, registration, revocation and introspection endpoints answer 401 for `INVALID_CLIENT` and 400 for the rest, with the exceptions in the table.

| Code | HTTP status | Description |
|------|-------------|-------------|
| `INVALID_REQUEST` | 400 | A required parameter is missing or malformed, or `code_challenge_method` is not `S256`. |
| `INVALID_CLIENT` | 401 | The `client_id` is unknown, or client authentication failed. |
| `INVALID_GRANT` | 400 | The authorization code or refresh token is invalid, expired or consumed, the `redirect_uri` does not match, or PKCE verification failed. |
| `INVALID_REDIRECT_URI` | 400 | The `redirect_uri` does not match the registered client. |
| `INVALID_SCOPE` | 400 | A requested scope is not allowed for this client or grant. |
| `INVALID_TARGET` | 400 | The `resource` parameter does not match the one bound to the grant. |
| `INVALID_CLIENT_METADATA` | 400 | Dynamic client registration metadata is invalid. |
| `INVALID_DPOP_PROOF` | 400 | A DPoP proof is missing or invalid. |
| `USE_DPOP_NONCE` | 400 | The client must retry with the server-issued DPoP nonce. |
| `UNAUTHORIZED_CLIENT` | 400 | The client is not allowed to use this grant type. |
| `UNSUPPORTED_GRANT_TYPE` | 400 | The grant type is not supported. |
| `LOGIN_REQUIRED` | 400 | The user is not signed in at the authorization endpoint. With a `loginPage` configured the response redirects there instead. |
| `INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE` | 403 | The token does not carry a required scope. See below. |
| `SERVER_ERROR` | 503 | `/mcp/revoke` and `/mcp/introspect` only: the revocation store could not be written or read. The body is `temporarily_unavailable` and `Retry-After` is set on `/mcp/revoke`. Retry the call. |
| `CONSENT_REQUIRED` | none | The client is identified by a [metadata document](/mcp-client-id-metadata) and no `consentPage` is configured, so no code is issued. Returned as a `Result` error from the authorize step. |
| `ACCESS_DENIED` | 400 | Token exchange was refused by the `tokenExchange.authorize` policy. |
| `REGISTRATION_DISABLED` | 404 | Dynamic registration is off (`registration: { enabled: false }`). Returned by `registerClient` as a `Result` error; the route answers 404. |
| `RATE_LIMITED` | 429 | Introspection only: the client is over `introspection.maxRequestsPerMinute`. A `Retry-After` header is set. |
| `UNAUTHORIZED` | 401 | No Bearer token was presented. |
| `SERVER_ERROR` | 500 | The server could not complete validation. |

`requireMcpAuth`, `requireScopes` and gateway policies with `requiredScopes` answer a scope shortfall with 403 and a `WWW-Authenticate` challenge carrying `error="insufficient_scope"`, the missing `scope` and `resource_metadata`. The body lists `required_scopes` and `current_scopes`. The step-up helper adds an `upgrade_url` so the client can re-authorize with the extra scopes.

### General errors

| Code | HTTP status | Description |
|------|-------------|-------------|
| `BAD_REQUEST` | 400 | The request body or parameters failed validation. |
| `UNAUTHORIZED` | 401 | No valid credential was provided. |
| `FORBIDDEN` | 403 | The credential is valid but does not have access to this resource. The gateway also uses it for a disallowed origin or a failed `requiredPermissions` check. |
| `NOT_FOUND` | 404 | The requested resource does not exist. |
| `RATE_LIMITED` | 429 | Too many requests. A `Retry-After` header says when to retry. |
| `CSRF_REJECTED` | 403 | A cross-site write was refused for a cookie session. |
| `PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE` | 413 | Gateway only: the request body is over the limit. |
| `BAD_GATEWAY` | 502 | Gateway only: the upstream is unreachable. |
| `GATEWAY_TIMEOUT` | 504 | Gateway only: the upstream did not respond in time. |
| `INTERNAL_ERROR` | 500 | An unexpected error occurred. Check server logs for details. |

# Test utilities

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/test-utils

`@glinr/theauth-test-utils` provides factories, mock servers, and assertion helpers so you can test auth-dependent code without a real database or network.

## Install

```bash
pnpm add -D @glinr/theauth-test-utils
```

## Factories

Factory functions create realistic mock entities with sensible defaults. Pass overrides for any fields relevant to the test.

```ts
import {
  createMockUser,
  createMockSession,
  createMockAgent,
  createMockPermission,
} from '@glinr/theauth-test-utils';

const user = createMockUser({ email: 'alice@example.com' });
const session = createMockSession({ user });
const agent = createMockAgent({ type: 'service', permissions: [] });
const perm = createMockPermission({ resource: 'files', actions: ['read', 'write'] });
```

Each call generates unique IDs, so you can create multiple entities in the same test without collisions.

## Mock auth server

`createMockAuthServer` returns an in-memory `AuthAdapter` implementation with zero network or database calls. Use it in server-side unit tests that exercise code paths calling `resolveUser`, `getUser`, or `syncUser`.

```ts
import { createMockAuthServer, createMockUser } from '@glinr/theauth-test-utils';

const server = createMockAuthServer();
const user = createMockUser();

server.addUser(user);
server.setActiveUser(user.id);

const resolved = await server.resolveUser(new Request('https://example.com'));
// resolved.id === user.id
```

### Per-request user override

Set the `x-mock-theauth-user-id` header on a `Request` to override the active user for that specific request only, without calling `setActiveUser`:

```ts
import { MOCK_USER_ID_HEADER } from '@glinr/theauth-test-utils';

const req = new Request('https://example.com', {
  headers: { [MOCK_USER_ID_HEADER]: user.id },
});

const resolved = await server.resolveUser(req);
```

### Cleanup

```ts
afterEach(() => server.reset()); // clears the store and active session
```

## Assertions

Three typed assertion helpers narrow `ActionResult<T>` (the result type used by `@glinr/theauth-react`, where a failure carries an `error` string) and throw descriptive errors on failure.

```ts
import {
  expectAuthenticated,
  expectUnauthenticated,
  expectPermissionDenied,
} from '@glinr/theauth-test-utils';

// Passes only when result.success === true
expectAuthenticated(result);
console.log(result.data); // typed

// Passes only when result.success === false
expectUnauthenticated(result);

// Passes only when result.success === false and error contains "permission" (case-insensitive)
expectPermissionDenied(result);

// Custom substring match
expectPermissionDenied(result, 'not allowed');
```

## Mock React provider

For component tests, `MockTheAuthProvider` replaces `<TheAuthProvider>` with fixed values. It accepts `user`, `session`, `isAuthenticated`, `isLoading`, and optional `signIn`, `signUp`, `signOut`, and `refresh` overrides. The actions default to `vi.fn()` spies, so you can assert on calls.

```tsx
import { MockTheAuthProvider, createMockUser, createMockSession } from '@glinr/theauth-test-utils';

const user = createMockUser();
const session = createMockSession({ user });

render(
  <MockTheAuthProvider user={user} session={session}>
    <ProfileButton />
  </MockTheAuthProvider>
);
```

<Note>
The mock server itself has no dependencies. It matches the `AuthAdapter` interface structurally, so TypeScript will accept it anywhere an `AuthAdapter` is expected. The package entry point also exports `MockTheAuthProvider`, which imports `vitest`, `react` and `@glinr/theauth-react` (`react` and `@glinr/theauth-react` are optional peer dependencies), so use the package from a Vitest setup.
</Note>

# A2A protocol

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/a2a

## What A2A is

The Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol is an open standard from Google that lets AI agents discover and communicate with each other. Where MCP handles the connection between agents and tools, A2A handles the connection between agents themselves.

Think of it this way: MCP is how an agent uses a tool. A2A is how an agent talks to another agent.

theAuth implements A2A with built-in authentication, so every agent interaction is identity-verified and audited.

### A2A and MCP compared

| | MCP | A2A |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Agent-to-tool communication | Agent-to-agent communication |
| Discovery | OAuth metadata endpoints | `/.well-known/agent.json` |
| Protocol | Tool-specific RPC | JSON-RPC 2.0 |
| Auth | OAuth 2.1 | OAuth 2.1, API keys, OIDC, mTLS |
| Lifecycle | Stateless tool calls | Stateful task lifecycle |
| Streaming | Not defined | SSE via `message/stream` |

## Setup

### Install

```bash
pnpm add @glinr/theauth
```

### Create an A2A server

The A2A server exposes your agent as a JSON-RPC endpoint that other agents can call.

```typescript
import { createTheAuth } from '@glinr/theauth';
import { createAgentCard, createA2AServer } from '@glinr/theauth/a2a';

const theauth = await createTheAuth({
  database: { provider: 'sqlite-native', url: 'theauth.db' },
});

// Register an agent identity
const agent = await theauth.agent.create({
  ownerId: 'user-1',
  name: 'Code Reviewer',
  type: 'service',
  permissions: [{ resource: 'a2a:*', actions: ['execute'] }],
});

// Build the A2A Agent Card
const card = createAgentCard({
  agent: { id: agent.id, name: agent.name, type: agent.type },
  url: 'https://your-app.com/a2a',
  description: 'Reviews pull requests and suggests improvements',
  version: '1.0.0',
  skills: [
    {
      id: 'review-code',
      name: 'Code review',
      description: 'Analyzes code changes and provides feedback',
      tags: ['code', 'review', 'quality'],
    },
  ],
  capabilities: { streaming: true },
  securitySchemes: {
    bearer: { type: 'http', scheme: 'bearer', bearerFormat: 'JWT' },
  },
  security: [{ bearer: [] }],
});

// Create the server
const server = createA2AServer({
  agentCard: card,
  handler: {
    onMessage: async (message) => {
      // Your agent logic here
      const text = message.parts
        .filter((p) => p.type === 'text')
        .map((p) => p.text)
        .join('\n');

      return {
        id: crypto.randomUUID(),
        contextId: crypto.randomUUID(),
        status: { code: 'completed' },
        createdAt: new Date().toISOString(),
        updatedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
        artifacts: [
          {
            id: crypto.randomUUID(),
            parts: [{ type: 'text', text: `Review complete for: ${text}` }],
            createdAt: new Date().toISOString(),
          },
        ],
      };
    },
  },
  authenticate: async (request) => {
    const token = request.headers.get('Authorization')?.replace('Bearer ', '');
    if (!token) return null;
    // Agent bearer tokens (ta_...) are validated against the stored hash
    const caller = await theauth.agent.validateToken(token);
    return caller?.id ?? null;
  },
  onAudit: async (event) => {
    console.log('[A2A audit]', event.method, event.agentId, event.success);
  },
});

// Mount in your framework
// app.all('/a2a', (req) => server.handleRequest(req));
// app.get('/.well-known/agent.json', (req) => server.handleRequest(req));
```

### A2A server config

<ParamField path="agentCard" type="A2AAgentCard">The Agent Card that describes this agent. Served at /.well-known/agent.json.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="handler" type="A2ATaskHandler">Callbacks for handling incoming messages, cancellations, and streaming.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="authenticate" type={`(request: Request) => Promise<string | null>`}>Validates the caller. Return an agent/user ID or null to reject. Optional, omit to allow unauthenticated calls.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="onAudit" type={`(event: A2AAuditEvent) => Promise<void>`}>Called after each A2A interaction for audit logging.</ParamField>
<ParamField path="taskStore" type="A2ATaskStore">Custom task persistence. Defaults to an in-memory Map.</ParamField>

## Agent Cards

An Agent Card is a JSON document that describes what an agent can do, how to authenticate with it, and where to reach it. Other agents fetch this card to decide whether and how to communicate.

### Creating a card

```typescript
import { createAgentCard } from '@glinr/theauth/a2a';

const card = createAgentCard({
  agent: { id: 'agent-1', name: 'Translator', type: 'service' },
  url: 'https://translator.example.com/a2a',
  description: 'Translates text between languages',
  version: '2.1.0',
  skills: [
    {
      id: 'translate',
      name: 'Translate text',
      description: 'Translates text from one language to another',
      supportedMediaTypes: ['text/plain'],
      tags: ['translation', 'i18n'],
    },
  ],
  provider: { name: 'Acme Corp', url: 'https://acme.com' },
  defaultInputModes: ['text/plain'],
  defaultOutputModes: ['text/plain'],
});
```

### Validating a card

```typescript
import { validateAgentCard } from '@glinr/theauth/a2a';

const result = validateAgentCard(incomingJson);
if (!result.success) {
  console.error('Bad card:', result.error.message);
}
```

### Signing and verifying

Agent Cards can be signed with a private key so that consumers can verify the card hasn't been tampered with.

```typescript
import { generateKeyPair } from 'jose';
import { signAgentCard, verifyAgentCard } from '@glinr/theauth/a2a';

const { publicKey, privateKey } = await generateKeyPair('ES256');

// Sign
const signed = await signAgentCard({ card, privateKey });
if (!signed.success) throw new Error(signed.error.message);

// Verify
const verified = await verifyAgentCard({
  card: signed.data,
  publicKey,
});
if (verified.success) console.log('Valid:', verified.data.valid); // true
```

## Calling other agents

The A2A client discovers remote agents and sends them tasks.

```typescript
import { createA2AClient } from '@glinr/theauth/a2a';

const client = createA2AClient({
  agent: 'https://remote-agent.example.com',
  // The bearer token for the calling agent: the `token` returned by
  // theauth.agent.create() or theauth.agent.rotate(). It is shown only once,
  // so keep it in your secret store.
  getAuthToken: async () => process.env.AGENT_TOKEN!,
});

// Discover the remote agent's capabilities
const discovery = await client.discover();
if (discovery.success) {
  console.log('Skills:', discovery.data.skills.map((s) => s.name));
}

// Send a message
const result = await client.sendMessage({
  message: {
    id: crypto.randomUUID(),
    role: 'user',
    parts: [{ type: 'text', text: 'Review this PR: https://github.com/...' }],
    createdAt: new Date().toISOString(),
  },
});

if (result.success) {
  console.log('Task status:', result.data.status.code);
  console.log('Artifacts:', result.data.artifacts);
}
```

### Retrieving and canceling tasks

```typescript
// Get a task by ID
const task = await client.getTask({ id: 'task-123' });

// Cancel a running task
const canceled = await client.cancelTask({ id: 'task-123' });
```

## Authentication between agents

theAuth supports all A2A security schemes. You declare them in the Agent Card and enforce them in the server's `authenticate` callback.

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Bearer token">
    ```typescript
    const card = createAgentCard({
      // ...
      securitySchemes: {
        bearer: { type: 'http', scheme: 'bearer', bearerFormat: 'JWT' },
      },
      security: [{ bearer: [] }],
    });

    const server = createA2AServer({
      agentCard: card,
      handler: { onMessage: handleMessage },
      authenticate: async (req) => {
        const token = req.headers.get('Authorization')?.slice(7);
        if (!token) return null;
        const caller = await theauth.agent.validateToken(token);
        return caller?.id ?? null;
      },
    });
    ```
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="API key">
    ```typescript
    const card = createAgentCard({
      // ...
      securitySchemes: {
        apiKey: { type: 'apiKey', name: 'X-API-Key', in: 'header' },
      },
      security: [{ apiKey: [] }],
    });

    const server = createA2AServer({
      agentCard: card,
      handler: { onMessage: handleMessage },
      authenticate: async (req) => {
        const key = req.headers.get('X-API-Key');
        if (!key) return null;
        // An agent bearer token sent in a custom header
        const agent = await theauth.agent.validateToken(key);
        return agent?.id ?? null;
      },
    });
    ```
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="OAuth 2.0">
    ```typescript
    const card = createAgentCard({
      // ...
      securitySchemes: {
        oauth2: {
          type: 'oauth2',
          flows: {
            clientCredentials: {
              tokenUrl: 'https://auth.example.com/oauth/token',
              scopes: { 'a2a:call': 'Call this agent' },
            },
          },
        },
      },
      security: [{ oauth2: ['a2a:call'] }],
    });
    ```
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Task lifecycle

A2A tasks go through a defined state machine:

```
submitted -> working -> completed
                    \-> failed
                    \-> canceled
                    \-> input-required -> working -> ...
                    \-> auth-required -> working -> ...
                    \-> rejected
```

Each state transition is tracked with timestamps. When the server's `onAudit` callback is set, every interaction is logged with the method name, caller identity, task ID, and outcome.

<Info>
  A2A tasks are independent from MCP tool calls. An agent might use MCP to call tools internally while processing an A2A task, but the two protocols operate at different layers.
</Info>

## JSON-RPC methods

| Method | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `message/send` | Send a message and get a task result |
| `message/stream` | Send a message and receive SSE events |
| `tasks/get` | Retrieve a task by ID |
| `tasks/cancel` | Cancel a running task |

# Compare theAuth

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/compare/index

Auth is a crowded space. Every fact on these pages was checked on 2026-10-18, and a row that says "we did not find X" means we did not find it on the pages we fetched that day. These pages are meant to help you pick the right tool, not sell you on any particular one. If a competitor does something better, we say so.

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="theAuth vs better-auth" icon="code-compare" href="/compare/vs-ba">
    Both are MIT TypeScript libraries and both ship an MCP OAuth 2.1 server and an agent plugin or module. better-auth is the larger project with the larger community. theAuth adds delegation chains, approvals bound to arguments, an audit chain, devices and a Go library, some of which are on the release branch and not yet in a published release (npm `@glinr/theauth` is 1.2.0). The page lists each row with its source.
  </Card>
  <Card title="theAuth vs Keycloak" icon="key" href="/compare/vs-keycloak">
    Keycloak is the closest rival on devices and delegation: CIBA, Device Grant, DPoP and RFC 8693 are supported, with delegation and SPIFFE in Preview. It is a server you deploy, not a library. The page shows where its own docs stop.

  <Card title="theAuth vs Hanko" icon="fingerprint" href="/compare/vs-hanko">

  </Card>
  <Card title="theAuth vs Casdoor" icon="server" href="/compare/vs-casdoor">
    Casdoor is a deployed Go IAM service with LDAP, CAS, and RADIUS support. It targets employee SSO in Go shops. theAuth is a library, not a service, and it's built for agent-native TypeScript apps.
  </Card>
  <Card title="theAuth vs paid options" icon="building" href="/compare/vs-paid">
    Clerk and Auth0 are polished, fast to start, and expensive at scale. Both are proprietary hosted services with MIT licensed SDKs, and Auth0 sells a private deployment add-on on Enterprise. This page covers the open-source vs. managed tradeoff without reproducing any pricing tables.

# theAuth vs better-auth

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/compare/vs-ba

better-auth and theAuth are both open-source TypeScript auth libraries, and they start from different places. better-auth grew out of human sign-in and added a plugin system on top. theAuth is built around identities that can be humans, agents or devices, so permissions, delegation and audit apply to all of them.

better-auth is the larger project with the larger community, and it has an agent plugin of its own. Its latest stable release on 2026-10-18 was v1.7.10, published 2026-10-15 (a v1.8.0 beta was out the day after). This page lists what each documents, with the source for each row, so you can check the rows that matter to you. Where we did not verify a row for better-auth, we left it out instead of guessing. Last checked: 2026-10-18.

Status words for theAuth rows: "Published" means it is in the npm release `@glinr/theauth` 1.2.0 (or the Go release named). "Release branch" means it is written and tested on `release/agent-wave9-2026-10-18` and is not in a published release.

A migration guide is available: [Migrate from better-auth](/migrate/from-better-auth).

## What both do

| Capability | theAuth | theAuth status | better-auth |
|---|---|---|---|
| License and language | MIT, TypeScript, plus a Go library | Published | MIT, TypeScript |
| MCP OAuth 2.1 server | PKCE, RFC 7591, RFC 8707, RFC 9728 and Client ID Metadata Documents | Published | MCP plugin built on its OAuth 2.1 Provider, PKCE, RFC 8414 and RFC 9728 metadata, DCR off unless you enable it, CIMD recommended ([docs](https://www.better-auth.com/docs/plugins/mcp)). Its OAuth Provider page also lists RFC 7009, RFC 7662, RFC 8707 and the device_code grant ([docs](https://www.better-auth.com/docs/plugins/oauth-provider)) |
| Agent identity | `AgentIdentity` entity next to `User`, with delegation chains between agents | Published | Agent Auth plugin with agent, host, grant and approval records and capability grants. Its docs label it "not yet stable" ([docs](https://www.better-auth.com/docs/plugins/agent-auth)) |
| Human approval of agent actions | Approval module with decision codes | Published | `device_authorization` and `ciba` approval methods in the Agent Auth plugin ([docs](https://www.better-auth.com/docs/plugins/agent-auth)) |
| Passkeys, two factor, SAML, SCIM, organizations, API keys | Plugins for each | Published | Plugins for each, documented on its site. Organizations have owner, admin and member roles, custom roles and optional teams ([docs](https://www.better-auth.com/docs/plugins/organization)). Two factor covers OTP and TOTP with backup codes ([docs](https://www.better-auth.com/docs/plugins/2fa)) |

## Where theAuth goes further

These come from our own repository. For each of the five differentiators below we did not find the same feature on the better-auth pages we fetched on 2026-10-18. That is a statement about those pages, not proof that the feature is missing elsewhere or in a later release.

- Approvals bound to arguments: we did not find this on the Agent Auth page we fetched on 2026-10-18. Grants can carry `constraints`, but the page does not define a schema or say they bind call arguments.
- Tamper evident audit chain: we did not find one on the pages we fetched on 2026-10-18. The `onEvent` hook is described as a place to write audit logs, with no integrity mechanism mentioned.
- Device principals and MQTT: we did not find these on the pages we fetched on 2026-10-18. The plugin's "device authorization" is for a human to approve an agent.
- ROS 2 or robotics: we did not find this on the Agent Auth page we fetched on 2026-10-18.
- Delegation chains with revocation that reaches issued tokens: we did not find multi-hop chains on the pages we fetched on 2026-10-18. Its OAuth Provider docs say opaque access tokens are deleted at once on revocation and that revoking a refresh token removes the access tokens it minted. JWT access tokens cannot be revoked server side.

| Capability | theAuth | theAuth status |
|---|---|---|
| Approvals bound to the arguments the human saw, with a mismatch code | Canonical hash of action, resource and arguments, spent once | Release branch |
| Tamper evident audit chain with Ed25519 signed checkpoints and portable receipts | Chained rows, Merkle tree head signed with Ed25519, inclusion and consistency proofs | Published (1.2.0) |
| Verifier in TypeScript for the Go library's signed head checkpoints | Detects tail truncation of a Go chain | Release branch |
| Revocation that reaches issued MCP tokens | A signed delegation claim and a shared denylist, checked live, cached or offline | Release branch |
| Devices as principals: enrollment, offline signed policy bundles | `device` principal with the same permissions, delegation and audit | Release branch |
| MQTT broker authorization | Backend for EMQX and Mosquitto, tested against EMQX 5.8.6 and Mosquitto 2.0.15 | Release branch (Go) |
| ROS 2 permissions | Export to SROS2 and DDS Security files, tested with enforcement on ROS 2 Humble | Release branch |
| Go library with the same model | Memory, SQLite, Postgres and MySQL stores | Published (Go v2.12.0) |
| No `node:crypto` imports in core | Runs on Workers, Deno and Bun | Published |

"Release branch" means the code is written and tested but is not in the npm or Go release you get today (npm `@glinr/theauth` is 1.2.0). Check the [GitHub releases](https://github.com/glincker/theauth/releases) before you rely on a row.

## Where better-auth is ahead or equal

- Adoption and ecosystem. better-auth had 30.4k GitHub stars on 2026-10-18 and a large plugin and integration community. It also ships more named social providers than we do. We counted 36 provider source files in its repository on 2026-10-18, which is a file count and not a figure from its docs. theAuth is new and has no user numbers we can quote.
- Databases. better-auth documents Kysely (SQLite and D1, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MSSQL), Prisma, Drizzle and MongoDB. theAuth has Drizzle and a Prisma adapter, and the Go library has memory, SQLite, Postgres and MySQL. If you need MongoDB or MSSQL, better-auth covers it today. Redis in better-auth is secondary storage, not a database.
- MCP. Both ship an OAuth 2.1 server for MCP, so that alone does not separate them.
- Approvals. Both support human approval of agent actions. The difference is the argument binding noted above.
- SAML. theAuth's SAML verifier has not had an independent audit, and the docs say so. Treat it as experimental.

## Pick theAuth if

- Your app runs AI agents, devices or robots that need their own identity, scoped permissions, delegation and an audit trail.
- You want one model across TypeScript and Go services.
- You need approvals tied to the exact arguments, or revocation that reaches tokens already issued, and you can run the release branch or wait for the release.

## Pick better-auth if

- You are building a human-facing web app and want the larger community and ecosystem.
- You need a database or provider that theAuth does not cover. Check both lists first.
- You want its agent plugin and are fine with it being marked not yet stable.

# theAuth vs Keycloak

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/compare/vs-keycloak

Keycloak is a mature identity server that you deploy and run. theAuth is a library you embed in your app. Of the products we checked, Keycloak comes closest to theAuth on device flows and delegation, so it is the one to read carefully if you need those. Every Keycloak fact below comes from its own documentation, fetched on 2026-10-18. Its latest release on that date was 26.8.1, published 2026-10-13.

Status words for theAuth rows: "Published" means it is in npm `@glinr/theauth` 1.2.0. "Release branch" means it is on `release/agent-wave9-2026-10-18` and not in a published release.

## What Keycloak documents

| Capability | Keycloak | Source |
|---|---|---|
| CIBA (backchannel approval) | Supported, on by default | [features](https://www.keycloak.org/server/features) |
| Device Authorization Grant | Supported, on by default | [features](https://www.keycloak.org/server/features) |
| DPoP | Supported | [features](https://www.keycloak.org/server/features) |
| RFC 8693 token exchange | Standard exchange v2 Supported | [token exchange](https://www.keycloak.org/securing-apps/token-exchange) |
| Delegation with `actor_token` and the `act` claim | Preview, off by default | [token exchange](https://www.keycloak.org/securing-apps/token-exchange) |
| SPIFFE trust provider | Preview. Kubernetes service accounts are Supported | [features](https://www.keycloak.org/server/features) |
| MCP authorization server | OAuth 2.1 Supported for MCP spec 2025-03-26, later spec versions Experimental. RFC 8414 and RFC 7591 Supported. RFC 8707 and Client ID Metadata Documents Experimental | [MCP](https://www.keycloak.org/securing-apps/mcp-authz-server) |
| Organizations, SCIM, themed login pages | Organizations Supported, `scim-api:v1` Supported, server rendered themes | [features](https://www.keycloak.org/server/features) |
| Databases | PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server and others | [db](https://www.keycloak.org/server/db) |

## Where its docs stop

On 2026-10-18 we did not find the following on the Keycloak pages we fetched. This is not proof that Keycloak lacks them.

- Approvals bound to call arguments: not found. We did not find it in the CIBA material we read.
- A tamper evident audit chain: not found. The admin guide covers auditing user events and admin events, and we saw no hash chain or integrity mechanism. We read only the first 200k of 688k characters of that guide.
- IoT device principals and MQTT: partly. The Device Authorization Grant exists, but we found MQTT only in third party tutorials, which we did not verify.
- ROS 2 or robotics: not found in Keycloak's documentation.
- Revocation that reaches exchanged tokens: its token exchange documentation says revoking an access token does not revoke the exchanged access token. A refresh token revocation chain does exist. We did not find multi-hop nested `act` chains described.

## How theAuth differs

| Capability | theAuth | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Form factor | Library in your process, with a Go library alongside | Published |
| Delegation chains between agents, revoked as a cascade | `agent.revoke()` revokes the delegation chains downstream | Published |
| Approvals bound to action, resource and arguments, spent once | Canonical hash with a mismatch code | Release branch |
| Revocation that reaches issued MCP tokens | Signed delegation claim and shared denylist | Release branch |
| Devices as principals with offline signed policy bundles | `device` principal | Release branch |
| MQTT broker authorization | EMQX and Mosquitto backends | Release branch (Go) |
| ROS 2 permissions | SROS2 and DDS Security export | Release branch |

## Where Keycloak is ahead

- It is a full identity server with years of production use, a supported standards list, an admin console, themed login pages, and many database backends.
- Device Authorization Grant, CIBA and DPoP are marked Supported today. The theAuth device work is not in a published release.
- It covers SAML, LDAP style federation and social login out of the box. Our SAML verifier has not had an independent audit.

## Pick theAuth if

- You want auth as a library inside a TypeScript or Go app, with agents and devices as principals.
- You need approvals tied to exact arguments or revocation that reaches issued tokens, and you can run the release branch or wait for it.

## Pick Keycloak if

- You want a standalone identity server for employees and customers, with a supported standards list.
- You need device grant, CIBA or DPoP now, from a stable release.

# theAuth vs Hanko

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/compare/vs-hanko

Hanko is built around one idea: passkeys should be the default, not the fallback. It's a focused library with a Go backend, official TypeScript bindings, and an AGPL license. If passkeys are your entire auth surface and you have zero agent workloads, it's worth a serious look.

theAuth includes passkey support as one method among many. The bigger difference is what happens after the human authenticates: theAuth was designed for the agent layer that comes next.

A migration guide from Hanko is coming soon.

## Feature matrix

| Capability | theAuth | Hanko |
|---|---|---|
| License | MIT | AGPL (backend), MIT (JS SDK) |
| Primary focus | Agent-first auth SDK | Passkey-first auth |
| TypeScript SDK | Yes, first-party | Yes, first-party |
| Named OAuth providers | 48 (22 first class, 26 presets) | ~3 (Google, Apple, GitHub) |
| Passkey support | Yes | Yes, core focus |
| MCP OAuth 2.1 server | Built in | Not shipped |
| Agent identity | First-class `AgentIdentity` entity | Not shipped |
| RBAC / permissions | Unified RBAC + ABAC + ReBAC | Not shipped |
| Ephemeral sessions | Built in with auto-expiry and audit grouping | Not shipped |
| Edge runtime | Web Crypto throughout | Go backend required |
| Self-hostable | Yes | Yes |

## Pick theAuth if

- You need more than passkeys: OAuth providers, agent identity, or a policy engine.
- You're building AI-powered products where agents need their own auth layer.
- You want a permissive MIT license for the full stack, not just the client SDK.

## Pick Hanko if

- You want the smallest possible passkey-only library with a tight scope.
- You have no agent story and passkey-first is exactly the feature you need.
- You're comfortable with AGPL for your backend auth service.

Hanko does one thing well. theAuth does more, which is a tradeoff in either direction.

# theAuth vs Casdoor

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/compare/vs-casdoor

Casdoor is a deployed Go IAM service. You run it as a separate process alongside your app, and it handles SSO, LDAP, CAS, RADIUS, and a native MCP OAuth server. It's designed for organizations that need a standalone identity provider, especially in Go environments.

theAuth is a library, not a service. You import it into your TypeScript app and it runs in-process. Same MCP OAuth 2.1 spec, very different deployment model.

A migration guide from Casdoor is coming soon.

## Feature matrix

| Capability | theAuth | Casdoor |
|---|---|---|
| Language | TypeScript library | Go service |
| First-party TypeScript SDK | Yes | No (third-party only) |
| Deployment model | In-process library | Standalone IAM server |
| MCP OAuth 2.1 server | Built in with agent delegation | Built in |
| Agent identity | First-class `AgentIdentity` entity with delegation and audit | Not shipped |
| LDAP / CAS / RADIUS | Not shipped | Yes |
| RBAC | Unified RBAC + ABAC + ReBAC | RBAC via Casbin |
| Ephemeral agent sessions | Built in | Not shipped |
| Cost attribution | Built in | Not shipped |
| Trust scoring | 5-level built in | Not shipped |
| Edge runtime | Web Crypto throughout | Go, not applicable |
| Self-hostable | Yes | Yes |
| License | MIT | Apache 2.0 |

## Pick theAuth if

- You're building a TypeScript or edge-native app and want auth in-process, not as a sidecar.
- You need first-class agent primitives: delegation, ephemeral sessions, trust scoring, and cost attribution.
- Your MCP OAuth story needs to know which agent made which call, not just which client.

## Pick Casdoor if

- You want a deployed IAM service that your whole organization can log into, including non-TypeScript services.
- You need LDAP, CAS, or RADIUS compatibility for employee SSO.
- You're in a Go shop and want to own the full server.

The clearest signal: if you're writing `import { createTheAuth }`, theAuth. If you're writing `docker run casdoor`, Casdoor.

# theAuth vs paid auth platforms

Source: https://docs.theauth.dev/compare/vs-paid

Clerk and Auth0 are polished products. The onboarding is fast, the UI components are good, and you can be in production in an afternoon. That's a real advantage worth naming before anything else.

The tradeoff is real too. You run on their service, and the bill scales with your user count. Both have free tiers that feel generous until you hit the ceiling. Check their pricing pages directly, [Clerk pricing](https://clerk.com/pricing) and [Auth0 pricing](https://auth0.com/pricing), before making a spreadsheet.

## The structural differences

**Open source vs. closed.** theAuth is MIT. You can read every line, fork it, run it anywhere. Clerk and Auth0 are hosted platforms, so you rely on their security posture, their uptime commitments and their product roadmap. Both services are proprietary. Clerk's terms keep all rights in the service and give customers a limited, revocable right to use it ([terms](https://clerk.com/legal/terms), fetched 2026-10-18). Only their SDKs are open source: Clerk's `clerk/javascript` repository and Auth0's `node-auth0` are MIT licensed (GitHub, 2026-10-18). Auth0 does list a Private Deployment add-on on its pricing page as an Enterprise option with a custom quote ([pricing](https://auth0.com/pricing), 2026-10-18). We did not find a self-hosting offer for Clerk on the pages we fetched.

**Self-hosted vs. vendor.** Running theAuth means you control the database, the logs, and the data residency. That matters if you're in healthcare, finance, or working under GDPR data locality requirements. Vendor platforms handle the infrastructure, which also means your auth logs live in their service.

**Agent identity in the core.** theAuth models agents directly: `AgentIdentity`, delegation chains, ephemeral sessions and cost attribution are part of the library. Clerk and Auth0 now document MCP and agent features of their own, so compare what each one covers (Auth0 labels parts of this early access, as of 2026-10-18). Clerk's Agent Tasks create authenticated sessions on behalf of users, and Auth0 documents Token Vault and CIBA (CIBA needs an Enterprise plan or add-on). On 2026-10-18 we did not find approvals bound to call arguments, a tamper evident audit chain, device or IoT principals, ROS 2 support, or delegation chains with revocation that reaches issued tokens on the Clerk and Auth0 pages we fetched. That says nothing about pages we did not read.

Status of the theAuth pieces named here: `AgentIdentity` and delegation chains are Published (npm `@glinr/theauth` 1.2.0). Devices, MQTT and ROS 2 support, and revocation that reaches issued MCP tokens, are on the release branch and not yet in a published release. With theAuth the model lives in the library you run.

## When managed platforms make sense

Managed auth is the right call when speed matters more than cost or control. If you're validating a product idea, a startup in week two, or a solo developer who doesn't want to run a database, the vendor handles the operational complexity.

It's also worth considering if your team has no one who wants to own auth infrastructure. theAuth is simple to run, but it still runs on your stack.

## When open source makes sense

Once you have a stable user base, the cost curve of managed platforms typically exceeds what it costs to run a database and a self-hosted SDK. Beyond cost, open source gives you the ability to audit the code for compliance, patch issues without waiting on a vendor, and keep sensitive auth data inside your own infrastructure.

For a product with AI agents, compare the agent features of each option. Better Auth, an open-source library, also has an agent plugin; see [theAuth vs better-auth](/compare/vs-ba) for the differences we verified.
